It is this understanding that is paramount, at least in this book. From this vantage point, computing is seen as simply a means to an end to getting the job done. Now, of course if your work involves databases of humongous size, then the ability to even compute on such large databases comes into question. Though we do touch on these areas slightly in this book, computational complexity is not our chief concern. 25For the most part, we assume that the data you will be working with is of reasonable computational size. This book is not about data engineering. It is about statistics, science, and machine learning.

1.3.1 The Nature of Algorithms

In discussing the role of computers in today’s climate, it is an ideal time to note that today’s statistical and machine learning “Zeitgeist” seems to be all about algorithms, almost as if such things are new and were invented yesterday! Indeed, the very word algorithm carries with it a “sexy” appeal among students.

But what is an algorithm exactly? A very general definition is that it is a method or set of instructions for carrying out a procedure (Tanton, 2005). Under this general definition, preparing a meal is an example of an algorithm, just as walking your dog is an algorithm. Driving a car is an algorithm just as brushing your teeth is one. Writing this book was an algorithm. Algorithms are present in virtually every facet of our lives. Quantitatively, an algorithm can be as simple as long division or one could argue that even adding two numbers is an example of an algorithm. Misconceptions of algorithms being “new” to modern data science are just that, misconceptions.

1.3.2 Algorithmic Stability

As we have discussed, the focus of machine learning is a bit less on the data and a bit more on the actual algorithms that carry out the data analysis. How stable are they? How stable is a procedure such as regression across similar or different samples? Does it have such high variance that even slight perturbations of the data would result in wildly different outcomes? Questions such as these fall under the general rubric of algorithm stability. A stable algorithm is generally one for which if the training data are altered or perturbed slightly, the output of the algorithm more or less matches the degree of perturbation in the data and that as n increases these changes eventually disappear altogether (Liu et al., 2017).

Uniform stability specifies a bound by which two samples cannot exceed in order to be considered stable. More narrowly, a learning algorithm is uniformly β-stable if when a hypothesis trained on two different samples, h s and h s′ that differ by only a single point, the difference in loss functions L is equal to or smaller than a constant β with probability equal to 1. That is,


p[(|L(hS)−L(hS′)|) ≤β] = 1
(1.1)

where S is the original sample, S′ the sample with perturbation, and β is the stability coefficient that sets the upper bound (Liu et al., 2017; Mohri et al., 2018).

A related concern is how fast or efficient is the algorithm or computation more generally. A computation is said to run in polynomial time if the number of elementary steps can be expressed as a polynomial function of the size of the input. Running in polynomial time is generally considered a favorable characteristic of an algorithm. A computation not running in polynomial time is often running in exponential time.

1.4 The Importance of Design, Experimental or Otherwise

Statistics and machine learning without consideration of design issues, from a scientific point of view, is vacuous. Indeed, one of many features that makes this book unique from other books on multivariate analysis and machine learning is the constant reminder throughout that design issues are most important from a scientific point of view, not the actual method or algorithm applied to 26the data. That is, if you are doing science, then design matters most. Statistics, machine learning, and computing come in second.

For example, you can perform a cluster analysis with your fancy machine learning software and algorithm, but it will never tell you “why” people who drive Hondas form a cluster from those who drive Nissans. It will tell you what is associated with each cluster possibly but it will likely not tell you why. Only experimental designs can even come close to approximating such conclusions. Hence, throughout the book, we remind the reader that this or that statistical or machine learning tool often cannot answer the deeper scientific questions of most interest. Only good design can provide approximate answers to those questions. A statistical or machine learning model cannot tell us whether vaccine A is better than vaccine B when it comes to treating COVID-19, but a good experimental design might.

1.5 Inductive, Deductive, and Other Logics

In philosophy there are generally two broad ways of reasoning, of “getting to the truth” as it were, inductively and deductively. Crudely, inductive logic is that of drawing conclusions from the specific to the general, whereas deductive logic implies drawing conclusions from the general to the specific. As an example, if I have never seen dogs before and witness ten dogs all with four legs, I may wager that all dogs have four legs based on the observations I have witnessed. This is an example of inductive logic, where the particular is the set of dogs I have witnessed and the general is that of all dogs, most of which I have not witnessed and may never witness. The larger set of observations could even be infinite in size. On the other hand, if I somehow already knew that all dogs have four legs, then it is an easy matter to deduce that the next dog I meet will have four legs. In this case, we are going from the general to the particular and is an example of deductive logic. Boolean logic is an example of a deductive process; for instance, statements such as if a > b and b > c, then a > c, the law of transitivity, is an example of a deductive “implication” statement in Boolean logic (Lucci & Kopec, 2016). Empirical science is necessarily inductive as in most cases we simply cannot have access or observe all events and must draw conclusions based on only a select few. Science can be said to have deduction envy in that it would love to be deductive, but such is generally not philosophically possible.

Generalizing from the specific to the general is usually imperfect and comes with error. Statistical inference is a way of generalizing from the specific to the general and relies heavily on probability theory. When we see ten dogs with four legs and induce that all dogs have four legs, we are taking a “leap” in such a conclusion. That is, we do not know if all dogs have four legs; we are “gambling” or “betting” that they do based on our current observations. This is how science generally proceeds. Science is a gamble. Indeed, inductive learning is about finding functions that best approximate an unknown function, which is essentially what statistical learning is about.

There also exists fuzzy logic, which implies that a proposition can be “sort of true.” This is related to the more broad idea of fuzzy sets. In fuzzy logic, one is not either dead or alive, but instead one is dead to a matter of degree. Likewise, fuzzy set theory assigns membership to sets by matter of degree, not absolutely. It must be emphasized that inductive and deductive logic are well a part of our lives and science; they form the basis of much of our thinking about what is “true” or “false.” The Greeks are largely responsible for providing us with the rigors of deductive logic, where mathematical statements, for instance, are only regarded as true if they can be rigorously deduced.

More recently, theoretical logicians such as Boole and Frege elevated logic into its own mathematical discipline. Despite the long and historical study of logic, it should be emphasized that the “goodness” of logic relies on the assumption that logic itself is correct. If our assumptions about 27the power of these logics ends up being found false one day (presumably by way of even more logical thinking!), much of mathematics if not all would fall to the ground as would other modes of thinking as well. That is, if essential arguments such as the following could somehow be refuted one day (e.g., through a truth table shown to be false), or at minimum no longer generally assumed to be true, it would pose a revolution (to put it mildly) in science and thinking in general:


$$\begin{array}{l} \left. p\rightarrow q \right. \\ p \\ {\therefore q} \\ \end{array}$$

where the above reads that if p then q, p, therefore q. Of course, at first glance, the proposition that the above modus ponens could actually be incorrect as a way of concluding q sounds entirely irrational if not idiotic. More than likely, these essential capstones of inference will continue to hold the test of time. We merely point out the nature of constructing knowledge of this kind, that so much of it depends on prior assumptions, or provable assumptions based on even deeper assumptions no matter how “convincing” or “obvious” those assumptions may be. History can sometimes surprise us, as we will soon discuss in reference to Gödel’s theorems.

We can demonstrate simple logical arguments in software. In R, for instance, logical arguments can be carried out quite easily. For example, we can ask R to evaluate certain expressions as true or false:

> 1==5
[1] FALSE

where in the above, == is called a relational operator (Davies, 2016). Another example is the following:

> 5 == 4+2
[1] FALSE

Since logic contains “1” and “0” values corresponding to true and false, we can treat logical values as numbers as in the following where we add up “true” values:

> T + T + T
[1] 3

1.5.1 Consistency and Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems

Euclid’s Elements is regarded as one of the most famous of all mathematical texts ever written, and more specifically in geometry. The fifth postulate of the text was for a couple thousand years assumed to be an axiom, but in the 1800s it was shown that Euclidean geometry was not the only geometry possible. One could construct an edifice of non-Euclidean geometry. This event helped to introduce a crisis into mathematics.

Up to late 19th century (1800s), much of mathematics was thought to be based on logic, and given this, one could reasonably expect that the entire edifice of mathematics would be essentially a closed system that is entirely logically consistent. Consistency, in this regard, refers to the idea that if a statement is true, it cannot simultaneously be false. More succinctly, a consistent system is one that is free from contradictions. For instance, if p→q, a contradiction here, for example, 28might conclude q and ¬q (i.e., not q) simultaneously. A consistent system does not contain such contradictions.

After the invention of the calculus in the 1600s, it was discovered that calculus was not based on a theoretically solid foundation. A group of mathematicians attempted to rigorize calculus and were largely successful. The new discipline became known as real analysis, or simply analysis, and purported to be a rigorized and deeper version of calculus. For example, the notion of continuity at the time of Newton and Leibnitz was quite informal. Real analysis rigorized continuity and gave it a very precise definition. There would be no more informal talk regarding what was meant by notions such as continuity. Mathematicians delivered a rigorous definition for these and other key mathematical ideas. Mathematics prided itself on rigor, precision, and well-defined statements and definitions.

While the attempt to put mathematics on a rigorous logical foundation was relatively successful, the idea that it could be entirely put on such a coherent and consistent foundation was challenged by Gödel. Gödel showed that there are some statements in mathematics that could not be proved from other statements within the system. The theorems advanced by Gödel in showing this were known as his incompleteness theorems. The second of his theorems essentially held that it is impossible to program a computer to answer all mathematical questions. As Tantom (2005, p. 229) notes, “Gödel’s work dashed centuries of hope of finding a small set of basic axioms on which to base all of mathematics.”

The above surprise was just the beginning of reconceiving mathematics not as a bullet-proof edifice of irreversible truths, but rather as a construction which like many other things requires something to initiate the construction. Not everything within the constructed system can be proved or justified. This was exactly what was found by Gödel who propositioned that mathematics, more precisely Peano’s axiomatization of arithmetic, contains within it statements that cannot be proved with reference to the system. That is, it must require something external to the system for the rest of the system to be proved. In other words, any first-order theory containing Peano’s axiomatization “is either self-contradictory or incomplete for the purposes of deriving certain [emphasis added] arithmetic statements” (Muggleton, 1991). As Kline (1972, p. 1026) remarked:

The rigorization of mathematics may have filled a nineteenth-century need, but it also teaches us something about the development of the subject. The newly founded logical structure presumably guaranteed the soundness of mathematics; but the guarantee was somewhat of a sham. Not a theorem of arithmetic, algebra, or Euclidean geometry was changed as a consequence, and the theorems of analysis had only to be more carefully formulated. In fact, all that the new axiomatic structures and rigor did was substantiate what mathematicians knew had to be the case. Indeed, the axioms had to yield the existing theorems rather than determine them. All of which means that mathematics rests not on logic but on sound intuitions.

Kline hits the nail on the head. Dead center. While analysis provided a rigorous “foundation” for calculus, it was essentially yet still a human construction for ideas already assumed to be true. Again, the classic case here is that of continuity. Continuity was assumed to already exist; all that mathematicians did was provide a more rigorous description or account of it. The contributions were extraordinary in nature, no doubt, but many of such contributions simply provided justification for concepts already assumed to exist without justification. The assumptions (and intuition, as Kline put it) still came first.29

1.5.1.1 What Is the Relevance of Gödel?

The reader may reasonably ask why any of this Gödel talk is relevant to this book. In truth, it isn’t, other than to augment awareness of the mathematical system on which statistics and machine learning are based. In all of the statistical and machine learning principles and methods we will survey, it should be recognized that these are essentially human constructions; they are not written in stone and not entirely deductions from a smaller set of fundamental truths. Too often students believe that mathematics is rigid, dry, and outside of the realm of creativity. Nothing could be further from the truth. Mathematics, and by extension statistics and machine learning, are creative enterprises. Rigorous ones, but creative just the same. Rigor does not imply the absence of creativity; it simply requires stronger justification for new ideas and principles born out of such creativity. The rules are much “stiffer” than creativity in music or art. Sure, in jazz there are “rules,” but in the end, you can play what sounds “good.” When reflected on even more deeply, it may be realized that we make up the rules in all of these, including in mathematics, statistics, and machine learning, yet more accountability for such rules exists in these latter three since most rules are a consequence of logic.

1.6 Supervised vs. Unsupervised Learning

In an attempt to classify statistical and machine learning methods, the distinction supervised vs. unsupervised is often made. We first discuss the distinction, then explain why such a delineation is incomplete and insufficient. As is true of many ways of “splitting” a concept, what may at first seem clear and useful quickly becomes “fuzzy” and “muddied” upon closer and deeper philosophical scrutiny. As we will see, the difference between what is supervised vs. unsupervised gets quite “murky” very fast.

As the story goes, in supervised learning we have prior-established designated labels on the response. Supervised learning is sometimes called learning by teacher because we have already defined the classes we are trying to predict. For example, if we are using education level to predict salaries equal to or greater than vs. less than $100,000, we have clearly identified the labels ≥100k and <100k; thus, the problem is supervised. Methods such as linear regression and discriminant analysis are generally regarded as supervised learning. We know what we are trying to predict or model.

In unsupervised learning, on the other hand, we do not have prior-established classes or labels. That is, we are not attempting to predict or classify into categories because the categories are currently unknown, or, at minimum, unused. Dimension-reduction techniques such as principal components analysis (PCA) or cluster analysis are often regarded as unsupervised. Unsupervised methods are often considered more exploratory in nature than their supervised counterparts.

There is also a third category, that of semi-supervised learning, which is when we do not have all of the data and can alleviate the need for labeled data by capitalizing on the unlabeled data (Mohri et al., 2018). Semi-supervised learning approaches are beyond the scope of this book.

1.6.1 Fuzzy Distinctions

Despite the traditional arguments for the distinction between supervised vs. unsupervised, if forced to choose one over the other for all methods, we would likely conclude that most techniques are supervised in some sense and that unsupervised techniques really do not exist. To do this requires us to generalize our idea of “supervised” somewhat to a bit more than simply denoting labels on the response. It requires us to accept that most if not all methods are, in one way or another, user-driven at least to some extent, even if minimal in some cases.30

Consider that the moment the user is required to make any decisions regarding the method, he or she is either directly or implicitly supervising the approach. Consider principal components as an example, which is usually assumed to be an unsupervised method. As we will see later in the book, there are many different ways of conducting PCA. Choosing among these versions is an act of supervision, just as are choices regarding whether to standardize data and analyze the covariance or correlation matrix as input. Further, once the dimension reduction has been performed, the decision of how many components to retain is a supervised act. The situation is even more supervisory in a related so-called unsupervised method, that of factor analysis, where the user often must decide a priori how many factors to extract from the covariance or correlation matrix before even running the procedure. Telling the computer how many factors to compute is an extremely “supervisory” decision based on our revised version of what supervisory means.

As another example, consider cluster analysis, another so-called unsupervised technique. Such a procedure requires a priori for the user to select a metric by which distances will be operationalized. Once these inputs have been made, we allow the algorithm to “do its thing” in a non-supervised way, but the choices that govern the use of these methods are quite similar to the choice made in, for instance, the type of regression one performs in a supervised learning context. Should the user go with ordinary least-squares for a given problem or weighted least-squares? How about least-angle regression? In the end then, though the distinction between supervised and unsupervised is useful, when considered in a deeper way and with a bit of tinkering with the definitions, we arrive at the conclusion that all methods are supervised, some less so than others, and some not as explicitly as others.

It should be emphasized that many distinctions such as these in multivariate statistics or machine learning, when critically challenged, become quite fuzzy and blurry to the point where the distinction has trouble holding water, as it were. This is perfectly fine and does not mean the distinction isn’t useful or wrong; it simply means we should not think too rigidly about any of these definitions. Definitions such as these are useful, but they are often weakened when we put them under a microscope and tweak them slightly. Never memorize. Instead, conceptualize.

1.7 Theoretical vs. Empirical Justification

In philosophy, there is a difference between theoretical vs. empirical justification. We illustrate these differences with a couple of powerful and recent examples.

1.7.1 Airplanes and Oceanic Submersibles

The airplane lifting off the runway is an empirical demonstration that airplanes fly. It is only one demonstration of the idea. If many such airplanes successfully lift off the ground, we gain confidence in the idea that “airplanes fly.” That is, the certainty that airplanes fly is due to empirical justification, empirical “proof” we might crudely say.

The above is different from theoretical justification. The theoretical justification comes from an analytical argument, usually based on mathematics in this context, that airplanes should fly. That is, if the theory of flight is correct based on precise engineering aeronautic principles, then the airplane should fly. As much as possible, scientists should analytically justify what they seek to observe, or even have observed, empirically.

Why is this important? Recall the OceanGate expedition of 2023. The Titan oceanic submersible was successful in delving to the bottom of the ocean in visiting the Titanic many times such as to suggest the idea that it was a safe vessel to embark on such excursions. However, as critics noted after the submersible went missing (and was later found destroyed due to implosion), theoretical justification for the suitability of the vessel was lacking. That is, the vessel was not analytically 31justified for such excursions. Empiricism may reveal something to “work” a few times, but only theoretical justification can give us increased certainty that such will work in general for a large number or even infinite number of trials.

1.7.2 Will the Bridge Stay Up If the Mathematics Fail?

A classic example of the distinction between theoretical vs. empirical justification is perhaps the construction of a bridge. If one day the mathematics that led to the construction of the strong bridge suddenly were found faulty, would the bridge still stay up, or would it immediately fall? Of course, it would likely stay up, at least for a little while, maybe even longer. However, it is the theoretical justification of the bridge’s construction that we typically rely on to ensure its long-term reliability and sturdiness. Theory, or rational argument, makes the knowledge on which the bridge is constructed more certain; not guaranteed, since the theory itself is tentative, but simply more certain.

Theoretical and empirical justification must work hand in hand, however, and serve to inform each other, but one should never take a few empirical demonstrations to “justify” a theory that has not been justified a priori independent of those empirical demonstrations. This is the strength of sound mathematics and proofs, or more generally, rigorous philosophical argument. Such serves as a rational “guarantee” that the way we are thinking about constructing the bridge is sound.

With regard to the OceanGate submersible, perhaps to a large extent its prior success was based on capitalizing on random chance. Without theoretical justification, the experiences or instances of what you have obtained could simply be lucky instances. The fact that the submersible successfully visited the Titanic n times does not guarantee a successful visit on the (n + 1)th time. Regardless of how many successful trips there were prior to the accident, those successful trips were nonetheless a sample, and in this case not a random sample of all potential trips since most likely the probability of failure of the submersible structure increased the more times it traveled down to see the Titanic due to increasing structural fatigue of the vessel. A sample of successful voyages was observed, but making any kind of inference to the population of potential voyages requires some guesswork. Statistical inference is guesswork. It is the art of imposing rigorous quantification on such guesswork.

1.8 Level of Analysis Problem

Some physicists will claim that their discipline is the “fundamental” one, meaning that subjects such as biology, psychology, etc., are merely special cases of this fundamental discipline. Let’s briefly examine what this might mean, and how it introduces the level of analysis problem.

Suppose for a moment the physicist is correct, that all science reduces down to near infinitesimal particles, the presumed true building blocks of the universe of which all else is constructed. For the moment, we will call this the deepest level of analysis. Even if this is the case, the psychology experiment that finds a group difference in psychological health between those who practice mindfulness vs. those who do not could be considered a higher-level analysis (in the sense of a top-down view only) of these infinitesimally small particles. Whether the particles also conform to this group difference structure is simply a different perspective. The point is that the psychology experiment has revealed at a higher “bird’s eye” level a group difference and that group difference is just as meaningful as analyzing the atoms at a lower level. The representation of the data is at different levels, but the phenomenon under study may be essentially the same.

Hence, aspiring scientists should be aware that there are different levels of analysis and that they all contribute to understanding. Debating over which is the most “fundamental” unit of analysis is an interesting debate, but is not one that should detract from the triangulation of many different approaches to studying a given phenomenon.32

1.9 Base Rates, Common Denominators, and Degrees

So much of everything in research is about base rates. As a data analyst or researcher, you should always be aware of the base rate phenomenon whenever you either conduct or perform research. It is literally impossible to contextualize research correctly without such an awareness. Regarding the Titan, many experts in the area warned that the submersible may have problems due to its structural integrity or lack thereof. Upon first hearing there were concerns about the sub, it may have been tempting to interpret this information as unique to that particular submersible. The news reports brought to mind of a particular sub with significant weaknesses and dangers. Upon hearing these reports, however, it behooves the critical listener to consider whether such dangers were unique to all submersibles of which the dangers with this one were simply a special case.

What we are getting at with the above question is the concept of a base rate. Surface knowledge can be very misleading and is too often the only knowledge we “see.” There is usually always a base rate to any knowledge, but too often it’s the surface knowledge that will be incorrectly emphasized at the expense of the background or context layers. Now, it turns out that the issues with the submersible were uniquely significant and likely led to the demise of the sub and all who were aboard, but the point is that when you learn of abnormality or presumably “unique” problems with anything, always ask yourself whether those things are truly unique to the object you are working with or whether there is a deeper underlying base rate such that the unique characteristic is actually much more common than initially believed. Simply because an event is observed does not imply that such an event is unique to the particular object you are working with, even if on the surface the mind can quickly treat the characteristic as if it is unique.

Gigerenzer (2003) calls this awareness of base rates a mind tool that all researchers or anyone consuming research should practice and nurture in their thinking. The (first) attempted assassination on President Trump in 2024 was presumably carried out by a “loner” type. However, many human beings would fit that description and many more human beings likely have psychologies exponentially darker than that of the gunman. Simply because we observed a characteristic of the gunman does not explain, by itself, the behavior. Awareness of base rates here is essential. When the “warning signs” are characteristic of say, 20–30% of the population, they are not warning signs anymore. They are features of human nature.

Relativity also plays a role in the consideration of base rates. One begins to think less in terms of categories and more in terms of degrees along a continuum. Once more referring to the Titan submersible, it was said in the aftermath of the implosion that passengers should not be allowed into experimental submersibles or indeed any experimental transport due to the risks involved. But what is not experimental? Few would regard airline travel as experimental. Due to its safety record it has been put into the “category” of non-experimental travel. However, from a philosophy of science perspective, airline travel is indeed still experimental; it is simply less so than venturing on the OceanGate submersible. Airline travel is still a relatively recent invention. Relative to the entire span of humanity, people have been flying airplanes for a very short time. Contextualizing events along a continuum instead of assigning such events “black and white” labels is epistemologically fruitful. For many travelers, their Delta flight tomorrow may be “experimental” enough of a risk!

1.9.1 Base Rates and Splenic Masses

A failure to consider base rates can have drastic consequences on decision-making. German Shepherd Dogs are well known to be very intelligent and for the most part well-tempered and trainable dogs, which is one reason why they are often employed as officers in police departments and beloved by owners as family. However, they are unfortunately known to have health problems, especially as they age. One typical health problem is that of tumors of the spleen, which may be benign or malignant (cancerous). Though cancer is of course detrimental, the worst part of a splenic mass is the chance that it ruptures into the abdomen and the dog bleeds internally.33

Suppose you perform an elective ultrasound on an 11-year-old male German Shepherd. The ultrasound reveals a splenic mass. As a dog owner, you are of course concerned that the mass could rupture but have no idea how long the mass has actually been there. The mass, of course, is an abnormality on the spleen, meaning that the dog was unlikely to have been born with the mass. It appeared at some point during the dog’s life, though at what point, you do not know. You lack an ultrasound baseline with which to compare the current data. It is an abnormality on the spleen, but is it an abnormality for an 11-year-old German Shepherd? Likely not. Consider data reported recently on the prevalence of splenic masses on a random sample of Golden Retrievers aged 6 through 13 that found that a whopping 52.8% of Golden Retrievers in this sample were found to have splenic masses! Further, since it is well known that splenic masses are much more common in elderly German Shepherds than young ones, the percentage of elderly dogs (i.e., a conditional distribution) carrying splenic masses is probably closer to 70–80%. Hence, the detection of a splenic mass on the ultrasound of the 11-year-old is most likely an expected finding, not an anomaly. The point here is that there are likely many dogs that carry splenic masses, many of which are likely benign and for which those masses never pose a problem or the dogs die of other causes. Indeed, the next 11-year-old (or older) German Shepherd that you observe on a walk down the street with their owner likely has a splenic mass. That a mass was found on the ultrasound does not make it an anomaly; the detection of the mass and doing an ultrasound on the dog may be the actual anomaly. This is what we mean by base rate thinking, and once you start thinking in terms of base rates, you will see them everywhere.

Indeed, in the literature on splenic tumors in dogs, suppose it is reported that approximately ½ of tumors on the spleen are benign and ½ malignant (this statistic is not entirely accurate, but is convenient for this discussion). However, suppose this estimate is typically based on the presentation of the tumor in an emergency bleeding state, that is, when the dog begins bleeding from the tumor and is brought in for emergency treatment. The correct statement should be ½ of bleeding tumors are benign and ½ malignant, not ½ of tumors unconditionally (i.e., bleeding or not bleeding). The Venn diagram in Figure 1.2 depicts the base rate idea we are referring to.34

The ½ and ½ estimate is based on tumors that are based on presentation in a vet’s office, and hence “known” because they are usually bleeding or causing symptoms in the dog. Dogs that do not have reason to present, however, may have tumors as well, as evidenced by the Golden Retriever study. Many of these dogs will die of other causes, and hence the probability of a tumor being malignant is much less if the tumor is not bleeding.

Awareness of base rates is a powerful tool in this regard such that even experienced veterinarians may neglect when interpreting novel cases. Veterinarians and other medical professionals are trained in medicine, not statistical decision theory. As a student learning statistics you will become very aware of when your medical provider is not thinking clearly when it comes to important decisions.

1.9.2 Probability Neglect

The above discussion of base rates is also related to another idea that dominates the interpretation of probabilities, that of probability neglect. For the German Shepherd, a veterinarian discussing a few cases of ruptured tumors might arouse great concern over the possibility that the current tumor in your dog ruptures. The focus is then on the rupturing tumor but ignoring the true probability that the tumor does not rupture. It is as much a statistical phenomenon as it is a psychological one, where intensity is magnified for the current event at the expense of other events that are likely more probable. The idea of the tumor rupturing is at the forefront of our minds, yet we ignore the probability that it does not rupture, which could be much higher.

Another example of probability neglect is that of the experience post-9/11, 2001, in which the population at large was afraid to fly. The presenting information of the tragedy of seeing the planes crash into the towers (and Pentagon and field in Pennsylvania) dominated people’s consciousness, when in reality, the probability of a plane crashing, even after the tragedy, continued to likely be remote. “I don’t want to fly because it is too dangerous,” says the individual post-9/11, but then travels by car on the interstate where the probability is significantly higher of an adverse event. We must be very cautious not to ignore probabilities simply because the event we are currently considering evokes strong emotion.

1.9.3 The “Zero Group”

Yet another general application or instance of base rate thinking is what we shall refer to as the zero group in research. This is the group that is not participating in the study but may actually be of most interest. Without awareness of there being such a group, the investigator may entirely miss it and not be aware of it.

As an example, consider the online question of whether people like Honda vehicles. The ratings are exceptionally high, but what may be being recorded are only those who like Hondas! If the true percentage of individuals liking Hondas is 30%, and those 30% are the only ones responding to the survey, it can be falsely concluded that 100% of individuals like Hondas. The 70% who do not like Hondas never responded. This is what we are calling the zero group in research. It is the group that never makes its way into the study but is of utmost interest to the calculation of the effect or the prevalence of what is being measured.

There is usually (perhaps always) a zero group that may be out of sight that one actually does want to study. The key is to be aware of this possibility so that you can incorporate it into your scientific conclusions even if you cannot directly analyze the group. Another example of a zero group was the 2016 election (or possibly 2024 as well, for that matter) where Trump voters refused to be polled or were hesitant to admit they would vote for Trump. The pollster was attempting 35to measure something called voting preference, but the most important group, the Trump voter, eluded them either through improper sampling or no tried and true way to vet dishonest responses.

1.10 Statistical Regularities and Perceptions of Risk

To extend on the above discussion, statistical regularities often make extremely risky engagement seem less so. For example, consider once more airline travel. Is airline travel risky? Is it dangerous? Of course it is! Traveling at greater than 30,000 feet in what is essentially still an experimental capsule is a risky endeavor. Yet, from a statistical point of view driving to the supermarket in your car is riskier. How we qualify risk changes depending on the perspective we adopt. A car traveling on a highway at 65 mph is less risky than an airplane traveling at 30,000 feet going 400 mph, but not statistically.

Statistical regularities are well known for reducing our perception of risk, but this is only so in the sense of past behavior. That is, if an airline flight is similar to most other airplane flights before it, then statistically it comes with little risk. However, despite the modeling of your flight today as having come from a distribution of past flights, we simply have no knowledge of the current event. It is entirely new. It is entirely possible (though highly improbable) that most flights from now on go on to crash; we simply do not know as we have not yet observed these new instances. All we have for certain are probabilities which we apply to new data under the assumption that such data are being drawn from similar probability distributions as past events.

Hence, one might say that the flight at 30,000 feet is risky in absolute terms, but statistically, it is much less so. In statistical parlance, the flight is relatively risk-free because the Bayesian prior of it being successful is quite high (we will discuss Bayesian statistics shortly). However, philosophically, the prior tells us nothing about the actual new physical event. It only models its probability under the assumption that the new event was drawn from a distribution made up of similar prior events.

1.10.1 Beck Depression Inventory: How Depressed Are You?

Risk is of course also prevalent in the diagnosing of clinical disorders. Suppose as a clinician you administer the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) to a new client and that client scores in the range of mild depression. The BDI is a well-known screener for depression. A good clinician knows that no sole diagnostic criteria should be used to diagnose a client. However, what does a high BDI score signify? It does not signify the disorder. It instead can only indicate a “sign” of the disorder and classic Bayes reasoning needs to be applied to obtain the actual probability of depression. If the client’s prior probability of the disorder is low, then a high BDI score may simply not be enough to indicate or diagnose depression. This is a basic principle of revising probabilities, yet it has been shown time and time again that such basics are not understood or appreciated by many who diagnose medical and clinical disorders. Patients’ lives have been turned upside down due to inaccurate reporting of HIV test results, for instance. This is more than a triviality; it is of vital importance. A failure to communicate statistical results properly to a clientele is equivalent to malpractice. Patients and customers have a right to be told accurate probability estimates and given guidance on how to interpret them.

1.11 Decision, Risk Analysis, and Optimization

The above discussion of risk and decision-making quite naturally ties into ideas of formal optimization in mathematics and statistics. In many methods featured in this book, the objective, from 36an optimization point of view is to minimize or maximize some function, which in the end is essentially translated into minimizing the risk of making a wrong decision with as little error as possible. The area of study called risk analysis or the related area of decision analysis are fascinating disciplines of study and permeate many applied areas of practice. In the end, many statistical analyses are performed with the end goal of making a good decision. However, few if any decisions come without risk. Though one can argue there are, in theory, perfect decisions, they are only “perfect” in the sense of being rigorously thought out and rationally conceived. They all contain consequences and costs of being wrong, at least in the short term.

Every day we are confronted with decisions and we make them with imperfect knowledge. Whether we formally conduct a decision analysis on such decisions or intuitively try to balance the risk of making a wrong decision with the benefit of making a right decision, these decision tasks permeate our lives. There is a whole literature on the psychology of risk and how human beings manage risk and the interested reader is encouraged to consult such literature should these topics be of interest to her. For now, it is simply enough to survey a few features of this wide and exciting area of research.

1.11.1 The Risk of Making a Wrong Decision

Consider the following hypothetical scenario – you have just paid off your home, valued at approximately $400,000. While legally you were required to have fire homeowners insurance when assuming a mortgage with the bank, now that you own it outright you are no longer required to hold any insurance. You ponder the question carefully as to whether you should still purchase insurance or pocket the premium you would pay and devote those dollars to something else. The only way to truly address this decision problem is to assign probabilities to competing events and evaluate expectations or utility. If the price of insurance is $1,000 per year, it may seem a no-brainer to pay the premium since the cost of losing the home to a fire would be devastating financially at a total loss of $400,000, the market value of the home. However, if you are one to seldom leave your home and the risk of fire is remote, perhaps the $1,000 spent on an insurance premium is best spent elsewhere. Of course, most homeowners would pay the premium as the risk of losing the home, even if small, is too large as to not guard against such an event. Yet, at the same time of not being able to presumably tolerate such risk, the same individual regularly and voluntarily goes joy-riding in their car on a very dangerous stretch of highway where the risk of losing one’s life is much greater than the risk of losing one’s home to a fire. The point we are making is that risk tolerances can vary widely depending on the given problem and the perception of risk, rational or irrational, can be variable depending on the context and situation.

1.11.2 Statistical Lives and Optimization

The idea of risk also translates to notions of statistical lives. Returning to the airline example discussed earlier, airlines seek to minimize loss in terms of injury and deaths. Yet at what cost? Certainly not at any cost. Airplanes regularly land in thunderstorms and adverse conditions even though such conditions pose more risk than others, yet such risk is calibrated against other interests, such as retaining customer satisfaction by a timely landing, keeping flight schedules on track, as well as the interests of the crew in wanting to be done with their flight as a result of fatigue. That isn’t to suggest a flight crew would recklessly land in a severely dangerous thunderstorm, but it would be tremendously naïve to think that tolerable amounts of risk are not existent and implicit in such landings. When those calibrations begin to impose too much, such that they risk exceeding the risk threshold, which is usually probably subjectively determined case-by-case, then a more dangerous level of risk arises which may lead to accidents. The point we are making here is simply 37to say that no behaviors are risk-free, and an airline that purports to manage a risk-free operation of flight is simply not being truthful. Risk is minimized but such minimization is subject to constraints and competing interests. Optimization algorithms in statistics and machine learning also optimize, but usually not unconditionally. They usually optimize subject to constraints and conditions.

1.11.3 Medical Decision-Making and Dominating Criteria

In basic decision theory, we say a decision is dominated by one or more criteria if that decision trumps a competing decision based on selective input or information. For example, consider the dog owner once more regarding the detection of a splenic mass via ultrasound. Is it benign or is it cancerous? Of course, a benign mass will not spread to other parts of the body, whereas a malignant mass is more likely to do so. The decision is whether to remove the spleen via surgery. In this example, one can spend much time and expense trying to determine whether the mass is benign or malignant, yet the decision to remove vs. not remove the spleen may be dominated by the possibility of the mass bleeding or rupturing, which could put the dog’s life in danger regardless. One could CT-scan the body to look for microscopic metastasis; however, at what value would that be to the decision of whether or not to proceed with surgery? Likely minimal, given that the possibility of a bleed dominates the surgery decision. The decision for surgery is said to be dominated by the bleed possibility over the nature of the mass (benign vs. malignant) and hence surgery is recommended (base rates aside) regardless of whether the mass ends up being benign or malignant. Many times we spend countless hours grappling over inputs to a decision that in the end do not matter as these elements are dominated by other criteria.

The above is just one example of how certain decision criteria might dominate others in particular situations. As another example, have you ever witnessed the perfectly built home, but in the wrong location? A true majestic masterpiece of a home, but in such a poor location! The house fails to sell because the location decision dominates the favorability of the home.

In statistics, decisions you make along the way in your analysis dominate others. For example, if you build your entire analysis on the arithmetic mean as a basis of central tendency, when in fact the median would have been a more accurate portrayal of the data, even if the analysis is quite complex and detailed this crucial decision dominates all others. If you build on a questionable foundation, strong as the edifice may appear, it will be structurally unsound. Foundations first! Newton’s theory of physics, impressive as it is, Einstein found was built on incomplete foundations. Critical questions about foundations are what lead to scientific and other revolutions.

1.12 All Knowledge, Scientific and Other, Is Tentative

As a final point regarding our review of scientific principles, we should emphasize the fact that all knowledge is tentative pending further development or discovery. Within the realm of science, this idea is well known. Perhaps the clearest example of this is with Newtonian physics. It was “correct” years ago, but now is less correct given Einstein’s theory of relativity. Likewise, aspartame used to not be considered a carcinogen, but only recently has it been classified as possibly one. What is true scientifically yesterday is no longer today. This is how science functions and is the norm. Scientific “facts” are always conditionally or tentatively true based on further evidence.

Surely then, statistical and mathematical knowledge must be unconditionally always true, right? No! While at first glance it may appear that such knowledge is steadfastly certain, history has shown us differently. Perhaps the most alarming example of this was with Euclidean geometry and the discovery of non-Euclidean geometries. Euclidean geometry was for certain the only geometry for over a couple thousand years. Had that “fact” not been considered tentative by very bright minds who investigated foundations while all others busied themselves in further building on the 38edifice of Euclidean geometry, we would have never come to know that Euclidean geometry was not a “fact” of mathematics. Likewise with theorems of mathematics or statistics, a proven theorem is generally considered true and timeless, but errors in proofs are regularly found such that it makes them less certain and enduring almost overnight.

The moral of the story here is to always hold knowledge, whatever the kind, as tentative given more information. One might act as though such knowledge is true, while at the same time being open to revising one’s opinion of such knowledge if new information contradicts it. The earth is currently known to be approximately round, or so, but if tomorrow’s discovery provides contradicting information we must have an open mindset such that we are willing to revise our beliefs. Likewise, climate change is a theory, not a fact. As new evidence enters into the equation we must be prepared to revise our belief in climate change. As we will see, this way of thinking has very strong Bayesian undertones.

1.13 Occam’s Razor

Occam’s razor is the idea that if there are competing theories to explain data, the simplest explanation shall be preferred over the more complex assuming that each competing theory accounts for the data equally well. While the principle is usually appealed to be based on intuition and plausibility (i.e., it sounds like a reasonable position to take with regards to theory-building), the principal can actually be more rigorously theoretically defended (Stoffi et al., 2022). Occam’s razor is far from being a statistical or machine learning concept alone as we can apply the principle even informally to everyday life.

One area where Occam’s razor is especially applicable as it relates to machine learning models is when constructing a neural network where as we will see, one of the decisions faced by the user is the number of hidden nodes and layers to include in the network. All else equal and given that competing neural network constructions result in more or less the same predictive power, Occam’s razor requires keeping the model as simple as possible while still maintaining its ability to generalize well. Hence, if a neural network with a single simple hidden layer does as well as one with multiple complex layers, the simpler model is to be preferred. However, as Einstein (and others) reminded us, everything should be made as simple as possible, but no simpler. A “too simple” of an explanation or theory that hinders explainability is not optimal either.

Theoretical explanations can become quite complex in science and industry. Pragmatic and simple explanations are often better. Why does a stock go up in the stock market? Yes, we can consider the multidimensional and multifactorial economic influences and market forces, yet on a more descriptive, pragmatic level, stocks go up for primarily one reason and one reason only: more people than not are buying it. Of course, such isn’t much of a theory as to why more investors are buying the stock, but it is the simplest and most practical explanation regarding why the stock is increasing.

1.13.1 Parsimony vs. Complexity Trade-Off

Choosing the simplest theory or model is not the only priority of the scientist or quantitative modeler. Even if a very complex model explains the data better than a simpler one, it does not necessarily imply the more complex model should be chosen. For example, in a multiple regression model one can make the model as complex as one desires by adding more and more predictors. As is well known, R 2 for the model will necessarily increase given the inclusion of an increasing number of predictors even if the addition in variance explained (greater than zero) by those predictors is negligible. Hence, a model with 1,000 predictors will have a higher R 2 than a model 39with 100, but variance explained should not be our only criterion for model selection, especially if the purpose is scientific explanation. If the goal is simply raw prediction and the availability of such data on multiple variables is easy to come by, then choosing the model with 1,000 predictors is the correct choice. One example of this might be Amazon collecting numerous predictors from online purchases that add to its ability to predict your next purchase. Choosing the simpler, more parsimonious model is not priority given the ease by which such data are collected by Amazon’s virtually unlimited storage and upper-limit computing power.

However, if we are trying to explain the behavior of migrating birds, for instance, building a theory on 1,000 predictors may be unwieldy if not impossible. The complexity of the model is too rich, and hence simplifying the model, even at the risk of lowering predictive power, may be called for. From a scientific perspective, the goal of modeling is rarely to generate models that fit perfectly, but instead to explain as much as possible using the least amount of information as possible.

These ideas motivate the use of penalized model fit statistics that attempt to strike a balance between providing a good fit while minimizing the number of predictors providing that fit. In this book we will survey a number of penalized versions of statistics and unpack them to see exactly how they work.

1.14 Overfitting vs. Underfitting

In continuing our discussion of theory and model-fitting, we note there to be a delicate balance between overfitting versus underfitting a theory to data. The general idea behind overfitting is when a model is tailored too specifically to the training data and will likely not generalize well to the test data. At the opposite extreme, underfitting is when it is not specific enough to the training data. The goal of statistical inference and machine learning is that of generalization and hence both overfitting and underfitting have consequences. Not surprisingly, the magnitude of these consequences is related to the sample sizes used in such generalization or lack thereof. If the sample size is too small and the complexity of the hypothesis class too rich, overfitting is almost guaranteed to occur. On the opposite end, for increasingly larger sample sizes, a lack of complexity in a model will be more prone to underfitting.

Consider a very simple conceptual example of over vs. underfitting. Suppose you are a therapist attempting to identify the issue with your client’s daily anxiety and elevated heart rate. After referrals to medical practitioners, you have successfully ruled out any biological issues. You suspect however that the “jitters” have to do with the amount of caffeine intake by the client. After asking the client to change their caffeine intake over the next while, you theorize that their anxiety is a function of having exactly 4.357 cups of coffee per day. Perhaps you have good reason to theorize that exact amount for this particular client after experimenting with various caffeine intake amounts. That is, your theory “fits” the client extremely well and seems to explain his behavior. However, as a general theory, how well will it do? Suppose you take your results and seek to generalize to future clients, telling them, “You must drink less than 4.357 cups of coffee per day.” Of course, common sense tells us that the theory built on the specific individual will not generalize to future clients, at least not very well.

What has happened here from a theoretical point of view is that you have overfit the data. You paid too much attention to particulars of the given individual (sample data) and likely capitalized on random noise in the individual’s specific caffeine sensitivity, so that when you attempted to generalize to new clients, the theory failed miserably as essentially a point prediction. How might you change the theory so that it generalizes better? You might instead fit a theory such as “Moderate intake of caffeine is predictive of anxiety level.” This theory will likely generalize 40better to new individuals (i.e., to new data) because it no longer relies as heavily on the specifics of the given individual you are dealing with.

On the opposite end of things, consider what underfitting would look like in this case. Suppose you tested the theory on your client as to simply not drink hot beverages. That is, you theorize that if your client avoids hot beverages altogether, such will have the effect of decreasing anxiety. Of course, that’s far too general of a theory; you must make it more specific. You have underfit the data. Murphy (2022) gives an even simpler example using a coin-flipping paradigm. Suppose you flip a coin 20 times and obtain 15 heads on the 20 flips. The maximum likelihood estimator resulting from this exercise would be heads for future flips. But clearly, this overfits on the training data as most likely all future flips will not be all heads. That is, we overfit the theory on too small a sample of data.

The above examples can be generalized easily and more broadly to statistical and machine-learning problems. Consider the data in Figure 1.3 (1), a bivariate plot of points.

Consider what overfitting would look like in this case. We could simply connect the dots (Figure 1.3, (2)). That is, we are modeling the theory (curve) too closely to the training data. What would underfitting look like? Suppose we simply modeled the mean (Figure 1.3, (3)). This is an example of underfitting as it essentially ignores the richness of the data. A nice compromise would be the line of best fit, typically the regression line (Figure 1.3, (4)). The regression line provides an inexact fit, but the theory here is general enough to possibly generalize to new test data.

In all of the models we refer to in this book, the more specific and detailed the model fit to data, in general, the more likely it is to overfit. Do not be in a hurry to produce a model that fits the (training) data perfectly. Any such model can easily be built! The interest in model/theory-building is to produce a model that not only fits the current data reasonably well, but that also generalizes to new data.

Of all the models we will study in this book, models such as neural networks are especially prone to overfitting. Why? Because, as we will see, due to allowing complex nonlinear relationships, they tend to capitalize on small perturbations in the data that may fail to generalize to new data. This is one reason why, despite the meteoric advances in model complexity in the statistics and machine learning literatures, classic linear models are still often preferred over more complex models in many contexts.41

1.14.1 Solutions to Overfitting

There are usually a variety of ways to deal with and cope with overfitting. Many depend on the specific method used. Sometimes simply taking averages of predictions made by a number of different models fit to the training data is sufficient for minimizing the effects of overfitting. As we will see later in the book, such is the approach essentially advocated by such procedures as bagging.

Perhaps the most common strategy to deal with overfitting is simply to regularize a model. Regularization is a general technique in which, all else being equal, simpler models are favored over more complex models and hence in general is in the spirit of Occam’s razor. This often translates to adding a penalty term to the loss or empirical risk function. We now briefly discuss regularization and then develop it at a deeper level later in the book.

1.14.2 The Idea of Regularization

The idea of regularization permeates several models in statistics and machine learning and we will see this principle applied regularly throughout the book. The principle of regularization, or shall we say the spirit of it, is much more general than the specific instances in which it is used or the individual method to which it is applied. If the principle is understood, then every time regularization is encountered, even in different forms, the reader will more easily understand it despite the precise details of how it is being applied in the given context. But what is regularization exactly? Probably the most general idea of regularization is the following:

Regularization simplifies models to reduce the probability of overfitting.

By guarding against overfitting, generalization error is reduced (Goodfellow et al., 2016). Regularization helps stabilize a model, and stable learners (or models) are less likely to overfit. If small changes to input data result in large changes in outcomes, as already discussed, the model is regarded as unstable. As a human analogy, a good friendship can withstand turbulence; that is, the outcome does not change in the face of adverse events. The friendship still remains strong. A weaker friendship is easily changed based on an input that breaks the friendship apart.

Most often in practice, regularization involves adding a penalty term to the maximized or minimized objective function (Murphy, 2022). Early stopping of an algorithm also constitutes an attempt to regularize a model. Other times, simply collecting more data on which the model is applied is a suitable solution. While a polynomial may overfit say, 20 data points, it is unlikely to overfit 200 or 2,000, and the generalizability of the model will often improve.

1.15 The Measurement Problem

In the age of sophisticated algorithms and terabytes of data, it can be all too easy to pay insufficient attention to what the data actually consist of, that is, what they actually represent. Sure, we all desire novel algorithmic fancy and modern ways of analyzing such data, but what if the data are not representing that which we sought out to measure? What if that number in the spreadsheet does not correspond to what we believe it represents? If the data point does not represent what we sought to measure, no sophisticated statistical or machine learning algorithm will save it. What the data point is a function of can be easily taken for granted, an assumption that what we sought to measure we are in fact measuring. This can be a very dangerous assumption. In this section, we briefly survey some issues related to the larger problem of measurement in the social and natural 42sciences and discuss some of the more common ways of thinking of scales of measurement. We then very briefly discuss Likert scale data.

1.15.1 What Is Data?

To begin a discussion of measurement and reliability and validity, we should first ask ourselves what data are in the first place. At a philosophical level, which as mentioned virtually everything boils down to sooner or later when scrutinized enough, data is simply information. In the age of computerized data analysis, we of course associate a piece of data with a number in a spreadsheet, but it should be recognized that that numerical representation of data is simply a special case of the wider possibility of what data could be. For example, learning that your friend is not trustworthy is a piece of data. Looking up in the sky and seeing a sunny day is data. Your internet connection going out momentarily is yet another piece of data. The first to walk the planet were data analysts, not very good ones we might argue from our modern point of view, but data analysts just the same. What distinguishes today’s data analyst from centuries ago is that today we are more systematic and precise in how we go about defining, storing, and analyzing data.

1.15.2 The Philosophy and Scales of Measurement

Measurement can be interpreted as the assignment of numbers to objects via a set of rules. Crudely, if I am much taller than you, measurement implies that we have a rule that says I should get a higher number (measurement) than you and preferably by a well-defined amount on precisely measured units (e.g., inches). The problem with measurement, at a philosophical level, is the extent to which what we are actually measuring is a reflection of the true score we wish to measure. Make no mistake, the score we obtain with whatever instrument we use is but a measurement. It is not a pure reflection of the true score. In measurement theory, the true score T is a function of the observed score O plus error E:


T = O + E
(1.2)

To cut right to the chase, the measurement of something like height or weight contains more O than E, whereas the measurement of something like personality or intelligence, likely, or at minimum one could argue, contains more E than O. The key to (1.2) is that just because you measure something this does not necessarily imply that you are tapping into the true score. Much of your measurement may simply be error. The measurement of temperature with a dysfunctional thermometer may be more error than actual temperature, for instance.

1.15.3 Reliability

Measurement of data is only as good as such a process is reliable and valid. Reliability generally refers to the idea of consistency just as it does in ordinary speech. Informally, a measurement process is reliable, in one sense, if repeating the measurement produces the same or at least similar recording if the attribute under consideration has not changed. For example, measuring your height today and then tomorrow should provide the same (or at least nearly so) measurement. Such a measurement process is deemed reliable if it does. If your height measurement today was 60 inches and tomorrow 65, and assuming you didn’t experience a growth spurt overnight, the measurement process would be deemed quite unreliable.43

Following McDonald (1999), we assume that the population correlation ρ between T and E is equal to 0, that is, ρ TE = 0. By the variance-sum law which holds that the variance of uncorrelated variables can be summed, the variance of Y, now the observed score, is a sum of the variances of both T and E, that is,


σY2 = σT2 + σE2
(1.3)

From (1.3) we can deduce that σT2 ≤ σY2 and σE2 ≤ σY2, which implies


$$\rho = \frac{\sigma_{T}^{2}}{\sigma_{Y}^{2}} = \frac{\sigma_{T}^{2}}{\sigma_{T}^{2} + \sigma_{E}^{2}}$$
(1.4)

and where it can be easily shown that ρ is bound between 0 and 1 where ρ is called the reliability coefficient of Y. There are different forms of reliability. We survey one of the most popular ones now, that of internal consistency.

1.15.3.1 Coefficient Alpha

The split-half reliability is the correlation between two halves of a test corrected to full length by the Spearman-Brown prophecy formula (Cortina, 1993),


$$r_{sh} = \frac{2r_{12}}{1 + r_{12}}$$
(1.5)

where r 12 is the Pearson correlation between the two halves. Cronbach’s alpha is equal to the mean of all split-half reliabilities assuming item standard deviations are equal (Cortina, 1993; Sijtsma, 2009). The package coefficientalpha (Zhang & Yuan, 2023) can be used in R for carrying out reliability analyses. An example from the package’s documentation yields the following data on ten items:

> library(coefficientalpha)
> data(example)
> head(example)
item1 item2 item3 item4 item5 item6 item7 item8 item9 item10

We see that alpha is relatively high at 0.915. In general, alpha values of 0.80 or higher are usually deemed acceptable. While alpha is regularly used, on a theoretical level there are problems with the coefficient and it can be especially prone to misunderstanding (Panayides, 2013; Sijtsma, 2009).

1.15.3.2 Test-Retest Reliability

Test-retest reliability generally refers to the consistency or stability of a measure across two or more time points. It is generally assessed using the correlation coefficient. For example, suppose we administer a test at time A then correlate that to test results at time B. To the extent that the correlation is strong indicates that reliability is likewise tenable.

Special software functions are usually not needed to assess test-retest reliability as it can easily be evaluated using a Pearson (or other, such as intraclass) correlation coefficient.

1.15.4 Validity

The validity of a measuring instrument is an assessment of whether that instrument measures what it is designed to measure. For instance, a tire pressure gauge that reports the correct tire pressure is a valid measure of tire pressure. Flight instruments on an airplane are valid if they report correct readings of such things as speed, altitude, and so on. An intelligence quotient (IQ) test is considered valid if it actually measures something called “intelligence.”

How do we know altitude readings on an aircraft measure something called altitude? We know because engineers correlate such readings to measurement instruments having readings that are already known to measure altitude. Hence, when a new altitude measure is developed, it is a fairly easy matter to correlate it to well-known measures. Likewise with a temperature gauge, you can be quite confident that you have 36 psi (pounds per square inch) in your tires measured by your new gauge if your old and reliable gauge also measures 36 psi.

The measurement of IQ or similar psychological constructs is not as easily validated because, for one, there is no agreement on not only how IQ is best measured, but also whether even something called “intelligence” exists! It can be exceedingly difficult to validate something for which there is no agreed-upon criterion such as speed, altitude, or tire pressure. Psychological sciences have attempted to define IQ rigorously, but such definitions ultimately come down to what experts in the area wish to call intelligence. Of course, the criteria are not simply “made up” or contrived. Far from it. Experts spend a great deal of time pondering over what kinds of items reflect processing ability and such, and hence IQ tests are often based on rather strong theoretical underpinnings. Despite this, “capturing” the essence of IQ with a psychometric test that features subjective responses some believe to be an impossible task. If, however, we can agree on a particular test as a criterion, then validating newer instruments can be correlated to the original criterion, just as the aforementioned altitude readings can be correlated to more well-known readings.

It should be emphasized as well that at a philosophical level, the criterion for something like IQ and that of altitude is always human judgment. We are the ones who “invented” the idea of altitude, just as we are the ones who invented the idea of intelligence. Of course, that may be exaggerating the point slightly, but it is simply to say that constructs are always constructed. It just so happens that some constructs are extremely well-agreed upon and have lasted centuries without much disagreement, while others (such as IQ) are more novel and their existence is even subject to debate.

There are different kinds of validity which all more or less rely on the correlation coefficient in some form or another in the establishment of evidence. For instance, if an instrument has convergent validity, it should correlate highly with other tests purported to measure the same criterion, 45whereas if the instrument has divergent validity then it should not correlate with tests that purport to measure different constructs. For an excellent overview of validity, see McDonald (1999).

1.15.5 Scales of Measurement

Stevens (1946) proposed four scales of measurement: nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio. We let o i represent the object we wish to measure. The measured object is denoted by m(o i) while the true object is denoted by t(o i). Nominal scales are not true measurement at all, since they simply assign a different label to each object as merely an identifier. That is, m(oi)≠m(oj)⇒t(oi)≠t(oj). The classic example of nominal scales is that of football jersey numbers on the backs of football players. That one football player has a different number than another simply implies that it is a different football player and nothing more. The numerical assignment certainly does not imply that one football player is “better” than the other.

Ordinal measurement also carries the implication of nominal measurement, m(oi)≠m(oj)⇒t(oi)≠t(oj), but now with an added magnitude property. That is, if m(o i) > m(o j), such implies that t(o i) > t(o j). Ordinal measurement is the first instance of what we regard as measurement instead of simply assigning numbers to different objects as in the nominal case. Be sure to note, however, that m(o i) > m(o j) does not imply how much t(oi) > t(oj), it only implies that o i has more of the quantity than o j. Hence, that you finished first in the race, me second, and our mutual friend third tells us nothing about the magnitude or distance between first and second vs. second and third place. It only tells us the order, hence the name ordinal. To assume distances between objects to be equal, we require interval measurement, which we discuss next.

The interval scale is characterized by being an ordinal scale but with the added quality that for all distances i, j, m(o i) > m(o j) = c, where c is some amount or constant, implies t(o i+1) > t(o j+1) = c. That is, exact distance between objects is a characteristic of the interval scale. As an example, the distance in temperature on the Fahrenheit scale between 0 and 10 is the same amount of temperature change as the temperature change from 10 to 20, at least measurably.

The ratio scale has all the properties of the interval scale but with an important addition. Zero on the ratio scale implies zero of the quantity we are working with. That is, m(o i) / m(o j) = c implies t(o i) / t(o j) = c. The only adjustment we need to make to express the scale as ratio distinct from an interval one is to denote the origin as a true zero point. On the interval scale, zero is simply an arbitrary point; that is, it is just another point on the scale. That it is zero carries no special meaning. On the ratio scale, however, zero means zero.

If a scale is ordinal, then it necessarily possesses characteristics of a nominal scale. If a scale is ratio, it necessarily possesses characteristics of an interval, ordinal, and nominal scale, and so on for all scales in between. For example, temperature on an interval scale simultaneously implies a scale weaker than interval such that a temperature of 10 degrees is more than a temperature of 5, which is characteristic of an ordinal scale. We leave it to the reader to think up more examples. The idea that more primitive scales (e.g., nominal) can be considered special cases of more advanced scales (e.g., ratio) is referred to generally as collapsing scales.

1.15.6 Likert Scales

Likert scales were invented by Likert (1932) and are designed to elicit subjective measurement from individuals on a scale arbitrarily constructed by the researcher. In sciences such as psychology and sociology, measuring attributes of interest can be extremely difficult; some would even 46say impossible in many cases. For example, how can we measure how much you like pizza? We could observe how much you like pizza by following you around to see how much you eat of it every day, but such would be too timely and obtrusive. A more efficient way, if less valid, may simply be to ask you how much you like pizza and numerically scale your response. This is an example of a Likert scale.

Likert scales are a useful attempt to measure what we want to measure, but to be precise, they are not actually measuring the question in the scale. Instead, they are measuring the individual’s response to the question. For example, when we measure the person’s opinion on the overall quality of healthcare, their actual opinion might differ from the response they are providing. Their response and their actual opinion are not a one-to-one guarantee. This is the first problem with Likert scale data.

Second, the type of Likert scale can have a great influence on the accuracy of measurement. It is not difficult to come up with examples where participants will either be too optimistic or pessimistic on a particular item. It is equally easy to come up with examples where a participant may purposely mislead on the particular item. Human beings are not always honest, and if they are, they likely are not aware of their biases. A wealth of psychological research has been done in support of this idea. Asking a participant their level of anxiety is a subjective representation of their level of anxiety. There is no guarantee that it is their actual anxiety. This is especially true since nobody really knows precisely what anxiety is in the first place! We think it exists, but we can’t “point to it” as we can something like height or weight.

Hence, so long as the weaknesses and drawbacks of Likert scale data are recognized, they can be useful, but they need to be used and interpreted with care. Research has also been performed to help determine whether numerical distances on Likert scale data actually correspond to psychological measurement. See Wakita et al. (2012) for details.

1.15.6.1 Statistical Models for Likert Data

How should Likert data be analyzed? A first thing to note regarding any data is that the numbers do not know where they came from nor how they should be treated. Scales of measurement are ideas we impose on data. Hence, a data set can be analyzed in any way we wish, though the analysis will only be reasonable if it conforms to properties we impose on or assume of the data.

Categorical data methods are usually most appropriate for data at the nominal level since numbers in the nominal scale most often represent categories. Chi-squared analyses and log-linear models are well-suited for these types of data. Data that are at the ordinal level of measurement have more options for analysis. For one, we could simply treat the data as interval or ratio, drawing conclusions quite cautiously. Or, we could adopt methods specifically targeted for ordinal data, which we now briefly discuss.

1.15.6.2 Models for Ordinal and Monotonically Increasing/Decreasing Data

For two variables, continuous or not, Spearman’s ρ (pronounced “rho”) measures the monotonic relationship between variables where the relationship can be monotonically increasing or monotonically decreasing. This is in contrast to the classic Pearson r which assesses linearity.
