As depicted in Figure 1.4, Spearman’s ρ only cares that data on x are increasing or decreasing with data on y and does not require linearity or any other parametric structure.47

Other tests that can be used with ordinal response variables include Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney for two groups and the Kruskal-Wallis test for multiple groups as a counterpart to parametric ANOVA. The sign test can be used for nominal or ordinal data and the Friedman test is also a useful alternative for repeated-measures data. Space does not allow us to discuss nor demonstrate these tests here. For details, see Siegel and Castellan Jr (1988) which is a classic resource on nonparametric tests. For more cohesive models, ordinal logistic and the ordered probit model can be used. If the odds in the model are proportional to one another and differ only by a constant, this gives rise to the proportional odds model. For details, see Fox (2016, pp. 401–402).

Another option for modeling monotonic data is that of isotonic regression, which in contrast to ordinary least-squares regression specifically models data as a non-decreasing approximation. See Neykov (2019) for details. Isotonic regression for the two-variable case, that is, bivariate isotonic regression, can be carried out using the R package Iso (Turner, 2023).

1.16 Overview of Statistical and Machine Learning Concepts

Having surveyed some fundamental philosophical assumptions and ideas underlying science, statistics, and machine learning, we now turn to surveying statistical and machine learning concepts themselves. Many of these concepts have long histories in statistics where others are more modern and apply mostly to machine learning. Topics surveyed here are selective; they are the ones the reader should be familiar with in order to understand the rest of the book.

1.16.1 Probably Approximately Correct

The idea of probably approximately correct (PAC) learnability arose from statistical learning theory for the purpose of identifying hypothesis classes or sets (usually infinite in nature) that are actually learnable and provide low generalization error (Haussler, 1990; Valiant, 2013). Hypothesis classes are essentially subsets of virtually all functions that could be selected in modeling some phenomenon. For instance, suppose we select a hypothesis that minimizes empirical risk on a 48sample. How do we know such a hypothesis will also minimize population risk? If the hypothesis class is so-called PAC learnable, then we know it will probably also minimize population risk. That is, PAC learnability tells us that the selected function will, essentially, likely have low generalization error. That is, a PAC model will probably generalize well to new data.

A more direct and pragmatic way of understanding PAC learnability is to consider how well a hypothesis or concept class will not predict. That is, any hypothesis that is seriously wrong will almost certainly be “discovered” with high probability after a small number of examples or data points in a sample because it will (very soon) make an incorrect prediction. Thus, any hypothesis that is consistent with a sufficiently large set of training examples is unlikely to be seriously wrong. That is, it has been “tested” via experience, which implies it must be probably approximately correct. Any learning algorithm that returns hypotheses that are probably approximately correct is called a PAC learning algorithm, and such a designation can help provide bounds on the performance of various learning algorithms. For a precise and technical characterization of PAC learnability, see Mohri et al. (2018, p. 11).

1.16.2 No-Free-Lunch Theorem

As mentioned at the outset of this book, one element that distinguishes the machine learning paradigm from that of classical statistics is a focus more on the algorithm or method than the data. That is not to say the data are not important; they most certainly are of course, but the performance of the algorithm or procedure is what is studied most. Questions such as “Does logistic regression outperform discriminant analysis, and if so, under what conditions?” dominate the current machine learning zeitgeist.

Given this emphasis on the algorithm, it makes sense to ask then whether one algorithm dominates all others. That is, we ask the question:

Is there a best universal learner?

The answer to this question is contained in what is known as the No-Free-Lunch Theorem, which essentially holds that there is no universal learner. There is no “best” algorithm under all conditions for all data. Unpacked, what this implies is that for any learning algorithm there is a data set for which it may be very accurate and another data set for which it is very poor. The assumptions we enter with in one substantive situation, often called the inductive bias, are not the same as in another domain, and hence a universal learner across all domains does not exist. When we say a learning algorithm is “good,” we are only quantifying how well its inductive bias matches the properties of the data we are currently working with (Alpaydin, 2020). However, as good as the learner may be in one setting, there is always a task in which it will fail.

As a simple example, linear regression may work wonderfully in predicting income based on education levels but fail miserably in predicting COVID-19 probabilities of death. An equivalent and more crude interpretation of the theorem is that for even the most sophisticated algorithm one can conceive, over all conceivable possible tasks it will have the same average performance as merely predicting that every point belongs to a particular class (Goodfellow, 2016). Why will the performance of an algorithm chosen to model a specific situation likely be better? Because we will have chosen that algorithm for the specific task at hand coupled with our knowledge of the data. In other words, we are no longer averaging across all tasks. We are selecting a specific task and using an algorithm well-suited to that task.

As an analogy, modeling IQs across all possible theoretical distributions is hopeless and if we combined (or averaged) all distributions, our model of IQ would be quite poor. Fortunately, we do not employ all distributions; we usually employ a normal distribution because it best approximates 49the empirical shape of the distribution of IQ. The normal distribution isn’t the “best” distribution for all tasks; it is the best for particular tasks such as the modeling of IQ. That is, we “narrow down” from all distributions by making assumptions regarding the task we are working with. This is a powerful way to conceive of assumption-making when it comes to fitting statistical distributions – assumptions help narrow down the search and selection of an algorithm.

Think of this next time your chosen algorithm fits well to a given data set and be sure to not exaggerate how “good” your algorithm actually is. There is no best algorithm for all circumstances. Algorithms and statistical procedures must be chosen wisely for each task, which implies knowing not only something about the data but also something about the substantive area to which it is being applied. Linear regression, for instance, can never be the “best algorithm.” It can only be the best coupled with a particular data set which suits it well (e.g., one that exhibits linearity and homoscedasticity of variances).

1.17 V-C Dimension and Complexity

The Vapnik-Chervonenkis or “V-C” dimension is a measure of a classifier to perform. It characterizes its learnability. It is the maximum number of points that can be “shattered” or less formally, “separated” by a hypothesis class. As a simple example of the theory, consider the following plots (adapted from Hastie et al., 2009, p. 238), where each point takes its turn as class = 1 (bolded square) vs. class = 2:

As shown above, we can see that a linear function is able to “shatter” the two-group structure in each case. Hence, we would say that the class of linear functions for the above is able to shatter three points.

The above is but a trivial example of V-C dimension, as its theory gets much more complex. The details of the theorem can be found in Vapnik and Chervonenkis (1971). The theorem effectively can help provide an upper bound on optimism of a set of algorithms (Hastie et al., 2009) and tells us the capability or capacity of a concept class, that is, what the class is able to do, such as in the above example of lines shattering three points. A learning machine with a high number of parameters in general has a high V-C dimension; however, this is not necessarily always the case. One could have a very wiggly line that shatters many points yet only has a single parameter (see Hastie et al., 2009, for an example).

1.18 Parametric vs. Nonparametric Learning Methods

Virtually all statistical and machine learning approaches can be distinguished between parametric vs. nonparametric, though in reality many approaches will fall in between these two extremes. What distinguishes a parametric vs. a nonparametric approach? As with most things in statistics, the distinction quickly becomes fuzzy, but we will do our best to delineate the primary features.50

Parametric methods make assumptions about the functional form thought or assumed to underlie the observed sample data. Nonparametric methods do not assume such a form, but instead try to estimate the functional form more directly from the observed data. In a sense then, we can generally say that parametric models arrive on the scene with a Bayesian prior of sorts about the kind of distribution and function that may have given rise to the observed data, whereas nonparametric methods generally simply want to “get to know the data” without prior beliefs or functional form assumptions getting in the way. This is an oversimplification of the distinction, but still useful as an approximation.

Why make parametric assumptions at all? Why not just let the data “speak?” Making parametric assumptions often facilitates the analysis so that one does not have to start all the time at the very “beginning” as though one knows absolutely nothing at all about what functional form might have given rise to the data. As a result, parametric approaches typically require less data than do their nonparametric counterparts. For example, if you already have a good idea that the parametric form of the relationship will be linear, then you will need less data to fit your model than if you allowed the functional form to be entirely determined by the data, which would entail a more nonparametric approach. There are usually benefits to being able to assume a prior functional form to data. However, if the assumption is incorrect, accuracy and validity of the analysis will be compromised.

Another way of appreciating this difference is with respect to the number of parameters required in each type of modeling. Using the linear model as an example once more, once we fit the intercept and slope, the job is done, regardless of how much data we are fitting the line to. Two parameters get the job done regardless of whether we fit the line to ten observations or 10,000. The parametric line for a smaller sample size keeps the data from “speaking too loudly,” which is reasonable, since there isn’t much data to begin with. In other words, we are, through our imposing of a parametric form, helping the data determine its underlying form. However, as sample size increases and we get more data, we begin to “trust” the data more with determining its own underlying structure, and hence are more likely to allow it to “speak for itself” than restrict what it can say via a smaller allowance of a parametric form. After millions of observations, if the data suggest the underlying form is a very complex polynomial, we will have more trust than if the data were quite small in number. When the data were smaller, we imposed a line (or some other parametric form) so that the conclusions do not get too unrealistic by perhaps “connecting the dots” in the smaller sample.

1.18.1 Flexibility and Number of Parameters

Another and very useful way to think about the distinction between parametric vs. nonparametric approaches is via flexibility and the number of parameters required to carry out the modeling. As we have said, parametric models (e.g., a linear model) have a fixed number of parameters coming to the modeling scene already packaged and ready to be fit to the data. In the nonparametric situation, however, the number of parameters needed for the modeling is theoretically and pragmatically unbounded. As we will see when we fit such things as regression splines, we can pretty much fit as many knots as we wish to best approximate the curve. We have greater flexibility in how we model the data when compared to a parametric approach. The effective number of parameters is essentially unbounded (James et al., 2013).51

1.18.1.1 Concept of Degrees of Freedom

Degrees of freedom can be conceptualized in a variety of ways. All ways pretty much point to the same concept. For example, in a system of equations, degrees of freedom refer to the number of variables needed to complete the solution set, that is, if we know values for x, y, but not z, then the degrees of freedom for the system are equal to one. In a physical system, degrees of freedom refer to the minimum number of coordinates required to describe the state of the system (Tanton, 2005).

The basic sample variance as an estimator of the population variance is probably the simplest statistical illustration of this concept, where n–1 is used as the denominator to express the loss of a degree of freedom in


$$s^{2} = \frac{\left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right.} \right)^{2}}{n - 1}$$
(1.6)

The numerator $\left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right.} \right)^{2}$ features the estimation of μ through y, hence the loss of the degree of freedom.

More universally in terms of fitting models, the concept of degrees of freedom is related to the complexity of a model. In general, the more complex a model fit to training data, the more degrees of freedom that model possesses (e.g., spline with several knots or higher-order polynomial fit). A model with more degrees of freedom will generally fit better than a model with less, and hence overfitting becomes very probable as degrees of freedom increase (Murphy, 2022). An example is that of an exaggerated higher-order polynomial fit essentially at some point accounting for mostly noise in the empirical observations.

1.18.2 Instance or Memory-Based Learning

Nonparametric methods in the machine learning literature sometimes go by the name of instance-based learning methods or memory-based learning as a result of their heavy reliance on the data in determining fit. At a computational level, memory-based methods store the entire or at least much of the data set when making predictions about future data. As a result of this storage requirement, such memory-based methods are generally fast to train but can be slower to make predictions (Bishop, 2006).

1.18.3 Revisiting Classical Nonparametric Tests

If the reader has taken a classic statistics course, she may recall encountering nonparametric statistics, at least in a single chapter usually toward the end of the book. Nonparametric statistical tests included such things as the Kruskal-Wallis test and a host of others. Given our characterization of nonparametric tests above in the most general way, we can now revisit earlier teachings on nonparametric tests as traditionally and “classically” taught. What was it about those tests that made them nonparametric? In line with our definition above, it was the fact that they presumably did not make parametric assumptions that made them nonparametric. Or, at minimum, made fewer of them. For instance, the Kruskal-Wallis test does not assume observations come from normal populations as the competing parametric ANOVA test does. These nonparametric tests often operate on ranks and such, and thus often make minimal, if any, assumptions about the underlying population.52

The problem with this characterization of nonparametric tests is that the modern statistician versed in machine learning may not recognize those “simple” nonparametric tests as being examples of today’s nonparametric expanse largely due to increased computing power. Today’s nonparametric methods can seem much more vast, much more elaborate, much “bigger” than those simpler nonparametric tests of the classical age in statistics. When we say “nonparametric” today, we typically are not referring to those simpler tests, we are instead referring to things like the bootstrap, splines or other algorithms that make fewer assumptions about the underlying population, and for good pragmatic reason as well, such that in many cases of “Big Data” today we are closer to being able to approximate the entire population in our data recruitment anyhow. The key to today’s nonparametric methodologies isn’t so much about not making parametric assumptions, even though this still is their defining characteristic. The “spirit” of today’s nonparametric landscape is that of letting the data speak for itself. It’s about getting the parametric assumptions out of the way and replacing them with modern computing capabilities. Efron and Hastie (2016) summarize the newfound rise of nonparametric methods:

Two words [parametric and nonparametric] explain the classic preference for parametric models: mathematical tractability. In a world of sliderules [sic] and slow mechanical arithmetic, mathematical formulation, by necessity, becomes the computational tool of choice. Our new computation-rich environment has unplugged the mathematical bottleneck, giving us a more realistic, flexible, and far-reaching body of statistical techniques. But the classic parametric families still play an important role in computer-age statistics, often assembled as small parts of larger methodologies.

(p. 53)

As referenced earlier, a good resource on classic nonparametric tests is Siegel and Castellan Jr (1988).

1.19 Dimension Reduction, Distance, and Error Functions: Commonalities in Modeling

Most processes or data do not have thousands of intrinsic parameters that underlie them. Instead, there are usually only a few that govern things at a lower dimension. The lower-dimensional structure is said to be embedded in the higher-dimensional space that we come across in our work. That is, we say there is a manifold or subspace that “lives” within this higher-dimensional space. Dimensionality reduction seeks to reveal or uncover that manifold or subspace.

The search for essential dimensions has dominated science in one way or another since its infancy. Instead of thousands of “things going on,” there may be just a few things underlying the surface. At first glance, dimensionality reduction is quite naturally associated with techniques such as principal components analysis, factor analysis, etc., but the truth is that dimensionality reduction is implicitly present in virtually almost every technique we deal with. Even the basic t-test and its transformations (e.g., linear contrasts, ANOVA) can be shown to contain essential primitive concepts of dimension reduction, though at an elementary level of presentation this is not immediately apparent nor would it make sense to teach t-tests as related to dimensionality-reduction techniques in an introductory course.

1.19.1 Dimension Reduction: What’s the Big Idea?

The idea of dimension reduction is to project data points onto lower dimensions. The general question posed by dimensionality reduction is the following:53

What would these data points look like if they existed in these lower dimensions?

As we will see later in the book, this is basically what PCA is all about, assuming the underlying dimensions are linear functions. We may have 1000 variables, but when we reduce the dimensionality from 1000 to say, 3, we then want to know what the scores would have been on these 3 dimensions. This will be answered by projecting the data onto those three dimensions and then computing component scores, which are the scores yielded on those now three dimensions.

As an example of what we are talking about and to preview what lies ahead in the book, PCA can be defined most generally as


li = a1y1 + a2y2 +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + apyp
(1.7)

where li is a linear combination of weighted values of observed variables y 1 through y p. Even if the data are not truly on a linear manifold (we will define “manifold” later in the book; for now it may be regarded as simply a shape of sorts), PCA is often still useful and a very good approximation to the true underlying manifold. PCA, as we will see later, is essentially seeking to discover a new basis from which to project the data. A basis, as we will review in our survey of linear algebra, is the maximum set of linearly independent vectors that spans the space. When we collect data in its raw form, it is already on a basis but that basis is relatively arbitrary. For instance, the typical Cartesian plane, from this perspective, is an arbitrary basis but constrained at a 90-degree angle. Transforming the data to a new basis is what PCA and many other techniques accomplish. We then project the data from that basis to learn what the data look like from that vantage point, the vantage point being the new basis. The basis in the case of PCA is the set of orthogonal eigenvectors that result from the eigen decomposition (or singular value decomposition). The basis is orthonormal, which means orthogonal and each eigenvector having a length equal to unity.

What shall our dimensionality reduction look like? What is the form of these lower dimensions? We have two general possibilities: linear vs. nonlinear dimensionality reduction. While traditionally linear dimensionality reduction has been the norm, relatively recent techniques have allowed for sophisticated nonlinear reduction, or what is more generally called nonlinear manifold learning. While linear reduction may capture a process relatively well, in some cases a nonlinear manifold is required to capture more of the complexities and intricacies of the underlying manifold.

1.19.2 The Curse of Dimensionality

Given that many methods come down to dimensionality reduction, it is well worth noting at this point that dimensionality can be extraordinarily difficult to tame. Nonparametric methods, as we have discussed, often attempt to model data at a very local level. It would at first seem that these methods are well-suited for handling the dimensionality problem. However, as the number of dimensions increases, modeling local behavior becomes unwieldy. Hastie et al. (2009) describe the curse of dimensionality with reference to local regression, a technique that models the regression surface at a more local level than typically can be accomplished by ordinary least-squares:

Local regression becomes less useful in dimensions much higher than two or three … It is impossible to simultaneously maintain localness (low bias) and a sizeable sample in the neighborhood (low variance) as the dimension increases, without the total sample size increasing exponentially … When the dimension to sample-size ratio is unfavorable, local regression 54does not help as much, unless we are willing to make some structural assumptions about the model.

(pp. 200–201)

To paraphrase, locality is a relative term and not simply a function of a distance metric. As we will revisit when we discuss k-nearest neighbors, as the dimensionality of the space we are working in grows, even to capture a relatively local neighborhood of that sizable dimensionality often involves covering a significant quantitative range of the variable(s) in the model. Considered another way, as dimensionality grows, it becomes virtually impossible to account for all possible “cells” in a multidimensional matrix, and hence the very definition of locality becomes less meaningful unless sample size grows substantially to account for the increasing volume of the space.

To use a k-nearest neighbor analogy that we will refer to when considering that method in more detail later in the book, if your nearest neighbor mathematically is a house on the planet Mars, such fails to convey the true spirit of locality. That is, it’s hard to argue a house on Mars is a neighbor of yours. It may be a neighbor mathematically, but such is only because of the huge dimensionality of the problem in which there is a necessarily insufficient sample size to account for all “cells” in the data from your house to the house on Mars. In other words, that there is no house on the moon should not, by itself, make Mars, by default, a nearest neighbor. Mars being a neighbor is more an artifact of the dimensionality of the space you are working in, not because Mars is truly a neighbor. Increasing sample size would eventually, and most likely, put a house on the moon, and the moon would be your neighbor now instead of Mars. In brief, as the dimensionality of the problem increases, that Mars may be your “nearest neighbor” becomes a much less meaningful statement than if we were to truly identify your nearest neighbors more locally, that is, in a smaller volume of space.

1.20 Distance

Perhaps even more rudimentary of a “unifier” of the methods and models of this book is that of distance. Every approach and method, whether in multivariate statistics or machine learning, in some way assesses distance between objects (Johnson & Wichern, 2007). For instance, “patterns” and “clusters” can only be discerned if we are able to measure distance between observations. Which objects are similar? Which are different? One important point to keep in mind, however, is the following:

Similarity, measured by a distance function, does not necessarily imply “alikeness.”

For example, a weight of 10 pounds is alike a height of 10 inches, but only in terms of measured distance, not in terms of substantive material. As is the case with most statistical procedures, we must be acutely aware of the distinction between numerical representations of data and the scientific nature of the material underlying the numbers. As William James once said, we must not confuse data with the abstractions we use to analyze them.

We discuss the concept of distance further in the following chapter on mathematical foundations, there highlighting the most common measure of distance, that of Euclidean distance.

1.21 Error Minimization

Error minimization is yet another unifying theme of most of the methods in this book. In all methods we seek to, in a sense, hit a nail straight on the head as much as possible and minimize error 55in doing so. This idea of minimizing error occurs in virtually every method, either implicitly or covertly behind the scenes.

As an example, consider once more principal components analysis. Though typically performed using eigen analysis or SVD (singular value decomposition) and reproducing all the original variance in the variables, the most sought-after result of a PCA is that of a single component accounting for all the variance. Hence, the target can be considered a single component. The error function is the extent to which we require other components to make reasonable sense of the data, or, depending on the application, to reproduce the given image via data compression if the substantive application is that of image compression. Likewise, in structural equation modeling we seek to reproduce the covariance matrix; the extent to which we are unable to exactly is the extent to which we are in error. Minimizing error when imposing some kind of functional or near-functional form onto data is a goal of many statistical and machine learning methods.

1.22 Training vs. Test Error

When we consider f (x), this is regarded as the true unknown function. We typically estimate f (x) using f̂(x), where f̂(x) is the estimated function. Do we care whether the function is a “black box” or something we can “unpack” and get to know better? If we do, then we would like to know exactly what f (x) is; if we do not, then black-box predictability may be of primary interest without actually getting to know the functional form. Perhaps Amazon.com simply wishes to know what product you will most likely buy next; it may not care why; it simply cares to know which one.

When we train a model, we fit it to sample data. However, as we will discuss later in the book, training error (i.e., lack of fit) is usually not of primary interest. Rather, we instead wish to know how well the model fits on data it has not yet seen before. This is known as test error and is usually the final verdict on how well a model fits, at least for the given instance of fitting it to sample data. A useful analogy is that of a boxer training for a fight; we care less about how the boxer does on sparring practice opponents and instead care more about how he or she does against a new fighter. “Fight night” is the true test of the boxer’s skill, not the training sessions in preparation for the fight.

1.23 Cross-Validation and Model Selection

Cross-validation is a major “theme” of statistical learning and machine learning that differentiates itself somewhat from “classical” statistics of the past. When we come across a research paper that applies a statistical method to data and reports a measure of fit, the magnitude of the fit statistic is usually optimistic because by fitting the model to the sample data we may have capitalized on random or chance factors. As we have already discussed, we may have overfit the model. That is, the R-squared reported of say, 0.80, may be much too high of a realistic assessment of model fit. Yes, it is accurate on the training data, but as we have emphasized, we are much more interested in how the model performs on the test data.

The test error is the average error that results from using a statistical learning method to predict the response on a new observation – that is, a measurement that was not used in training the method. This definition and the wider concept are critical in evaluating a model. As mentioned, training error typically underestimates the test error rate. Estimating test error is not as easy as it sounds, however. Ideally, we would have a designated test set of observations (say, 20–30% of the original data set) that we could directly apply the statistical model to in order to observe how it performs. However, often we do not have such a data set at our disposal and hence a number of 56techniques have been developed to aid in estimating test error by simply using the available training data (e.g., Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)).

For the moment, assume we do have enough data such that we can set aside some of it for empirical cross-validation. There are different approaches that have been developed for cross-validating on the new sample. The validation set approach designates a subset or holdout of observations on which to test (e.g., 20–30%). Leave-one-out cross-validation adopts a similar philosophy but sets aside a single observation to predict and hence can be considered a special case of the validation approach for which n = 1. The test observation is (x 1, y 1) and is not used in the fitting, so (y1−ŷ1)2 provides an approximately unbiased estimate of the test error. It is unbiased, but highly variable since it is only a single observation. By “highly variable” is implied that if we used a different observation we might get a quite different result. So, we repeat for all observations and thus the leave-one-out estimate for the test mean squared error (MSE) is the average of all n test error estimates:


$$CV_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{MSE_{i}}}$$
(1.8)

where MSE i is used for quantitative responses (for discrete or categorical responses, other measures of error are typically used). Leave-one-out cross-validation is less biased than the validation set approach. That is, it is less likely to overestimate test error as the validation approach typically will. Also, there is no randomness in this approach as with the validation approach. Since we use all n, the idea of random sampling or splitting into arbitrary validation sets does not exist. Yet another approach is that of k-fold cross-validation, a kind of compromise between the validation set and leave-one-out approaches. K-fold cross-validation produces “folds” of greater number than n = 1 as in the leave-one-out case. Keep in mind that when we examine real data, we do not know the true test MSE, and so we can’t fully determine the accuracy of the cross-validation estimate. When performing cross-validation, sometimes we want to know the exact value of the minimum, whereas other times we just want to know which method gives the lowest minimum.

We will revisit cross-validation as we apply it to select methods throughout the book. However, we need to issue an important caveat: the process of cross-validating a model can result in a relatively elaborate exercise of simulating various parameters via grid searches and other exploratory visual tools as to seek out and arrive at the “best” model or tuning parameter(s) in terms of minimizing error, but these tools should also be interpreted in conjunction with substantive concerns of the area you are working in. In this way, “fine-tuning” a model is not usually as straightforward as following this or that computational cross-validation “routine” and should be considered in a wider scientific context.

Further, trying ranges of tuning parameters via grid searches and varying other settings is often recommended instead of relying too much on one or two parameters exclusively. For example, in methods such as ridge and lasso regression, good cross-validation often involves grid searches with varying ranges of input parameters to determine the best values to minimize error, not simply one or two values that have been “tuned” on the train data. Our select “snipet” discussions of cross-validation in this book usually simplify this process greatly for the purpose of keeping the treatment brief and space-wise manageable. However, this is in no way meant to suggest the process of cross-validation and arriving at the final model is therefore complete. In actual data analysis, it may be just the beginning. It would be a mistake for the reader to assume that because our discussion of cross-validation is brief or often omitted that it is therefore not necessary or important for the 57given method. It most often and surely is; however, extensive cross-validating via computational demonstrations would take us far beyond where we want to go in an introductory text that seeks to strike an ideal balance of theory, method, and practice. In many cases, we provide the requisite references to packages where extensive cross-validation direction can be sought out. As mentioned earlier in the book, most software examples in the book are simply meant as “foot in the door” glimpses into the computational aspects and in most cases are meant only to selectively demonstrate the technique; these easy demonstrations are not meant to be exhaustive or in any way complete “cookbook” or necessarily thorough or exhaustive steps to conducting any of the analyses.

1.24 Monte Carlo Methods

Monte Carlo methods feature the use of repeated iterative sampling facilitated by the computer. Note that we do not need the computer to do such sampling but suffice to say that it would be virtually impossible to sample extensively without the convenience of a computer that can easily and very quickly automate such a process. Any time a method features repeated sampling of some kind by computer, it is, by definition, a Monte Carlo method. Of course, the evolution of the computer and advanced computing speed has made the idea of resampling relatively easy to implement. It should be noted, however, that despite a Monte Carlo method being advertised as executing random sampling, resampling by computer could never truly be random. That is, once we have an algorithm choosing the next “random” number, the true randomness idea is forever lost.

One common use of the technique is in estimating the sampling distribution of a statistic, either because the sampling distribution cannot be derived analytically or simply because we want to compare the Monte Carlo method to its analytical counterpart. When we estimate a quantity and its sampling distribution using such methods, it often goes by the name of bootstrapping. We survey the bootstrap in the following chapter. The bootstrap is a special case of the more general Monte Carlo method because it features resampling. However, note that bootstrapping is not equivalent to the Monte Carlo method.

Monte Carlo methods are also often used to solve complicated optimization problems via randomized algorithms and hence are often employed in statistics and machine learning. Such approaches can also quite easily be used to estimate statistical power against competing alternatives. For a good example of this, see Rizzo (2019).

1.25 Missing Data

Missing data should never be ignored as there is often a reason for the missingness. The fact that an individual did not answer a particular question on a survey is not missing data; rather, it is extremely informative data and may signal the most important of responses. Perhaps the individual did not want to admit to ever stealing anything? Hence, the question, “Have you ever stolen anything?” is answered by not answering! That is the data that becomes of most interest. Never ignore missing data. Instead, get curious as to why it is missing.

Missing data is sometimes discussed under the more general topic of “cleaning data” in textbooks. Cleaning data typically refers to not only replacing or imputing missing data but also correcting for erroneous entries and detecting other abnormalities in the data file. For these latter uses, data cleaning is fine, but for replacing missing data, as mentioned, the analyst should proceed with caution. Empirical data is experience; it is the “stuff” that is of paramount importance in your entire analysis; it should not have to be “cleaned” that much. If you find yourself spending lots of time “cleaning” a data file, you may want to reconsider how your data was collected.58

1.26 Qualitative Approaches to Data Analysis

The topics of this book are from statistics and machine learning, and hence are considered quantitative or numerical in nature. Quantitative approaches dominate science. However, qualitative approaches can be just as useful and in some cases even more fruitful. Such approaches are often used in the social sciences as well as humanities (e.g., history, anthropology, etc.). A philosophical attempt to distinguish between what is “qualitative” vs. “quantitative” usually turns to “mush” rather quickly and there ends up being more similarity between the approaches than differences (numbers are, after all, qualitative categories). As discussed earlier in the book, categorization can be a dangerous thing, epistemologically. Most forms of knowledge and language end up being about patterns and structures among objects, and whether we measure them as quantitative or qualitative becomes a side issue. Quantitative approaches are usually regarded as more rigorous because numbers and mathematical operations have less flexibility than other epistemological objects or structures.

The qualitative tradition, in general, prefers to not reduce information to numbers. There is a very good reason for this, as numbers may actually mask and detract from underlying processes if not used correctly. As noted by Carrera-Fernández et al. (2012), who discuss qualitative research,

in which the researcher trusts textual data more than numerical data and analyzes this data in its textual form instead of transforming it into numbers for analysis, with the objective of understanding the meaning of human action … not only textual data but also visual, verbal, bodily, audio and spatial data are used … data are analyzed in their original dimension, without being previously transformed into numbers.

(p. 3)

Of course, a qualitative approach to determining the proper flap angle on an airplane at take-off is out of the question, unless of course the qualitative categories are precise numerical measurements. Numerical accuracy in this area of investigation is imperative. Note it is still qualitative, only that the qualitative nature is one of precise mathematical categories. In investigations where numbers may not represent underlying essences, for instance the study of poetry, literature, or the study of the soul, history, and so on, quantitative approaches may actually detract from such underlying essences. Quantitative approaches, especially in the social sciences, are largely overrated. In certain domains, they give the appearance of rigor, but underneath the numbers is too often a weak foundation. Rollo May’s The Meaning of Anxiety (2015) may tell us more about anxiety, its essence, than this or that statistical model applied to imperfectly measured anxiety data. The important point here is to keep an open mind and not discount qualitative approaches simply because they are not “math heavy.” Not everything is reducible to numbers. However, not adopting such a reductionist philosophy can make the communication of qualitative characterizations much more difficult. Perhaps in the end what is needed is a proper mixture of approaches in accounting for complex phenomena.59

1.27 Chapter Review Exercises

  1. 1. Through an online internet search, try to distinguish between statistics, machine learning, data science, and artificial intelligence. Is making the distinction easy or hard? Why? Where does computation fit into these distinctions?
  2. 2. Explain what it means for an algorithm to be stable, both conceptually and technically.
  3. 3. Distinguish between inductive vs. deductive logic.
  4. 4. In R, try computing 5 = 5, and then 5 == 5. How is the output different in each case?
  5. 5. Distinguish between supervised and unsupervised learning and discuss why the distinction can quickly become artificial.
  6. 6. Distinguish between overfitting and underfitting and give an example in each case, whether of a model fit to data or a more general theory or narrative that seeks to explain empirical events.
  7. 7. In reliability theory, under what case would σY2 = σT2? Do you think such a situation is realistic in measurement and science more generally? Why or why not?
  8. 8. Why is something measurable at the ratio scale also necessarily measurable at the nominal scale? Explain.
  9. 9. Distinguish between probably approximately correct and the V-C dimension.
  10. 10. Distinguish between parametric vs. nonparametric statistical and machine learning methods. Do you encounter any difficulties when trying to differentiate between them?
  11. 11. What is the curse of dimensionality? Why might it be a problem in dimension-reduction methods?
  12. 12. Distinguish between training vs. test error and discuss where the concept of cross-validation “fits” in between these two types of error.
  13. 13. If you had to collapse all approaches into quantitative or qualitative, which would you choose? That is, can qualitative approaches be “subsumed” under quantitative, or are quantitative approaches best subsumed under qualitative? Explain.

60

2 Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

DOI: 10.4324/9781003376941-4

In this chapter we provide an overview of the general mathematical and statistical background required for understanding the rest of the book. Most readers of this book will arrive with a varied background; some may be coming to this book having taken prior mathematics, statistics, and methodology courses, while others may only have the bare minimum introductory first- or second-year statistics course as their only preparation that they took likely as a follow-up to introductory courses in linear algebra and calculus which they may or may not have understood. Sadly, in today’s climate, it is very common for students to be able to pass a course in calculus, for example, without being able to describe what calculus is even about afterward; one can apply the power rule of differentiation to the function f(x) = 2x2 to get f′(x) = 4x, but one may not understand at all the work that has been just performed. What does f′(x) mean here? How should 4x be interpreted? It has been remarked by many that far too much mathematics education is about computation rather than truly understanding. For such readers who may not have been encouraged to understand in prior coursework, some or much of the material surveyed in this chapter may not quite be “review” and will instead essentially be introduced for the first time. Readers with a limited background are encouraged to supplement their study of these topics with references provided throughout and suggested readings at the close of the chapter.

As mentioned in the previous chapter, the foundations of statistics and machine learning are not really in mathematics. Mathematics only serves as the vehicle by which such concepts are communicated. For instance, in a simple linear regression problem, the “idea” is to minimize error in prediction. That’s the concept. To operationalize the concept requires more than words or a general idea; it requires precise symbolic definition and representation, that is, mathematics. The two are not one and the same. And while statistics and mathematics are challenging in their own right, the more significant challenge as it concerns the applied scientist is to understand why the given mathematics is being used in the given context. This helps to motivate the big-picture ideas behind the mathematics.

As an example, kernels, while all the rage in modern machine learning, are in fact quite old and not new to linear algebra and can be used in a variety of contexts well beyond machine learning. But why use them at all? What is the general “theme” underlying their use? The general big-picture idea to using them is to both facilitate computation while also providing a shorthand to approximating functions in higher dimensions. The underlying mathematics allows us to define what this looks like symbolically, but understanding how, why, and when to use kernels is the more “global” picture that is most important to grasp. “Big-picture” understanding is what is needed most and which is most often lacking from typical undergraduate and graduate courses, especially in quantitative courses targeted to applied scientists. Students need to be taught why, not just how. When one understands the “why” the how either reveals itself or can be dug up. Learning the how at the 61expense of the why is not pedagogically meaningful, yet sadly is often encouraged in the teaching of students. Students are not robots; they are creative minds and should be educated as such.

The technical “underground” of statistics, multivariate statistics, machine learning, and data science more generally is typically found in what are often regarded as the three “pillar” areas of mathematics: probability and statistics, linear algebra, and calculus and optimization. Indeed, it is not out of the ordinary for a statistician or researcher to simultaneously be somewhat of a “mini expert” in linear algebra or calculus, or both, since so much of linear models and multivariate modeling has its technical basis in these areas. As an example, consider the topic of eigenvalues and eigenvectors. These objects show up throughout statistics and machine learning, yet one can also study them in their own right, far removed from any applied statistical use. They are mathematical objects in and of themselves. As discussed at the outset of this book, the researcher or scientist, or more generally the “user” of these methods must be continuously aware of how much of a “sub-area” to study while also keeping focused on the primary area of their investigation. For example, too much of a focus on linear algebra eventually detracts from their applied experimental science, whatever that specialization may be (e.g., biology, psychology, forestry, chemistry, etc.).

2.1 Mathematical Previews vs. the “Appendix” Approach

2.1.1 Why Previews Are Better

Too often requisite mathematical underpinnings in books like this are given either as a disconnected review of fundamentals or as an appendix. All the “good stuff” is packed away in the appendix for the reader to look up as needed. This approach is limiting, however, as it fails to connect the material to the more substantive areas of the text. Our approach is to provide an overview of these technical fundamentals but most importantly, preview where we will see them again throughout the book. This last point is especially important. It does little good for the reader to learn or review a bunch of seemingly “abstract” mathematics if it is not properly motivated. At least not in an applied sense. Of course, the reader may not always readily fully appreciate the preview as it will be an incomplete description of the new concept (if it is indeed new to the reader); however, it will still serve the purpose of exposing the concepts to the reader as a preview of where such mathematics are used in statistics and machine learning. These early foundations help make understanding the pillars of statistics and machine learning (probability, linear algebra, calculus) a more continuous process rather than a discrete one. In this sense, the foundations are the method, but one is largely unaware of this until they see the foundations “in motion” or “at work” when studying the method later in the book, then returns back to these earlier pages to better recognize the connections that were being previewed.

As an example, the concept of a linear combination, taught in the abstract, may come across as an arcane and pointless symbolic mathematical object, until one realizes that so much of multivariate statistics and machine learning are about these very objects. If the reader is coming to the book with virtually no prior experience, then they will not appreciate our preview of where linear combinations will be used later in the book. On the other hand, if they are coming to the book with such prior experience, they will likely immediately recognize the connection which may help “tie” together concepts for that reader.

As another example, understanding the problems associated with linear dependence in a regression problem will only truly make sense once we get to linear regression, even though the concept of linear dependence is introduced and previewed in the current chapter. Books like this one are written in a more or less linear fashion, but the understanding of these subjects is not always linear. Chapters later in the book may help make something “click” in earlier chapters, and the reader should be pedagogically open to these types of connections.62

2.1.2 About Proofs

We avoid formal proofs in this chapter and throughout the book. However, this does not imply that basic proofs cannot be constructed based on the details we do present. Proofs are often a lot “closer” in proximity to the reader’s capacity than they may at first realize, especially if they are truly grasping the material.

As an example, it is well known that the Pearson correlation coefficient is bounded by limits of −1 and +1. Why this is so we explain in the book, though the explanation would not constitute a “formal proof.” However, if desired, a proof can be constructed from pieces of the explanation, and this typically makes for a great exercise. As gifted educator Morris Kline has said numerous times in reference to teaching calculus, it is better to understand the intuition behind the object than to learn a rigorous proof, at least on first reading and exposure. Indeed, historically, physicists and other scientists have relied on this approach quite heavily in the invention of new concepts. The mathematical and statistically specialized communities rightfully have high and very rigorous standards for what denotes a “formal proof,” (they should be applauded for their appreciation of rigor), but it is important for the reader to recognize that they themselves are sometimes not that far off from that “ideal” formal justification in at least some cases. Approximations are okay, so long as one realizes they are not the be-all and end-all and may lack formality. So long as the approximation does justice to the concept, you’re fine. If the approximation leads you astray from the concept, then that’s a problem.

Where results are very important, we provide the requisite technical references to more formal proofs and justification. For example, understanding what the central limit theorem is and why it works is most important in an applied sense, but if one were adamant on learning “why” via formal proof and had the ambition to work through it, select references are provided that further justify the theorem. Understanding why and how a theorem is “proved” and not the details of the proof may be enough, even for the curious reader. Proofs can be complex, but the idea of proof is (generally) not.

What is a proof, exactly? A quote by Abbott (2015, pp. 8–9) on famed mathematician Hardy is helpful here:

As Hardy indicates, there is an artistic quality to mathematics of this type, which may or may not come easily, but that is not to say that anything especially mysterious is happening. A proof is an essay of sorts. It is a set of carefully crafted directions, which, when followed, should leave the reader absolutely convinced of the truth of the proposition in question. To achieve this, the steps in a proof must follow logically from previous steps or be justified by some other agreed-upon set of facts. In addition to being valid, these steps must also fit coherently together to form a cogent argument. Mathematics has a specialized vocabulary, to be sure, but that does not exempt a good proof from being written in grammatically correct English.

Hence, a proof is a way of justifying that a mathematical statement is correct; it is an argument of sorts, just as arguments abound in other areas of inquiry (e.g., science, history, politics, etc.). Mathematical proofs, however, are much more rigorous because they are on objects that we can operationalize as specific quantities and variables.

One final point for now before we begin. Obviously, it is impossible to cover all the mathematics used in statistics or machine learning in one single chapter. It is even not possible to cover it all in one single book, or series of books, or encyclopedia! You get the idea. Our primary goal here is to simply survey the most common, relevant, and foundationally important prerequisite mathematics and statistics for an understanding of the contents to follow in the remainder of the book. 63A related goal is to provide additional insight for readers who may already have an introductory grasp of these topics and to help such a reader see the bigger picture. For example, has the reader ever appreciated how similar basic neural networks are to other statistical methods? As mentioned at the outset of this book, one of the chief goals is to emphasize such connections to augment the student’s understanding of these more global notions.

2.2 Elementary Probability and Fundamental Statistics

Probability theory is the quantification of uncertainty and is at the foundation of most statistical and machine learning ideas. As R.A. Fisher (1925, 1935), the “father of statistics” put it, we may not be able to make certain predictions, but we can often rigorously quantify the degree to which we are uncertain. This is a powerful idea, one that essentially revolutionized how scientific thought and conclusions are “packaged.” We may not know whether it will rain tomorrow, but the extent to which we can quantify our uncertainty regarding whether or not it will rain nonetheless provides us with knowledge and gives us a “handle” on the problem. We have become relatively certain about the uncertainty. That’s a big idea. Historically, the invention or discovery of probability was somewhat of a paradigm shift, not only in science, but in everyday communication.

Ideas and concepts of probability go back at least to the ancient Greeks and probably much before then, as most important ideas do. However, probability was only mathematically formalized into a system relatively recently beginning in the 1600s. Most mathematical (and other) inventions have histories where the key concepts germinate over time. Few innovators truly work alone and few important ideas are unmotivated by other equally important ideas. The formalized interpretation of probability, considered in proper context, was more of a culmination of ideas that germinated for centuries.

2.3 Interpretations of Probability

There are generally three schools of probability: classical, frequentist, and subjective. Classical views are, for the most part, not really part of mainstream probability. The probability of getting a “1” on a roll of a die is 1/6 since there are six sides to the die and all appear to have equal probability. That’s an example of the classical view. Historically, frequentist and subjective notions have dominated statistics and hence also more or less dominate machine learning.

For the frequentist, probability is a long-run frequency; that is, if you want to know the probability of something, you need to experience the event over repeated trials and take the fraction of times the event occurs to the total number of trials. The typical classic and easy example is that of flipping a coin. If we flip the coin 100 times and get 50 heads, we say the probability of heads is equal to 50/100 = 0.5, even though theoretically this is only an approximation to the true probability. The 0.5 is not the true probability. For the true probability under this approach, we would require flipping the coin an infinite number of times. From this perspective, true probabilities are only arrived at in the limit as sample size grows infinitely large, that is,


$$\lim\limits_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{n_{H}}{N} = p\left( H \right)$$
(2.1)

Unfortunately, “infinitely large” could never be a reality, and hence one weakness of the relative-frequency approach is that obtaining such a large number of trials is nothing more than a fanciful idea, even if it does serve as a useful working model for defining probabilities. Many scholars have critiqued the relative-frequency interpretation of probability precisely on this basis.64

The subjectivist, also commonly known as the Bayesian (since Bayesians typically adopt a subjective viewpoint of probability), takes probability to be an opinion, a degree of belief and hence does not require the unrealistic and unattainable infinite number of trials idea that is mandatory for the frequentist to accept. As we will see later however when we survey Bayesian statistics, subjective probability has its problems as well.

The key point to take away from this discussion so far is that the nature of probability has historically, and is still currently, open to debate. You are understanding this point correctly; nobody knows what a probability actually is! All that can be offered is an interpretation of probability. Which interpretation is correct is not a debate we will have here, and in fact, if you studied and wrote a dissertation on the topic, you’d most likely end up in the same place you started. That is, probability is a relatively elusive concept, and the best we can do is simply adopt a way of thinking about it. The frequentist and subjectivist notions of probability dominate modern science.

2.4 Mathematical Probability

Regardless of the interpretation of probability adopted, virtually all probability theorists agree on the fundamental mathematics of probability. That is, while the nature of probability (i.e., frequentist vs. subjectivist) is and has been up for debate for literally centuries, the essential mathematics underlying fundamental probability are usually not contested, except perhaps by true rebels and nonconformists! Hence, in what follows in our brief presentation of mathematical probability, there are no true “debates.” Most are “on board” with these basic notions and definitions. Much of modern probability is based on the theory of sets, which we do not review here, except as it applies directly to the concepts we do present.

The probability of the event A is denoted P(A), and is a number between 0 and 1:


0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1
(2.2)

The complement of A denoted $\overline{A}$ is the probability that A does not occur. Since the probability of the entire sample space, by definition (and convenience) must equal 1, this implies that


$$P\left( \overline{A} \right) = 1 - P\left( A \right)$$
(2.3)

The joint probability, that is, of A and B occurring at the same time is denoted


P(A∩B)
(2.4)

If A and B cannot occur simultaneously, then


P(A∩B) = 0
(2.5)

and we say the two events A and B are disjoint or mutually exclusive. Examples of mutually exclusive events include the events “head” and “tail” on the flipping of a single coin since one cannot obtain a head and a tail on the same flip.

To know if two events are mutually exclusive, one must know about the context or physical model of the problem. For example, the events “heads” and “tails” are not intrinsically and organically mutually exclusive events; they are only so under the model of a single flip. For successive flips, they are not typically mutually exclusive. The only absolutely necessary criterion for mutually exclusive events is as stated in (2.5), that of P(A∩B) = 0, and hence so long as this condition 65is satisfied, even in the abstract, the two events are mutually exclusive. Knowledge of temporal conditions of the physical model imposed serves to help us know whether the condition is met.

Why is this point so important? Why are we going on about it? The reason is that physical models (which include temporal sequences as a special case) are special cases or circumstances of a more general “real-world” context. Abstract mathematics (or philosophy, for that matter) does not require such a basis in reality. To emphasize the point, if the aliens come one day and have no conception of time, the concept of mutual exclusiveness would still be “communicable” by simply drawing the idea in Figure 2.1 with Venn diagrams on a sheet of paper.

The depiction in Figure 2.1 is what mutual exclusiveness is, at least from a geometrical point of view. Knowing whether mutual exclusiveness applies to the objects under study must come from the context. If there is only one flip of the coin, head and tail are mutually exclusive events. If there are two flips, they are not. Context matters. Everything happens in a given context; this includes scientific, mathematical, statistical, and machine learning matters. This “theme” will return time and time again throughout this book and it is worth emphasizing and repeating here:

Context Matters!

2.4.1 Unions and Intersections of Events

The probability of A or B occurring on a given trial is denoted by their union,


P(A∪B)
(2.6)

and is equal to the sum of probabilities of A and B minus their intersection,


P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B)
(2.7)

where P(A∩B) defines the probability of the intersection.

It is easy to see that for mutually exclusive events, where P(A∩B) = 0, the union of A and B is equal to66


$$\begin{array}{l} {P\left( A \cup B \right) = P\left( A \right) + P\left( B \right) - P\left( A \cap B \right)} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = P\left( A \right) + P\left( B \right) - 0} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = P\left( A \right) + P\left( B \right)} \\ \end{array}$$

This is sometimes referred to as the special rule for the addition of probabilities, that is, where the intersection is equal to 0 and we can simply compute the union by adding probabilities. To be on the safe side, it is good advice to always plan on subtracting an intersection from the addition to ensure for yourself that there is no overlap. It is obvious and easily provable that the intersection of a number of sets must be a subset of their union as the overlap, no matter how large, cannot be larger than the sum of all sets. The reader may recall that a subset can consist of the entire set, whereas a proper subset must be smaller than the full set.

2.5 Conditional Probability

Most phenomena in science are not about probabilities; they are instead about conditional probabilities. We rarely care about the probability of an event occurring; we care more about the probability of an event occurring, given something else has already occurred. This “conditional” statement translates to a reduction in the original sample space from what it originally was for the unconditional probability estimate. The probability of cancer is interesting, but the probability of cancer given that you do or do not smoke two packs of cigarettes per day is much more interesting. Virtually every problem and finding in science, no matter how simple or complex the model or lack thereof, can be translated into a statement of conditional probabilities.

Conditional probabilities add the aforementioned “context” to the problem since unconditional probabilities, while often accurate in and of themselves, can be grossly misleading. In passing, this is precisely why some detest statistics, because depending on what other factors or conditions are imposed on a problem, one can draw one of many conclusions. For instance, while the probability of perishing from COVID-19 may be 0.05, the probability of one dying given that one is an otherwise healthy 30-year-old is likely significantly less. Unconditional probabilities are, in a sense, “averages” across objects and conditions, and as we will discuss later, averages can be grossly misleading. Conditional probabilities are specialized focused slices within that spectrum. They help us narrow in on the probability estimate of most interest and provide that necessary context to the problem. The difficulty is that in many or most problems, there is no theoretical limit to how much context can be included which makes arriving at the “true” conditional probability in many situations very difficult or even impossible. At worst, a lack of context will simply make the probability estimate unmeaningful and very misleading. The probability of a human being currently eating baby formula is very low. It’s a silly probability estimate because we have not conditioned it on age and thus have not provided proper context to the problem. The probability estimate is accurate. The lack of context to the problem is foolish and makes the unconditional probability estimate uninteresting.

The concept of so-called risk factors also evolves from the general principle of conditional probabilities. For instance, when a practitioner asks about the past suicidality in your family as a way of estimating your own probability of suicide, she is attempting to narrow the sample space such as to ascribe past suicidality as a risk factor in estimating your own risk of suicide. The concept of risk factors plays a significant role in many branches of epidemiology and science in general. When you hear the word “risk factor,” think “conditional probability.”67

Mathematically, the conditional probability of A given B is defined as


$$P\left( A \middle| B \right) = \frac{P\left( A \cap B \right)}{P\left( B \right)}$$
(2.8)

while the conditional probability of B given A is given by


$$P\left( B \middle| A \right) = \frac{P\left( A \cap B \right)}{P\left( A \right)}$$
(2.9)

depending on which variable we are conditioning the other on. Using conditional probabilities and simple algebra, we can now define the aforementioned intersection between A and B more formally:


$$\begin{array}{l} {\,\,\, P\left( B \middle| A \right) = \frac{P\left( A \cap B \right)}{P\left( A \right)}} \\ {P\left( A \cap B \right) = P\left( A \right)P\left( B \middle| A \right)} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = P\left( B \right)P\left( A \middle| B \right)} \\ \end{array}$$

That is, the probability of A and B occurring simultaneously (i.e., P(A∩B)) is equal to the product of an unconditional probability – either P(A) or P(B) – with a conditional probability where it is also true that


P(A)P(B|A) = P(B)P(A|B)
.

2.5.1 Unconditional vs. Conditional Statistical Models

As emphasized in our discussion of unconditional vs. conditional probabilities, much of statistical modeling in the end is about conditional probabilities. In most cases, however, we do not evaluate such probabilities in a vacuum. Rather, we evaluate them relative to a particular statistical model. Hence, when we write the unconditional probability of P(A), it will now be understood that we are assuming a statistical model, whether that statistical model is specified explicitly or not.

Referring to our previous example, the unconditional probability of cancer is, by itself, though useful, rather uninteresting, and would denote a much too simplistic statistical model similar to the idea of predicting overall suicide rates in a regression context based on no predictors would also be much too simple of a model. The intercept-only model is limiting. To enrichen the model, we should want to include covariates and variables to provide a meaningful context to the evaluation of the probability. This is the very essence of much of statistical modeling, to provide a context for evaluating and estimating particular probabilities of most interest. Many statistical models are, in the end, nothing more than generalizations of ideas of conditional probabilities. Of course, that’s a simplification, but it’s a good start to understanding statistical modeling.

Going from conditional probabilities to statistical models, we need to generalize our notation. Instead of speaking of the unconditional probability P(A), we need to speak instead of the unconditional model, not simply probability. The conditional model is given by the following,68


p(y|θ)
(2.10)

where the response is now y and the parameter vector is now θ. The model is unconditional because there are no covariates. We now add a covariate x as follows:


p(y|x,θ)
(2.11)

which yields a conditional model where now y is “conditioned” on x, for which the parameters in θ will be estimated. Under the circumstance where y and x are independent, then p(y|θ) = p(y|x,θ). Contrarily, when y and x are dependent, then it should be obvious that p(y|θ) ≠ p(y|x,θ).

2.6 Probabilistic Independence

From the definition of conditional probability, we can quite easily obtain the concept of statistical or probabilistic independence. If P(A) = P(A|B), then events A and B are said to be independent, which implies that knowing B has occurred tells us nothing about the probability of A occurring. Note that the qualifier “has occurred” implies a temporal dimension, but as was the case for mutual exclusiveness, we need not assume a temporal context at all. All we really require is a reduction in the sample space so that the event of interest is referenced to that reduced space instead of to the original wider space.

We can easily see from the rule for joint events that if A and B are independent, then


$$\begin{array}{l} {P\left( A \cap B \right) = P\left( A \right)P\left( B \middle| A \right)} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = P\left( A \right)P\left( B \right)} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.12)

since if A and B are independent, then P(B|A) = P(B). That is, if we can assume events A and B are independent, then we can simply multiply their unconditional probabilities in determining P(A∩B). This is known as the multiplication rule for independent events. If we cannot assume they are independent, then we cannot simplify the rule and must always invoke the conditional probability P(B|A) rather than simply P(B) in the second term. That is, the more complete rule for computing the probability of the intersection is the first above, that of


P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B|A)

The multiplication of unconditional probabilities is simply a special case of the above more general rule. But how do you know if events A and B are independent or not? We discuss this issue next.

2.6.1 Everything Is about Independence vs. Dependence!

Whenever new concepts are introduced in statistics, they are often so fundamental that it is tempting to conclude that the whole discipline revolves around them. We just experienced this idea in our discussion of conditional probabilities, concluding that everything is about conditional probabilities. Even more fundamental is the idea of independence versus dependence. The unifying principle of these concepts cannot be overstated. It is what probability and thus virtually all statistics and science are about. On the one hand, statistically, probabilistic independence is at the heart of many probability calculations and often simplifies matters a great deal. On the other hand, in terms of real scientific empirical objects, establishing independence can be extremely difficult (and many times impossible) to demonstrate, and instead is often simply an assumption that 69must be (conveniently, and even unrealistically in many cases) made, often on reasonable grounds given the experts concluding the independence have knowledge of the system(s) they are working with. Determining empirically that two events are independent can often be next to impossible. Statistical modeling is about making assumptions, often lots of them.

As an example of what we are talking about, consider an airplane system. Probabilistic independence is a sought-after goal when conceptualizing and manufacturing aircraft components and running failure analysis scenarios. Engineers purposely design airplane systems to be as independent as possible so that a failure in one system does not change the probability of a failure in another system. Why is this so important? Well, consider the possibilities when flying on an airplane; it would be a terrible thing if the probability of a failure of one engine increased the probability of a failure of a second engine, or if the probability of the landing gear detracting was not independent of the probability of the hydraulic system working. In these cases, it would take but one failure to influence other failures, and hence a single failure could, in theory, take down the airplane through a chain reaction of events. Hence, as much as possible, system events on airplanes are designed to be probabilistically independent. The probability of one engine failing should, ideally, not have an effect on the probability that the plane experiences a decompression, for instance.

But how do these experts “know” the systems are independent? They don’t! Well, not for certain, anyway. However, rational argument, a plausible argument, knowledge of the systems under consideration, increasing empirical evidence, and making assumptions that align with such knowledge typically lead such professionals to conclude that operating the flaps on the wings, for instance, is independent of the ability of the fuel tank to hold fuel, just as a failure of the landing gear to retract is independent of the plane’s engines to generate power. Of course, these seem like “obvious” assumptions to make, but the point is that they are often nonetheless assumptions (assumptions often supported by increasing amounts of evidence, in this case). The goal of science is to reject “obvious” assumptions with newly established empirical evidence that potentially counter or challenge existing assumptions.

For instance, it was once assumed that a simple cigarette could never cause any harm, just as it was once assumed that chemicals used in paint (e.g., benzene) could never pose a threat to our health and the health of our pets. Social media was never thought to be associated with depression and anxiety in our children. Science is about cutting through “established” beliefs with evidence that suggests such “establishment” should be rejected. Newtonian mechanics was once assumed correct until Einstein’s “unlikely” theory led us to believe differently. The point is that all scientific “fact” is tentative to new evidence and revision, and the idea of probabilistic independence is no different. We can assume events to be independent to get on with business (and fly the plane, for instance), but we must always allow the possibility that they are not, subject to new evidence. It was once assumed that a thin layer of icing on wings could never influence the capacity of the plane to stay airborne. We now know differently, largely due to experiencing (i.e., data) planes fall from the sky because of a thin layer of such ice. Such has encouraged us to “update” our belief about the impact of ice on wings, which is why that 20-minute delay we are so impatient about as travelers (while de-icing equipment clears our wings) could be saving our lives. The 20-minute delay is a “good thing” and has been informed by prior deaths and tragedies, that is, experience.

2.7 Marginal vs. Conditional Distributions

As we have seen, the concept of conditional probabilities is vitally important to both statistics and science. However, we have also discussed that conditional probabilities are often applied to statistical models, not individual probabilities. With these two elements, we can generalize concepts 70of conditional probabilities to that of joint and conditional distributions. Further, for a continuous distribution, the marginal probability density function (PDF) over all possible values of y can be obtained from the joint PDF by integrating out all other p variables that may be present and summing (via integration) over all possible values of y,


f(x) = ∫ − ∞ + ∞f(x,y)dy
(2.13)

The PDF integrates to 1, that is,


f(x) = ∫ − ∞ + ∞f(x,y)dy = 1
(2.14)

In the discrete case, we can simply visualize summing up or down a 2 × 2 table across categories of the second variable. As was the simpler case for the rule of independence for individual probabilities, random variables are independent if the joint PDF is equal to the product of marginal PDFs. If the joint PDF is not equal to the product of marginal PDFs, then the two random variables are said to be dependent.

2.8 Independence Implies Covariance of Zero, but Covariance of Zero Does Not (Necessarily) Imply Independence

As we will discuss in more detail later, the covariance between variables is a measure of the extent to which the variance of one variable is linearly associated with the variance of another. The covariance is given by


$$Cov_{xy} = \frac{\left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( x_{i} - \overline{x} \right.} \right)\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right)}{n}$$
(2.15)

For any two variables that are statistically independent, this necessarily implies a covariance equal to 0. However, the converse is not necessarily true. That is, a covariance equal to 0 does not necessarily imply that two events are independent. They may turn out to be independent, but the covariance equal to 0 is not enough to imply it. This is because the relationship between the two variables may simply be one that is nonlinear. The covariance between two variables is a measure of linear association or relationship only.
