Hence, two variables may be strongly dependent or related to one another, yet still have a covariance (and hence, also correlation, though as we will see later the two are not equivalent) equal to 0. This is one reason why interpreting a measure of covariance or correlation should never be done without also inspecting a scatterplot of the association. Always plot your data! This is worth repeating:

Always plot your data!

Numerical summaries are never enough. As an extreme instance and very insightful example of this effect, we refer to Anscombe’s Graphs in Statistical Analysis (Anscombe, 1973) in Figure 2.2 which consists of three different data sets that yield identical summary statistics.71

Remarkably, all four plots share the same means on x and y ($\overline{x} = 9.0$, $\overline{y} = 7.5$), regression of y on x (slope of 0.5), regression equation y = 3 + 0.5x, sum of squares $x - \overline{x} = 110.0$, regression sum of squares (27.50), residual sum of squares (13.75), estimated standard error (0.118), and R2 = 0.667. If such a demonstration does not convince the reader to always plot their data, nothing will!

Other examples of this effect abound (see Murphy, 2022, p. 42 for examples). In short, visualization is a must for good data analysis and exploration, not an option. Let’s put this another way; if you are not visualizing your data in at least some capacity, you are usually conducting a poor data analysis. There are special cases where one may be able to circumvent visualization, but the point is that visualization will tell you things about your data that numerical summaries may never. Numerical summaries alone will never provide the widest or most complete picture or understanding of the data, and as we have said already ad nauseam by now, and will continue to repeat throughout the book, all variables exist in a wider context of other variables. Visualization helps provide a description of that context, which is why so much effort is put toward developing new visualization techniques in statistics. As we will see later in relation to manifold learning, multivariate visualization can be especially challenging and difficult, and as the dimensionality of the data increases, can be virtually impossible.

We will revisit covariance and correlation in more detail shortly.

2.9 Sensitivity and Specificity: More Conditional Probabilities

Another area where conditional probabilities are featured and used is when determining the sensitivity and specificity of diagnostic tests. A diagnostic test is a sign. It is a piece of data. It is a moment of experience. It is not a deterministic indication that the disease or condition is present. A classic and modern example of this is diagnosing COVID-19. A diagnostic test may indicate the presence of the virus, but there is also associated with that a probability that the disease is not present. A test that detects the disease when the disease is present is called the sensitivity of the test. A test that fails to detect a disease that is not present is called the specificity of the test. Good tests have strong sensitivity and specificity though the two will seldom, if ever, be perfect or equal to one another.

Of course, we desire any test to have maximum sensitivity and maximum specificity. That is the ideal we shoot for. Where things go wrong with diagnostic tests is when a test indicates the virus or condition is present when the virus or condition is not present. This is known as a false positive, or more commonly in the statistical literature as a Type I error in hypothesis testing. On the other hand, a test that fails to detect a virus when the virus is present has committed a Type II error. 72Which is the worst error? Which error has the greater consequence? Such, of course, depends, again, on the context of the problem. Context matters! Again! Which is most important depends on which type of error the scientist wishes to minimize. Surely, we do not want to misdiagnose the virus. Yet at the same time, diagnosing the virus when it is not present can lead to many problems, such as emotional distress, financial costs, the inconvenience of further testing, etc. Indeed, this has been one of the controversies surrounding habitual mammogram testing, for example; some argue that due to the error rates involved, yearly mammograms may be doing more harm than good. The risks of diagnosing a disease when none exists are real and can have great consequences. At the same time, missing a condition when the condition is present can likewise have serious consequences. Which error is more consequential largely depends on the situation, context, and the inclination of the scientist or subject.

2.10 Bayes’ Theorem and Conditional Probabilities

There is perhaps no better or more important of an example of conditional probabilities as with Bayes’ theorem. Recall that we mentioned at the outset of this chapter that the two primary camps in statistics are those of the frequentist and subjective perspectives. Maximum likelihood estimation, the most common method for estimating parameters, generally stems from and is governed by a frequentist approach in which the probability of the data given a parameter is evaluated, that of p(y|x), where here y is the data and x is the parameter (in place of the notation θ for our discussion here). The conditional probability p(y|x) is referred to in frequentist probability as the likelihood.

In Bayesian reasoning, the probability of the parameter given the data is instead evaluated, that of p(x|y). Bayes’ theorem inverts conditional probabilities from p(y|x) to p(x|y):


$$p\left( x \middle| y \right) = \frac{p\left( y \middle| x \right)p\left( x \right)}{p\left( y \right)}$$
(2.16)

where p(y|x), as before, is called the likelihood, p(x) is the prior probability, and p(x|y) is the posterior probability. The denominator, p(y) is the total probability of the data, or evidence more generally.

An even more meaningful way to interpret Baye’s theorem is by replacing x with T (theory) and y with D (data):


$$\begin{array}{l} {\, p\left( x \middle| y \right) = \frac{p\left( y \middle| x \right)p\left( x \right)}{p\left( y \right)}} \\ {p\left( T \middle| D \right) = \frac{p\left( D \middle| T \right)p\left( T \right)}{p\left( D \right)}} \\ \end{array}$$

That is, p(T|D) is the probability of the theory given the evidence or data. The difficulty with Baye’s theorem is that one must enter a prior probability, which can be quite subjective in nature. Note that no matter the strength of the data, if the prior probability p(T) is equal to 0, then the posterior probability will also equal 0, since,73


$$\begin{array}{l} {p\left( T \middle| D \right) = \frac{p\left( D \middle| T \right)\left( 0 \right)}{p\left( D \right)}} \\ {p\left( T \middle| D \right) = 0} \\ \end{array}$$

The big idea in Bayesian analysis is that contrary to frequentist approaches where parameters are regarded as fixed constants, Bayesian analysis treats parameters as random variables.

2.10.1 Bayes Factor

In the case where we have two competing models, M0 and M1, we can form the Bayes factor, which is a ratio of likelihoods of the data under these two hypothetical conditions:


$$B = \frac{p\left( D \middle| M_{1} \right)}{p\left( D \middle| M_{0} \right)}$$
(2.17)

where p(D|M1) is the probability of the data under the condition of the alternative hypothesis, M1, and p(D|M0) is the probability of the data under the condition of the null hypothesis, M0. If the two likelihoods are the same, then we would, obviously, expect B to equal 1, whereas if M1 is preferred over M0 then we would expect B > 1. The Bayes factor provides a competing alternative to classical frequentist statistics that focuses on the p-value as a means of making a decision between the two states. According to Jeffreys, a Bayes factor greater than 10 indicates strong evidence for M1 while a Bayes factor greater than 100 indicates exceptionally strong evidence for M1 (Murphy, 2022). However, as always, the size of the ratio should be evaluated, at least in part, relative to the context of the investigation. A Bayes factor of 2 in some research settings may be considered relatively large, whereas a Bayes factor of 10 in another research setting may be considered trivially small. Have we mentioned before that context matters?

2.10.2 Bayesian Model Selection

Suppose we run a host of competing models and wish to select the “best” one in some sense. The qualifier “in some sense” is necessary here, as selecting a “best” model is in no way a straightforward task and will usually depend on much more than a single criterion for selection.

By a Bayesian approach, that model should be the one that maximizes p(m|D), where m is now the model and D is, as before, the data:


$$p\left( m \middle| D \right) = \frac{p\left( D \middle| m \right)p\left( m \right)}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}{p\left( D \middle| m \right)p\left( m \right)}}$$
(2.18)

We recognize in the above the quantity p(D|m), which, when unpacked, is equal to


p(D|m) = ∫p(D|θ,m)p(θ|m)dθ

and is called the marginal likelihood (Murphy, 2022). If p(D|m) holds strong under different settings of the parameter θ, then m is likely to be considered a reasonable model. The key to the marginal likelihood is the summing (via integration) across a variety of parameter values (θ). This is why it is called “marginal,” as a result of the summation over all values of θ. If it were for a particular value of θ = θi, then it would be “conditional” instead of marginal. Under the condition of two competing models m1 and m2, should p(D|θ̂1,m1) and p(D|θ̂2,m2) both be large, Occam’s razor requires us to select the model that is simplest. Marginal likelihoods then help us select a suitably complex model, which has analogies to cross-validation and other model selection guidelines in a frequentist context (see Murphy, 2022, pp. 179–180 for details). However, 74marginal likelihoods can be difficult to compute in practice because they require integrating over the entire parameter space (Murphy, 2022). The Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) can be considered a kind of approximation to the log marginal likelihood, which, as we will see later in the book, is used in many contexts, including regression and cluster density estimation, among others.

2.10.3 Bayes’ Theorem as Rational Belief or Theorizing

Bayes’ theorem is not a trivial idea. Far from it. By itself, Bayes’ theorem tells us how, as rational agents, we should update our belief about T in light of new D, where T is nothing more than a belief or theory and D is nothing more than experience in its fullest generality. Bayes’ theorem is not a statistical idea; first and foremost it is a philosophical one. Bayesian inference essentially tells us how a rational agent should update their belief in light of new experience. “Should” equates to being rational. It is not equivalent to how human beings actually update their beliefs. Indeed, much psychological research has been conducted on human subjects to demonstrate that human beings are far from being Bayesian.

As one might imagine, this idea has made Bayes central to not only statistics, but also other areas where the study of rational behavior is of primary interest. The application of Bayes’ theorem, whether formal or informal, is a way of being “intelligent” about updating one’s belief. Game theory, psychology of beliefs, economic theory, etc., are all areas that, in the end, study human behavior. Sub-specialties of these domains have interests in learning whether human beings update their beliefs in correspondence with what Bayesian theory would prescribe. The Bayes estimator tells us which action to take, if acting rationally, to minimize the risk of making a wrong decision. Maximizing expectation, however, is not always equivalent to maximizing utility, and hence Bayesian decision theory will often have us maximize the latter instead of the former, except if the problem is relatively simple and both expectation and utility coincide. Utility, simply put, is a measure of how beneficial this or that action is to the agent, not simply evaluated based on probability or mathematical expectation. Not buying that overpriced post-pandemic McDonald’s hamburger may maximize budgeting constraints, but buying it because it tastes so good maximizes utility. A fiscally poor and irrational choice, but has much utility for the buyer and thus becomes rational from that perspective. Utility theory is a fascinating area of investigation. For an excellent discussion, consult Winkler (2003).

While Bayes’ theorem is generally useful, it should be remarked that it could introduce bias and discrimination into the process of updating belief. For example, the high probability of a black person committing a crime may be justified by reference to Bayes’ theorem because for a given crime, past crimes may have featured a disproportionate number of blacks, causing the prior probability to skyrocket. Bayes’ theorem is rational updating of belief, but it may be considered discrimination to use it in this particular context. Likewise, the probability of a mass in a dog being cancerous may be high upon application of Bayes’ theorem, given the age and breed of the dog. While Bayes’ theorem is doing its work, it can also be terrifying that a dog is put down because of their breed and without the result of a biopsy. The prior probability makes a cancer diagnosis more likely, perhaps even highly probable, but if it’s a decision of life vs. death for the dog, putting the dog down on the “gamble” that it is cancer is an unwise action. The cost of making an error in this regard may be too high, even if the posterior probability is exceedingly high. Bayes theorem can only estimate the probability of the theory; it cannot, by itself, tell you how to act, nor is a posterior probability ever equal to unity in most real-world applications. Further, it must always be remembered that we do not know anything about the current event; we only know about past events, and the prior probability in Bayes’ theorem, even if estimated correctly, is not about the current event under consideration. Calculate Bayes’ theorem with reckless abandon, but use, and most importantly 75interpret Bayes’ theorem with caution . As a result of the prior probability potentially having an overwhelming influence on the posterior, work has been done on what are called noninformative priors (Bishop, 2006), which, as the name suggests, attempts to reduce the influence of the prior.

We will revisit Bayes’ theorem often in this book, such as when determining the optimal decision boundary when discussing discriminant analysis, or when considering Naïve Bayes as a nonparametric alternative to classification. The idea of including prior information in a model is not new and can be witnessed throughout statistics and science, as well as more modernly with machine learning. For instance, a new paradigm in machine learning called physics-informed machine learning has the goal of informing machine learning models using physically relevant prior information (Pateras et al., 2023). That is, the model or algorithm is “informed” by prior knowledge of the object or system that is being modeled.

2.11 Law of Large Numbers

The law of large numbers is a fundamental law in statistics that in words essentially says the larger the sample size, the closer one gets to the true probability of an event. As a simple example, getting 9 heads out of 10 trials yields an estimate of the probability of heads equal to 9/10 = 0.90. The estimate of the probability of heads is not that great in this instance because it is based on only a few observations, that is, a relatively small sample. As sample size n increases, the approximation gets better, until in the limit as n→∞, the true probability is known. The limit, in this case, infinity ∞, is never achieved. The true probability, at least in this frequentist perspective, will never be known. All we really have are estimates. The bigger the sample size, in general, the better the estimate.

The law can be formalized as follows for the case of the sample mean $\overline{y}$ when used as an estimator of the population mean, μ: for any ε > 0, the probability of any deviation of the kind $\overline{y} - \mu$ goes to 0 as n increases, eventually without bound, that is, n→∞. Alternatively, we could express the same thing by saying for any |ε|>0, the probability that $\overline{y} - \mu$ is between  − ε and ε goes to 0 as n→∞. Incidentally, it is worth noting that infinity, ∞, is not regarded as a number in mathematics, but is simply a concept. The symbol for positive infinity in R is Inf.

The law stems from a relative-frequency interpretation of probability and more pragmatically means that if you want to know the true probability of an event, the more data you collect, in general, the better your estimate of that probability. Note that this does not necessarily imply that collecting more data is always advisable. A million data points can do no worse than a thousand, unless of course the cost of collecting such extra observations is prohibitive and one can conclude about just as much knowledge from the initial sample of a thousand than the million. While the law of large numbers wants us to collect more data, it is a theoretical argument only. It may not be practical in reality. That thing we call the “real world” and is the unpleasant distraction from the theoretical mathematician often interferes with our capacity to collect more data and if the identical conclusion can be drawn with lesser data points, then collecting more data may simply be a waste of time and resources. Limiting theorems such as the above are attractive, but we must not get lost in their beauty at the expense of practical, real-world considerations.

An implication of the above is that statistical power curves tend to asymptote (horizontally) as sample size increases, and hence the cost of collecting more data may simply not be worth it. In the age of big data and the facility by which large data sets can be collected, these truths still hold, but since collecting data can be done rather cheaply these days in many contexts, such costs are unlikely to deter businesses such as Amazon from collecting terabytes of data and hence ignore power curves altogether. When “Big Data” is available, power curves are left in the wind. In such contexts, data is far too easy to come by to be concerned with power curves.

However, in other settings, such as smaller experimental ones where collecting data may be very difficult and vastly expensive, establishing just how much information is needed to draw 76conclusions is a very worthwhile activity. For example, if your units of observation consist of children with a particular rare disorder, each single data point may be extremely difficult to collect and the difference between 20 and 25 observations may be a huge undertaking. Collecting data may be prohibitively expensive. The development of small-sample statistics in the early 1900s made it possible to study populations without having to sample huge numbers. This was the gift of inferential statistics. We seem to be coming full circle in the current climate where collecting bigger data sets is the norm in some areas (definitely not all), mostly due to the facility by which such data can be collected (i.e., electronically) and easily stored. Early inferential statistical procedures were originally designed to circumvent this activity and make the most out of small data. Will the age of “small data” ever return? Let’s imagine what that might look like in the following fictional academic news report headline:

An amazing new quantitative technology is being popularized for which one only requires very small samples to make generalizations to much wider populations. We call this new age of data analysis, SDA, or “Small Data Analysis.”

Increasing sample size can also have an influence on Bayesian posteriors. For example, in choosing a model, for small sample size, a posterior may indicate one model, whereas as sample size grows, a competing model may have a higher posterior due to the increase in information. Weak vs. strong laws of large numbers can also be distinguished though not discussed here. For details, see Shao (2023) for a clear but relatively theoretical discussion. Casella and Berger (2002) also feature a discussion (p. 235).

2.11.1 Law of Large Numbers and the Idea of Committee Machines

One indirect application of the law of large numbers that we will revisit later in the book is contained in the idea that average prediction functions converge to expected prediction functions. For instance, ten prediction functions, when averaged, get us closer to the true expected (i.e., in terms of long-run probability) prediction function than any of the single prediction functions. That is, when we combine many weak learners, we often achieve better predictions than the capacity of any of the weak learners that make up the combination.

An analogy to sports would be that a team of weak players produces a better outcome than any of the individual teammates. Indirectly, the law of averages is present in this statement, since it implies that the greater the n, where “n” in this case is the number of prediction functions (players), the better we will converge to the true function. This idea of combining so-called “weak learners” to produce a stronger learner generally falls under the general category of committee machines.

2.12 Random Variables and Probability Density Functions

A random variable is a mathematical variable that is associated with a probability distribution. More precisely, a random variable is a function from a sample space into the real numbers (Casella & Berger, 2002) such that for any “slice” or interval, that is, for any subset of the sample space is called an event. The function must as well be measurable (Mohri et al., 2018) though measurability of functions is well beyond the scope of the current text. We simply make mention of the word “measurability” here to denote the fact that not all functions are measurable, and hence saying that random variables are a function onto the real numbers is incomplete. Deeper and more sophisticated definitions of a random variable will first distinguish between measurable versus nonmeasurable functions (e.g., see Shao, 2023).77

As an example of a random variable, consider the variable xi having values 0, 1, 2, 3. The variable xi, as it currently stands, is often called a mathematical variable. The descriptor “mathematical” is usually implicit, but such a variable may often be called such in a statistics text simply to distinguish it from a random variable. As the reader will recall, it is a variable because xi can take on different values in the set. If xi could only take on a single value (e.g., 0 or any other value), it would not be a variable but instead would be a constant. It becomes a random variable when we associate probabilities with those values in the set such that they sum to unity. For instance, the aforementioned xi is now a random variable in the table below, where each value of xi is now associated with a probability of 0.25:

xi p(xi)

0

0.25

1

0.25

2

0.25

3

0.25

∑ = 1.0

Note that there is no requirement that probabilities be equal across values of xi for xi to be a random variable. The only requirement is that the sum of probabilities is equal to 1.0. That is, we could have just as easily distributed the probabilities as 0.20, 0.40, 0.30, and 0.10 to illustrate the concept.

2.13 Convergence of Random Variables

Where a random variable “is going” is often of theoretical interest. That is, we often would like to know what value a random variable converges to in the limit. As sample size increases without bound to infinity, that is, n→∞, we would like to know properties of this convergence.

We say a sequence of random variables converges in probability to a random variable x if:


$$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}p\left\lbrack \middle| x_{n} - x \middle| \geq \varepsilon \right\rbrack = 0$$
(2.19)

In passing, note we have used the word infinity above, and do so as well in other places in the book. And while it seems convenient to use it and the spirit of what is meant by statements such as n→∞ is quite easily understood, the concept of infinity itself is quite rich historically and comes with it many philosophical difficulties and challenges, many of which are still ongoing today. Our inclusion of it in no way is meant to trivialize the depth of the object. Indeed, a dissertation with the title The History and Theory of Infinity in Philosophy and Mathematics would be no easy undertaking! Some hold that concepts of infinity, coupled with abstraction and proof, open the gateway to advanced mathematics (Stillwell, 2016). Make no mistake as well, by our mention of philosophy of mathematics, we are in no way meaning to communicate anything less than extremely rigorous. An in-depth study of infinity would not only require deeper mathematics, but also deeper philosophy. Whether such philosophy utilizes symbols (as does mathematics) has no bearing on the depth required to investigate such a topic.

2.14 Probability Density Functions

A probability density function is a function f that is associated with a continuous random variable x and that integrates to one:78


p(a≤x≤b) = ∫abf(x)dx = 1

The probability of any particular value in a continuous probability density has a limiting value equal to 0. That is, p(x=xi) = 0. Continuity is defined very precisely and rigorously in mathematics using epsilon-delta definitions; however, intuitively, continuity can be thought of as drawing a curve without lifting one’s pencil from the page. Because it is a probability density function, its CDF is also regarded as absolutely continuous, where absolute continuity implies, among other things, that we can integrate for all values of a, b. The distinction here between absolutely continuous vs. simply continuous has no bearing on the work we do in the current book. However, to the real analyst in mathematics, such a distinction is very important.

At first consideration, this may seem like an odd result. How can any particular value in a continuous distribution have (limiting) probability equal to 0? To make this more intuitive, consider the probability between any two particular values, a and b, to equal a number greater than 0. As the distance a − b decreases, the probability of that interval gets smaller and smaller, until in the limit the distance a − b is such a thin slice that the probability of that thin slice is, theoretically, equal to 0. Numerically, one can think of this as the impossibility of grabbing hold of a number with an infinite number of decimals; only an interval of numbers can be seized; any particular number in that interval is elusive. One can also liken the idea to that of Zeno’s paradox, in which as one approaches an object, the distances are continuously “halved” on route to that object, until one gets so close to that object that the distance between the person and the object has a limiting value of zero.

If the probability distribution is of a discrete rather than a continuous variable, then it usually goes by the name of a probability mass function. In such distributions, we can assign a positive probability of a given value of the random variable, p(x=xi) ≠ 0, unless of course the probability of a particular value of x is, in actuality, zero. The point, however, is that the probability of any particular value does not need to be zero as was the case for a continuous distribution. In a discrete distribution, we can assign probabilities to specific events. In a continuous distribution, we can only assign probabilities to intervals. That is, in a continuous density, the “events” are, in actuality, the interval “cuts” along the real line.

An example of a discrete vs. continuous probability distribution is given in Figure 2.3.79

2.15 Normal (Gaussian) Distributions

Normal distributions and densities in statistics are everywhere. They are often called “Gaussian” because of their innovator, Friedrich Gauss. Not only do many physical phenomena approximate normality, but assuming normality theoretically provides a great deal of convenience in deriving new statistics and sampling distributions. Normality of a single variable is referred to as univariate normality, for two variables is bivariate normality, and for greater than two, multivariate normality. We survey each of these densities below.

2.15.1 Univariate Gaussian

The univariate normal density is given by


$$f\left( x \right) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{- {(x - \mu)}^{2}/2\sigma^{2}}$$
(2.20)

There are two parameters in the univariate density, that of μ and σ2, where x is simply the “input” value and π and e are constants. The density (or crudely, “area”) under the normal distribution integrates to 1,


$$\int\limits_{- \infty}^{\infty}{N\left( x \middle| \mu,\sigma^{2} \right)dx = 1}$$

If we set μ = 0 and σ2 = 1, the normal density is called the standard normal density and is the classic z-distribution that appears at the back of most introductory statistics texts and serves to reveal various areas (proportions) under the curve. Having a single “standard” distribution to refer to provides a single “scale” from which other distributions with different μ and σ2 can be transformed via z-scores. When we compute a z-score,


$$z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$$
(2.21)

we are transforming the given distribution to have a mean equal to 0 and standard deviation equal to 1 where (x−μ)2/σ2 = (x−μ)(σ2) − 1(x−μ). Hence, for a given μ and σ2, the “action” of the univariate density is a function of its exponent. If we take the reciprocal of σ2, that is, 1/σ2,we obtain the precision of the distribution (Bishop, 2006, p. 24). As we will see later, writing the exponent in the way of (x−μ)(σ2) − 1(x−μ) will translate nicely in going from univariate to multivariate dimensions.

The transformation to z is an example of a linear transformation (the meaning of which we review shortly). It being an example of a linear transformation means that conversion to z does not change the shape of the distribution of the original data. This is very important! At first glance it can seem that conversion to z should normalize a distribution and hence give it a normal shape. But this intuition is incorrect and is a perfect example where what one feels should be correct is, in actuality, not. Intuition in mathematics and statistics can be a boon but at times a dangerous thing which is why proofs are usually required before a statement is considered true.80

2.15.2 Mixtures of Gaussians

Mixture models are those that combine different distributions, typically linearly, at arriving at a probability estimate. Oftentimes those individual distributions are Gaussian, and hence Gaussian mixture models are quite common. We write a mixture of Gaussians as


$$p\left( x \right) = {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{K}\pi_{k}}N\left( x \middle| \mu_{k},\Sigma_{k} \right)$$
(2.22)

The components k = 1 through K of a mixture model are the different k distributions that are “mixed” into a single distribution, each having its own mean μ and covariance matrix ∑ and where π is the mixing parameter or “weight” applied for each distribution. Combined, we wish to model the probability of x, p(x). The sum of mixing proportions must equal 1, that is, ${\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{K}\pi_{k}} = 1$ and where 0 ≤ πk ≤ 1. We can also impose equality constraints in a mixture distribution such that certain parameters are set to be equal across distributions, such as that of equal covariance matrices in a multivariate setting (Goodfellow et al., 2016).

A Gaussian mixture model is a universal approximator, which, as we will see when we survey neural networks, implies that any smooth function (or density) can be approximated to any small degree of error given enough components (Goodfellow et al., 2016). Hence, given enough mixtures of distributions, function approximation becomes a certainty just as with neural networks; if we are given enough hidden layers and nodes, they too become universal approximators. Mixture models, as we will see, are also useful in methods ranging from random effects models to cluster analysis to neural networks and beyond and are much more general than simply mixing normal densities. Our example here is of normal densities only for the reason that we are currently surveying the normal distribution. Mixtures for discrete variables, for instance, might include mixing Bernoulli distributions (Bishop, 2006).

2.15.3 Evaluating Univariate Normality

Many methods and techniques have been proposed for evaluating the normality of distributions. Perhaps the most useful are simple graphical and visualization techniques; however, inferential methods exist as well to estimate how likely it is the current sample distribution was selected from a population distribution that is normal. Tests for univariate normality include the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Shapiro-Wilk test, the Anderson-Darling test, and many others. According to Bilodeau and Brenner (1999), the Shapiro-Wilk test has been found to be the best omnibus test. We assume the reader has some experience with interpreting these tests, especially the Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Shapiro-Wilk tests. Further details can be found in Denis (2021a).

We can demonstrate the Shapiro-Wilk test very easily in R:

> shapiro.test(rnorm(100, mean = 5, sd = 3))
  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
data: rnorm(100, mean = 5, sd = 3)
W = 0.99085, p-value = 0.7331

The null hypothesis is that the population from which the sample data were drawn is normally distributed. Since the p-value is not even close to a traditional cut-off, such as p < 0.05 (p = 0.7331), we do not have evidence to reject the null. Note that this in no way confirms the population to be normal, but it does not give us evidence to suggest it is not normal.81

There are many ways and packages available for plotting all kinds of densities in R. For example, we can easily obtain a plot of the normal distribution in R by the following (Figure 2.4):

> x <- seq(-3, 3, length = 100)
> y <- dnorm(x)
>plot(y)

2.15.4 Multivariate Gaussian

As we have just seen, in the univariate density,


$$f\left( x \right) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{- {(x - \mu)}^{2}/2\sigma^{2}}$$

the exponent featured  − (x−μ)2/2σ2. When we generalize the univariate Gaussian to the multivariate setting, we replace observations x with vectors x, μ with μ, and individual variances, σ2 with covariance matrices Σ:


$$f\left( x \right) = \frac{1}{\left. \left( \sqrt{2\pi} \right)^{p} \middle| \sum \right|^{1/2}}e^{- (x - \mu)'\Sigma^{- 1}(x - \mu)/2}$$
(2.23)

For μ = 0 and Σ = σ2I, where σ2 = 1, this is the parallel setting for the standard normal distribution with μ = 0 and σ2 = 1, where now I is the identity matrix. But how exactly is Σ = σ2I the analogous condition to σ2 = 1? Recall that when Σ = I, this means that all values along the main diagonal are equal to 1 and all elsewhere is equal to 0 indicating that there is zero pairwise covariance between all variables. This implies that all variances in the multivariate density for Σ = I are equal to σ2, where σ2 = 1 in this case, just as σ2 = 1 is true for the univariate density under a standard normal distribution.

We can easily compare respective univariate and multivariate densities. In the univariate density, note that the density begins with82


$$\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}$$

In the multivariate setting, this is generalized to


$$\frac{1}{\left. \left( \sqrt{2\pi} \right)^{p} \middle| \sum \right|^{1/2}}$$

and now reflects volume as opposed to area as was the case in the univariate setting due to the now multidimensional space occupied by the multivariate density. The reason why it reflects volume instead of area is because we are now working in greater than two dimensions (i.e., think of a cube or cuboid, for example, instead of a square). The univariate distribution is often referred to as a one-dimensional distribution statistically, but such refers to the number of variables being studied, which is one. On paper, geometrically, the distribution occurs in two dimensions.

But what of the bivariate density? The bivariate density is simply a special case of the multivariate density for the case of two variables and hence, we find it more convenient to simply regard it as a multivariate density. However, it can also be written in the following form:


$$f\left( x_{1},x_{2} \right) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{1}{\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\left( 1 - \rho^{2} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}\exp\left\{ {- \frac{1}{2\left( 1 - \rho^{2} \right)}\left\lbrack {\left\lbrack \frac{x_{1} - \mu_{1}}{\sigma_{1}} \right\rbrack^{2} - 2\rho\left\lbrack \frac{x_{1} - \mu_{1}}{\sigma_{1}} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack \frac{x_{2} - \mu_{2}}{\sigma_{2}} \right\rbrack + \left\lbrack \frac{x_{2} - \mu_{2}}{\sigma_{2}} \right\rbrack^{2}} \right\rbrack} \right\}$$
(2.24)

where ρ2 is the squared correlation between variables x1 and x2. For further details on the bivariate density, see Johnson and Wichern (2007, p. 151).

The multivariate density is significant for many reasons, most of which parallel the reasons for the popularity of the univariate density in statistics and science more generally. However, there is an added feature of importance as regards the multivariate density, and that is, if we can assume multivariate normality, we can be assured that any linear combination of the random vector X is also normally distributed. While this may seem like an intuitive result, it has huge implications for statistical inference in multivariate models. The theorem also implies that conditional distributions will be multivariate normal as well.

2.15.5 Evaluating Multivariate Normality

Assessing multivariate normality is exponentially more difficult than assessing univariate normality due to it being a higher-dimensional problem. The best advice for such evaluation is probably given by Johnson and Wichern (2007, p. 177):

It will become clear that our investigations of normality will concentrate on the behavior of the observations in one or two dimensions (for example, marginal distributions and scatter plots). As might be expected, it has proved difficult to construct a “good” overall test of joint normality in more than two dimensions because of the large number of things that can go wrong. To some extent, we must pay a price for concentrating on univariate and bivariate examinations of normality: We can never be sure that we have not missed some feature that is revealed only in higher dimensions … for most practical work, one-dimensional and two-dimensional investigations are ordinarily sufficient. Fortunately, pathological data sets that are normal in lower dimensional representations, but nonnormal in higher dimensions, are not frequently encountered in practice.83

Still, there are tests that can be used to evaluate normality, even in the multivariate domain. A generalization of the Shapiro-Wilk test can be used, as well as a more recent test called the Henze-Zirkler test. See Zhou and Shao (2014) for details. The consequence of not ensuring multivariate normality is that the asymptotic distribution of many statistical tests becomes much more complicated (Bilodeau & Brenner, 1999). Recall that the asymptotic distribution is that obtained as n→∞.

In practice, researchers often use visualization and graphical techniques to verify univariate (e.g., Q-Q plots, histograms, etc.) and bivariate normality (e.g., scatterplots), and if such are more or less approximately satisfied, they then make the inferential “leap” to assuming that multivariate normality holds as well. However, it needs to be emphasized that while multivariate normality implies bivariate and univariate normality, the reverse is not necessarily true. That is, univariate and bivariate normality does not automatically imply multivariate normality. Hence the aforementioned “leap” required. Univariate and bivariate normality may increase the probability of multivariate normality, but it does not necessarily imply it.

2.16 Binomial Distributions

When a variable has a binary outcome, such as pass vs. fail, and whose probability of a success is constant or stationary over a series of trials, the binomial distribution is a plausible distribution for modeling such data. A random variable x is binomially distributed if x can take on one of two binary-valued numbers. For convenience, we denote these numbers 0 and 1; however in theory they could be any two numbers. We assume that 1 occurs with probability π and 0 occurs with probability 1 − π, where of course π is bound by limits 0 and 1 as is true of all probabilities.

The binomial density is given by


$$p\left( x;n,\pi \right) = \frac{n!}{x!\left( n - x \right)!}\pi^{x}\left( 1 - \pi \right)^{n - x}$$
(2.25)

where x is the number of outcomes that we are modeling, n is the total number of trials, and π is the probability of a success on any given trial. A classic example of the binomial in practice is modeling the probability of getting 2 heads out of 5 flips on a fair coin (i.e., where “fair” implies π = 0.5). This probability is easily computed,


$$\begin{array}{l} {\,\, p\left( x;n,\pi \right) = \frac{n!}{x!\left( n - x \right)!}\pi^{x}\left( 1 - \pi \right){n - x}} \\ {p\left( 2;5,0.5 \right) = \frac{5!}{2!\left( 5 - 2 \right)!}\left( 0.5 \right)2\left( 1 - 0.5 \right){5 - 2}} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = 0.3125} \\ \end{array}$$

Knowing that the probability of getting 2 heads out of 5 flips of a fair coin is equal to 0.3125, or about 31% of the time, such can help us evaluate the null hypothesis that a given coin is fair. Surely, if the coin is producing 2 heads out of 5 flips, this would give us no reason to suspect the coin is not fair. On the other hand, had the coin produced, say, 0 heads out of 5 flips, such would have yielded a probability of 0.03125. That is, the probability of getting zero heads out of five flips on a fair coin is quite low. It is so low that it might suggest we reject the null hypothesis that the coin is fair and infer the alternative that it is not, or at minimum, that the probability of heads is not equal to 0.5.84

We can compute binomial probabilities very easily in R. For the case of 2 heads out of 5 flips with a stationary success set at 0.5, the probability is computed as

> dbinom(2, 5, 0.5)
[1] 0.3125

The mean of a binomial distribution is nπ, that is, the number of trials multiplied by the probability of success on any given trial. For the above data, this number is 5(0.5) = 2.5. That is, on 5 flips, we would expect an average of 2.5 heads. Of course, since the variable is a discrete one, this interpretation should be made with caution as it is not possible to obtain “fractions” of heads. Recall that averages do not care about fractions. The mean number of persons per household may very well be 3.4, impossible as this number is for human beings (or any discrete objects, for that matter).

The variance of a binomial random variable is equal to nπ(1−π). For example, the variance of a binomial distribution with probability π = 0.5, and as before n = 5, is equal to nπ(1−π) = 5(0.5)(1−0.5) = 2.5(0.5) = 1.25, with standard deviation (square root) equal to 1.118.

2.16.1 Approximation to the Normal Distribution

The binomial distribution approximates the normal distribution for large number of trials, and in the limit, converges to the normal distribution. We can easily demonstrate in R how increasing n approximates normality via the plots in Figure 2.5.

Notice that as n increases for the same probability p = 0.5, the distribution increasingly resembles a smooth normal distribution. This is just one example, and perhaps the simplest and easiest to demonstrate, of how virtually all distributions in statistics are related. Many distributions converge to others under sufficient conditions. The Poisson distribution, to be surveyed shortly, in the limit converges to the normal distribution as well.

2.17 Multinomial Distributions

The binomial distribution just surveyed is actually a special case of the more general multinomial distribution:85


$$p\left( x_{1},...,x_{k} \right) = \frac{n!}{x_{1}!x_{2}!...x_{k}{}_{!}}\pi_{1}^{x_{1}}\pi_{2}^{x_{2}}...\pi_{k}^{x_{k}}$$
(2.26)

where now π1x1π2x2...πkxk are the different probabilities associated with individual events x1, x2,xk. That is, instead of having only two possibilities on the discrete variable (binomial), the variable now has several possibilities, each having their own respective probabilities, π1, π2, … πk.

2.18 Poisson Distributions

The Poisson density is given by


$$p\left( x/\mu \right) = \frac{e^{- \mu}\mu^{x}}{x!}$$
(2.27)

where e is a constant and x is the number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time. The expectation (i.e., mean) of the Poisson density and that of its variance are both equal to μ. For further details on the Poisson density, see Casella and Berger (2002, p. 92).

2.19 Chi-Square Distributions

The chi-square density is given by


$$f\left( x \right) = \frac{1}{2^{v/2}\Gamma\left( v/2 \right)}x^{\lbrack(v/2) - 1\rbrack}e^{- x/2}$$
(2.28)

where Γ is the gamma function and v are the degrees of freedom of the density. The chi-square distribution of a random variable is equal to the sum of squares of n independent and normally distributed z-scores (see Fisher, 1922 for details):


$$\chi_{n}^{2} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}z_{i}^{2}} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\frac{\left( x_{i} - \mu \right)^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}}$$

A final thought on statistical distributions and densities. Not surprisingly, there are many more than we have highlighted here in our brief review. Most times, the type of problem you are modeling will quite naturally dictate or strongly suggest the density you should use to model the given phenomenon. The key is recognizing from the problem you are facing which statistical distribution might be most appropriate. Such insight can be difficult and often depends on relying on one’s experience or expertise in the given substantive area. It is not unusual, however, for an analyst to spend some time contemplating which density would be best in modeling this or that phenomenon, especially when the problem is difficult.

2.20 Expectation and Expected Value

When we talk about “expectation” in statistics, we are generally referring to the long-run average behavior of a random variable. Since we are dealing with a random variable, this idea necessarily invokes and implies the probability concept. The expected value of a function g is the sum (or 86integral) of that function multiplied by its corresponding probability, for a continuous random variable,


$$E_{X}\left\lbrack g\left( x \right) \right\rbrack = {\int\limits_{x}{g\left( x \right)p\left( x \right)dx}}$$
(2.29)

For a discrete random variable, the expectation is


$$E_{X}\left\lbrack g\left( x \right) \right\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{x}{g\left( x \right)p\left( x \right)}}$$
(2.30)

The expectation for a discrete variable is different from that of a continuous variable since, with a discrete one, we can assign individual probabilities to values of the variable and sum up products, g(x)p(x). With a continuous variable, products are technically also summed, but they require integral calculus to do the summation and not simply sigma as in the discrete case.

We can compute expected values of single random variables as above, but we can also compute expected values of elements of vectors and matrices as well. The expectation of a random matrix is the expectation of each of its random variables,


$$E\left( X \right) = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} {E\left( x_{11} \right)\,\,\,\,\, E\left( x_{12} \right)\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \cdot \cdot \,\,\,\,\, E\left( x_{1}{}_{p} \right)} \\ {E\left( x_{21} \right)\,\,\,\,\, E\left( x_{22} \right)\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \cdot \cdot \,\,\,\,\, E\left( x_{2}{}_{p} \right)} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, \cdot} \\ {E\left( x_{n1} \right)\,\,\,\,\, E\left( x_{n2} \right)\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \cdot \cdot \,\,\,\,\, E\left( x_{n}{}_{p} \right)} \\ \end{array} \right\rbrack$$
(2.31)

Since E(x11) through to E(xnp) is equal to μ11 to μnp, we can write:


$$E\left( X \right) = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} {E\left( x_{11} \right)\,\,\,\,\, E\left( x_{12} \right)\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \cdot \cdot \,\,\,\,\, E\left( x_{1}{}_{p} \right)} \\ {E\left( x_{21} \right)\,\,\,\,\, E\left( x_{22} \right)\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \cdot \cdot \,\,\,\,\, E\left( x_{2}{}_{p} \right)} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, \cdot} \\ {E\left( x_{n1} \right)\,\,\,\,\, E\left( x_{n2} \right)\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \cdot \cdot \,\,\,\,\, E\left( x_{n}{}_{p} \right)} \\ \end{array} \right\rbrack = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} {\mu_{11}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\mu_{12}\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \cdot \cdot \,\,\,\,\,\mu_{1}{}_{p}} \\ {\mu_{21}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\mu_{22}\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \cdot \cdot \,\,\,\,\,\mu_{2}{}_{p}} \\ {\,\,\,\, \cdot \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, \cdot} \\ {\mu_{n1}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\mu_{n2}\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \cdot \cdot \,\,\,\,\,\mu_{n}{}_{p}} \\ \end{array} \right\rbrack$$
(2.32)

2.21 Measures of Central Tendency

Observing every data point in a data set, especially for large data sets, provides a weak summary of that data and we usually wish instead to summarize the data with one or two measures that, in some sense, “represent” the data. We emphasize “in some sense,” because no single measure could ever summarize any data perfectly. To understand what central tendency means with regard to a particular measure used, one must understand in some depth the measure, that is, the abstract “idea” of what central tendency might mean. Of course, if the data set consists of only say, 2–3 data points, then inspecting the data set point by point is well advised and it makes little sense in trying to reduce such data into a smaller set of summary statistics. Usually, however, our data sets are medium-sized to very large, and graphical or numerical summaries are required in getting to know our data.

Measures of central tendency are data reduction measures; they take a set of observations and reduce such data down to a single measure.87

2.21.1 The Arithmetic Mean (Average)

The arithmetic mean is without question the most popular measure of central tendency. The arithmetic mean is given by


$$\overline{x} = \frac{1}{n}{\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{N}x_{n}}$$
(2.33)

Note that the arithmetic average consists of summing all observations, and then dividing by how many numbers went into that sum. Hence, the mean is often regarded as the center of gravity in a distribution. Since it is the center of gravity, it is also true that the sum of deviations from the mean is equal to 0; that is,


$$\left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( x_{i} - \overline{x} \right.} \right) = 0$$
(2.34)

The fact that deviations from the mean sum to zero is one reason why such deviations are typically squared (or absolute values taken under some circumstances) when producing the variance or standard deviation.

For a random variable, the mean is given by


μ = ∫ − ∞ + ∞xf(x)dx
(2.35)

where x will denote a specific value of the variable and f(x) is the density under the curve for that value, and for discrete random variables,


$$\mu = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}x}p\left( x \right)$$
(2.36)

where p(x) will be the probability of the specific value x since with discrete random variables we can assign an individual probability to x, whereas with continuous variables recall, we cannot.

The arithmetic mean is only one of many means that can be computed on a set of data. Other means include the geometric mean and the harmonic mean. The geometric mean is given by


$${\overline{x}}_{g} = \left( {\prod\limits_{i = 1}^{n}x_{i}} \right)^{\frac{1}{n}} = \sqrt[n]{x_{1} \cdot x_{2} \cdot \cdot \cdot x_{n}}$$
(2.37)

Note that in the geometric mean, we are taking products of values (via the product operator, $\prod\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{}$) instead of sums as in the arithmetic mean and taking the root equal to the number of observations n (i.e., 1/n).

The harmonic mean is given by88


$${\overline{x}}_{h} = \frac{n}{\frac{1}{x_{1}} + \frac{1}{x_{2}} + \cdot \cdot \cdot \frac{1}{x_{n}}} = \frac{n}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\frac{1}{x_{i}}}$$
(2.38)

The important point is that when someone reports computing the mean on a set of data, be sure to inquire which mean is being computed. Typically, when the word “mean” is used, it refers to the arithmetic mean, but not always. In the reporting of scientific research, it would be irresponsible of a researcher to not specify which mean is being reported if it were not the arithmetic mean. Further, though the arithmetic mean is often advertised as a measure of central tendency, it only reveals the center of a distribution in the sense of $\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{\left( {x_{i} - \overline{x}} \right) = 0}$, and in no other sense. In a perfectly normal distribution, the mean will be at the center of the distribution with symmetrical and equal areas on each side of the distribution. In a skewed distribution, however, the mean will no longer be at the “center” of the distribution and will simply fall where the condition $\left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( x_{i} - \overline{x} \right.} \right) = 0$ is satisfied. For example, consider the location of the arithmetic mean in the distribution in Figure 2.6.

Note that the mean is not at the center of the distribution, however it is still defined as a measure of “central tendency.” If you memorize “mean = central tendency,” you will never truly understand the mean! The only way to understand it is to inspect its structure and appreciate what it actually does. This is true of all equations and formulas in statistics and machine learning. Never rely on “verbal” definitions to describe them; only their equations and formulas reveal what they actually accomplish.

It is a good computing exercise to compute the mean the “long way” in R or Python (try devising a function to generate the mean). In Python, we can easily compute the mean by using numpy.mean():89

import numpy as np
x = [10, 20, 30]
np.mean(x)
Out[56]: 20.0

The mean of the observations 10, 20, and 30 is, not surprisingly, equal to 20.

2.21.1.1 Averaging Over Cases: Why Thinking in Terms of Averages Can Be Dangerous

Means and averages are much more than about the above computations. Though averaging incorporates all deviations from a center point, it simultaneously ignores individual information. If averaging is held as a policy to govern by, then it will naturally and necessarily ignore important individual cases. The “spirit” of an average need not be numerical either; it can be entirely conceptual as the following example illustrates.

Consider the case of canine vaccines. Many states require all dogs to be vaccinated routinely every one to three years. However, there is increasing evidence, some published, and some based on clinical observation and experience, that over-vaccinating may have detrimental health effects. If this is the case, then why have a blanket policy of vaccinating all dogs every one to three years? The answer is an easy one, because of convenience and a lack of attention paid to each particular case. Since the goal of vaccination is to not only protect any individual dog but also to offer protection to all human beings, the policy of vaccination is very general. But this greatly ignores individual cases. Not all dogs are the same and not all dogs have the same behavior patterns. For the dog whose owner doesn’t know where the dog is at 11 p.m. as the dog roams about the neighborhood searching for mischief and wrestling with potentially rabid foxes and raccoons, the one-to-three-year vaccination policy is a good one! However, for the dog who is primarily an “inside dog” who goes outside only periodically and is in virtually no danger of contracting the disease due to hypervigilant supervision by his owner, the one-to-three-year policy is overkill for that particular dog. Averaging makes things “easy” and allows a blanket policy, and essentially discriminates against cases that do not “fit” into requiring the policy. The law says your 11-year-old senior dog requires vaccination, yet science may suggest doing so is a bad idea because the dog is elderly, has medical conditions, and in all probability the prior vaccination is probably still providing immunity (a titer test for immunity may be a better option). Given such risk factors, vaccinating again would be somewhat reckless, yet by the “easy” and convenient policy of averages, the law often does not take into account these individual cases.

The moral of the story is that while thinking (and computing) in terms of averages can be productive, it can also be very dangerous. Individual case analysis is almost always better, despite how more expensive and time-consuming such an analysis may be. Means and averages are balance points, yet often, “balancing” should not be of primary interest. Case studies and more focused analysis should be the priority when the data, resources, and time allow it. Indeed, this is one criticism against numerical “summative” statistical research in general, that it focuses too heavily on the common person rather than the individual person. In clinical settings, case studies will typically do away with averages and instead focus on the individual.

Averages can also be dangerous when it comes to interpreting data. For instance, our interpretation of the mean implicitly assumes linear interpolation between values. For example, consider the mean of two numbers, 2 and 4. The mean is, of course, 3. Denoting 3 as the “center of mass” assumes that the distance and importance between 2 and 3 and 3 to 4 is the same, which in this case is linear. Linear interpolation, in general, can be risky because the intermediate values may not be 90linear, but are often assumed to be out of convenience. This is a simple idea but can have drastic and important consequences when interpreting real data.

2.21.2 The Median

Another measure of central tendency is that of the median. The median is the data point that divides the ordered data set into exactly two equal parts. The computation of the median will depend on how many observations are in the data set. For instance, if n is odd, then the location of the median ỹ is equal to (n+1)/2, yielding a median value equal to


$$\widetilde{y} = y_{(\frac{n + 1}{2})}$$
(2.39)

If n is even, then the location of the median is between (n/2) and (n/2) + 1, yielding a median of


ỹ = [[yn/2]+[y(n/2)+1]]/2
(2.40)

While means can be said to be sensitive to extreme observations, medians are not. Medians, and other median-like statistics (such as quartiles), are said to be robust to extreme or outlying observations. Because medians only consider the “middle” value of the distribution, one can easily change other values in the data set while still retaining the same median. For example, the median of the data set 9, 10, 11 is 10, while the median of the data set 9, 10, 100 is also equal to 10. If a researcher reports the median of their data, ask to see a plot! Resist engaging in the cognitive bias that the median (or the mean, for that matter) implies a normal distribution. “Normality” is a theoretical notion. Empirical normality never truly exists; it can only be approximated by the theoretical ideal, that is, by the mathematical definition of a normal density.

Recall that the arithmetic mean is not robust to extreme scores or outliers. That is, since the mean is a weighted sum of deviations, even changing one value in the distribution will alter the mean. Is this a benefit or drawback? Such will depend on what you want the measure to accomplish. The scientist is, of course, interested in the data, but without knowledge of the functions (e.g., mean, median, etc.) imposed on such data, statistics computed on that data become amenable to misunderstanding and misinterpretation.

2.22 Measures of Variability

Measuring the variability in an empirical or theoretical distribution can take many forms, some better than others depending on the context of the situation and the characteristics of the data. Measures such as the range, interquartile range, which is equal to the 75th minus the 25th percentile, semi-interquartile range, equal to the 75th minus the 25th percentile divided by 2, and others are useful as “median-like” measures of variability. Being median measures, they are insensitive and robust to outlier observations, and hence, if such influence is not desired when summarizing a data set, these types of measures come highly recommended. Most commonly, however, we wish to calculate more sensitive measures that utilize the arithmetic mean as their locus or center from which we take deviations. For this reason, the variance and standard deviation dominate statistics as measures of variability, which we now review.91

2.22.1 Variance and Standard Deviation

The sample variance is defined as


$$S^{2} = \frac{\left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right.} \right)^{2}}{n}$$
(2.41)

where $\overline{y}$ is the mean of the distribution and yi any particular data point in that distribution. The sample size is given by n. The sample variance requires us to sum squared deviations from the mean and take the average of that sum. The sample variance with n in the denominator is a biased estimator of the population variance, σ2,


$$\sigma^{2} = \frac{\left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( y_{i} - \mu \right.} \right)^{2}}{n}$$
(2.42)

where now μ is the population mean to replace $\overline{y}$ in the aforementioned sample variance. Formally, S2 is a biased estimator because its expected value does not equal the population parameter, σ2. More succinctly, we write E(S2) ≠ σ2. To make it an unbiased estimator, we can correct the denominator by subtracting a degree of freedom, which yields,


$$s^{2} = \frac{\left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right.} \right)^{2}}{n - 1}$$
(2.43)

and now makes it true that E(s2) = σ2. The positive square root of the sample variance is the sample standard deviation s,


$$s = \sqrt{\frac{\left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right.} \right)^{2}}{n - 1}}$$
(2.44)

which provides a measure of average deviation from the mean, now no longer in squared units as was true for the variance. As an example, if the standard deviation for a distribution is computed to be equal to 5, we can conclude that on average, scores deviate from the mean by five units. However, without knowing the characteristics of the distribution and whether it is normal or not, we cannot use the normal density to compute proportions under the curve. That is, we cannot automatically assume that nearly 68% of cases fall within +1 or −1 units (i.e., a single standard deviation on either side of zero). We need to know more about the shape of the distribution in order to make such statements.

The variance and standard deviation so far discussed are for empirical variables, not theoretical random variables. For a continuous random variable, the variance is given by


σ2 = ∫ − ∞ + ∞(x−μ)2f(x)dx
(2.45)

If the variable is discrete, then we can associate a probability pi with any particular value x in the distribution, yielding92


$$\sigma_{}^{2} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{\left( x - \mu \right)^{2}p_{i}\left( x \right)}}$$
(2.46)

In Python, the variance can be computed by numpy.var(). In R, the var() function will return the variance.

2.22.2 Mean Absolute Deviation

The reader may wonder why squared deviations of the kind $\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right)^{2}$ are taken when computing the standard deviation. Indeed, we must take at least some function of the deviations since taking the sum of deviations, $\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right)$, will always result in a value of zero, no matter the extent of variability or dispersion present in the distribution. That is, recall it can easily be shown that ${\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right)} = 0$ for any conceivable distribution, which thus makes it a poor measure of dispersion. Why do we always get zero? The reason is because deviations from the mean are made up of both positive and negative deviations which balance out when taking the sum. By squaring deviations, we eliminate the negatively-signed differences and hence obtain a value greater than zero only if there is indeed variability present in the distribution. If there is no variability, then $\left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right.} \right)^{2} = 0$ will be true but only because there is indeed no variability, not because it is a constant for any distribution of data we may consider.

Squaring deviations is not the only operation that will negate negative deviations. We could have also taken a simpler function, that of absolute values of deviations. That is, taking absolute-valued deviations,


$$\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left| {y_{i} - \overline{y}} \right|$$

would have also generated a value greater than zero only in the situation where there is variability in the distribution. So why take squares? Why not take absolute deviations instead? It turns out that taking squared deviations is mathematically more tractable and facilitates differentiation easier than would absolute values. However, it should be emphasized that taking absolute-valued deviations is permissible and is done in many contexts, especially those in which outliers in the distribution may make the squared sum especially large. That is, squaring a deviation magnifies its deviation much more than taking an absolute value. For example, a deviation of 4 has a squared value of 16, whereas it only has a value of 4 in absolute value. Hence, if you wish to minimize the influence of outlying data, then taking absolute deviations may be preferable in some cases to taking squared deviations. There is a whole literature on taking absolute-valued deviations in a variety of statistical and machine learning methods. Such a procedure is usually called least-absolute-value (deviation) regression in a linear model context.

2.23 Skewness and Kurtosis

The skewness of a distribution is a measure of the general shape of that distribution away from the typical bell-shaped normal distribution and is given by93


$$\gamma = \frac{E\left\lbrack \left( y_{i} - \mu \right)^{3} \right\rbrack}{\left( {E\left\lbrack \left( y_{i} - \mu \right)^{2} \right\rbrack} \right)^{3/2}}$$
(2.47)

A distribution that is positively skewed has a tail that stretches out toward the right (i.e., higher scores), while a distribution that is negatively skewed has a tail that stretches out toward the left (i.e., lower scores). A distribution with an absence of skew may have a single mode (i.e., the classic normal distribution) or may have several modes (e.g., a bimodal distribution). A lack of skew in a distribution should not automatically be associated with or imply a normal shape. For example, the distribution in Figure 2.7 exhibits virtually no skew.

To reiterate, it can be easy to assume that upon hearing a distribution has no skew to visualize a normal distribution with a single mode. However, this could be in error, as the plot in Figure 2.7 reveals. An absence of skewness does not necessarily imply a single mode. This is one more reason to always plot data. Numerical summaries are usually never enough to draw strong conclusions about distributional characteristics.

The kurtosis of a distribution measures the general “tailness” of that distribution (Upton & Cook, 2014) and more succinctly the behavior of the distribution’s tails with regard to how “heavy” they are, meaning how much mass exists in the tails (DeCarlo, 1997). It is given by


$$k = \frac{E\left\lbrack \left( y_{i} - \mu \right)^{4} \right\rbrack}{\left( {E\left\lbrack \left( y_{i} - \mu \right)^{2} \right\rbrack} \right)^{2}}$$
(2.48)

A distribution is said to be mesokurtic if the distribution exhibits kurtosis typical of a bell-shaped curve, platykurtic if the distribution has lighter tails and is often flatter toward the center of the distribution when compared to the normal, and leptokurtic if the distribution exhibits heavier tails and is often more narrow in the middle of the distribution, typically making it more “peaked” than what would be expected in the normal density. While degree of “peakness” of a distribution is not the formal definition of kurtosis, the heaviness of tails often to some extent (though definitely not always) corresponds to whether the distribution is wider or more narrow toward the center of the distribution. However, associating kurtosis entirely with the peakness of a distribution has largely been jettisoned.94

2.24 Coefficient of Variation

The coefficient of variation is yet another measure of dispersion in a data set, and essentially “scales” the standard deviation σ by the value of the mean, μ. It can be useful in this regard to know how the standard deviation for a set of data (sample or population) relates to the size of that data’s mean. Hence, if we report the standard deviation equal to 2, knowing what the mean is can help us assess the extent to which a standard deviation of 2 is considered “big” or “small.”

The coefficient of variation is given by


$$CV = \frac{\sigma}{\left| \mu \right|}$$
(2.49)

where σ is the population standard deviation and |μ| is the absolute value of the population mean. As an example, for σ = 5, the coefficient of variation when μ = 5 is much smaller (i.e., 1) than if μ = 1 (i.e., 5). Hence, comparing standard deviations of distributions without incorporating respective means may, in some cases, be misleading, and a useful practice when comparing variability in distributions is to also incorporate the coefficient of variation into the discussion.

2.25 Statistical Estimation

Classical (and Bayesian, for that matter) statistics is all about estimation. Unless we have entire populations, we cannot know, for certain, the parameters of those populations and instead must estimate them using sample data. Recall that if you have the population data at your disposal, there is nothing to estimate, as one can simply compute descriptive statistics on the parameters of interest. This is sometimes misunderstood by newcomers to statistics, many of whom, upon learning about significance tests and p-values become in a hurry to conduct such tests on every data situation they encounter, all too proud to report p-values! However, a significance test on population parameters provides no additional insight beyond observing the parameters themselves. Significance tests are only meaningful when performed on sample data and when we wish to know something about the population parameters from which the sample data was presumably collected.

We say that θ̂ is an estimator of the population parameter θ. More precisely, it is a point estimator because it seeks to estimate one particular and specific value of the parameter, θ. In general, an estimator is any function of the sample data that is used to estimate a population parameter. When we apply the estimator to some data and obtain a value for it, for instance, applying the mean estimator and obtaining a numerical mean, we say that the estimator has produced an estimate. Point estimators are almost always statistics (since they are computed on samples), but statistics are not always point estimators. As an example, if we compute the mean salary of a university department, such a mean is a descriptive statistic on the sample; however, it is not a point estimator because we are not using it to estimate any parameter.

An estimator is unbiased if the expectation of θ̂ is equal to θ, that is,


E(θ̂) = θ
(2.50)

In contrast, an estimator is biased if the above equality does not hold,95


E(θ̂) ≠ θ
(2.51)

with the amount of bias being equal to the difference between the expectation and the actual parameter value:

Bias = E(θ̂) − θ(2.52)

Many estimators exhibit bias in samples but are not asymptotically biased. That is, as sample size grows indefinitely, bias eventually vanishes. More succinctly, an estimator is asymptotically unbiased if bias tends toward zero as sample size increases toward infinity. We can express this more formally as,


$$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left( {E\left( \hat{\theta} \right) - \theta} \right) = 0$$

where in the above recall that E(θ̂) − θ is the degree of bias present. As n increases, bias increasingly disappears, and is nonexistent in the limit. That is, E(θ̂) = θ in the limit as n→∞.

The variance of an estimator is a measure of how much the estimate would change if we changed or perturbed the data. That is, in repeated sampling where we experience random fluctuations in sample data, the variance of an estimator captures how much the estimate changes as a result of this fluctuation. We define the variance of an estimator as:


Varθ̂ = E(θ̂2) − (E(θ̂))2
(2.53)

It seems intuitive to conclude that favorable estimators are those that have minimal to no bias while simultaneously having minimal variance. In most cases, this is the ideal to shoot for. However, as we will see later in the book, such estimators are not always most favorable for all situations. There are times where purposely allowing bias into an estimator is actually a “good thing” if it helps reduce variance. Of course, the most ideal situation would be to both reduce variance and reduce bias, but this is usually an unattainable goal. As bias decreases, we usually experience an upshoot in variance, and as variance decreases, an upshoot in bias. This trade-off is well known in statistical circles and not surprisingly goes by the name of the bias-variance trade-off. Biased estimators include those of the ridge and lasso, which are detailed later in the book. For now, we unpack in more detail the bias-variance trade-off.

2.26 Bias-Variance Trade-Off

We just mentioned that two things we need to be concerned about regarding an estimator are its bias and variance. We can unpack this idea into the following fundamental identity:


E(y0−f̂(x0))2 = Var(f̂(x0)) + [Bias(f̂(x0))]2 + Var(ε)
(2.54)

where E(y0−f̂(x0))2 is the expected test mean squared error (MSE) at the value of the predictor, x0. It is important to realize here that the variance and bias in this context refer to the statistical learning method or model, not the data. That is, we are not interested in the variance of the sample data in this context; we are interested instead in the variance generated by using such and such statistical methodology or model estimate. Variance is how much the estimated function, f̂, would 96change if a different training data set was used, or if the current one was “perturbed,” and bias is how “off” the learning method is in actually capturing the true function, f(x0). The more flexible the method, the higher the variance, while the lower the bias. The relative change of these two quantities will influence test MSE. As flexibility increases, bias initially decreases faster than the variance increases (James et al., 2013). However, beyond this initial state, an increase in flexibility impacts the bias much less but instead increases the variance, at which point test MSE likewise increases. The objective is to have both low variance and low bias as much as possible; however, a reduction in bias often results in an increase in variance, and vice versa.

2.26.1 Is Irreducible Error Really Irreducible?

It is typically held that variance of a statistical method, Var(f̂(x)), can be mitigated or reduced; however, Var(ε) is considered to be irreducible variance, which implies it cannot be mitigated and we are essentially “stuck” with it. That is, Var(ε) is sometimes regarded as a constant that cannot be decreased. But is Var(ε) truly irreducible? No! Yes, we can find a better function to fit, that is, f̂(x) to better approximate the “truth” in the form of f(x), which will get us closer to E(y−f̂(x0))2 = 0, but we can also reduce ε via measurement, or at minimum, make ε less variable. It is only “irreducible” in the sense that it may be independent of the function one is fitting, but it is not irreducible in the sense of simply reducing the overall squared error. That is, ε exists not solely as a result of not fitting the “correct” function or using a better statistical learning technique, but can decrease simply by an improvement in measurement. Reducing Var(ε) becomes a realistic possibility.

Are we theoretically able to get ε completely to zero? Probably not, but such will depend on what we consider ε to actually “be” at a deeper philosophical level. If one believes in true chance or true error, then it may be impossible to get error down to zero and we will always have at least some fluctuation. As noted in James et al. (2013, p. 19), “the irreducible error will always provide an upper bound on the accuracy of our prediction for Y. This bound is almost always unknown in practice.” While this is true, our point is merely that this does not take into consideration whether error can theoretically ever go to zero. More formally, we may write,


limVar(ε) → 0 = E(y − ŷ)2=[f(x)–f̂(x)]2

That is, as Var(ε)→0 in the limit, we simply obtain the squared difference between the observed f(x) and estimated f̂(x) functions (note that we dropped Var(ε)). This “ideal” is theoretically possible as we find ways to decrease ε and its Var(ε). While this is a hugely interesting topic on a psychometric and philosophical level, we will not explore the issue further here.

2.27 Maximum Likelihood Estimation

Maximum likelihood is, historically, the most common method of estimating parameters in a variety of statistical models and contexts. It is due primarily to Fisher (1922) though in concept at least, its origins and germination span several hundred years before Fisher (Stigler, 1986). The idea of maximum likelihood is very simple. Suppose you have observed data in the form of a sample. Maximum likelihood asks the question:97

What values of parameters should we choose, that would maximize the likelihood function of such data?

Note carefully that the data have already been observed. The question we are asking is what value for parameters of interest would have made such data most likely?

As a simple example, consider flipping a coin ten times and observing five heads. The five heads constitute the observed data. What parameter value for the probability of heads would have given this observed result a “maximum likelihood” of occurring? The answer, of course, is the probability of heads equal to 0.5, or, more succinctly, p(H) = 0.5. An alternative parameter value such as p(H) = 0.4 would have made the data less likely than p(H) = 0.5, and hence θ̂ = 0.5 is the maximum likelihood estimator in this case. The estimates for the parameter values (e.g., p(H) = 0.5) are referred to as maximum likelihood estimates.

More formally, the maximum likelihood estimator, or MLE, is defined by


$$\left. {\hat{\theta}}_{mle} \triangleq \underset{\theta}{\arg\max}p\text{(}D \middle| \theta\text{)} \right.$$
(2.55)
