which simply expresses the argument value (i.e., arg ) that makes the data D most likely given the parameter value, θ. That is, maximum likelihood (ML) provides which value for θ makes p(D|θ) (the likelihood function) most probable. The logarithm of a function is a monotonically increasing function, which means that whether we take the likelihood or the log of the likelihood essentially amounts to the same thing in terms of assessing the size of likelihoods. For technical reasons, and for convenience, taking the log is useful, and hence the log-likelihood is given by


log L(θ) = log p(D/θ)
(2.56)

In practice, it will often be the negative of the log-likelihood that is minimized instead of the log being maximized,


$${\hat{\theta}}_{mle} \triangleq \underset{\theta}{\text{arg}\min}\text{-log}\, p\text{(}D/\theta\text{)}$$
(2.57)

which is generally known as the error function (Bishop, 2006).

All of the above is quite general. For instance, we can unpack these elements for the multivariate situation specifically in which we desire maximum likelihood estimators. Hence, suppose we seek maximum likelihood estimates of μ, the multivariate mean, and Σ, the covariance matrix, that will maximize the likelihood of the data. In the multivariate setting, the aforementioned estimates are found by


$$\hat{\mu} = \overline{y}$$

for the multivariate mean vector, and98


$$\left. \hat{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{n}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right.} \right)\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right)'$$

which can also be given by $\frac{n - 1}{n}S$, where S is the sample covariance matrix. For justification for these particular maximum likelihood estimators, see Rencher and Christensen (2012, p. 99). Maximum likelihood requires us to select the parameters that maximize the joint density evaluated at the observations (Johnson & Wichern, 2007). The maximizing parameter values, as before, are called maximum likelihood estimates. That is, the maximum likelihood estimates of μ and Σ are those values, μ̂ and Σ̂ that maximize the likelihood function L(μ,Σ). In practice, as in the univariate case, often the negative of the log of the likelihood is computed. As mentioned, maximizing the likelihood is equivalent to minimizing error (Bishop, 2006).

2.27.1 Why ML Is So Popular and Alternatives

Maximum likelihood estimators possess many favorable properties. It is the default estimation for many if not most statistical and machine learning problems. For instance, it is commonly used in neural networks (Goodfellow et al., 2016).

Despite its popularity, maximum likelihood is by no means the only method of estimation in statistical modeling and machine learning. Numerous other methods have been advanced to accommodate data situations for which assuming multivariate normality is unrealistic. For instance, quasi-maximum likelihood (QML) is a method of estimation advanced in structural equation modeling featuring nonlinear terms such as quadratic effects (Klein & Muthén, 2007). Two-stage least-squares estimation for nonlinear SEM models has also been advanced (Holst & Budtz-Jorgensen, 2020). Adaptive Gaussian Quadrature (AGQ) has also been proposed for estimating nonlinearity in SEM models. The method of moments is an alternative approach to ML estimation when the solution is either unavailable or computationally difficult (Murray, 2022). Online recursive estimation is yet another possibility (Murray, 2022). All of these estimation methods are complex and discussions of them could fill an entire chapter or even book.

The key takeaway from this discussion is that when it comes to estimation methods, though maximum likelihood is probably the most popular method, there are numerous alternative methods which are already in existence and others which are being developed in statistics and machine learning. Hence, when one comes across the term “estimation,” one should be curious to learn what type of estimation is being referred to as it will not always be maximum likelihood.

2.27.2 Estimation and Confidence Intervals

In classical statistics, we can either attempt to estimate a particular point in a distribution, such as the arithmetic mean, or we can attempt instead to estimate an interval of values. Theoretical statistics tells us that the expected value of the sample mean, $\overline{y}$, is equal to the population mean, μ. That is, $E\left( \overline{y} \right) = \mu$. However, we also know that the probability of “hitting” the precise value of the population mean has a limiting value of zero. Hence, we seek usually to build an interval of values around the sample estimator and instead of seeking point predictions, we will use an interval estimator, the most common of which is the confidence interval.

The confidence for the mean is given by


$$\overline{y} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$$
(2.58)

where zα/2 is the critical value of z given the desired accuracy for the confidence interval. For a 95% interval, that value is 1.96, and so we have99


$$\overline{y} \pm 1.96\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$$

Recall that seldom do we actually know the value of σ and must instead estimate it based on sample data. When we use the sample standard deviation s as an estimator of the population standard deviation σ, the mean is no longer distributed as z, but instead is distributed as a t-statistic, and hence the confidence interval becomes:


$$\overline{y} \pm t_{\alpha/2}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$
(2.59)

Confidence intervals are by no means limited to means. Interval estimators can be used for a variety of statistics. In many cases, analytical solutions tell us how to construct the standard errors for such intervals. In other cases, standard errors are intractable and difficult or even impossible to calculate. When we cannot compute standard errors directly, one option is to bootstrap samples of observations and determine interval bounds via repeated sampling. We discuss the bootstrap shortly.

Be sure to note that as was true for the point estimator, an interval estimator is the random variable. The parameter that is being estimated is not the random variable. While there are a few different ways of interpreting confidence intervals in practice, the most correct way is to refer to the procedure for computing such intervals of which one interval has been calculated. Hence, the most correct interpretation of a computed 95% interval on data becomes

The probability that the given interval, based on the procedure used to compute the interval, covers the parameter, is 0.95. Repeating the procedure of calculating intervals this way would result in 95% of them covering the true parameter.

There is a whole literature on the correct interpretation of confidence intervals and how researchers presumably always get it wrong. Yes, formality matters here, but the above is not the only way a confidence interval can be conceptualized, especially in a real research setting. The above interpretation is rather awkward when it comes to interpreting real research, but is arguably near the most theoretically correct interpretation. For a brief discussion on this point and a brief argument for why competing ways of interpreting confidence intervals may be useful in practice, consult Denis (2020).

2.28 The Bootstrap: A Way of Estimating Nonparametrically

Perhaps more than any other statistical technique, the bootstrap is the one that has benefited the most from the computer age revolution and the speed and facility that such computation provides. Though theoretically the bootstrap would still be possible without computers, it would be so laborious and impractical computationally that it is fair to say the technique would have likely forever been abandoned and have never risen to fame. Thanks to computation, however, the bootstrap has, in the world of statistics and machine learning, become a “household name.”

The origins of the bootstrap are usually credited with Efron (1979) and is actually a special case of what is generally known as the jackknife which came before it, but is far more applicable and generalizable than the jackknife. The jackknife itself can be thought of as a linear expansion method (called the delta method) for approximating the bootstrap (Efron, 1979). As noted by Efron and Hastie (2016), “Before computers, applied statisticians needed to be Taylor series experts in 100laboriously pursuing the accuracy of even moderately complicated statistics” (p. 155). The jackknife, originating in 1957, was a first step toward a computational approach to standard errors.

The basic idea of the bootstrap is to capitalize on computing power to draw repeated samples from a sample that, for the given bootstrap scenario, serves as a pseudo-population. We include the bootstrap here in our discussion of estimation as it is yet another way to estimate parameters of a distribution; while the methods we have just surveyed do so parametrically through time-tested analytical formulae, the bootstrap is a nonparametric way of estimation through simulations of resampling using the computer.

Even more generally, bootstrap methods are a special case of the wider family of Monte Carlo methods, which is a general name given for resampling. To be clear, the bootstrap is not equivalent to Monte Carlo methods by any stretch, as many other techniques that utilize Monte Carlo sampling exist. However, in applied statistics and machine learning circles the bootstrap is undoubtedly one of the more popular applications of the general Monte Carlo technique. As a result of the bootstrap typically being used for estimation, we have included a discussion of it here instead of under Monte Carlo techniques, but including it under a general discussion of Monte Carlo techniques would not have been wrong.

2.28.1 Simple Examples of the Bootstrap

As discussed, the bootstrapped sample is to the original sample as the original sample is to the population. Why would we ever want to sample from a sample? There are a few reasons, but one primary reason is that obtaining things like standard errors and such analytically is sometimes not feasible and in many cases, actually impossible. True, we know what the standard error is for the mean, for instance, equal to


$$\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$$

but we are less sure, for instance, what the standard error is for the median (i.e., the standard error for the median is less exact). That is, the standard error of the median is less analytically available. However, thanks to the bootstrap, we can assess “empirically” the standard deviation of medians (i.e., the standard error of the median). This is a chief benefit to being able to bootstrap, that of being able to “simulate” statistics empirically via resampling that have no analytical sampling distribution or that deriving such sampling distributions proves very difficult. In theory, we could “invent” a new statistic tomorrow that has no known sampling distribution and simply bootstrap the statistic via resampling to determine its “behavior” over the long run. This is perhaps the biggest reason why the bootstrap is such a “big deal” in statistics.

More formally, assume we have a training set, denoted by Z = (z1,z2,...,zN), where any given zi corresponds to data on x, y, that is, zi = (xi,yi). Imagine now we resample from Z a total of B = 100 samples. We will refer to these samples as the bootstrapped samples. To use our example of the standard error, we would compute standard deviations on each of the bootstrapped samples and observe standard deviation behavior over the 100 samples. This would denote the standard error we want to compute. However, we need not necessarily be computing standard errors; we could be computing virtually anything on these bootstrapped samples. As mentioned, bootstrapping is widely applicable to virtually any statistic, even those for which deriving sampling distributions is impossible.

As an example, we could compute linear regressions on the bootstrapped samples and observe the behavior of the linear equations across the samples, or any other models or statistics. This is the 101power of the bootstrap and Monte Carlo simulation in general; it allows us to resample repeatedly and build a distribution of functions of the data, whatever those functions may be. The bootstrap in this regard is very flexible and has wide application. It is nonparametric, meaning it assumes nothing about the population, making it extremely flexible and well-suited for creative ventures pertaining to whatever you wish to calculate on the repeated samples. Bootstrapping allows you to create an actual empirical distribution of computed statistics instead of deriving a theoretical one analytically.

More formally, consider once more Z = (z1,z2,...,zN). Suppose we compute some quantity on Z, that is, some function of Z which we will appropriately denote f(Z). Suppose that function f(Z) is the variance of Z, that is, Var(Z) defined as


$$f\left( Z \right) = Var\left( Z \right) = \frac{\sum\limits_{b = 1}^{B}\left( Z_{}^{{}^{*b}} - {\overline{Z}}^{*b} \right)^{2}}{B}$$

where Z * b is a particular computed bootstrapped sample and ${\overline{Z}}^{*b}$ is the mean of all bootstrapped samples. Notice carefully that Var(Z) here is just an ordinary variance but computed on the B bootstrapped samples. All of this looks familiar based on our earlier study of the variance. For instance, if we wished for the more typical estimator, we could use B − 1 instead of B in the denominator,


$$f\left( Z \right) = Var\left( Z \right) = \frac{\sum\limits_{b = 1}^{B}\left( Z^{*b} - {\overline{Z}}^{*b} \right)^{2}}{B - 1}$$

It is easy to see then that Var(Z) is yielding a measure of variance around bootstrapped samples.

2.28.2 Why Not Bootstrap Everything?

As we have seen, the bootstrap is quite universal and general and can be applied in many different contexts. Indeed, we can literally bootstrap virtually any function on a sample if we have sufficient reason for doing so. It does not need to be something familiar, such as a mean, median, or other well-known statistic. This is precisely the advantage of the bootstrap, in that it allows us to estimate statistical quantities for which we may have literally no theory to guide us and for which there may be no chance of ever knowing the sampling distribution without resampling.

So, why isn’t the bootstrap used more often? Why don’t we bootstrap virtually everything? The reason is that except when assumptions are violated, analytically-derived solutions may produce more favorable results than resampling. Computer simulations can be inexact when compared to timeless analytical derivations. Hence, when statistical theory is available and analytical solutions possible, classic formulas may dominate bootstrapped approaches. As a general guideline as to when or not to bootstrap, first check to see if an analytical solution is available and use it if it is a valid one that is strongly supported theoretically. Second, try the bootstrap. Of course, there is never any harm in trying out both approaches and comparing results.

When bootstrapping, the question that also naturally arises regards how many replicates are sufficient to get a reasonable estimate of the distribution of the bootstrapped statistic. Though there is some debate on this, a general recommendation is in the neighborhood of B = 50, and rarely greater than 200 (Rizzo, 2019). Bootstrapping also allows for replacement, and hence one bootstrapped sample might contain the same sampling element as another bootstrapped sample. The 102probability that a data point is not included in a sample is equal to 1 − (1/n) which implies that the probability that the given data point is not included in n samples is equal to (1−1/n)n, which is a well-known approximation to 1/e in the limit as n→∞ (Aggarwal, 2015).

Bootstrapping in Python can be easily performed using SciPy. Bootstrapping in R can be performed several ways. One way is by using the bootstrap package (Original et al., 2019).

2.28.3 Variations and Extensions of the Bootstrap

There are numerous variations on the bootstrap. Among these include the leave-one-out bootstrap, where the accuracy of an instance is computed using all the data except that instance (Aggarwal, 2015). Kleiner et al. (2014) proposed a sub-sampling method called bag of little bootstraps (BLB) to help deal with the massive data that may be too large for computer memory or take too long to analyze efficiently. In the BLB approach, one draws a number of subsamples of a given size on each sample from the original collected data set. For each of the subsets, a number of bootstrapped samples are chosen and we compute statistical methods on those subsets (e.g., computation of the mean). These are thus, the point estimates. These measures are then combined by averaging to yield the overall point estimates and quality measures.

The fractional bootstrap, also known as the Bayesian bootstrap, draws random weights and instead of applying such to resampling units, applies them to the actual data. For details and implementation in R, see the fwb package (Greifer, 2023).

2.29 Elements of Classic Null Hypothesis Significance Testing

For better or for worse, much of classical statistics is based on the method of null hypothesis significance testing, or “NHST” for short, which provides the basis for rejecting a hypothesis if the data are unlikely to have occurred under the presumed model. This yields the classic “p-value” from which a scientist decides “yay” or “nay” whether to retain or discard the null. The null hypothesis, contrary to misconception, is not necessarily the hypothesis of a null result or zero effect, nor is it necessarily the hypothesis of equality in a comparison scenario of two populations. R.A. Fisher, the inventor of ANOVA, coined the null hypothesis to be the hypothesis to be nullified if observed data contradict it. More specifically, if the probability of an observed statistic is relatively small in light of the null, the null is rejected and a statistical alternative hypothesis is inferred. The designation of “statistical” in statistical alternative is important. A statistical alternative hypothesis is a statement of “not the null,” and is not a statement confirming the researcher’s substantive alternative hypothesis. Classical null hypothesis significance testing, or really any statistical theory, does not have the ability to confirm a research hypothesis. Misunderstanding this point can easily lead to misunderstanding the results of a significance test.

As an example to illustrate the point, suppose we posit a null hypothesis that the mean IQ of a population is equal to 100. That is,


H0 : μ = 100

The statistical alternative hypothesis is that the mean is not equal to 100; that is,


H1 : μ ≠ 100

But why would it not be equal to 100? Perhaps because the investigator treated the group with a magic pill that would increase their IQ. In this context, that is the research alternative hypothesis. 103Note that rejection of the null and inference of the statistical alternative hypothesis is not equivalent to inference of the research alternative. The null hypothesis does not know “why” it is being rejected; it is simply being rejected based on the low probability of the test statistic. Hence, a rejection of the null could “happen” under a lot of conditions, especially if the study or experiment were done poorly. If the null is rejected under a properly done experiment, then inference of the statistical alternative naturally leads to a strong inference of the research alternative, but that “leap” is not automatic, and making it so can easily lead to inference of an incorrect research alternative. For instance, under a poorly performed study, perhaps it wasn’t the magic pill at all that was the effective agent; perhaps the increase in IQ was due to increased sunlight due to a change in seasons or a change in diet among participants that simulated an increase in IQ because of greater cognitive processing power.

To emphasize the abstraction that exists in the classical null hypothesis significance test, we can express the parameter value (or vector, in the case of multivariate models) as belonging to a particular parameter space under the null, Θ0, from which the parameter value is a member of that set,


H0 : θ ∈ Θ0
(2.60)

against an alternative hypothesis that the parameter value is a member of an alternative set,


H1 : θ ∈ Θ0c
(2.61)

where Θ0c is the complement to Θ0 and whose membership is that of not the null. Why the abstraction? To make things unnecessarily abstract and mathematical? No! This symbolism demonstrates the most general framework of the null hypothesis significance test and emphasizes that the complement to the null hypothesis is an abstraction. It is not “concrete.” Otherwise said, rejection of the null hypothesis does not necessarily mean anything other than inferring the complement to the null in terms of an abstract parameter space! Allowing this idea to sink in will prevent the reader from making egregious scientific inferences when rejecting a null hypothesis that are habitually made even by professionals in various fields. A rejection of the null does not imply the research alternative; it merely indicates the complement to the null statistically (not substantively).

Classical significance levels used in most scientific investigations include 0.05 and 0.01, though there is absolutely no statistical or philosophical grounds for using these levels. Fisher himself simply denoted the 0.05 level as “usual and convenient” in the establishment of evidence to contradict the null. Still, there is a long history of misunderstanding what 0.05 actually means, and often researchers incorrectly treat 0.05 as a “yes” vs. “no” decision on the presence of an effect in the experiment, which is a serious misunderstanding. Not only does 0.05 not necessarily indicate the presence or absence of a meaningful effect, but there is simply nothing “special” about 0.05. As many have noted before, surely God loves the 0.06 level as much as the 0.05. Determining an appropriate significance level should be done carefully with regard to the risk tolerances of making type I and type II errors depending on the given context of the situation. Once more, context matters!

A rejection of the null does not necessarily imply that the null is false. Of course, logically, the null can be said to be false even before collecting the data. Do we really expect population means to ever be exactly equal? Hardly ever! Even with a rejection, we do not know if the null is false; we are simply using the available sample data to hedge our bet. Science is a gamble! A false rejection of the null is called a type I error and is indicated by the level at which we set our statistical test, that of α. A type II error is the error committed when we fail to reject a null hypothesis that is, in actuality, false. The probability of such an error is indicated by β. 104Statistical power is equal to the balance of the type II error rate, computed as 1 − β. Power is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis given that it is false. Ideally, power for a study or experiment should be at least .80 or higher, where more power than not is usually a good thing if our goal is to reject a null.

2.29.1 One-Tailed vs. Two-Tailed Tests

A one-tailed test is when we commit all of our rejection region on one tail of the distribution and none on the opposite tail. A two-tailed test is when there are rejection regions on both ends of the sampling distribution. It is worth emphasizing that while typically two-tailed tests constitute an even “splitting up” of the alpha region, there is no requirement of such equality when performing a two-tailed test, so long as one adjusts their test appropriately. That is, one can allot 4% of the rejection region in one tail and 1% in the other if that is what substantive interest or theory indicates. In practice, however, for a 5% test, the researcher will usually allocate 2.5% to each tail. Since the event of the statistic falling in one tail or the other constitutes a sum of two mutually exclusive events, these areas can be added (i.e., 0.025 + 0.025) to produce the overall type I error rate.

2.29.2 Effect Size

A p-value essentially tells us the probability of the data given the null hypothesis. Because the standard error of a statistic is influenced heavily by sample size, it is entirely possible to reject a null hypothesis simply as a function of sample size, where the “effect” is extremely small. This can be very easily illustrated in the case of a one-sample z:


$$z = \frac{\overline{y} - \mu}{\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}}$$

Note that as n→∞, z→∞. More formally,


$$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}z = \infty$$

which reads that in the limit as n→∞, z will get increasingly larger and likewise go to ∞. Since its inception, it has long been argued that p-values do not tell the researcher or scientist what they actually want to know. What they want to know is a number characterizing the mean difference or the extent to which the independent variable “explains” variance in the dependent variable. The p-value will not tell you this information, no matter how small it is! Stop reporting p < 0.05, thinking that it alone justifies a scientific finding! Only effect sizes will yield explained variance and a true characterization of a scientific effect.

2.29.3 Cohen’s d Measure of Effect Size

Cohen’s d is a popular measure of effect size in either the one-sample case or two-sample case. Below is d for the one-sample case, where $\overline{y}$ is the sample mean, μ0 is the population mean under the null hypothesis, and σ is the population standard deviation,105


$$d = \left| \frac{\overline{y} - \mu_{0}}{\sigma} \right|$$
(2.62)

Note that d is effectively a ratio of quantities, the ratio of one deviation, $\overline{y} - \mu_{0}$ to another, σ. That is, the ratio answers the question “How large is the observed deviation relative to the standard deviation?” If the deviations are approximately the same, then d ≃ 1. Unlike R2, which is bound by 1, d does not have such an upper limit.

Note that d is not a function of sample size, as is the p-value. True, sample size n does appear in the denominator of d in the standard deviation,


$$\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\left( y_{i} - \mu \right)^{2}}{n}}$$

however, note that the standard deviation is not a function of n as is the standard error in the one-sample z-test for a mean, $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$. That is, σ will not necessarily increase or decrease simply as a function of n as is true of the standard error. Hence, though sample size appears in the denominator, it serves a different function. This is the precise difference between a p-value and an effect size: p-values are a (partial) function of sample size; effect sizes are (generally) not.

There are a whole host of effect sizes that can be computed in statistics. Sometimes the effect has to be gleamed from the research paper as the authors of the paper will not outwardly identify their effect size measure or mistakenly believe that the effect size is contained in the p-value. For example, they may report the odds of an effect occurring, which in itself serves as a useful effect size estimate, but will not identify the odds specifically as the effect size. It is up to the reader in many cases to understand and appreciate the nature of an effect size so they can identify it in the paper they are reading (and possibly compute or otherwise estimate it if it is omitted).

Transformations between effect sizes are well documented. For example, if a research paper reports a d statistic, one can convert from d to r via the following transformation:


$$r = \frac{d}{\sqrt{d^{2} + 4}}$$
(2.63)

The conversion of d into a log odds ratio is also easily obtained:


$$\frac{d\pi}{\sqrt{3}}$$
(2.64)

For example, suppose Cohen’s d is equal to 0.22. As the reader may verify, this translates into an approximate log odds ratio of 0.40. A wealth of other transformations between effect sizes exists in the literature, including many “conversion” calculators online that aid in translating effect sizes from one form to another.

2.29.4 Are P-values That Evil?

As mentioned, the misconception behind p-values, historically, is nothing short of shameful. The legacy of misusing such indicators in the establishment of scientific evidence is nothing short of embarrassing, and what is perhaps worst, it continues on today! While effect sizes are being 106increasingly emphasized in research, there are still numerous studies across various fields that report p-values as a sole indicator in the establishment of scientific evidence, almost as if p < 0.05 is reason enough on its own to somehow establish evidence or success in an experiment or study. As we have emphasized, without the inclusion of an effect size, the reporting of scientific evidence based on p-values alone is incomplete. Any good statistics course one takes should dramatically emphasize the distinction between p-values and effect sizes. From a scientific perspective, it is probably the most important piece of knowledge one can acquire in learning applied statistics.

Based on this discussion, it may seem as though p-values are evil and should forever be avoided. Indeed, some have even argued for a ban on p-values. Meehl (1978) has even accused Fisher of almost purposely “beffudling” researchers into believing in p-values! However, p-values are really not that bad and serve a purpose. Interpreting p-values incorrectly is where the real problem lies.

The p-value, by itself, serves a useful function. It allows for an inferential statement based on a rejection of the null hypothesis. This is not a bad thing. And though it may sound borderline criminal that one can obtain a small p-value based simply on increasing sample size n, this too is not a bad thing. An increase in sample size leading to an increasingly smaller p-value implies that the estimation of the parameter value is improving. That is, the strength of the evidence against the null should increase given the increase in n. In the limit, as n increases to infinity, the rejection of the null is guaranteed and assured, assuming at least some effect. An estimator is consistent if with increasing n, we obtain a better and more precise estimate of the parameter based on our sequence of estimates. That is, a consistent estimator is one such that


$$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}p\left( \middle| \hat{\theta} - \theta \middle| < \varepsilon \right) = 1$$
(2.65)

where θ̂ − θ is the difference between the estimator, θ̂, and the parameter value, θ. Consistency of an estimator assures us that as the distance θ̂ − θ gets smaller, less than some arbitrarily small number ε, the probability of that distance being smaller than ε is equal to 1 as n→∞. As Casella and Berger (2002, p. 468) note, an equivalent statement to the above is


$$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}p\left( \middle| \hat{\theta} - \theta \middle| \geq \varepsilon \right) = 0$$
(2.66)

which essentially says the same thing; in this case, the probability of any difference being equal or greater than some small magnitude ε is equal to 0 as n→∞.

The p-value is a reflection of this consistency and hence it getting smaller as n increases is what the p-value should be doing. What the user should not be doing is attributing the decreasing p-value as increasing support for the research or scientific alternative hypothesis. That is where the problem lies. The movement to ban p-values from particular journals is akin to banning firearms entirely 100% due to misuse. An argument can be made on both sides of the debate, but the gun (p-value) itself, as it sits there not harming anyone, is innocent. As with all innocent mathematics and statistics (and guns), it takes a human being to truly mess it up.

2.29.5 Absolute vs. Relative Size of Effect Size: Context Matters

An R2 effect size of 0.10 is relatively small numerically, since the maximum theoretically attainable effect size is 1.0. However, 0.10 may be quite large and impressive relative to the given research area. Effect sizes should be contextualized within the research area to better appreciate how large or small they really are. Cohen (1988) provided “rules of thumb” for effect sizes in social research of 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, and 0.7 or higher “large.” But it should be emphasized that these are nothing more than arbitrary guidelines and Cohen may have been better off not 107providing them at all, since too often researchers simply compare their obtained effect size to these arbitrary guidelines instead of comparing their obtained effect size to the effect sizes in competing research.

How large is an effect of d = 0.7 or so? That converts to an R2of approximately 0.11, which means we’re only explaining approximately 11% of the variance in the response variable. Is that “large?” Not in absolute terms; it’s very small, given R2 has a theoretical upper limit of 1.0. But, for many areas of social research (which is the area Cohen was referring to when he published his guidelines of 0.2, 0.5, and so on), explaining 11% is usually pretty decent as much social research will typically explain much less. Hence, in that context, 0.7 or so is considered relatively large. But only in that context. If the effect size of raising or lowering the flaps on the response variable of flight on an airplane were that low, we’d all be taking the bus. In that context, explaining 11% of the variance is comical, negligibly small, and outright dangerous. We could easily devise a social study where 11% would be negligible as well, yet we could also imagine a social study where 11% is whoppingly large and impressive. Imagine if the way people smiled or did not smile explained 11% of the variance in their lifespan; that would probably be considered ground-breaking and extremely large! Yet the same effect size explaining flap angles and flight has the plane crashing into the ground way too often.

Hence, effect size without context is very difficult to interpret other than in a purely absolute sense (e.g., 11% of the variance explained is better than 0% but still a long way to maximum variance, which is 100%). In an absolute sense, regardless of the research area, 11% is small. Or, we could say, “Relative to the range of theoretically possible effect sizes, 11% is small, because the theoretical maximum is 100%. We’re only explaining approximately one tenth of what is theoretically possible to explain in terms of variance.” But when we step away from the abstract and say things like “This drug explains variance in blood pressure by 30%,” that may have tremendous practical value and save many lives, especially if given most other drugs explain only up to 5%. In other words, the drug is clinically relevant. It is clinically significant. In this way, that drug’s effect size is extremely impressive and large, because we’re comparing it to the research area and also thinking about its practical implications. Summer tires vs. winter tires probably explains a reasonable amount of variance in traffic deaths in winter, let’s say 5%. That 5% might represent thousands and thousands of lives saved and may be the most significant thing we can do to curb traffic deaths in winter because all other “treatments” (like brighter headlight bulbs or other alternatives) explain only 0.3%, for instance. Hence, the effect size of 5% is very big in the particular area. Are we going to compare that to Cohen’s guidelines? No, because his guidelines were specific to a narrow area of research and may at best be arbitrary in relation to other areas.

2.29.6 Comparability of Effect Sizes Across Studies

The question often arises as to whether effect sizes are comparable across experiments and studies. The simple answer is that some effect sizes, such as Cohen’s d, are comparable, but with many caveats. First, the comparison will rarely if ever be perfect, as the standard deviation for each study can differ from study to study, as well as what measuring instruments were used, the reliability of those measures, and so on. Cohen’s d is the standardized mean difference within a given study, but across studies those differences are not necessarily standardized. This is the key point.

For example, suppose that d = 0.5 in one study vs. d = 0.6 in another. We are choosing these effect sizes to be relatively close on purpose. The second study has the higher effect size, but are we prepared to say the second study has truly found a larger effect? Perhaps the effect size in the one study is larger or smaller simply as a function of variability and not mean difference. For this 108reason and others, some (e.g., Baguley, 2009) even suggest reporting simple effect sizes without standardization. A simple effect size does not incorporate the standard deviation and features only the mean difference. The problem is that even a few outlying cases can push the variability up so that all of a sudden the mean difference in the numerator does not look quite as impressive (since we are dividing by an increasingly large denominator).

For the above reasons, for most comparisons of effect sizes, it may be best to simply report general ranges of effect sizes and focus less on specific effect sizes, especially if the material under study is also expected to exhibit much measurement error. For example, if we were working with pristine measures that are reliable and repeatable to multiple decimal places (e.g., speed of an engine or angle of descent of an airplane), then a difference of 0.6 to 0.5 would be more meaningful than with say, a social measure that may be more prone to measurement error and error due simply to the way the data were sampled. Of course, if you suspect that the multiple issues that could affect the size of effect are more or less constant across studies, then perhaps you could conclude 0.6 is greater than 0.5 and all the factors which may influence this difference we assume are randomly distributed or more or less equivalent across the studies, which allows for a more blanket and general statement. However, barring such equivalency, there may be good reasons why one study reported the 0.6 vs. 0.5 even if in reality both effect sizes are in fact, and for all purposes, virtually equivalent.

Cohen’s d, or any other effect size, is a function of the specific data that went into it, so in that sense it is unique to the data set. If a second data set exhibits the same (or very similar) numerical properties as the first data set, then d values are much more comparable. Differences in scaling can also mean tremendously different effect sizes to the point where we may be not even sure of what is being compared when we compare d values. However, if a first study had an effect size of 3 and another 0.5, one might be, in general, fairly confident that the first study exhibits more of an effect than the second if both studies were similar in many characteristics, including scaling. As that difference gets smaller and smaller, the confidence in making such a conclusion decreases. If a researcher reports 0.51 vs. 0.52 in Cohen’s d values and concludes, “Therefore, the second study (0.52) found a larger effect,” yes, numerically it did, but each effect size computation is but an estimate of the true underlying effect and is riddled with all the measurement errors and random influences that went into the computation, not the least of which is the way the scale is set for the variables under study. A Likert scale with a range of 1 to 7 for responses is likely to elicit a much different distribution than a Likert scale of 1 to 3, even though in both cases the same variable may be being measured. This issue relates to the operationalization of the independent or predictor variables, which we now briefly discuss.

2.29.7 Operationalizing Predictors

How one chooses to operationalize the independent or predictor variable(s) can have a significant influence on whether an effect is found in statistical modeling. For example, consider η2 from ANOVA. Suppose that η2 = 0.80 in one study vs. η2 = 0.70 in another. Does such imply that the first study has a truly larger effect size? Without knowing any more details of each study, it is entirely possible that η2 = 0.80 has resulted more from the way the independent variable was operationalized than anything else. The following principle should be heeded:

Where each experiment or study “comes from” is just as important as the numerical measure one is choosing to contrast and compare studies because that numerical measure (e.g., Cohen’s d, η2, etc.) is a function of all those underlying influences.109

The above is key. When one traces the roots of the equation for d or η2, etc. one gets into the very numbers and characteristics of the data. Effect sizes are not simply summary statistics; they are general reports of the data. Just as comparing the sample mean from one study to another depends on what went into each sample mean, so it is also the case with effect sizes. To emphasize the point, consider the following statement: “The mean grade in one class is a bit higher than another.” What does that tell us? It tells us that the mean grade in one class is a bit higher than in the other! To go further into analysis would require us to examine what went into each mean, and so on, which is a much deeper investigation such that in some cases could even reverse the direction of the effect. The takeaway point here is that summary statistics never tell the full story. The deeper story is told in the actual data points, and the even deeper story is told in how the data were obtained and measured. “The student’s GPA is 4.0” means nothing unless we know more about what courses were taken, how courses were graded, difficulty of each course, and so on. Data is experience, and unless you know the experience intimately, summary statistics can only provide crude approximations.

2.30 Central Limit Theorem

There are many situations where theoretical results are facilitated by assuming a normal sampling distribution. For example, when we obtain a sample mean and wish to compare it to the sampling distribution of the mean, we need to assume the sampling distribution takes on a normal (or at minimum, approximately normal) shape. If the original population distribution from which we have sampled is known to be normal, then it stands that the sampling distribution will likewise be normal. However, in most cases we do not know the shape of the original population distribution and hence we need a way nonetheless to assure the normality of the sampling distribution. The central limit theorem, or CLT, allows us to know the shape of the sampling distribution, whatever the shape of the original parent population.

The univariate central limit theorem of the mean holds that if we let x1, x2, ..., xn be independent observations from any population with mean μ and finite variance σ2, then $\sqrt{n}\left( \overline{x} - \mu \right)/\sigma$ has an approximate normal distribution, N(μ,σ2) for large sample sizes. In the limit, as sample size increases, the sampling distribution of the mean takes on an increasingly normal shape.

Likewise, we can state the multivariate central limit theorem more formally as if we let X1, X2, ..., Xn be independent observations from any population with mean μ and finite covariance matrix Σ, then $\sqrt{n}\left( \overline{X} - \mu \right)$ has an approximate normal distribution, Np(μ,Σ) for large sample sizes (Johnson & Wichern, 2007). As in the univariate case, if the parent population is normal, the multivariate distribution of the sample will be normal. The extent to which the parent population is normal speeds up the process for normality of the sampling distribution as sample size increases. For a more formal definition and characterization of the central limit theorem, see Casella and Berger (2002, p. 236). Note that in general, the central limit theorem is about the behavior of random variables, not specifically the mean μ or mean vector μ. In this sense, there are many different “versions” of the central limit theorem. Most students come across the CLT in the context of the behavior of the mean, but such should not imply the CLT is uniquely about the mean.

2.31 Covariance and Correlation

A mathematical relation, or simply a relationship between two variables, is a subset of the Cartesian product (Figure 2.8). That is, if any pairs are not represented in a given correspondence between two (or more) variables, this, by definition, denotes a relationship between the two (or more) variables.110

Take a moment and note how general and nonspecific the idea of a relationship is between variables. If we delete even one pair out of the totality of pairs, we have illustrated a relationship! Why are we emphasizing this matter? For the reason that the next time someone says to you, “There is a relationship between x and y in my data,” it should be answered with “Well, of course there is, but more importantly, is the relationship in any way interesting?” The point we are making here is that between any two or more variables, there is virtually always a relationship that exists among them in the sample and in the population. How could there not be? Do you really think all pairs in any Cartesian plot could ever be represented for any empirical pairing of x and y? Of course not! Hence, the naming of a relationship between two or more variables is usually an obvious and uninteresting statement. Now, usually, professing a relationship means more. Let’s consider what it could mean now.

A relationship between variables can take on many forms. For two continuous variables, a literal infinite number of curves can be drawn. Said differently, a literal infinite number of pair deletions could occur in the Cartesian plot such as to generate a relationship. Often, of most interest (and convenience) is that of linear relationships. Both the covariance and correlation are measures of the linear association or relationship between two variables.

The covariance between two random variables x and y is given by


Cov(x,y) = E[(xi−μx)(yi−μy)]
(2.67)

which we can also express as the integration of areas for the continuous case,


∫ − ∞ + ∞∫ − ∞ + ∞(xi−μx)(yi−μy)f(xi,yi)dxdy
(2.68)

and111


$$\sum\limits_{x_{i = 1}}^{n}{\sum\limits_{y_{i = 1}}^{n}{\left( x_{i} - \mu_{x} \right)\left( y_{i} - \mu_{y} \right)p\left( x_{i},y_{i} \right)}}$$
(2.69)

for discrete random variables.

The sample covariance between variables x and y is given by


$$s_{xy} = \frac{\left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( x_{i} - \overline{x} \right.} \right)\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right)}{n - 1}$$
(2.70)

or, less commonly, can also be written as


$$s_{xy} = \frac{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{x_{i}y_{i} - n\overline{x}\overline{y}}}{n - 1}$$

We can see that the covariance, of course, requires variation in both x and y since if either $\left( x_{i} - \overline{x} \right)$ or $\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right)$ are equal to 0, then


$$\begin{array}{l} {s_{xy} = \frac{\left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( x_{i} - \overline{x} \right.} \right)\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right)}{n - 1}} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = \frac{0}{n - 1} = 0} \\ \end{array}$$

That is, if you have no variation, you cannot quantitatively assess relationship. Relating age in years to income level won’t work if everyone in your sample has the same income. Statistical relationships do not work well with constants. You need variability in both variables.

The covariance is in natural or original units of both x and y, and hence it is possible that a small or large covariance is mostly reflective of the scale on which x and y are measured. That is, a scale on which there is little variation on either x or y or both might reflect a data set with small covariance even if the degree of linear relationship is relatively strong. For this reason, it is useful to standardize the covariance. We do this by dividing the covariance by the product of standard deviations on x and y. Doing so gives us the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient, rxy,


$$r_{xy} = \frac{\frac{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{\left( x_{i} - \overline{x} \right)\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right)}}{n - 1}}{\sqrt{s_{x_{i}}^{2} \cdot s_{y_{i}}^{2}}} = \frac{{cov}_{xy}}{\sqrt{s_{x_{i}}^{2} \cdot s_{y_{i}}^{2}}}$$
(2.71)

which has a theoretical range from −1, a perfect negative linear relationship, to +1, a perfect positive linear relationship. A value of rxy = 0 indicates no linear relationship between variables. Again, the word “linear” here is emphasized, since it is entirely possible that there still is a relationship between variables, only that it is not linear. For example, the scatterplot in Figure 2.9 will likely yield a correlation close to 0, yet the relationship is still relatively apparent.112

It is easy to see as well that if either sxi2 or syi2or both equal 0, indicating no variation in variables, then rxy is undefined. Again, just as was the case for the covariance, the correlation coefficient is a measure of (standardized) co-variation in variables. If there is no variation in one or both variables, the correlation coefficient is not defined. The correlation coefficient rxy is a consistent estimator, that is, rxy→ρ as n→∞. There are multiple ways to interpret the correlation coefficient. For an excellent discussion, see Thirteen Ways to Look at the Correlation Coefficient (Rodgers & Nicewander, 1988).

2.31.1 Why Does rxy Have Limits −1 to +1?

The limits of −1 to +1 on rxy are such as a result of the product of variances, sxi2 ⋅ syi2 in the denominator, which implies that the numerator covxycan be no larger in absolute magnitude than the denominator $\sqrt{s_{x_{i}}^{2} \cdot s_{y_{i}}^{2}}$. The denominator in rxy essentially provides the maximum “variability” that is available to be accounted for in the numerator, and hence the numerator covxy can never be larger, in absolute value, than the denominator. The sign of the covariance will indicate whether rxy is positive or negative, but the magnitude of rxy can be no greater than |1|. A more formal proof of this can be found in Casella and Berger (2002, p. 172).

2.31.2 Covariance and Correlation in R and Python

We can quite easily compute covariance and correlation in R via the cov() and cor() functions. As an example, consider the following two vectors of data:113

> x <- c(0, 4, 7, 9, 10)
> y <- c(3, 4, 6, 7, 8)
> cov(x, y)
[1] 8.25
> cor(x, y)
[1] 0.9794398

We see above that the covariance between the two vectors is 8.25, while the standardized covariance, or correlation, is equal to 0.979. Note that the covariance is not that large, yet the correlation has a very large magnitude. This is due to the standardization of the covariance. Never assume that simply because the covariance is relatively small (or large) that the correlation will likewise be small (or large). They are distinct numerical measures. A large covariance does not necessarily imply an equally large correlation.

In Python, we can compute the correlation very easily, where we first produce data vectors on number of coins in your pocket and money in your bank account using scipy.stats:

coins = [0, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12, 15, 20, 25, 28, 30, 35]
money = [20000, 30000, 40000, 45000, 55000, 60000, 80000, 100000, 130000, 150000, 200000, 230000, 250000, 300000, 350000, 400000]
import scipy.stats as stats
corr, _ = stats.pearsonr (coins, money)
corr
0.9923

The Pearson correlation between coins and money is estimated to be 0.9923.

2.31.3 Correlating Linear Combinations

Just as we can covary or correlate random variables, we can also covary or correlate linear combinations of random variables. For example, consider the following two linear combinations,


z = a′x = a1x1 + a2x2 +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + apxp

and


w = b′y = b1y1 + b2y2 +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + bpyp

The covariance between these linear combinations is given by


$$s_{zw} = \frac{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{\left( z_{i} - \overline{z} \right)\left( w_{i} - \overline{w} \right)}}{n - 1}$$
(2.72)

and likewise, the sample correlation between z and w is114


$$r_{zw} = \frac{s_{zw}}{\sqrt{s_{z}^{2}s_{w}^{2}}}$$
(2.73)

Why would we want to covary or correlate linear combinations? For the same reason why we would want to correlate any two random variables. A linear combination is just a composite of variables. What is a single variable? It is also a composite variable, only a very simple composite made up of only itself. To illustrate, consider once more the linear combination for w:


w = b′y = b1y1 + b2y2 +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + bpyp

Now, simplify w so that it becomes only a function of y1, that is, w = b′y = b1y1. If b1 = 1, then b1y1 = y1 and hence, w = y1. Thus, the linear combination is simply composed of y1. That is, the motivation for correlating linear combinations is the same as that for single variables, only that linear combinations are usually more complex than single variables; they are “made up” of more “stuff” (i.e., variables) than a single random variable. However, the concept is the same. Many multivariate methods, in one way or another, correlate linear combinations, though it may not appear this way on the surface. As an example, analysis of variance and discriminant analysis do so, which are all versions of an underlying multivariate correlational methodology called canonical correlation. We discuss canonical correlation more thoroughly later in the book.

2.31.4 Covariance and Correlation Matrices

Many statistical procedures, such as principal components analysis or factor analysis, do not operate on individual variables. Rather, they operate on matrices of variables. That is, the object of analysis is not a variable but instead a matrix. As an example, principal components analysis performs (linear) dimension reduction on the covariance matrix directly. The covariance matrix for the population is given by


$$\Sigma = \left( \begin{array}{l} {\sigma_{11}\,\,\,\,\,\sigma_{12}\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \cdot \cdot \,\,\,\,\,\sigma_{1p}} \\ {\sigma_{21}\,\,\,\,\,\sigma_{22}\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \cdot \cdot \,\,\,\,\,\sigma_{2p}} \\ {\,\, \cdot \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, \cdot} \\ {\sigma_{p1}\,\,\,\,\,\sigma_{p2}\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \cdot \cdot \,\,\,\,\sigma_{pp}} \\ \end{array} \right)$$
(2.74)

where σ12, for instance, is the covariance between variables 1 and 2, and σ11 is the covariance of a variable with itself, which is the variance, since


$$\left. s_{xy} = \frac{\left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( x_{i} - \overline{x} \right.} \right)\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right)}{n - 1}\rightarrow\frac{\left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( x_{i} - \overline{x} \right.} \right)\left( x_{i} - \overline{x} \right)}{n - 1}\rightarrow\frac{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( x_{i} - \overline{x} \right)^{2}}{n - 1} = s_{x}^{2} \right.$$

Of course, as usual in statistics, we rarely if ever have access to the population covariance matrix, and hence instead of Σ, we usually only have S, the sample covariance matrix, which, when corrected by n/(n−1), is an unbiased estimator of Σ. That is, $E\left( {\frac{n}{n - 1}S} \right) = \Sigma$.

The sample correlation matrix is the standardized covariance matrix, given by115


$$R = \left( \begin{array}{l} {1\,\,\,\,\,\,\, r_{12}\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \cdot \cdot \,\,\, r_{1p}} \\ {r_{21}\,\,\,\,\, 1\,\,\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \cdot \cdot \,\,\, r_{2p}} \\ {\,\, \cdot \,\,\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, \cdot} \\ {r_{p1}\,\,\, r_{p2}\,\,\,\,\, \cdot \cdot \cdot \,\,\,\, 1} \\ \end{array} \right)$$
(2.75)

Both the covariance and correlation matrices are symmetric matrices, which, as we will see in our review of linear algebra, implies that for an arbitrary matrix A,


A = AT

That is, the original matrix is equal to that of its transpose, or, otherwise said, if we exchange rows for columns and columns for rows, we will obtain the same matrix. Why is this fact important? It is important because there are special properties associated with symmetric matrices, including the fact that eigenvectors are guaranteed to be pairwise orthogonal only for symmetric matrices whose eigenvectors correspond to distinct eigenvalues, which will have significant implications for methods such as principal components. Symmetric matrices are also necessarily square matrices (i.e., same number of rows as columns), which allows for eigen decomposition to be performed on such matrices, whereas for nonsquare and asymmetrical matrices the more general SVD (singular value decomposition) is typically preferred.

2.32 Z-Scores and Z-Tests

Recall the definition of a z-score, or standardized score,


$$z = \frac{y_{i} - \mu}{\sigma}$$

A z-score is actually a comparison of two deviations, one in the numerator, yi − μ, to one in the denominator, σ, the standard deviation. Thus, one can interpret the z-score as a comparison of how large the current raw score deviation is to what is “standard” in the given distribution we are working with. A z-score of 0 arises only if yi − μ = 0, which means the raw score does not deviate at all from the mean. Should the distribution have no dispersion, then σ will equal 0 and the z-score will be undefined. It is also worth noting that the numerator represents a centering of yi. That is, whenever we subtract the mean, we are centering the given observation. Hence, the z-score can also be defined as the standardized centered observation. Centering plays a significant role in statistical modeling and will be revisited when we survey regression analysis and other methods in the book. Many times, we wish to center predictors by subtracting the mean so that the predictor value at zero is more meaningful. Centering often makes the intercept of a model more interpretable.

We can easily demonstrate centering and computing z-scores in R. Consider the following distribution of raw scores:

> x <- c(0, 4, 8, 9, 10)
> mean(x)
[1] 6.2

We now center the distribution by subtracting the mean,

> x.center <- x – mean(x)
> x.center
[1] -6.2 -2.2 1.8 2.8 3.8
> mean(x.center)
[1] -1.775489e-16

116Note that the mean of the new centered distribution is equal to 0 (within rounding error). To produce z-scores, we can then divide by the standard deviation, while also confirming that the mean of the new z-scores is equal to 0 and the standard deviation is equal to 1:

> z = (x-mean(x))/sd(x)
> z
[1] -1.4949527 -0.5304671 0.4340185 0.6751400 0.9162614
> mean(z)
[1] -2.218278e-17
> sd(z)
[1] 1

Z-scores form the basis for the standard normal distribution which has a mean equal to 0 and a standard deviation equal to 1. Pay notice to the word “standard” here. Most empirical distributions that are normal (or approximately so) do not have a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1.

2.32.1 Z-Tests and T-Tests for the Mean

Recall the one-sample z-test for the mean,


$$z_{M} = \frac{\overline{y} - E\left( \overline{y} \right)}{\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}} = \frac{\overline{y} - \mu_{0}}{\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}}$$
(2.76)

The reader will recall from introductory courses that we typically do not know the standard error of the mean, $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$, and instead require an estimate of it,


$${\hat{\sigma}}_{M} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$
(2.77)

When we use s as an estimate of σ, the resulting statistic is no longer a z statistic; it is instead distributed as t, which gives rise to the t-test for one sample,


$$t = \frac{\overline{y} - E\left( \overline{y} \right)}{\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}}$$
(2.78)

It is a fact of mathematical statistics that the t-distribution converges to the z-distribution as degrees of freedom increase without bound. This is the case because the variance of t is defined as


σt2 = v/(v−2)
(2.79)

and so as v→∞, the above ratio goes to one, that is,


$$\lim\limits_{v\rightarrow\infty}\left( \frac{v}{v - 2} \right) = 1$$

For two samples, the z-test for means is given by117


$$z_{M} = \frac{E\left( {\overline{y}}_{1} \right) - E\left( {\overline{y}}_{2} \right)}{\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}}{n_{1}} + \frac{\sigma_{2}^{2}}{n_{2}}}} = \frac{\mu_{1} - \mu_{2}}{\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}}{n_{1}} + \frac{\sigma_{2}^{2}}{n_{2}}}}$$
(2.80)

The justification for summing the variances in the standard error is due to the variance-sum law that holds that if y1 and y2 are normally distributed and independent random variables with means μ1 and μ2 and variances σ12 and σ22, the difference between the random variables has a mean equal to μ1 − μ2 with variance σ12 + σ22. That is, the standard error of the difference between means is equal to,


$$\sigma_{{\overline{y}}_{1} - {\overline{y}}_{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}}{n_{1}} + \frac{\sigma_{2}^{2}}{n_{2}}}$$
(2.81)

What is more, due to the central limit theorem, the sampling distribution of ${\overline{y}}_{1} - {\overline{y}}_{2}$ is approximately normal for increasingly large samples and is theoretically normal for n→∞.

As for the one-sample situation, we rarely, if ever, know the values of σ12 and σ22 and hence estimate them with s12 and s22,


$$t = \frac{E\left( {\overline{y}}_{1} \right) - E\left( {\overline{y}}_{2} \right)}{\sqrt{\frac{s_{1}^{2}}{n_{1}} + \frac{s_{2}^{2}}{n_{2}}}} = \frac{\mu_{1} - \mu_{2}}{\sqrt{\frac{s_{1}^{2}}{n_{1}} + \frac{s_{2}^{2}}{n_{2}}}}$$
(2.82)

For unequal sample sizes (not unequal variances), we pool variances, which means we will require an estimated standard error not of the mean, but of the difference between means,


$$\begin{array}{l} {{\hat{\sigma}}_{diff} = \sqrt{{\hat{\sigma}}_{pooled}^{2}\left( {\frac{1}{n_{1}} + \frac{1}{n_{2}}} \right)}} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = \sqrt{\frac{\left( n_{1} - 1 \right)s_{1}^{2} + \left( n_{2} - 1 \right)s_{2}^{2}}{n_{1} + n_{2} - 2}\left( \frac{n_{1} + n_{2}}{n_{1}n_{2}} \right)}} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.83)

The classic two-sided null and alternative hypotheses for the t-test is

H0: μ1 = μ2 H1: μ1 ≠ μ2

With the pooled variance estimator, the t-test becomes


$$t = \frac{E\left( {\overline{y}}_{1} \right) - E\left( {\overline{y}}_{2} \right)}{\sqrt{\frac{\left( n_{1} - 1 \right)s_{1}^{2} + \left( n_{2} - 1 \right)s_{2}^{2}}{n_{1} + n_{2} - 2}\left( \frac{n_{1} + n_{2}}{n_{1}n_{2}} \right)}}$$
(2.84)

evaluated on (n1−1) + (n2−1) degrees of freedom. It should be noted that sometimes the numerator of these difference tests are stated with an assumed value D0 under H0 for the difference, $E\left( {\overline{y}}_{1} \right) - E\left( {\overline{y}}_{2} \right) - D_{0}$. In theory at least, this allows the researcher to specify a value for D0 other 118than zero; however, zero will typically be taken as the default value unless there is good substantive reason to set it unequal to zero.

2.33 Unequal Variances: Welch-Satterthwaite Approximation

Recall that the two-sample t-test assumes equal population variances, that is, σ12 = σ22. If there is evidence to suggest that variances are unequal, then an approximation can be used. The approximation adjusts for the degrees of freedom of the test where instead of degrees of freedom equaling (n1−1) + (n2−1), they are computed as


$$df = \frac{\left( n_{1} - 1 \right)\left( n_{2} - 1 \right)}{\left( 1 - c \right)^{2}\left( n_{1} - 1 \right) + c^{2}\left( n_{2} - 1 \right)}$$
(2.85)

where,


$$c = \frac{s_{1}^{2}/n_{1}}{\frac{s_{1}^{2}}{n_{1}} + \frac{s_{2}^{2}}{n_{2}}}$$

Likewise, approximate confidence intervals may be computed via


$$\left( {\overline{y}}_{1} - {\overline{y}}_{2} \right) \pm t_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{s_{1}^{2}}{n_{1}} + \frac{s_{2}^{2}}{n_{2}}}$$
(2.86)

2.34 Paired Data

When working with paired data, we require making inferences about μ1 − μ2 just as in the independent-samples t-test, only that now, observations are not independent; they are matched or naturally paired. What is interesting about paired data on relatively simple data sets is that the concept of paired data generalizes to much more complex models (e.g., elaborate longitudinal models, blocking designs, and multilevel models with repeated measures). The numerator of the t-test is the same, since $E\left( {\overline{y}}_{1} - {\overline{y}}_{1} \right)$ is still μ1 − μ2. However, the standard error of the difference in means incorporates the fact that the samples are paired, and is equal to


$$\sigma_{{\overline{y}}_{1} - {\overline{y}}_{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2} + \sigma_{2}^{2} - 2\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\rho}{n}}$$
(2.87)

where ρ is the correlation between variables y1 and y2. Note that for ρ = 0, the numerator under the radical sign is simply σ12 + σ22 as it was in the unpaired situation, that is, σ12 + σ22 − 2σ1σ2(0) = σ12 + σ22. However, for ρ ≠ 0, the standard error for paired data has an expectation less than that of independent data, since 2σ1σ2ρ is being subtracted from the sum, σ12 + σ22. In practice, the t-test usually takes the form of computing mean difference $\overline{d}$ between columns, and like in the independent-samples t-test, subtracting a null value of D0, which yields,119


$$t = \frac{\overline{d} - D_{0}}{s_{d}/\sqrt{n}}$$
(2.88)

The resulting t is evaluated on n−1 degrees of freedom since there is now only a single column of differences, in effect, it is now a one-sample test. A confidence interval for the mean difference can be computed,


$$\overline{d} \pm t_{\alpha/2}\frac{s_{d}}{\sqrt{n}}$$
(2.89)

where sd is the standard deviation of the column of difference scores.

This concludes our brief overview and review of fundamental statistics typically taught in introductory courses. If any of the information in this chapter seemed entirely “new” to you, it is suggested that you review a relatively deep introductory statistics text to review the essentials of statistical inference. Ott and Longnecker (2016) is a very good choice in this regard.

We now move on to the second major pillar of statistics and machine learning, that of linear algebra.

2.35 Review Exercises

  1. 1. Precisely define the frequentist approach to probability.
  2. 2.Distinguish between unconditional and conditional probability.
  3. 3. Distinguish between statistical independence and mutual exclusiveness. Can two events that are independent simultaneously be mutually exclusive? Why or why not?
  4. 4. Discuss some of the benefits and dangers of adopting a Bayesian approach to updating belief, specifically in reference to Bayes’ theorem.
  5. 5.Discuss what happens to the normal density as σ2→0. In the limit, as variance becomes equal to 0, what shape does the normal density take on?
  6. 6. Using the Shapiro-Wilk test in R, evaluate the null of normality for a random sample of 10,000 observations having mean equal to 0 and standard deviation equal to 1.
  7. 7. Compare the univariate density to that of the multivariate density. How are they similar? Different?
  8. 8. Using the binomial distribution, compute the probability of obtaining 10 heads out of 10 flips of a presumably fair coin, where “fair” implies a probability of heads equal to 0.5.
  9. 9. How can irreducible error become reducible when measurement is taken into account in the bias-variance trade-off? How can the variance of error be reduced?
  10. 10. Clearly distinguish between a p-value and an effect size.
  11. 11. Distinguish between covariance and Pearson’s correlation. Under what condition(s) would they be equivalent?

2.36 Linear Algebra and Matrices

Linear algebra is at the heart of virtually all multivariate statistics and machine learning. It is largely the vehicle by which many concepts in these domains are communicated and operationalized. Without linear algebra, though we could still in theory conceptualize what might be meant by a principal component or other multivariate objects for example, we would not be able to operationalize or define it narrowly or precisely. Linear combinations and other objects from linear algebra, in this case, allow us to do so. They allow for precise and rigorous definition. Through the language of linear algebra, we can define exactly what we mean by a host of statistical objects. Linear algebra is the technical “bedrock” of much of multivariate statistics and machine learning.120

We proceed rather briskly and review and recap the most relevant aspects of linear algebra for a general understanding of multivariate statistics and machine learning and preview topics featured in the book. Readers having a prior course in the subject will undoubtedly recognize most, if not all, of this material. Readers new to the area will find the topics informative, yet may wish to supplement this section with one or more of the excellent books that have been written on the subject for a slower and more inclusive gradual introduction. As promised, we do not simply present a bunch of concepts and expect the reader to figure out their relevance later. Instead, we take great care in foreshadowing and previewing where many of these concepts will find their place in later sections in the book.

As an example, the idea of orthogonality is meaningful to the specialist in linear algebra in its own right, but for the learner of statistics and machine learning it will be helpful to recognize how the concept is featured in multivariate and machine learning models. We will need to survey the actual models later to fully appreciate its relevance, but the foreshadowing of how it (and other concepts) will be used will help make these concepts a bit more “applied” in the sense of appreciating where they belong in the big multivariate/machine learning universe.

2.36.1 Vectors

A vector is an array or listing of numbers, where the following is a column vector with elements x1 through xn,


$$x = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ x_{n} \\ \end{array} \right\rbrack$$

Because we are working in the real numbers, we denote x ∈ ℝn and the listing of numbers x1 through xn denotes the elements of the vector x. In this book, if not indicated specifically, it can be assumed that we are working in the field of real numbers, and hence where “x ∈ ℝn” is not indicated, it can be generally assumed. None of the work featured in this book features the use of complex numbers (x ∈ ℂn).

In R, we can create a simple vector by:

> x <- c(0, 2, 5, 8, 10)
> x
[1] 0 2 5 8 10

Creating the same vector in Python is just as easy:

import numpy as np
x = [0, 2, 5, 8, 10]
x
Out[294]: [0, 2, 5, 8, 10]
x_1 = [[0], [2], [5], [8], [10]]
x_1
Out[300]: [[0], [2], [5], [8], [10]]
121

2.36.1.1 Vector Spaces and Fields

A vector space is generally a space where vectors can be added and lengthened or shortened by scalars, which otherwise implies multiplication and obeys a series of rules featuring these two operations. That is, vector spaces generally describe spaces where the operations of addition and multiplication occur. A field is an algebraic structure that satisfies a list of properties such as commutative and associative laws of addition and many more. Many algebraic structures are special cases of others when certain properties are removed. For the purposes of this book, many of the mathematical operations that underlay methodologies occur in vector spaces because they feature vector and matrix operations.

2.36.1.2 Zero, Unit Vectors, and One-Hot Vectors

A vector of all zeroes is called the zero vector, while the unit vector has length or magnitude equal to one. Vectors that contain all zeroes except for a single value of “1” are also known as one-hot vectors, a term arising from electrical engineering where a circuit is either “on” or “off.” One-hot encoding can also mean changing status from text to a number, for instance, “red = 0” which is essentially similar to dummy coding variables.

2.36.1.3 Transpose of a Vector

The transpose of a column vector is obtained by writing columns as rows, in the case of


$$x = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ x_{n} \\ \end{array} \right\rbrack$$

we have


xT = [x1,x2,x3,⋅⋅⋅,xn]
(2.90)

where xT denotes the transpose of x. Often (as we do in this book), the transpose is written as x′. More formally, the transpose of a matrix is obtained by exchanging rows for columns and columns for rows in a matrix. Some properties of transposes include (AT)T = A, (AB)T = BTAT, (A+B)T = AT + BT, (cA)T = cAT, |AT|=|A|, among others.

Transposing vectors (and as we will see, matrices) is a useful operation in the computation of many statistics and quantities used in machine learning. For one, and as we will see, it allows for the multiplication of vectors and matrices. In R, the transpose function is t(). In Python, the relevant function is numpy.transpose().

Vectors can be conceived as simply a listing of numbers as above, which is often useful in a computer science context in which we simply would like to identify a listing of numbers. However, a geometrical or visual representation of a vector is often extremely useful, especially in scientific 122or physical contexts. As an example, consider a visual representation of the vector x′ = [3,2,1]in Figure 2.10.

Note that the first element of the vector, 3, is plotted along the x-axis, the second element (2) is plotted along the y-axis, and the third element, 1, is plotted along the z-axis. As a result of the vector being defined as a specific location in space defined by its coordinates, in a physical context a vector is often said to have magnitude and direction.

It is also worth noting that the plotting of the vector in Figure 2.10 generates a new geometrical object, in this case a cuboid. Many objects in linear algebra have geometrical counterparts. We will return to this point later in our survey of determinants.

2.36.1.4 Vector Addition and Length

Only vectors of the same dimension can be added or subtracted. We add vectors element by element,


$$x + y = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ x_{n} \\ \end{array} \right\rbrack + \left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} y_{1} \\ y_{2} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ y_{n} \\ \end{array} \right\rbrack = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} {x_{1} + y_{1}} \\ {x_{2} + y_{2}} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\, \cdot} \\ {x_{n} + y_{n}} \\ \end{array} \right\rbrack$$
(2.91)

The analogous operation holds for the subtraction of vectors as well. The length of a vector is the square root of the sum of squared terms (or “components”),


$$L_{x} = \sqrt{x_{1}^{2} + x_{2}^{2} + \cdot \cdot \cdot + x_{n}^{2}}$$
(2.92)

For reasons that will become clearer later, in many settings we often desire the length of a vector to be unity, which means the sum of squared elements is equal to 1, that is,123


$$L_{x} = \sqrt{x_{1}^{2} + x_{2}^{2} + \cdot \cdot \cdot + x_{n}^{2}} = 1$$
(2.93)

The length of a vector is also referred to as the Euclidean norm, also known as the l2 norm of that vector more generally defined as


$$\begin{array}{l} \left| \middle| x \middle| \middle| {}_{2} = \sqrt{x_{1}^{2} + x_{2}^{2} + \cdot \cdot \cdot + x_{n}^{2}} \right. \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = \sqrt{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}x_{i}^{2}}} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = \sqrt{x^{T}x}} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.94)

where xTx is the dot product (to be reviewed shortly). The l1 norm, on the other hand, instead of summing squares, sums absolute values,


$$\left| \middle| x \middle| \middle| {}_{1} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left| x_{i} \right|} \right.$$
(2.95)

As we will see later, eigenvectors will typically have length set (or constrained) to unity in methods such as principal components analysis. This is done mostly for convenience so that the variance accounted for by the component cannot grow simply as a function of its length. Setting lengths of vectors equal to unity is common practice in many other statistical methods as well. The important point for now is that what matters most in many of these procedures is not the actual length of the vector, but the relative distance between the values. “Normalizing” a vector to unit length does not disrupt these distances. That is, the ratios between values remain the same.

We can lengthen or shorten vectors by multiplication by a scalar or constant c, as in the following where each element of the vector x1, x2, x3, ..., xn is being multiplied by the constant c:


$$cx = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} {cx_{1}} \\ {cx_{2}} \\ {cx_{3}} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ {cx_{n}} \\ \end{array} \right\rbrack$$

In Figure 2.11 is an example of multiplying a vector by a constant of 2, which has the effect of lengthening (or “stretching”) the vector. In the same picture we multiply a vector by ½ (from the origin), forcing it into the opposite direction.

In R, we can easily add two vectors:

> x <- c(0, 2, 5, 8, 10)
> y <- c(3, 6, 8, 10, 12)
> x + y
[1] 3 8 13 18 22

Multiplying a vector by a constant is also easily accomplished in R. For example, we will assign124

z = x + y and multiply by a constant c = 2:
> z = x + y
> 2*z
[1] 6 16 26 36 44

Vectors can be added in Python as follows:

import numpy
a = numpy.array([1, 2, 3])
b = numpy.array([4, 5, 6])
a + b
Out[7]: array([5, 7, 9])

We can easily multiply a vector by a constant by:

x1 = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
x2 = 2 * x1
x2
Out[318]: array([2, 4, 6, 8])

2.36.1.5 Eigen Analysis and Decomposition

The idea of multiplication by a constant may seem trivial in this abstract context but is very significant in multivariate settings because many transformations by a matrix can be equated to the lengthening of a vector. For instance, in eigen analysis, as we will see later, the product of a matrix with a vector is equated to simply a lengthening of that vector by multiplication by a constant,125


Ax = λx
(2.96)

where A is some matrix, often a covariance or correlation matrix, post-multiplied by x, a vector. The equality states that this product Ax is equal to the pre-multiplication of x by a constant, λ. The constant λ is referred to as an eigenvalue of the transformation and x an associated eigenvector. As we will see, eigenvectors are unique only up to multiplication by a constant. Many seemingly complicated multivariate methods have eigen analysis at their core and feature this very simple idea of multiplying a vector by a constant, the constant in this case being the eigenvalue of the transformation.

To solve for λ and x we can start by rewriting Ax = λx as


(A−λI)x = 0

When we set the determinant equal to 0, that is, |A−λI|=0, we can then find values of λ to then solve for x.

As an example, consider the following matrix and the computation of the characteristic polynomial on matrix A to obtain eigenvalues:


$$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} {3\,\,\,\,\, 2\,\,\,\,\, 1} \\ {1\,\,\,\,\, 3\,\,\,\,\, 2} \\ {1\,\,\,\,\, 2\,\,\,\,\, 3} \\ \end{array} \right\rbrack$$

We calculate |A−λI|:

$\left| A - \lambda I \middle| = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} {3\,\,\,\,\, 2\,\,\,\,\, 1} \\ {1\,\,\,\,\, 3\,\,\,\,\, 2} \\ {1\,\,\,\,\, 2\,\,\,\,\, 3} \\ \end{array} \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} {\lambda\,\,\,\,\, 0\,\,\,\,\, 0} \\ {0\,\,\,\,\,\lambda\,\,\,\,\, 0} \\ {0\,\,\,\,\, 0\,\,\,\,\,\lambda\,\,} \\ \end{array} \right\rbrack = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} {3 - \lambda\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, 2\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, 1} \\ {\,\,\, 1\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, 3 - \lambda\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, 2} \\ {\,\,\, 1\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, 2\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, 3 - \lambda\,\,} \\ \end{array} \right\rbrack \right.$ =  − (λ−6)(λ−2)(λ−1)
