> bartlett.test(weight ~ group, data)
   Bartlett test of homogeneity of variances
data: weight by group
Bartlett’s K-squared = 2.8786, df = 2, p-value = 0.2371

We do not have evidence to reject the assumption of equal variances (p = 0.2371). It is wise to conduct various equality of variance tests on the same data to see if they report similar findings. If the assumption of equality of variances is rejected, while transformations on data are an option, what is even more important is to get curious as to the why behind the violation. Why are the variances unequal? Get curious from a scientific perspective before you address the problem statistically (e.g., such as with a transformation). Slight violations usually do not require any kind of remediation as ANOVA is quite robust to slight violations of assumptions. However, if violations of assumptions such as variances become more pronounced, especially for unequal sample sizes, corrective measures should be taken, or at minimum, results should be reported with requisite caveats. A nonparametric test such as the Kruskal-Wallis may be a useful option.

We assume the reader is already somewhat familiar with ANOVA and have only skimmed the surface as it pertains to applications of ANOVA in software. One should always verify assumptions (e.g., normality), check for equality of variances, and be sure that observations are independent of one another to the best of one’s ability. Excellent theoretical resources on ANOVA include Hays (1994) and Kirk (1995). Denis (2021a) covers ANOVA in much more detail and features more software demonstrations in R and SPSS as well. Denis (2021b) also features ANOVA using Python.

4.2 Factorial ANOVA and Higher-Order Models

We have surveyed the one-way classic ANOVA in which there is only a single independent variable. Factorial ANOVA features more than a single independent variable, usually with the goal of seeking out interactions, that of the effect of one variable being contingent upon one or more other variables.198

For example, it may be true that income (response variable) is found to be a function of education, but that relationship may depend, statistically, on what level of age we consider. Hence, there is said to be a statistical interaction between education and age. Note carefully that this conclusion alone does not imply that age “affects” education in any way, or that age or education “affect” income. Based on the statistical interaction alone, we do not have evidence to make any kind of “impact” statement. To even approximate such a claim would require a strong research design or feature variables that have such a naturally “organic” connection to one another (e.g., increasingly colder temperatures “affect” the rate at which water freezes).

Visualizing interactions is the best way to get a feel for them. For instance, in Figure 4.1 there is an interaction between gender and drug dose:

We can see from the plot that for females, scores increase from low dose to high dose. However, for males, the opposite effect holds. That is, scores begin high at low dose and then decrease to high dose. This interaction is rather pronounced; all that is technically required for an interaction is that lines be nonparallel. A bit of thought reveals that interactions in sample data are almost always present. The real question, however, is whether we can infer such a sample interaction in the population from which the data were sampled.

4.3 Random-Effects and Mixed Models

As we have said, the ANOVA we have surveyed thus far in this chapter has assumed that levels on the independent variable are fixed. To reiterate, in theoretical repetitions of an experiment, it was assumed we would be using the same levels each time. This is why it was called a fixed-effects analysis of variance.

When we do not assume levels are fixed but instead random samples of a population of possible levels, the factor is no longer fixed but instead random, which gives rise to the random-effects analysis of variance model. For example, if one were interested in the effects of dosage on headache symptoms, in a fixed-effects model, one could purposely and strategically select levels 1 vs. 2 vs. 3 mg of drug. The advantage of this approach is that once we obtain means, we can compare mean differences across the drug groups. The disadvantage of this approach is that we have no knowledge of differences between other possible levels of drug (e.g., 1.5 vs. 2.3, for instance). Is variance in headaches a function of these other levels as well? Under the fixed model comparing 1 vs. 2 vs. 3 mg, we simply do not know. The comparison of means does not allow us to infer such things. However, if instead we designate drug to be a random effect, and selected the levels 1, 2, 3 or others randomly, then if the factor is found to be statistically significant, we can conclude differences not only between doses 1, 2, and 3, but instead on drug doses in general, which includes levels not observed in the sample. This is the benefit of random effects; they allow us to conclude that levels not seen in the sample are also associated with variation in the response variable. Random effects allow for a more general statement.

When a model contains a blending of fixed and random factors, it is referred to as a mixed model. The classic general form of the linear mixed model is given as follows:


Y = Xβ + ZU + ε
(4.14)

where β are the fixed parameters and U the random, and where U and ε are independent zero mean random vectors. Both the random effects in U and ε are assumed to be normally distributed. The assumption that U is normally distributed may be unrealistic, however, and hence an alternative nonparametric random-effects model may be more appropriate. We survey that possibility a bit later in this section. For an excellent overview of both parametric and nonparametric random-effects and mixed models, see Nguéma et al. (2021).

In the model in (4.3), for fixed factors, mean comparisons are of interest. For the random factor, variance on the response variable is what is being modeled. Simple as this brief summary may sound, mixed models become theoretically complex very fast. In fact, books (and careers) are devoted to the subject. See Demidenko (2004) for a book-length treatment on the complexity of mixed models.201

4.3.1 The Meaning of a Fixed vs. Random Effect

A precise definition of fixed vs. random effects is critical. As we will discuss shortly, there is sometimes a misunderstanding in the literature that random effects are defined by simply having numerous statistics such as intercepts and slopes of which we would like to take an average. For example, consider Figure 4.2, where there are numerous intercepts which might represent starting points of trajectories for given individuals in a longitudinal study, as well as numerous slopes that emphasize a difference in trajectories over time. We see that there is quite a bit of variation in both intercepts and slopes in the sample.

What distinguishes an effect to be random or fixed in this case is not the fact that we have many intercepts or slopes in our sample data. Indeed, one could have a thousand different trajectories for different individuals and still identify the slope as a fixed effect. It may make more sense however to consider it random, but that identification is not determined by the fact that we have numerous slopes. It is determined by the fact that we consider the slopes as randomly sampled from a wider population of slopes and thus having their own probability distribution. This is the key component to considering an effect to be random, not the volume of variation in the sample. Whether to regard an effect as fixed or random is entirely a modeling decision and is embedded in the assumptions we make for the model. It is never “implicit” in the data, though that isn’t to say the data cannot “help” us make decisions on how to model the effect.

4.3.2 Is the Fixed-Effects Model Actually Fixed? A Look at the Error Term

The reader may recall that the standard linear model assumes an error term that is normally distributed with finite variance. That is, in the standard linear model, εi ∼ N(0,σε2) and εi, εi′ are independent for i ≠ i′. But what is the error term, εi, really? It is a random effect! Hence, when we are performing a fixed-effects ANOVA, we are, in reality, performing a mixed model. The random effect in the standard linear model is εi, the variance component is σε2, that is, V(εi). As put so 202well by Fox (2016, p. 701), “Unlike the standard linear model, linear mixed-effect models include more than one source of random variation – that is, more than one random effect.” And while this, logically, may be true, the custom is not to refer to fixed models as mixed models simply as a result of including an error term. By tradition, a mixed model is defined by having a blending of fixed and random factors beyond that of the error term. Our point is merely that if we look at these models in a bit of a deeper way, we come to realize that purely fixed-effects models actually do not exist unless we either fix the error term or leave it out entirely, which would be the same thing as setting it to zero.

4.3.3 Mixed Models in Python

We can fit a mixed model in Python using statsmodels. We adapt the following example from statsmodels.org where the growth curves of pigs are modeled. 4.3.4 Mixed Models in R

We now run the same mixed model on the pig data using lmer() in lme4 (Bates et al., 2015). The package lme4 has extensive mixed modeling capacities and is highly recommended for all things mixed models. We also load the package geepack (Hojsgaard et al., 2006) which contains the pig data:

> library(lme4)
> library(geepack)
> print(summary(lmer(‘Weight ~ Time + (1|Pig)’, data=dietox)))

Note that the designation (1|Pig) communicates the nesting or hierarchical structure of the data, such that weight is being modeled as a function of time, but nested within pig, where pig is a random effect, which implies in this case that it is a level 2 variable and that we wish to model the variance of its residuals. That is, our output should return a variance due to pig, since the model holds that pigs were randomly sampled from a larger population of potential pigs that could have appeared in the sample.

4.4 Multilevel Modeling

The standard linear model typically estimated by least-squares regression is appropriate for independent observations, which implies that errors will also typically be independent. That is, it is assumed that εi, εi′ are independent for i ≠ i′. The standard linear model is usually not appropriate, or at minimum severely compromised, when this assumption is violated.

One type of dependency that naturally arises in applied settings is that of clustering, where εi, εi′ are not independent for i ≠ i′. A classic example of where this type of clustering or dependency surfaces is in classrooms within a school, where students may share the same teacher. We say students are nested within classrooms. It would be unreasonable to expect that errors within classrooms are not related. However, this is only one potential source of nesting in the hierarchy that we may consider. Classrooms exist in schools, and schools exist in states. That is, schools within the same state, and their errors, are likely not independent of one another. As we build the nesting hierarchy from scores to groups, we develop a multilevel structure to observations, thus the name multilevel modeling. Multilevel modeling allows one to deal with the non-independence of errors that manifest at each level of the hierarchy.

4.4.1 A Garbled Mess of Jargon

The jargon and confusion of words and terminology that surrounds random, mixed, and multilevel modeling is nothing short of extraordinary. Historically, statistics is a discipline that has always had a difficult time having consistency in how it defines its terms because many concepts arise independently in different applied disciplines. Mixed models may arise independently in ecology, for instance, while also being developed (or “rediscovered”) in sociology as well. Slightly different names may be given to the models, which makes learning (and teaching) them very difficult for the newcomer. It’s as if in addition to learning the rather difficult method one has to become keen on how the vocabulary differs by area of specialization. This not only applies to mixed models, it applies to many statistical techniques; jargon can easily ruin your day in attempting to learn them.

It is exceptionally important however when discussing these models to be very exact and precise regarding what we are referring to. Multilevel models are often casually referred to as hierarchical linear models, random-effects models, mixed models, and other identifiers, and it can become greatly confusing for the newcomer to these models to appreciate or understand what these models are all about beyond these generalities.205

First, we need to make a distinction between structure vs. model. The term “multilevel” is a structure, it is not actually a “model,” though it is referred to as such in the literature (i.e., multilevel modeling), for reasons that will become clear shortly. It is best to reserve the word “multilevel” to describe structure, though in what follows we ourselves at times adopt the conventional phrase “multilevel modeling” as well and make no distinction. So long as one understands and appreciates the distinction, no harm is done. However, to the newcomer to multilevel models, a great deal of confusion can arise from not understanding what a structure is compared to a model. As we will see, multilevel structures can be analyzed in a host of different ways, only one of which is via random and mixed effects.

Second, a multilevel structure need not necessarily imply a mixed model, nor does a multilevel structure need to incorporate any random effects. They usually do include such random effects, but the definition of what is a multilevel (structure) does not absolutely require it. In reading the literature, however, the newcomer to these models is rarely made aware of this. Multilevel models are automatically assumed to consist of random effects. This implied association is not a necessary one. As we will see, for a multilevel model to have one or more random effects (other than the naturally occurring error terms), this must be assumed or imposed by the researcher. No multilevel structure, by itself, necessarily implies or must otherwise contain random effects.

As an example, consider the classic case once more of ten students per classroom in which there are five classrooms. Students are nested within classrooms, as students in one classroom will likely share features or common experiences over students in another classroom. They will be more similar than students in a competing classroom. Statistically, error terms of students within classroom will not be independent of one another. We can assume their errors will be correlated. In practice, if we desired, we could account for the multilevel structure by calculating separate regressions on each classroom. We could then compare the regressions by way of computing a product term that incorporates classroom. Notice that there is no random effect implied here and yet we are dealing with the multilevel structure just the same. The multilevel structure is still intact without requiring any random effects. It may not be the most “ideal” of solutions in modeling the multilevel structure, but the point is that addressing the multilevel structure does not necessarily imply, nor require, the modeling of random effects.

The purest or most accurate definition of a multilevel model often given or implied in the literature is that it allows for residual analyses at each level of the hierarchy. And while this is true, there is nothing in a multilevel structure that absolutely requires this level of analysis. The emphasis should be on “allows” in the previous phrase, not “necessitates.” Again, notice that we could quite easily analyze each regression or mean structure separately by classroom and assess residuals within each classroom. We do not require any random effects to do so. Including random effects, however, is often a very good idea, as we now discuss.

4.4.2 Why Do Multilevel Models Often Include Random Effects?

If a multilevel structure by itself does not necessarily imply the inclusion of random effects, how do random effects therefore come to rise in a multilevel model? The answer is that the researcher has to impose them on the multilevel structure through an assumption of the modeling. Take note again that we are imposing the random effect(s); they are not necessarily implied in the multilevel structure. Again, and referring to our previous example, observed variance in intercepts or slopes in exploratory analysis of data cannot serve as justification alone to model such as random effects.

To emphasize this important point, consider an excellent description of multilevel modeling by one of the chief leaders in this area:206

Given that the intercept and slope coefficients vary randomly over group …

The above is completely correct, but what does it mean? The key point to recognize from the above is that it is us who decides whether such coefficients “vary randomly” or not. The fact that there is observed variation in them is not enough. We have to decide to model the intercept and slope as fixed or random based on the assumptions we are imposing on the model. If there is no observed variation, we probably would not model them as random effects, but in theory, we still could.

Consider another typical presentation of the multilevel model:

Because multilevel models contain a mix of fixed effects and random effects, they are sometimes known as mixed-effects models.

The problem with the above is that, as mentioned, not only do multilevel structures not necessarily require the inclusion of random effects, but that even if they did, they do not need to be modeled using a traditional mixed-effects modeling approach. A structural equation modeling approach, for instance, could be just as fruitful. Once more, a multilevel structure does not necessarily imply a fixed, random, or mixed model.

In summary then, the intercepts and slopes typically found in hierarchical (or “nested” designs) do not know where they “came from.” We have to make those decisions as part of the assumptions we are imposing on our analysis. In writings about multilevel models, authors too often imply that because there is observed variation in intercepts and slopes, it necessarily implies the corresponding effect should be modeled as a random effect. This is simply not the case. Observed variation in statistics, whatever they may be (e.g., intercepts, slopes, means, standard deviations, etc.), is insufficient reason for modeling such as random effects. The decision to model as a random effect has all to do with how the observed realizations are conceptualized to have originated and how such statistics would likely behave in theoretical repetitions of the experiment. These are decisions made by the investigator.

A multilevel structure does not necessarily imply the presence of random effects. Random effects arise in such structures because the researcher decides to model them (intercepts and slopes) as such, but a multilevel structure need not necessarily imply the inclusion of these effects. Intercepts and slopes could, in theory, even when exhibiting much variation, be estimated as fixed effects.

4.4.3 A Priori vs. Post-Hoc “Nesting”

There is another important and key distinction to make with regard to multilevel ideas and nesting. In appreciating what a multilevel structure actually is, it is just as pedagogical to consider what a multilevel structure is not. Consider the classic one-way randomized analysis of variance design in which participants (n = 5 per sample, e.g., y11 is observation 1 in sample 1) are randomly assigned to treatments (Figure 4.3).207

Are participants nested within treatment groups? Are the errors within treatment groups expected to be related? No. Because of the random assignment to treatment groups, an individual’s score a priori is not expected to be related to any other individual’s score. Why is the qualifier “a priori” essential here? It is important because after they undergo treatment, we might indeed observe their errors to be related. For example, if being in the first treatment group involves ingesting a particular dosage of an energy drink, whereas other groups did not receive any energy drink, we would of course expect errors to be related within that first group relative to other groups. Those drinking energy drinks will become more “similar” due to the treatment they have received. They are now a “nest” due to receiving the treatment.

However, the above similarity is only apparent after the treatment has been administered, not before. Before receiving treatment, there was no reason to expect that the score of one participant would be related to the score (and error) of a second participant within that group. Participants in this case are not nested a priori, but once the treatment is applied, they are, in a sense, nested post-hoc. But this post-hoc nesting idea is immaterial to multilevel modeling. It would only play a role if we decided to build on the current study to perform a second one and used the treatment groups as starting points. In such a case, those drinking energy drinks would start out the new study having correlated errors. That is, those receiving the treatment would be more “alike” compared to others not receiving the treatment.

The key takeaway from this discussion is that for hierarchical, multilevel, or nesting structures to exist, errors should be expected to be related prior to receiving treatment, not after. Students in a classroom being taught by the same teacher are expected to have related errors well before they receive any treatment or intervention. This is the “likeness” that we wish to account for in multilevel structures. While the classic one-way ANOVA (for instance) can actually be considered a multilevel structure (the reader may want to think of how), the errors within each treatment group are expected to be independent even if they become correlated once the treatment is applied and measurement occurs. What is most important for modeling decisions such as this is the expectation of how errors will behave prior to treatment, not after.

4.4.4 Blocking as an Example of Hierarchical/Multilevel Structure

When a researcher forces observations into blocks, the so-called randomized block design, this is an example and special case of a multilevel structure. Observations are nested within blocks. The nesting is induced or created by the researcher. For instance, if we put all first-grade school 208children in one block and all second graders in another block, it stands that observations within each respective block will be more similar than observations across blocks. The observations are level-one units, while the blocks are level two. For this reason, blocking designs are often analyzed as mixed models where the blocking factor is regarded as random. For readers to whom blocking designs may be entirely new, Kirk (1995) provides a good and deep introduction.

4.4.5 Nonparametric Random-Effects Model

Most multilevel models include at least one random effect that aids in dealing with the nesting structure and dependencies of observations. In the classic random-effects model, it is assumed that random effects are normally distributed. This assumption, however, may be untenable and we may wish to adopt instead, as we will be doing in many places in this book, a nonparametric approach that makes no (or at least fewer) assumptions about the distribution of the random effects. The nonparametric random-effects model can be considered a special case of the wider latent class model. The random-effects regression model is also commonly known as a mixture model in regression since it combines a mixture of regressions that helps deal with the potential heterogeneity of groups (Jiang and Guntuboyina, 2021).

As an easy example of a nonparametric random-effects model and to get an idea of how it differs from the classic parametric random-effects model, consider first the typical (parametric) random-intercept model that contains no predictors,


g[E(yij)] = αj

where it is assumed that the intercept terms αj are normally distributed with a given mean and variance, that is, αj ∼ N(μ,σ2). Traditionally, we would like to estimate the mean μ of these intercepts and more importantly their variance (σ2). The approach is parametric because we are imposing a probability model on the intercepts. In a nonparametric approach, we assume that the distribution of αj is indexed by an unspecified discrete mixing distribution of latent classes, where the intercept associated with a given class x is denoted by αxand the size of the given class is given by P(x), where αx is the location and P(x) the “weight” of the given node or class.

Simplified, the nonparametric model is given by


g[E(yij|,x)] = αx
(4.15)

which is simply the expectation of yij for a given class x, which will be subject to P(x). A two-level model in which predictors are included is a natural extension of (4.15), where now zij denotes the inclusion of predictors into the model:


$$g\left\lbrack E\left( y_{ij} \middle| z_{ij},x \right) \right\rbrack = \alpha_{x} + {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{K}{\beta_{k} \cdot z_{ijk}}}$$
(4.16)

Key to note is that what makes the model nonparametric is not the inclusion of predictors in zij, but as was the case in the intercept-only model, the fact that yij is a function of a mixing distribution of classes, x. To reiterate, E(yij) is a function of a probability distribution in the classic parametric model, whereas it is a function of a mixing distribution (classes) in the nonparametric counterpart. Random slopes, in addition to random intercepts, can also be included, giving rise to a full-scale multilevel nonparametric random-effects model.209

Multilevel models, as was generally the case for mixed models, are best implemented using R (e.g., lme4) software instead of Python. Latent Gold is a software program that can estimate latent class models and the special case of nonparametric random-effects models. In R, the package npmlreg (Einbeck et al., 2018) can be used to fit these types of models as well.

4.5 Repeated-Measures and Longitudinal Models

Often in research studies, measurements are taken over a series of days, weeks, months, or years, or even epochs, as in the case of attempting to estimate whether today’s rising temperatures are just normal long-term temperature variation versus human-made climate change. Models that involve a temporal component are often called repeated-measures models or within-subjects designs, or, more generally, longitudinal models or time series. The reader should be aware, however, that longitudinal models can comprise a whole host of models and complexities which can include mixed-effects components as well as elements of structural equation models. As noted earlier, jargon and terminology are often not consistent from discipline to discipline, and hence it behooves the reader to be cautious when coming across these and similar terms to learn exactly what the author or researcher means by them. Making assumptions as to what they mean will typically only lead to misunderstandings!

4.5.1 Classic Repeated-Measures Models

For lack of a better terminology, and to differentiate among repeated-measures approaches, we will refer to the repeated measures that typically assumes a sphericity structure for the covariance matrix to be that of classic repeated measures. The assumption of sphericity is essentially that of equal variances among differences between all possible pairs of within-subject conditions. An even more stringent assumption is that of compound symmetry that assumes all variances and covariances in the matrix of within-subject variables are equal. Both of these assumptions give rise to what we are calling the “classic” repeated-measures model to distinguish it from more sophisticated models such as random-effects, mixed-effects, and structural equation longitudinal models and growth curves. Latent growth models are a sub-type of the more general structural equation model in which the latent variables are typically such things as intercepts and slopes that “give rise” to time points.

Just as we did for classic ANOVA, we assume the reader has had at least some exposure to basic repeated measures under the assumption of a spherical covariance matrix. Hence, we move quickly and simply provide the expected mean squares for the classic model. There is a lot of theory and explanation that goes along with these expected mean squares and for readers unfamiliar, Hays (1994) and Denis (2021a) are good sources that explain how these expected mean squares arise, including how MS residual is a function of the intraclass coefficient ρ below.

The expected mean squares for the classic additive “sphericity” repeated-measures model are thus:210


E(MS subjects) = σe2 + Kσsubjects2
(4.17)


$$E\left( \text{MS}\,\text{treatment} \right) = \sigma_{e}^{2} + \frac{J{\sum\limits_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}}}{K - 1}$$
(4.18)


E(MS residual) = σe2 = σT2(1−ρ)
(4.19)

where J is the number of rows for subjects, K is the number of columns for treatment, ρ is the intraclass coefficient, and σT2 and σe2 are the total and error variances, respectively.

There are numerous ways of fitting repeated-measures models in R. The function aov() in R has easy capabilities for fitting such models (see Denis, 2021a for details). Many packages are also devoted to fitting repeated-measures or longitudinal models, for example the mmrm package (Sabanes et al., 2024). Repeated-measures models can also be fit in a variety of ways in Python. Probably the easiest way is via statsmodels using AnovaRM. The following is sample code (output not shown) for a basic one-way repeated measures where the dependent variable is y, the subject variable is person, and the repeated measure is time:

from statsmodels.stats.anova import AnovaRM
print(AnovaRM(data=df, depvar=‘y’, subject=‘person’, within=[‘time’]).fit())

4.6 Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA)

Univariate ANOVA allows for more than a single independent variable or factor but only allows for a single response or dependent variable. The name univariate derives from this fact, that of a single response. When there exists more than a single response variable, we enter into multivariate territory. Multivariate analysis of variance, or “MANOVA” for short, is defined by having more than a single continuous response variable.

The multivariate hypothesis about mean vectors can be stated as follows,


$$H_{0}:\left( \begin{array}{l} \mu_{11} \\ \mu_{21} \\ \mu_{31} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ \mu_{j1} \\ \end{array} \right) = \left( \begin{array}{l} \mu_{12} \\ \mu_{22} \\ \mu_{32} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ \mu_{j2} \\ \end{array} \right) = \left( \begin{array}{l} \mu_{13} \\ \mu_{23} \\ \mu_{33} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ \mu_{j3} \\ \end{array} \right)... = \left( \begin{array}{l} \mu_{1p} \\ \mu_{2p} \\ \mu_{3p} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ \mu_{jp} \\ \end{array} \right)$$
(4.20)

which is evaluated against an alternative hypothesis that somewhere among the set of mean vectors is a difference, for example of one possibility, that of a mean vector difference between the first two groups (inequality statement is slightly informal here),211


$$H_{1}:\left( \begin{array}{l} \mu_{11} \\ \mu_{21} \\ \mu_{31} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ \mu_{j1} \\ \end{array} \right) \neq \left( \begin{array}{l} \mu_{12} \\ \mu_{22} \\ \mu_{32} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ \mu_{j2} \\ \end{array} \right) = \left( \begin{array}{l} \mu_{13} \\ \mu_{23} \\ \mu_{33} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ \mu_{j3} \\ \end{array} \right)... = \left( \begin{array}{l} \mu_{1p} \\ \mu_{2p} \\ \mu_{3p} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ {\,\, \cdot} \\ \mu_{jp} \\ \end{array} \right)$$
(4.21)

4.6.1 Suitability of MANOVA

When is it appropriate to perform a MANOVA over an ANOVA? The answer cannot simply be “when there is more than a single continuous response,” despite misleading cookbook approaches to data analysis sometimes advising on such a poor strategy. Indeed, analyzing sex differences on response variables IQ and amount of gasoline consumed in one’s vehicle in the past week would make little sense for the reason that the response “variate,” that is, the combination of variables on the response side, makes little if any substantive “sense.” Can it be analyzed? Yes, but on an applied level, is not a hypothesis we would likely be interested in. The key to MANOVA is not to analyze multiple responses simultaneously; it is to analyze multiple responses that in some sense “go together” to produce a variate. Simultaneous analysis of reading speed and grade point average would be a variate of more interest in an applied setting. Or, another example might be skull measurements as a function of prehistoric epoch (Anderson, 2003). The takeaway point is that when one combines multiple responses into a single model, one should have a reason for doing so over and above simply producing a multivariate model.

With that substantive rationale and caveat in place, there are statistical benefits to conducting a MANOVA over multiple ANOVAs, which include control over an inflating type I error rate. For instance, three different univariate ANOVAs conducted separately carries an increasingly large type I error rate (e.g., 0.05 per test, p = 0.05). The probability of making no type I errors (r = 0) across n = 3 tests each set at 0.05 is a binomial random variable,


$$\begin{array}{l} {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, p\left( r \right) = \left( \begin{array}{l} n \\ r \\ \end{array} \right)p^{r}\left( 1 - p \right){n - r}} \\ {p\left( 0,3,0.05 \right) = \left( \begin{array}{l} 3 \\ 0 \\ \end{array} \right)\left( 0.05 \right)0\left( 0.95 \right)3 = 0.86} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.22)

and hence the probability of at least one type I error is equal to 1 − 0.86 = 0.14. More formally, the probability of at least one type I error across k-tests can be approximated by


p(type  I  error≥1) = 1 − (1−αPC)k
(4.23)

A single MANOVA on the three response variables conducted simultaneously keeps the type I error rate fixed at whatever αis set to for the MANOVA (e.g., 0.05). This is a statistical benefit to performing a MANOVA over several ANOVAs; however, if substantively the MANOVA does not make sense, as discussed, a MANOVA model makes no sense to conduct for statistical reasons alone. The scientific or substantive rationale should dominate over the statistical here.

4.6.2 Extending the Univariate Model: Hotelling’s T2

The easiest and most direct way of extending the univariate model to the multivariate one is via the simple between-subjects t-test and generalization to Hotelling’s T 2, which is the multivariate counterpart where we model more than a single continuous response variable. This essentially will generalize to more complex models, but we focus on the t-test because it emphasizes the core principles in going from a univariate to multivariate landscape.

Recall the univariate t-test discussed earlier in our review of essential statistics:212


$$\begin{array}{l} {t = \frac{E\left( {\overline{y}}_{1} \right) - E\left( {\overline{y}}_{2} \right) - \delta_{0}}{\sqrt{\frac{\left( n_{1} - 1 \right)s_{1}^{2} + \left( n_{2} - 1 \right)s_{2}^{2}}{n_{1} - n_{2} - 2}\left( {\frac{1}{n_{1}} + \frac{1}{n_{2}}} \right)}}} \\ {\,\,\, = \frac{\mu_{1} - \mu_{2} - \delta_{0}}{\sqrt{\frac{\left( n_{1} - 1 \right)s_{1}^{2} + \left( n_{2} - 1 \right)s_{2}^{2}}{n_{1} - n_{2} - 2}\left( {\frac{1}{n_{1}} + \frac{1}{n_{2}}} \right)}}} \\ \end{array}$$

Consider now what happens when we square t,


$$t^{2} = \frac{\left( {\overline{y}}_{1} - {\overline{y}}_{2} \right)^{2}}{\frac{\left( n_{1} - 1 \right)s_{1}^{2} + \left( n_{2} - 1 \right)s_{2}^{2}}{n_{1} - n_{2} - 2}\left( {\frac{1}{n_{1}} + \frac{1}{n_{2}}} \right)}$$

Next, we express the denominator as an inverse so that there is no denominator:


$$t^{2} = \left( {\overline{y}}_{1} - {\overline{y}}_{2} \right)\left\lbrack {\frac{\left( n_{1} - 1 \right)s_{1}^{2} + \left( n_{2} - 1 \right)s_{2}^{2}}{n_{1} - n_{2} - 2}\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{n_{1}} + \frac{1}{n_{2}}} \right\rbrack} \right\rbrack^{- 1}\left( {\overline{y}}_{1} - {\overline{y}}_{2} \right)$$

Finally, we end up with


$$T^{2} = \frac{n_{1}n_{2}}{n_{1} + n_{2}}\left( {\overline{y}}_{1} - {\overline{y}}_{2} \right)'\left( S^{- 1} \right)\left( {\overline{y}}_{1} - {\overline{y}}_{2} \right)$$
(4.24)

For the one-sample mean vector, the corresponding T2 is the following:


$$\begin{array}{l} {T^{2} = \left( \overline{y} - \mu_{0} \right)'\left( {\frac{1}{n}S} \right)^{- 1}\left( \overline{y} - \mu_{0} \right)} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = n\left( \overline{y} - \mu_{0} \right)'S^{- 1}\left( \overline{y} - \mu_{0} \right)} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.25)

T2 is distributed as $\frac{\left( n - 1 \right)p}{\left( n - p \right)}F_{p,n - p}$, where p and n − p are degrees of freedom, where p is the number of variables and n is sample size. For details on likelihood ratio tests in relation to T2, see Johnson and Wichern (2007, pp. 217–218). Confidence regions can also be computed for T2 and multivariate populations (see Johnson & Wicher, 2007, pp. 220–221).

4.6.3 Multivariate Test Statistics

In the univariate ANOVA setting, there is only a single F-test to perform. In the multivariate setting, because of the alternative way covariances of response variables may be structured within groups on the independent variable(s), multiple multivariate tests have been developed and are available in virtually all software. These include Wilk’s lambda, Pillai’s trace, Roy’s largest root, and the Lawley-Hotelling’s trace. We provide only a cursory “glimpse” into the variety of multivariate tests. For a full development of how these tests come about, see Johnson and Wichern (2007).213

Wilk’s lambda, Λ, is given by


$$\Lambda = \frac{\left| E \right|}{\left| H + E \right|} = \frac{\left| E \right|}{\left| T \right|}$$
(4.26)

where under the null hypothesis,


$$\Lambda = \frac{\left| E \right|}{\left| 0 + E \right|} = \frac{\left| E \right|}{\left| E \right|} = 1.0$$

and where H is the “hypothesis” matrix and E the “error” matrix. Note that Wilk’s is an inverse criterion, meaning that if there is no effect, we would expect Λ to equal 1.0. This is unlike the F-ratio in univariate ANOVA, where larger F’s are preferred over smaller.

On the opposite extreme, if H accounts for all of the variation, then,


$$\Lambda = \frac{\left| 0 \right|}{\left| H + 0 \right|} = \frac{\left| 0 \right|}{\left| H \right|} = 0$$

Wilk’s lambda can also be expressed in terms of eigenvalues of E − 1H:


$$\Lambda = {\prod\limits_{i = 1}^{s}\frac{1}{1 + \lambda_{i}}}$$
(4.27)

where λi are the eigenvalues extracted from the analysis.

Pillai’s trace is defined as


$$V^{(s)} = {tr}\left\lbrack {\left( E + H \right)^{- 1}H} \right\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{s}\frac{\lambda_{i}}{1 + \lambda_{i}}}$$
(4.28)

Note that Pillai’s uses all eigenvalues (often called “roots”), λi. If we use only the largest of these roots, this gives rise to Roy’s largest root. That is, Roy’s largest root is simply the largest eigenvalue extracted and hence represents only the largest dimension underlying the data. Roy’s largest root is especially useful if one dimension dominates all others, which translates into one eigenvalue being much larger than the others. When the distribution of eigenvalues is more spread out, Pillai’s is more appropriate since presumably more than a single dimension is of interest.

Lastly, Lawley-Hotelling’s trace is simply a sum of eigenvalues and is thus given by


$$U^{(s)} = \text{tr}\left( E^{- 1}H \right) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{s}\lambda_{i}}$$
(4.29)

4.6.4 Evaluating Equality of Covariance Matrices: The Box-M Test

Recall that in univariate ANOVA, we were required to evaluate the assumption that all variances were equal. In the multivariate counterpart, we not only have variances to deal with; we also have covariances. Hence, the assumption now includes that all covariances across levels (or cells) of the independent variable are equal, that is,214


H0: Σ1 = Σ2 = Σ3... = Σp
(4.30)

where Σp are the p covariance matrices for each population under levels of the independent variable.

There are different approaches to evaluating this assumption. One is simply a crude (yet still useful) visual approach to learn whether the covariance matrices are relatively similar to one another to deem their population counterparts at least approximately equal and proceed with the MANOVA. The Box-M test is another approach that evaluates this assumption and is available in R in the biotools package (da Silva, 2021) under the boxM test, which can be easily demonstrated directly from the package on the iris data:

> library(biotools)
> data(iris)
> boxM(iris[, -5], iris[, 5])
Box M-test for Homogeneity of Covariance Matrices
data: iris[, -5]
Chi-Sq (approx.) = 140.94, df = 20, p-value < 2.2e-16

The assumption under the null is that population covariance matrices are equal. For these data, we reject the null (p = 2.2e-16) and infer the alternative hypothesis that at least two covariance matrices differ. When covariance matrices differ, it behooves the researcher to have a look at such matrices and to consider substantive reasons as to why they may differ. Never obtain a statistical result without carefully considering what it might imply about your data on a scientific, not only statistical, level. For additional theory on the test, see Johnson and Wichern (2007).

4.6.5 MANOVA in Python

We can conduct a basic MANOVA in Python using statsmodels. In the following we conduct a MANOVA on some random data where we generate 20 samples (n_samples = 20) on five responses (n_dim = 5) with three levels on an independent variable (n_classes = 3):

import numpy as np
from statsmodels.multivariate.manova import MANOVA
n_samples = 20
n_dim = 5
n_classes = 3

We produce the random data using np.random.randn() where X is the independent variable (or “exogenous” variable) side of the equation and y the response variable (or “endogenous” variable):

y = np.random.randn(n_samples, n_dim)
X = np.random.randint(n_classes, size=n_samples)

Note that the number of classes for X (i.e., 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, etc.) is designated to equal the size of the n_samples specified in y, so that each case gets assigned a class (we print only a few cases for y):215

y
Out[31]:
array([[-0.68321194, -1.17229168, 0.86179734, 1.26790702, 0.53352012],
  [-0.95366322, -1.06883607, 1.13404045, -0.71916984, -1.37089659],
  [ 0.18602881, -0.22453474, 0.02700791, 0.17279279, 0.13939027],
  [-1.45080321, -0.20265485, 0.57581133, -0.39974093, 0.93340395],
X
Out[33]: array([0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0])

In the following we specify the endogenous variable (i.e., the response variable) as well as the exogenous variable (the independent variable):

manova = MANOVA(endog=y, exog=X)
print(manova.mv_test())

We see that none of the multivariate tests reject the null having p-values equal to 0.3765, and hence we do not have sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis of equality of mean vectors.

4.6.6 MANOVA in R

Carrying out a MANOVA in R can be done in a variety of ways via several packages. In the following we conduct a MANOVA on the iris data. We construct the dependent variable “variate” by concatenating (i.e., joining) the iris features and identify species as the independent variable:

> data(iris)
> dv <- cbind(iris$Sepal.Length, iris$Sepal.Width, iris$Petal.Length, iris$Petal.Width)
> iv <- iris$Species
> manova <- manova(dv ~ iv, data = iris)
> summary(manova)
Df Pillai approx F num Df den Df Pr(>F)
iv 2 1.1919 53.466 8 290 < 2.2e-16 ***
Residuals 147
---
Signif. codes: 0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

We see that species yields a statistically (not necessarily substantively) significant effect (p < 0.001).216

To obtain effect sizes, we can use the package effect size (Ben-Shachar, 2020) to obtain a partial Eta-squared statistic:

> library(effectsize)
> effectsize::eta_squared(manova)
# Effect Size for ANOVA (Type I)
Parameter | Eta2 (partial) | 95% CI
-----------------------------------------
iv | 0.60 | [0.54, 1.00]
- One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00].>

We see that the partial Eta squared associated with the iv is 0.60, meaning that species explains approximately 60% of the variance in the response variable variate, that is, the linear combination of sepal length, sepal width, etc. Next, we conduct a discriminant analysis on species, a kind of follow-up analysis to MANOVA in the way of generating discriminant functions:

> library(MASS)
> discrim <- lda(iv ~ dv, CV=F)
> discrim

We can see that the first discriminant function accounts for a much larger proportion of the trace (0.9912) than the second (0.0088), which implies the first function is more “important” statistically than the second and better differentiates flower groups (i.e., the function has a greater eigenvalue). We are also given coefficients of the linear discriminants. But why are we seeing a discriminant analysis here? Though we introduce and discuss discriminant analysis in more detail later in the book as a classifier (if you have never studied discriminant analysis, you may choose to skip to that section now), it behooves us to briefly discuss here how discriminant analysis can be considered the “reverse” of the multivariate analysis of variance.

4.7 Linear Discriminant Analysis (as the “Reverse” of MANOVA)

The linear discriminant analysis model (that we have just briefly seen in our MANOVA example) features a binary or polytomous categorical response variable in which a linear combination of predictors is sought that maximizes group differences on the response. Discriminant analysis is sometimes referred to as a filter model and a feature selection method in the data mining literature (Aggarwal, 2015). While at first glance, this may be challenging for the reader to grasp or “see” the big picture, the LDA model can actually be regarded as a “hub” model, that is, a model from which many other models can be considered scaled-up or scaled-down versions of the LDA model structure.

For one, it can be operationalized in a few different ways, including being the “opposite” of the MANOVA model. This is the interpretation that most interests us here to supplement our discussion of MANOVA and also understand the above output provided in R by the MANOVA follow-up analysis or, crudely, “post-hoc” analysis (though it is not strictly a post-hoc test as we are not attempting to control for any error rates, we are using the word “post-hoc” here merely descriptively). MANOVA and LDA are often conceived as opposites of one another, and many times, a discriminant analysis will be performed as a follow-up to MANOVA to help learn more about the underlying function(s) (called the discriminant function(s)) responsible for separating groups so efficiently.

In the above output, we came across via our post-hoc of MANOVA a set of discriminant functions (technically, they are not discriminant functions yet until we weight the corresponding coefficients with the variables, which is why R calls them linear discriminants):

Coefficients of linear discriminants:
LD1 LD2

dv1

0.8293776

-0.02410215

dv2

1.5344731

-2.16452123

dv3

-2.2012117

0.93192121

dv4

-2.8104603

-2.83918785

A full understanding of what a discriminant function is will have to wait until we survey discriminant analysis later in the book. However, for now, it is enough to know that we have obtained two discriminant functions as a result of there being three groups in our data (i.e., type of species). LD1 above is nothing more than a linear combination (called linear discriminant or more generally linear discriminant function after weighting by variables) that is weighted with values of sepal length, sepal width, petal length and petal width (i.e., dv1 through dv4). The linear combination generated by LD1 is thus:218

LD1 = 0.82(sepal length) + 1.53(sepal width) + (-2.20)(petal length) + (-2.81)(petal width).

In the machine-learning community, LDA is hardly ever conceived as the opposite of MANOVA but instead simply as a “classifier” of group membership and as a similar and potential alternative to logistic regression. However, even more generally, both LDA and logistic can be interpreted as special cases of a wider model, that of the generalized linear model, which we discuss later in the book. Under this umbrella, LDA is an application of the generalized linear model in which the response is (typically) binary, yet the model is still linear. That is, in this context, the link function is simply the identity function. This serves to contrast the LDA model with that of the logistic in which the link function is the log of the odds. For readers coming to this discussion with some background, this likely makes perfect sense. Without such background however, what we have just said will be entirely confusing and the reader will have to wait until further in the book when we survey discriminant analysis and the generalized linear model in more detail. She may wish to return to this section after that discussion.

We “unpack” the LDA model later in the book where we treat it in much more detail as a classifier. For now, however, we simply wish to note that the unifying aspects of LDA and MANOVA cannot be overstated. Where MANOVA seeks to find mean vector differences, the LDA model seeks to use those linear combinations to distinguish between groups. Extensions and special cases of these models are numerous, and pedagogically, understanding discriminant analysis gives rise to a variety of related models. Indeed, it is not an exaggeration to say that we could, if desired, title an entire book called Linear Discriminant Analysis and Variations because of the “hub” nature of LDA.

5 Simple Linear and Multiple Regression Models (and Extensions)

DOI: 10.4324/9781003376941-8

Linear regression has historically been the workhorse of statistics and is still so today (Stigler, 1986). What is more, many of the common techniques that are in use today are, in one way or another, extensions or derivatives of the basic linear regression model. Entire books and treatises are written on linear regression as well as entire courses that study the topic in outstanding depth. This is for good reason; regression is literally at the center of the universe of statistical modeling and that of machine learning algorithms. Excellent textbook-length sources on regression analysis alone include Fox (2016) and Draper and Smith (1998).

The history of regression ideas and concepts dates back to antiquity (Stigler, 1986). More recently, the origin of least-squares generally is said to lay with Legendre (1805) and later in the same century with Galton (1888), who applied regression to problems of heredity. The essential idea of regression is that of making predictions on one variable based on another (or more) while minimizing some function of the error in making those predictions. Least-squares regression is all about exploiting the correlation between two or more variables with the goal of reducing error in prediction in the one based on knowledge of the other(s). Regression, the concept, is the essence of what statistical modeling is all about.

5.1 Simple Linear Regression – Fixed Predictor Case

The simplest linear regression model features a single predictor whose values are regarded as fixed in advance. This classic simple linear regression model is given by


yi = β0 + β1xi + εi
(5.1)

where yi is the response variable, β0 is the intercept of the regression line, β1 is the slope, xi is the explanatory or independent variable, and εi is the error term, that part of yi that is unaccounted for by the systematic part of the model and where E(εi) = 0. The intercept is sometimes referred to as the offset or bias term. This terminology is common in neural networks discussed later in the book.

The systematic part of the model is β0 + β1xi, and thus the expectation of yi, that is, E(yi) = β0 + β1xi is equal to β0 + β1xi. The model has expectation E(yi) = β0 when xi = 0 since220


$$\begin{array}{l} {E\left( y_{i} \right) = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{i}} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}\left( 0 \right)} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = \beta_{0}} \\ \end{array}$$

We note that the model is linear in the parameters β0 and β1. This is the meaning of linear in linear regression. Note that this definition of linearity does not require the model to be linear in the input variable xi. Hence, the following model is still a linear model even though the input enters as a squared term:


E(yi) = β0 + β1xi2

In our model of regression in (5.1), as mentioned, we assume that our predictor is fixed. That is, if we were to refit the model on new data and thus replicate the experiment, we would use the same values on our predictor xi. If xi were random, we would presumably use different values since such values were presumably, at least on a theoretical level, drawn from a probability distribution. The theory we develop below assumes a fixed-effects model. For a treatment of random effects in regression, see Fox (2016, p. 228).

5.1.1 Parameter Estimates

Recall that we usually do not know values for β0 and β1 and hence typically require estimating them from sample data,


ŷ = β̂0 + β̂1xi
(5.2)

How shall values of β̂0 and β̂1 be chosen? Certainly not arbitrarily or at random. As is true for most statistical models, parameter estimates are chosen in such a way that they accomplish some goal, which is usually to minimize or maximize some objective function. In the case of simple linear regression, these estimates are chosen such that they minimize the sum of squared errors around the regression line in simple linear regression and regression surface in multiple regression. That is, we wish to minimize the difference between observed and values predicted by the function f̂(xi):


$$\begin{array}{l} {RSS = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}\left( y_{i} - \hat{f}\left( x_{i} \right) \right)^{2}}} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}\left( y_{i} - {\hat{\beta}}_{0} - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}{x_{ij}{\hat{\beta}}_{j}}} \right)^{2}}} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.3)

The general form of the above loss function is of the type (a−h)2 which is a quadratic term, and hence the loss is a quadratic loss, often referred to as an L2 loss. Regression itself in no way requires us to minimize the L2 loss specifically. We could have instead, for instance, minimized the L1 loss, which is that of taking the absolute value of differences, |a−h|. Regression that minimizes L1 is often referred to as robust regression for the reason that through taking absolute deviations, it places less weight on outlying or more extreme scores (i.e., it is more “robust” to such extremes compared to L2). This is in contrast to the L2 loss, which magnifies extreme deviations through squaring them. Deviations from medians instead of means can also make regression more robust. The takeaway point for now is that there are many possible loss functions one may choose. For instance, yet another loss function is the Huber loss (for details, see Murphy, 2022). The point is that the fact that we are minimizing the L2 loss in classic regression in no way implies that this is the one and only loss function that should dominate all work. However, it is undoubtedly the most 221common among loss functions and is typically used as a default. Ideally, however, whatever loss function is chosen should depend on the problem at hand.

The least-squares estimates for β̂0 and β̂1 are found by differentiating the residual sums of squares (RSS) with respect to both β0 and βj, of which the solutions can be shown to be equal to


$${\hat{\beta}}_{0} = \overline{y} - {\hat{\beta}}_{1}\overline{x}$$
(5.4)

for β̂0 and


$${\hat{\beta}}_{1} = \frac{\left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{\left( x_{i} - \overline{x} \right)\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right.}} \right)}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( x_{i} - \overline{x} \right)^{2}}$$
(5.5)

for β1. It is easy to see that computing the slope requires variation in both x and y. For instance, without variation in x, $\sum\left( x_{i} - \overline{x} \right)^{2}$ is equal to 0 and hence β̂1 is undefined.

The slope, in the case of zero intercept, can also be written as the inner product of x and y relative to the inner product of x, that is,


$${\hat{\beta}}_{1} = \frac{\left\langle {x,y} \right\rangle}{\left\langle {x,x} \right\rangle}$$
(5.6)

As we will see when we survey multiple regression shortly, the variance of β̂1 is equal to (XTX) − 1σ2 where σ2 is estimated by


$$\left. {\hat{\sigma}}^{2} = \frac{1}{N - p - 1}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}\left( y_{i} - {\hat{y}}_{i} \right.} \right)^{2}$$
(5.7)

where N is the number of cases and p the number of predictors in the model. To compute significance tests on β̂0 and β̂1 we of course require standard errors, which in scalar form can be calculated from


$$SE\left( {\hat{\beta}}_{0} \right)^{2} = {\hat{\sigma}}^{2}\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{n} + \frac{{\overline{x}}^{2}}{\left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( x_{i} - \overline{x} \right.} \right)^{2}}} \right\rbrack$$
(5.8)

and222


$$SE\left( {\hat{\beta}}_{1} \right)^{2} = \frac{{\hat{\sigma}}^{2}}{\left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( x_{i} - \overline{x} \right.} \right)^{2}}$$
(5.9)

With standard errors computed, we can easily compute confidence intervals for both β̂0 and β̂1 as β̂0 ± 2 ⋅ SE(β̂0) and β̂1 ± 2 ⋅ SE(β̂1), respectively.

A test of the null hypothesis that the slope β1 is equal to zero takes the form,


H0 : β1 = 0
(5.10)

against the statistical alternative hypothesis,


Ha : β1 ≠ 0
(5.11)

To evaluate the null, we compute a t-statistic,


$$t = \frac{{\hat{\beta}}_{1} - 0}{SE\left( {\hat{\beta}}_{1} \right)}$$
(5.12)

evaluated on n − 2 degrees of freedom.

Recall that the correlation ryx between x and y is given by


$$Cor\left( x,y \right) = r_{xy} = \frac{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{\left( x_{i} - \overline{x} \right)\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right)}}{\sqrt{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( x_{i} - \overline{x} \right)^{2}}\sqrt{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right)^{2}}} = \frac{{cov}_{xy}}{s_{x}s_{y}}$$

The square of ryx, that is, ryx2, is the proportion of variance accounted for in y based on knowledge of x. For example, for ryx2 = 0.70, this means that 70% of the variance in y is accounted for by x.

Note that many of the equations and formulas just reviewed feature the use of scalar algebra and not matrix algebra (though we did use matrices a tiny bit). This is because in the simple linear regression case working with scalars generally suffices. As we turn shortly to multiple regression however, we will require working with matrices, where it stands that all the scalar algebra just surveyed can be just as well presented via matrices. Most books on regression will present the theory in matrices because these books aim for the widest and most general presentation of linear regression possible, for which using scalars (e.g., simple linear regression) is but a special case.

We see from the output that price is statistically significant (p < 0.001). The multiple R-squared associated with the model is 0.02046, which means only approximately 2% of the variance in mileage is accounted for by price. If the effect is so small, why is price statistically significant? This is likely occurring due to the sample size of the data. The cars data has a total of 804 observations and hence rejecting the null hypothesis is relatively easy. Recall that the sensitivity of the p-value to sample size is something that should always be kept in mind when interpreting statistical tests. It may be tempting based on the statistical significance of price to say that price is an “important” predictor of mileage, but the multiple R-squared and Adjusted R-squared tell a different story with such small amounts of variance explained. 5.2 Multiple Linear Regression

In a simple linear regression there is only a single response variable and a single predictor. In a multiple regression model, there are several predictor variables that we model simultaneously in predicting the single response. In a multivariate multiple regression, there are not only several predictor variables but also several responses modeled simultaneously.

The multiple linear regression model is given by


yi = β0 + β1x1 + β2x2 +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + βpxp + εi
(5.13)

where E(εi) = 0 and thus with expectation equal to227


E(yi) = β0 + β1x1 + β2x2 +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + βpxp

or when expressed as conditional on x,


$$\begin{array}{l} {y = E\left( y \middle| x_{1},...,x_{p} \right)} \\ {\,\,\,\,\, = \beta_{0} + {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}{x_{j}\beta_{j}\,}}} \\ \end{array}$$

We can more concisely state the above model more generally as a function f(x),


$$f\left( x \right) = \beta_{0} + {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}{x_{j}\beta_{j}}}$$
(5.14)

where “f(x)” represents the function f given the input of x. The summation $\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}{x_{j}\beta_{j}}$ allows for as many predictors that we wish to include into the regression model.

As was true for the simple linear regression model, parameter values β0, β1, β2, ..., βp are not known and must be estimated from the sample data; hence the estimated multiple regression model is given by


ŷi = β̂0 + β̂1x1 + β̂2x2 +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + β̂pxp
(5.15)

Parameter values are chosen via ordinary least-squares, which is an optimization problem to minimize the sum of squared errors. The least-squares solution is the following, where X is a matrix of predictors and y a vector of responses:


β̂ = (XTX) − 1XTy
(5.16)

Though the matrix representation for multiple regression looks more complex than for simple regression, it is not difficult to appreciate the solution. Recall that taking inverses is conceptually equivalent to division in ordinary scalar algebra, and hence if we were to naïvely (though mathematically incorrectly) rewrite (5.16) in the most “familiar” way, we could express it as


$$\begin{array}{l} {\hat{\beta} = \left( XTX \right){- 1}X^{T}y} \\ {\,\,\,\,\, = \frac{X^{T}y}{\left( X^{T}X \right)}} \\ \end{array}$$

We now easily see that the numerator contains in a general way a product of X and y whereas the denominator contains only a product of X. Hence, in words, the solution for β̂ is answering the question of the extent to which X and y “go together” relative to only X. If X and y are highly linearly related (emphasis on linear here), then XTy will be much larger than XTX and hence the coefficient for β̂ will be larger than not. On the opposite extreme, if X and y are not very much linearly related, then XTy < XTX and XTy will be only a fraction of the total “cross-variation” present in XTX in the hypothetical division of quantities. Note that this matrix representation then is nothing more than a generalization of the single variable case in which228


$$\hat{\beta} = \frac{Cov_{xy}}{S_{x}^{2}}$$

where in this simpler case Covxy is analogous, in concept at least, to XTy and Sx2 to XTX.

The term


X† = (XTX) − 1XT,
(5.17)

that is, with y dropped, is the left pseudo-inverse of the nonsquare matrix X (Murphy, 2022, p. 367). Hence, in cases where the inverse does not exist, a pseudo-inverse may be an option. This is especially useful for nonsquare matrices since ordinary inverses exist only for square matrices. Pseudo-inverses are best computed using the singular value decomposition, or “SVD” (Murphy, 2022).

5.2.1 Minimizing Squared vs. Absolute Deviations

Recall that instead of squared deviations from predicted values, one could also take least absolute deviations of the kind


|yi−ŷi|
(5.18)

But what is the relationship between minimizing (yi−ŷi)2 vs. minimizing |yi−ŷi|? Minimizing |yi−ŷi| instead of (yi−ŷi)2 places less emphasis on extreme scores. That is, when we square yi − ŷi, differences are magnified due to the squaring. If we instead minimize |yi−ŷi|, large deviations are not so emphasized.

Minimizing |yi−ŷi| is featured in least-absolute-value regression, or “LAV” regression for short. Historically, however, (yi−ŷi)2 is usually first choice in a regression context as squares are usually more tractable mathematically than are absolute value deviations (Fox, 2016).

5.2.2 Hypothesis-Testing in Multiple Regression

The null hypothesis under test in the multiple regression model is the following:


H0 : β1 = β2 =  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  = βp = 0
(5.19)

against the statistical alternative hypothesis that at least one of the coefficients, βj, is not equal to 0. To evaluate, as we did in analysis of variance (ANOVA), we compute an F-ratio, but not identical to that in ANOVA,


$$F = \frac{\left( TSS - RSS \right)/p}{RSS/\left( n - p - 1 \right)}$$
(5.20)

which is evaluated on p and n − p degrees of freedom, where p is the number of predictors and n is the number of data points. TSS and RSS are the total and residual sums of squares, respectively. If the probability of F under the null hypothesis of ρ2 = 0 is small, we reject the null hypothesis of no effect and conclude ρ2 ≠ 0 in the population from which the data were drawn.229

5.2.3 Multiple Linear Regression in Python

We can conduct a multiple linear regression in Python using sklearn. As an example, we fit a regression on 100 data points with four features:

from sklearn.datasets import make_regression

n_informative=3, noise=20, random_state=99)
df = pd.DataFrame(X,columns = [‘x1’,’x2’,’x3’,’x4’])
df[‘y’] = y
df
