5.3 Geometry of Least-Squares

A picture is worth a thousand words, and this holds true for visualizing how least-squares works. Figure 5.1 is a depiction of the projection of a least-squares line based on two predictors, x1 and x2.

We can see the response y and its estimated values ŷ as a function of x1 and x2, the space spanned by these predictors. The projection is the ordinary least-squares estimate. The extent to which x1 and x2 overlap is the extent to which there may be collinearity among the predictors and hence they are taking up a similar space. This overview just scratches the surface regarding visualizing regression and is only meant to whet the reader’s appetite should one wish to follow up on the interesting topic of the geometry of linear models. For an excellent and much more detailed treatment, see Fox, The Vector Geometry of Linear Models (2016, Chapter 10).232

5.4 Gauss-Markov Theorem: What We Like about Least-Squares Estimates

Why do we like least-squares estimators so much? What is so attractive about them? What is most important about them can be summarized in the Gauss-Markov theorem, which asserts that the least-squares estimates of the parameters aTβ̂ have the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators when the errors are independently distributed with zero expectation and constant variance (Fox, 2016, p. 212). Least-squares estimators are often called “BLUE” which stands for best linear unbiased estimator. As noted earlier, the least-squares estimate of aTβ̂ is


aTβ̂ = aT(XTX) − 1XTy
(5.21)

for which the expectation is equal to


$$\begin{array}{l} {E\left( a^{T}\hat{\beta} \right) = E\left( a^{T}\left( XTX \right){- 1}X^{T}y \right)} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = a^{T}\left( XTX \right){- 1}X^{T}X\beta} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = a^{T}\beta} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.22)

The Gauss-Markov theorem holds that for any other linear estimator for which the expectation is aTβ (unbiased), for example, E(wTŷ) = wTy, the variance of the least-squares estimates aTβ̂ is less than or equal to the variance of wTy. For a proof of this theorem, see Fox (2016, p. 213). An implication of the theorem is that the least-squares estimator has the smallest mean-squared error out of all the linear estimators we could consider that have no bias (Hastie et al., 2009).

5.4.1 Are Unbiased Estimators Always Best?

As we will see later, the restriction to unbiased estimators in regression and other methods is not necessarily always a wise one. Recall that the bias-variance trade-off is always at work in estimation. Most of the time, we would like to minimize bias in estimation. At times, however, it may be beneficial to permit some bias into an estimator for the purpose of reducing variance.

Biased estimators such as the ridge estimator in ridge regression may at times be preferred over an unbiased estimator. One such case when a biased estimator may be preferred is when least-squares estimates are unstable (Izenman, 2008). That is, if X in (XTX) − 1XTy is less than full rank, then singularity will result, which means the least-squares estimates will no longer be unique. When the assumptions of regression do not hold due to collinearity or other problems (e.g., correlated errors), alternative solutions for estimation must be sought. And while exact collinearity may rarely occur, variables that are “almost collinear” can happen quite often depending on the research context. A biased estimator can be a better choice when faced with these kinds of conditions as well as for data that are ill-conditioned, meaning that estimated quantities are rather sensitive to small changes in the data (Izenman, 2008). Collinearity and instability often go hand in hand, as the effects of collinearity are such that it can produce overly large positive or negative estimated coefficients whose very signs can be reversed under rather negligible changes to the data. Standard errors could be grossly inflated as well, which could yield non-statistically significant effects, whereas if collinearity were not present, those same effects may have been statistically significant.233

In addition to the above, for some data sets, the number of input variables in X might greatly exceed the number of observations in the data. Under these conditions, the OLS estimator still exists, but is not unique, and hence a biased estimator may be useful in this case. We discuss biased estimators such as ridge and the lasso shortly in the book.

5.5 Time Series: An Example of Correlated Errors

The standard linear model assumes independently and normally distributed errors, but the assumption of independence is rarely (if ever) quite right on empirical data. Just like most things in statistics, it is often a reasonable approximation, however. Recall that approximations are what statistical modeling is all about. Rarely, if ever, are any assumptions for any model exactly met.

When measurements are taken across a time period, the assumption of independent errors is usually not satisfied. That is, when the observations comprise a time series, εi are usually correlated. Indeed, dependencies among the errors can be very strong in such time-dependent data.

How is this dependency represented in the linear model? Recall in the classic linear model,


y = Xβ + ε

where ε ∼ N(0,∑εε) and where ∑εε is the covariance matrix of errors, symmetric and positive semi-definite. However, unlike in the typical non-time series least-squares regression model, the expectation for ∑εε is not one having zeroes on the off-diagonal. Instead, because measurements are usually related, we expect nonzero diagonal elements in the off-diagonal representing the correlated errors, which implies ∑εεwill have n(n + 1)/2 distinct elements. The dependency of errors in a time series model requires us to incorporate the covariances between time points similar to how we did so in the classic repeated measures models surveyed earlier in the book.

Time series is an enormous topic and we have only scratched the surface here in our cursory overview to give an example of where errors are often correlated in data. Books on time series include those by Chatfield and Xing (2019) and Cryer and Chan (2008). The package timeseries (Wuertz et al., 2024) can be used for time series in R, especially applicable to financial time series. The package pyts can be used to fit time series models in Python. Other packages such as sktime and tslearn can also be used. Fox (2016) provides a good, if not somewhat technical introduction to time series and comes highly recommended.

5.6 Model Selection in Regression: Is There an “Optimal” Model?

One of the biggest problems in regression analysis and related models is that of determining which model to maintain or keep. Model selection in statistics in general is a huge problem and is usually not quite as simple as using statistical criteria alone to determine which model to adopt. Research and scientific criteria should always enter the discussion. Too often researchers adopt a “kitchen-sink” approach (i.e., throw in everything but the kitchen sink) to variable selection which often leads to overly complex models, problems of collinearity, and poor generalizability of test data.

Among the statistical approaches, there are generally two common strategies used for selecting a model. Recall that in choosing a model, we are not interested in the model that minimizes training error; we are interested in the model that minimizes test error. The most direct way to evaluate test error would be to employ a cross-validation approach. For example, we could fit our model to 80% of the data and test on 20%. This gives us a direct estimate of the test error because it tells us exactly how the model performs on new data, that is, data the model has yet to “see.” This is a 234first strategy to choosing a model, that of evaluating the fitted model on test data to learn how it performs.

For many reasons, however, we may not want to follow the above direct cross-validation approach. Some of these reasons include the fact that historically, data may have been expensive and sometimes very inconvenient to collect in the given field, and hence training a model on anything less than the full data set is sometimes simply not feasible. Indeed, before computers came along, the idea of setting aside data to test on via fast computation was, of course, not even an option. Hence, what if we decided to not put aside test data and wanted simply to estimate the test error on the training data itself, even if imperfectly? Since we only have the training data, fortunately we can adjust the training error rate to, for some measures at least, better reflect test error. We consider these options next.

5.7 Effect Size, Model Selection, and Adjusting the Training Error Rate

A rejection of the null hypothesis in regression, crudely, suggests that the regression is predicting better than chance. However, on its own, a statistically significant p-value does not necessarily tell us much more than that, unless of course we have specific knowledge of the inputs to the computed p-value such as sample size, variance, and so on, to help make sense of the p-value finding for the given data set. As is usually the case with significance testing, it is entirely possible to reject a null hypothesis for regression yet it be a trivial scientific effect. Such can occur often when sample size is extremely large and hence even miniscule effects cause us to reject the null hypothesis. This is nothing new, as we have discussed in many other places in the book the influence that sample size has on computed p-values. As usual, what is needed is a measure of effect size. A good effect size is not sample size dependent. The problem with effect size, however, is that if we compute it only on the training data then we usually get an overly optimistic size of effect. This is not surprising and is in line with our understanding of how models fit to training data are generally too optimistic overall.

In what follows we first consider an effect size for training data, then survey a few strategies for measuring size of effect as well as model selection measures that better evaluate the parsimony of statistical models, and in some cases (e.g., Akaike’s Information Criterion), also help us better estimate test error.

5.7.1 R2, Adjusted R2, Cp, AIC, BIC

Recall that R2 in regression is given by


$$R^{2} = \frac{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( y_{i}^{'} - \overline{y} \right)^{2}}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right)^{2}}$$
(5.23)

The denominator, $\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( y_{i} - \overline{y} \right)^{2}$ is simply a sums of squares of actual data values from $\overline{y}$. This quantity will be large or small depending simply on how much variation we have in the current data set. However, look more closely at the numerator, $\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( y_{i}^{'} - \overline{y} \right)^{2}$; this term expresses the distance between predicted values, yi′ and the mean of the data, $\overline{y}$. If this distance is zero, then 235$\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( y_{i}^{'} - \overline{y} \right)^{2}$ is equal to 0 and R2 will equal 0. As this distance increases, R2 becomes larger, and the quadratic (i.e., squared) nature of sums of squares amplifies the magnitude, especially for deviations that are distant from the mean. Hence, it would appear at first glance that this R2 statistic is all we really need to choose a model, such that the larger the value of R2, the better the model. But this logic is problematic, since in almost all cases R2 will necessarily mathematically increase as the number of predictors entered into the model also increases. Hence, models with a greater number of predictors will result in larger R2 values. The value of 1 − R2 will give us a measure of what is typically called the apparent error rate. What we really want to know is the actual error rate.

One way around this difficulty is to interpret, instead of R2, an adjusted R2 statistic given by the following:


$$R_{adj}^{2} = 1 - \left( 1 - R^{2} \right)\left( \frac{n - 1}{n - p} \right)$$
(5.24)

where “p” here is the number of parameters in the model, including the intercept term. From (5.24) we can see that as p increases relative to a stable R2, Radj2 decreases instead of automatically increasing as was the case for R2. Hence, Radj2 essentially “penalizes” the user for including predictors that are not “worth their salt” in increasing R2.

The Cp statistic (“Mallow’s Cp”) is another approach to penalizing model fit,


$$C_{p} = \frac{1}{n}\left( RSS + 2d{\hat{\sigma}}^{2} \right)$$
(5.25)

where, as before, n is the number of cases or observations, RSS is the residual sums of squares on the training data, d now is the number of predictors (recall that p was the number of parameters in Radj2), and σ̂2 is an estimate of error variance using all predictors, usually MS residual. The nature of the penalty in Cp is by way of 2dσ̂2. Smaller values of Cp are preferred over larger values since smaller RSS implies a better-fitting model. However, this is offset by 2dσ̂2, where increasing d has the effect of increasing 2dσ̂2. Hence, Cp, if it could speak, would say, “Congrats on getting RSS down, but that decrease will be penalized by how many d it required to do so. If any of your d are not sufficiently contributing to the observed decrease in RSS, you may want to consider removing them instead of being penalized for including them.”

A similar statistic to the Cp, and one that is more popular, is that of the AIC (Akaike’s Information Criterion) statistic,


$$AIC = \frac{1}{n{\hat{\sigma}}^{2}}\left( RSS + 2d{\hat{\sigma}}^{2} \right)$$
(5.26)

which is very similar in logic to that of the Cp: the only difference is the multiplier $\frac{1}{n{\hat{\sigma}}^{2}}$ instead of $\frac{1}{n}$ in Cp. The penalty is still equal to 2dσ̂2, however. In this formulation, increasingly smaller values are preferred over larger values. The following is another version of AIC, the original version given by Akaike (1974),236


 − 2ln p(D|θ) + 2m
(5.27)

which is the familiar log-likelihood, ln p(D|θ), however pre-multiplied by −2. For this version of AIC, smaller is also better than larger, as the penalty m (number of parameters in the model) acts to increase AIC, and if the decrease in  − 2ln p(D|θ) isn’t “worth” the increase by m, it makes adding the extra parameter(s) less worthwhile in terms of maintaining model parsimony. However, “smaller is always better” does not always pertain to the report of an AIC statistic; it depends on how it is formulated. AIC could, in theory, appear as simply ln p(D|θ) − 2m where now a larger than not value is preferred. Notice that now the log-likelihood is positive without pre-multiplying it by −2 and as before we are subtracting the number of parameters in the way of 2m. Be sure you are clear on how AIC (or BIC) is specifically defined for your particular application (e.g., software, package, etc.) before you interpret it.

A derivative of both the Cp and AIC is the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC),


$$BIC = \frac{1}{n{\hat{\sigma}}^{2}}\left( RSS + \log\left( n \right)d{\hat{\sigma}}^{2} \right)$$
(5.28)

The BIC often penalizes to a greater extent than the AIC. The key difference in the two statistics is in what follows RSS in their respective formulations. In the AIC, that term is 2dσ̂2, where in the BIC, it is log(n)dσ̂2. All else equal, as sample size n increases, so does log (n) and BIC will typically “punish” more than AIC for the same RSS and σ̂2. As with AIC, be sure you know how the author is defining BIC before concluding that “smaller is better” (e.g., see Schwarz, 1978; Fraley & Raftery, 1998, where BIC is translated into a “larger is better” statistic).

As the name suggests, BIC originates from Bayesian decision theory and hence is derived from Bayesian principles. It can be shown that choosing a model with the minimum BIC is equivalent to choosing the model with the highest approximate posterior probability (Hastie et al., 2009). What is more, BIC is asymptotically consistent as a selection criterion, which implies that the probability that BIC will select the correct model increases toward unity (i.e., 1) as the amount of information (sample size) on which it is based increases. This is not true for AIC, which will too often select a model that is too rich or complex as information on which it is based increases (i.e., n→∞). For smaller sample sizes, BIC typically penalizes much more severely than AIC and hence may choose a model that is too simple (Hastie et al., 2009).

An additional measure of effect size that is sometimes recommended in regression is that of the semi-partial correlation coefficient (Hays, 1994). The semi-partial correlation partials out variance due to other predictors in the model before relating a predictor to the response variable. That is, it is the bivariate correlation between an adjusted variable (predictor) and an unadjusted variable (response). For details, see Hays (1994).

5.7.2 Comparing Radj2, Cp, AIC, and BIC to Cross-Validation

We have surveyed above a few ways of penalizing training data to assess model fit and model selection. Which measure is best? Should one use any of the Radj2, Cp, AIC, or BIC options, or should one use cross-validation? Cross-validation is usually first choice, since it is a direct estimate of the test error, whereas only Cp and AIC rather efficiently, though indirectly, estimate test error. Cross-validation also makes fewer assumptions about the underlying model (James et al., 2013). 237Historically, before high-speed computing power and very large data sets (at least in some fields), performing cross-validation directly was computationally quite difficult or borderline impossible and hence computing measures such as Cp, Radj2, etc. was more feasible and convenient. Today, however, with high-speed computing, cross-validation can be performed with relative ease. Hence, given the availability of relatively cheap computing speed, cross-validation is often the preferred option for model validation. Of course, nothing stops the investigator from simultaneously computing many competing effect-size measures and comparing them to see if they triangulate on the same data set. There is no “type I” error rate when computing effect sizes; the researcher can compute as many of them as she would like.

5.8 Assumptions for Regression

Virtually all statistical models are founded on a set of assumptions. Verifying assumptions for regression is important because least-squares estimates and inference are only as good as the assumptions on which they are based. Further, techniques have been developed that allow for users to evaluate the impact that data points have on the estimated least-squares solution. Thus, in addition to verifying assumptions such as linearity and homoscedasticity of variance, residual analyses that evaluate such things as leverage, raw, standardized, and studentized residuals are generally recommended.

Residual analysis in regression is a huge topic and due to space limitations, we do not survey it here. Defining such things as leverage and influence of data points requires more theoretical development than we can afford here. We also assume the reader may already have at least some exposure to this area in prior courses. We refer the reader to Fox (2016) for a thorough and excellent treatment of residual analyses, which can become quite complex and is an art unto itself. We cannot escape the topic of assumption analysis entirely, however, and must survey one of the most important areas of assumption-checking in regression and related models, that of collinearity.

5.8.1 Collinearity

Collinearity can have serious and deleterious effects on a regression solution. If the columns of X are not linearly independent, this equates to X not being of full rank, which implies that XTX is singular, the determinant is equal to 0, and the least-squares coefficients, though they theoretically can be estimated, are not uniquely defined. Hence, collinearity in regression is a serious problem and we need a way to address it.

5.8.1.1 Variance Inflation Factor

There are a few common ways of assessing collinearity. The first we survey is probably the most popular, that of computing a statistic called the variance inflation factor, or “VIF” for short. To understand VIF, we must first consider how we can write the variance of the ith partial regression coefficient (Cohen et al., 2003, p. 423):238


$$s_{\beta_{i}}^{2} = \frac{s_{y}^{2}}{s_{x_{i}}^{2}}\left( \frac{1 - R_{y.12...p}^{2}}{n - p - 1} \right)\left( \frac{1}{1 - R_{i.12...(i)...p}^{2}} \right)$$
(5.29)

where sβi2 is the variance of the βi coefficient, sy2 is the variance of the response, sxi2 is the variance of the given predictor xi corresponding to βi, and Ry.12...p2 is the coefficient of determination for the entire model with all predictors y.12...p. The variance inflation factor is the last term in (5.29):


$$\left( \frac{1}{1 - R_{i.12...(i)...p}^{2}} \right)$$
(5.30)

where Ri.12...(i)...p2 represents the explained variance of the predictor in question regressed on the rest of predictors in the model. The extent to which Ri.12...(i)...p2 is large is the extent to which the denominator 1 − Ri.12...(i)...p2 goes toward zero, and hence is the extent to which VIF will be larger than not. That is, the extent to which the predictor in question shares variance with other predictors in the model is the extent to which the variance inflation factor increases. The variance inflation factor, as the name suggests, measures the factor by which the variance of the given regression coefficient increases due to its collinearity with other variables in the model.

A second popular way of assessing ill-conditioning is through the condition number. The condition number k is the square root of the ratio of the largest to the smallest nonzero eigenvalues, that is, $k = \sqrt{\lambda_{1}/\lambda_{2}}$, where λ1 is the largest eigenvalue and λ2 is the smallest (Fox, 2016). If this ratio is large, X is considered ill-conditioned. It makes sense that a comparison of eigenvalues here can be used as an indicator of ill-conditioning. Consider what it means to have a very wide range between the largest and smallest eigenvalues. It implies that an increasing amount of variance is in one “component” (i.e., principal component) only in the data, which implies that there exists a large degree of correlation among variables “coagulating” into that component. Hence, the condition number can serve as an aid in detecting collinearity.

5.8.2 Collinearity Necessarily Implies Redundancy Only in Terms of Variance

In our discussion of collinearity thus far, it should be emphasized that two variables that are nearly perfectly collinear are redundant only in terms of shared variance, and not necessarily in terms of what they are actually individually measuring. A common misunderstanding when considering collinearity is to assume that two collinear variables are “getting at the same thing” on a substantive level simply because they are highly correlated. And while in some cases this may be true, it is not necessarily so across all cases.

For example, consider the classic case of correlating height and weight. Suppose the correlation is near 0.90. The shared variance between variables is relatively high, but we would all agree that weight is not the same thing as height. More generally, a statistical measure, whatever the kind, in no way necessarily reflects substantive reality. Whenever we apply an arbitrary statistical function to any “real object,” it is never a one-to-one relationship. The statistics are never enough; you have to know what the statistics are being applied to in order to draw the proper scientific conclusion. A lack of understanding of what statistics can vs. cannot tell you about empirical data is probably the greatest pitfall for users of statistics who have not considered these wider and deeper methodological and philosophical issues.

5.9 Variable Selection Methods: Building the Regression Model

Previously we discussed model fit and model selection measures, such as R2, Radj2, AIC, etc. While we discussed how to potentially choose the best model, we did not discuss how to select 239variables for a given model. This latter concern falls under the category of variable selection rather than the previously discussed topic of model selection. One way to conceive of variable selection in a very general sense is as suggested by Breiman (2001), such that a variable is important if dropping it from the model seriously affects prediction. And while variable selection may at first glance appear to be simple, it is an extremely complex problem, just as complex as model selection overall. Most variable selection procedures are quite unstable as well, such that tweaking or perturbing the original data even slightly can have a rather drastic effect on the final model (Breiman, 1996).

Variable selection methods include forward, backward, and stepwise techniques, where stepwise can be considered a hybrid version of forward and backward. Stepwise and selection algorithms often go by the name of wrapper models in the data-mining literature (Aggarwal, 2015). Versions of backward elimination algorithms are sometimes referred to as recursive feature elimination algorithms in the data and machine learning environments, and though there are distinctions between these types of algorithms, they pretty much get at the same thing in the end.

Other techniques include all-possible-subsets, forward-stagewise regression, and others. Both ridge and lasso regression, as we will see in the next chapter, can be considered in some sense variable selection techniques as well, especially the lasso since coefficients are explicitly driven to values of zero, while for ridge coefficients they are simply “shrunk” toward zero. For this reason, ridge is often not considered a “pure” variable selection procedure. However, nothing inhibits the user from simply dropping shrunken coefficients as they near zero or are much less in magnitude than other coefficients in the model. We will return to this discussion when we discuss both techniques in the following chapter.

In typical forward regression, predictors are entered based on some entry criteria, such as statistical significance (e.g., attaining p < 0.05). The procedure halts when no more predictors reach that criterion. In backward regression, all predictors begin in the model and are removed once they no longer reach p < 0.05 (or whatever level one chooses). Stepwise regression is typically a mix of both forward and backward approaches; however there are many stepwise programs and packages and it behooves the reader to study the details of the package they are using to clearly understand what the stepwise program does or does not do. The algorithms in various packages can become quite complex, which if not understood, provides ample opportunity for drawing false substantive conclusions from the stepwise results.

5.9.1 Forward, Backward, and Stepwise in R

There are several ways (and packages) for conducting forward, backward, or stepwise regressions in R. Many packages and routines will often combine routines, so as already emphasized, it is essential that one thoroughly familiarize oneself with the given package to know exactly what is being computed.

For our example here, we feature the mtcars data in R once more, on which we conduct both a forward and backward stepwise regression. In specifying mpg ~., we are implicitly requesting modeling mpg as a function of all other variables. We will now specify that we wish to conduct a stepwise, specifically:

> fit <- stepwise(formula = formula,
+ data = mtcars,
+ type = “linear”,
+ strategy = c(“forward”, “bidirection”, “backward”),
+ metric = c(“AIC”, “BIC”, “SL”))
> fit

We have requested above that forward, bidirection, and backward elimination be performed, and hence our output will be quite long. We have also requested AIC, BIC, and SL as the metrics for evaluating the regressions, where “SL” corresponds to “significance level.” Indeed, if we choose to look at the results from the stepwise (fit), we will get a listing of the model selection variables in the data set that is quite long and provides much detail. The benefit to using StepReg is that we can also visualize the results of the selection process where in Figure 5.2 is shown the effect of variable removal (e.g., (-)cyl) on each of AIC, BIC, and SL, this time resulting from the backward algorithm:

> plot(fit)

We see from the plot that at each step of the function, AIC, BIC, and SL drop in value as predictors are removed. The plot is a powerful way of visualizing the selection process. We see that SL drops rather dramatically toward the latter steps. BIC follows an almost perfect negative linear path across steps.

In Python, forward and stepwise regression can be performed using sklearn’s SequentialFeatureSelector() though not demonstrated here. For details, see Python’s sklearn site.

5.10 Mediated and Moderated Regression Models

Mediation has a relatively long history in statistics and has been motivated primarily by the substantive interests of social scientists, primarily psychologists. Despite its popularity and hype in 242some fields, it is important to understand what statistical mediation can vs. cannot do. Moderation, on the other hand, is most generally simply another word for interaction. In ANOVA-type models, we usually refer to such as interactions, whereas in regression models it has come to be known as moderation. It is vitally important to realize at the outset that mediation and moderation do not, by themselves, imply a physical process. That is, conducting a test of statistical mediation and concluding Z mediates the relationship between X and Y is only necessarily true statistically; it is not true substantively unless one has a substantive rationale or argument outside of the statistical model for inferring such a mediational process. There are countless published articles, even in “high impact factor” journals, where researchers conclude a mediational process simply based on statistical mediation, which exemplifies one of many philosophical and methodological abuses of statistics. We revisit and discuss this issue more extensively later.

5.10.1 Statistical Mediation

We purposely title this section by the name of statistical mediation for the reason that, as mentioned, far too often researchers tend to believe that if they apply a mediation model to data, it can thereby “extract” a mediational process. This is simply not the case. In addressing this important issue, let’s first very briefly survey how mediation (and moderation) is defined in the literature. For example, Little et al. (2007, p. 207) offer the following definition and distinction:

Generally speaking, a mediator can be thought of as the carrier or transporter of information along the causal chain of effects. A moderator, on the other hand, is the changer of a relationship in a system.

Pearl (2014, pp. 1–2) claims, “Scientifically, mediation tells us “how nature works” and, practically, it enables us to predict behavior under a rich variety of conditions and interventions.”

The classic mediation model is diagrammed in Figure 5.3, where X is the predictor, Y is the response, and M is the mediator.

The conditions for “classic” or traditional mediation typically include the following (MacKinnon et al., 2007):

  1. 1. X should bear a relationship to Y.
  2. 2. X should bear a relationship to M.
  3. 3. M should be related to Y when both X and M are predictors of Y.
  4. 4. The relationship of X to Y should diminish (in absolute value) when M is included in the model, presumably as a result of M “taking up” the correlation that would have otherwise been “transmitted” (in necessarily some statistical sense only) from X to Y.243

A more complex combination of mediator models is illustrated in Figure 5.4 where we now have three mediators, z1, z2, and z3, and where ε1, ε2, and ε3 are errors.

While including more than a single mediator may seem initially a good idea, it comes with many caveats. The models are only as valid as the assumptions imposed on those models. Indeed, as again noted by Pearl (2012, pp. 2–3), whom we paraphrase:

The validity of these two methods depends of course on the assumption [added emphasis] that the error terms … are uncorrelated, otherwise, some of the structural parameters would produce biased results. In randomized trials, where error can be identified with the randomization device, we are assured that error is uncorrelated with other errors and so the regressional estimates will be unbiased … However, randomization does not remove error from e2 and e3.

There is no end to how complex we can formulate a mediation model. For example, Figure 5.5 features a mediation model with a confounder that predicts the treatment, mediator, and outcome. Other than the confounder, the model is a classic three-variable mediation model.

Other than for rather simple mediation models, models such as these are often best analyzed as structural equation models, and hence we will revisit them to some degree later in the book when we survey SEM models in more detail. Estimation in mediation models includes the traditional coefficient product estimator (Hayes, 2018). Simulation-based estimators have also been proposed as well as semi-parametric estimators such as the inverse probability weighting estimator (Zhang, 2442023). The multiply-robust estimator, as well as the double-machine learning for mediation estimator, have also been proposed. For details, see Abécassis et al. (2023).

5.10.2 Statistical Moderation

As mentioned at the outset of our discussion of mediation and moderation, moderation analysis is nothing more than analyzing interactions. That is, quite literally, “moderation” is a fancy word for statistical interaction. When you conduct an analysis of variance and model the interaction, you are performing a moderation analysis. However, there is so much “hype” about moderation analyses in fields such as psychology and others that it is often advertised as being able to accomplish so much more than it can. Again, to reiterate, nowhere in the statistical procedure of moderation analysis is anything necessarily “moderating” anything else in a physical or substantive sense unless the variables you are working with and your theory suggest such a “physical” process. Statistical moderation alone does not afford that process in any way whatsoever. In fact, in many cases, statistical moderation can be rather anticlimactic.

As a basic example of moderation, consider the plot in Figure 5.6.

As a result of the slopes being different (nonparallel), we have a moderation effect. Of course, in the sample, there will virtually always be a moderation effect. Do you really think slopes could ever be exactly parallel in the sample? The real question is whether such an effect can be inferred toward the population, which is the inferential question we are ultimately interested in. We will survey an example of moderation later in the chapter using software.

5.10.3 Moderated Mediation

Just as in the test for any other interaction effect, one may be interested in learning whether an entire mediation model holds across values of a moderating variable. More specifically, we may be interested in learning whether an indirect effect (i.e., the effect of going “through” the mediator, so to speak) is conditional on values of a moderating variable. This is referred to as moderated mediation and more generally is found under the name of conditional process models (Hayes, 2018), or again, the search for conditional indirect effects. That is, the indirect (or “mediating”) effect is conditional upon some other third variable, illustrated in Figure 5.7.245

We see in Figure 5.7 the classic three-variable mediation model, however conditional upon the w variable as indicated by the xw interaction. Note that both w and the interaction term xw are included due to the principle of marginality (Fox, 2016) which holds that an interaction term should not be included without also including the individual terms that make up the interaction, which in this case is simply the w variable.

A mediated moderation model is when an interaction between an independent variable and a moderator variable “affects” (statistically) a mediator variable that in turn “affects” (again, only necessarily statistically) the outcome variable. According to Hayes (2018, p. 465), “mediated moderation is neither interesting nor meaningful” and ends up being mathematically equivalent under most conditions to moderated mediation. As such, Hayes recommends that questions of mediated moderation should be recast as moderated mediational hypotheses.

5.10.4 Mediation in Python

Mediation and moderation analyses are probably best left to R or similar software specifically designed for statistics (e.g., SPSS also has macros devoted to performing mediation). However, Python does afford some capabilities for this as well. The following is an example of mediation using the pingouin package (Vallat, 2018) in Python. The pingouin package is an open-source package originally written in Python 3 and uses primarily pandas and numpy.

The pingouin package can also easily fit mediation with binary variables as well as models with multiple mediators. Mediation models can also be fit with statsmodels.stats.mediation(), though we do not explore these usages here. The package moderate.mediation in R (Qin, 2024) can be used to fit rather complex mediation models and comes highly recommended for moderated mediation modeling. The package mediation (Tingley et al., 2014) also fits a variety of mediation models. Sensitivity analyses for mediation effects can also be performed. See Imai et al. (2010) for details. As a summary on mediation and moderation analyses in R, the package mediation (Tingley et al., 2014) is the “go-to” source for all types of mediation analyses using R.

5.11 Further Directions and a Final Word of Warning on Mediation and Moderation

Mediation and moderation in statistics is an enormous topic with books devoted to these methods (e.g., see Hayes, 2018). Recent work on mediation includes that of Ge et al. (2023) who develop a reinforcement learning framework for dynamic mediation analysis. In many cases, treatments are assigned over time and this work seeks to evaluate mediators along a longitudinal trajectory as well as sequential decision-making over an infinite number of decision points. Pearl (2012) critically assesses the habitual way of performing mediation, which assumes linearity and independence of errors, and proposes an alternative approach for modeling nonlinear relationships, which includes that with categorical variables. Judd et al. (2001) give details on estimating mediation and moderation models in within-subjects designs.

As mentioned at the outset of our discussion, however, mediation and moderation, if used and more importantly, interpreted incorrectly, can do more harm than good. Far too often in the social sciences are mediational and moderation processes concluded simply because statistical evidence supports it.

To reiterate, and as any good methodologist or philosopher of science will tell you, no statistical method, whatever the kind, can alone indicate a physical process (Fiedler et al., 2011). The problem with using these “power” and “action” words to describe statistical processes is dangerous. “Causal modeling” as mediational analysis has sometimes come to be known, is not causal at all unless there is a substantive context to induce such causality. There is absolutely nothing wrong with conducting a mediation or moderation analysis, but if more researchers actually understood how little it truly tells them about their data instead of recklessly imposing powers on their variables that they do not 247necessarily possess, the methods would probably be used less than they currently are. It behooves all researchers to understand the limitations of the statistical procedures they use before using and interpreting them on empirical data. Researchers regularly “empower” statistics to say much more from their data than they are able. Mathematical and statistical models are first and foremost abstractions; they have no knowledge of your empirical observations, they are simply using those numbers as inputs in their computations. Whether the statistical model says anything substantive about those empirical observations is a much more complex scientific and philosophical issue than simply fitting the statistical model. Narratives rarely correspond to “reality” one-to-one.

5.12 Principal Components Regression

Recall that in the typical multiple regression problem, a linear combination of predictors x1 through xp is sought such that it maximizes the correlation with the response variable, y. This maximum correlation is expressed via fit statistics such as R2. As we know already, multicollinearity can have detrimental effects on a regression model. Having several predictors that have high correlations with one another can, for one, inflate standard errors. Inflated standard errors reduce statistical power for detecting effects and hence make it more difficult to reject null hypotheses for predictors.

Statistical issues are not the only reason for disliking collinearity. From a scientific point of view, having correlated predictors is a waste of resources. For example, recording your birth date in months and then again in days is a waste of time, as one variable essentially does the job of two. They are essentially duplicates of one another. More precisely, one variable is a linear combination of the other. In such a case, the most likely solution is to simply drop one of the variables from the regression and simplify the model, both to eliminate or reduce collinearity but also to substantively reduce the scientific complexity of the model.

There are alternatives to simply eliminating variables from the set of predictors, however. One relatively popular alternative approach to this problem is to reduce the dimensionality of x1 through xp before making a prediction on y. Especially if p (the number of predictors) is very large, it may make more sense to transform p into a smaller number of components and then regress y onto this smaller number of components. Principal components regression attempts to do just this. To understand principal components regression, however, we must first get an idea of what principal components analysis is all about.

5.12.1 What Is Principal Components Analysis?

A more extensive discussion of principal components analysis (PCA) is reserved for later in the book where we discuss dimension-reduction techniques and manifold learning in more detail, devoting part of an entire chapter to the PCA technique. For now, we only survey the method briefly to learn how it serves the PCA regression technique.

Principal components analysis derives orthogonal linear combinations of the variables equal to the number of variables, such that successive linear combinations account for less and less variance in the observed variables. Recall that a linear combination is defined as248


li = a1y1 + a2y2 +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + apyp

That is, a linear combination is a weighted sum of products, where a1 through ap are the weights applied to observed variables y1 through yp. For our data on x1, ..., xp, the linear combination becomes


zi = a1x1 + a2x2 +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + apxp

where now zi is the name of the linear combination and x1 through xp are the observed variables. A principal component is a unique kind of linear combination such that the weights a1 through ap correspond to values of allied eigenvectors extracted from an eigen analysis performed on the covariance or correlation matrix of variables x1, ..., xp. Hence, if we denote the weights a1 through ap by e1 through ep to represent eigenvector weights, the first principal component is defined as


z1 = e1x1 + e2x2 +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + epxp
(5.31)

The first principal component accounts for the most variance in the observed variables. The second principal component accounts for the second-most variance in the observed variables but is orthogonal to the first. The goal of PCA is to capture as much variance in the first few components as possible to account for the variance in the set of observed variables. Principal components regression uses the first few principal components as predictors in a least-squares sense. In this way, the number of components retained in the PCR (principal components regression) can be likened to a tuning parameter (Boehmke & Greenwell, 2020). As we will see when we survey methods such as ridge and lasso regression, tuning parameters are useful in controlling the balance between the variance and bias of a statistical learning method and are useful in selecting a “best” model from a wider set of possibilities.

Principal components regression, useful as it may at first appear, makes one important assumption that may with empirical data not always hold. By regressing y on the set of components, we are implicitly assuming that the directions of most variance in x1 through xp are those same directions that are associated with y. While this assumption may not always hold, it is often considered a useful approximation for most data and PCA regression often gives reasonable results (James et al., 2013). As more precisely stated by Izenman (2008, p.132):

The extraction of the principal components is accomplished without any reference to the output variable Y, we have no reason to expect Yto be highly correlated with any of the principal components, in particular those having the largest eigenvalues. Indeed, Y may actually have its highest correlation with one of the last few principal components or even the last one.

Or, as even better elucidated by Artigue and Smith (2018, p. 9):

The promise of principal components regression is that it is an efficient way of selecting a relatively small number of explanatory variables from a vast array of possibilities, based on the correlations among the explanatory variables. The problem is that the eigenvector weights on the candidate variables have nothing to do with their relationship to the variable being predicted. Mildly important variables may be given larger weights than important variables. Nuisance variables may be given larger weights than the true explanatory variables. The coefficients of the true explanatory variables may be given the wrong signs.249

Even though principal components regression provides a simple way to use less than the full spectrum of predictors for the problem, it should not be regarded as a feature or variable selection method because of the lack of guarantee that the directions that best explain the predictors will also be the best directions to use for predicting the response. In fact, it is entirely possible to have variables only weakly related to the response, yet as the number of these variables increases, R-squared of 1.0 is nonetheless approached. In general, adding useless predictors, though resulting in an increase in dimensionality, will do so at the risk of overfitting and an increase in test error.

A more in-depth discussion of the above problems can be found in Jolliffe (1982). The key takeaway point is that though PCA regression is guaranteed to derive orthogonal components that maximize variance in the set of predictors, this will not necessarily be equivalent to maximizing R2between y and those components that account for the most variance in x1 through xp. For this reason, PCA regression should not be considered a variable selection technique (James et al., 2013) in the same spirit as techniques such as best-subsets or forward regression. PCA regression is also not scale-invariant, and hence standardization of predictors is typically (though not always) recommended.

5.12.2 PCA Regression and Singularity

As we have seen, PCA regression can be useful in situations where we wish to reduce the dimensionality of the predictors before using resulting components as predictors of a response. More to the point, PCA regression can be useful when predictors are highly correlated with one another.

There is another instance where PCA regression may be especially useful, and that is when the matrix of predictors, X, is singular and hence ill-conditioned. Recall that for a singular matrix X, it is implied that one row or column is a linear combination of one or more rows or columns. This condition always implies that the determinant of the matrix will equal zero, which implies the inverse of X cannot be computed. In such a case, one can substitute a generalized inverse when computing least-squares estimates. There are many generalized inverses, but the most common is that of the Moore-Penrose inverse, the use of which will yield the generalized inverse regression estimator (Izenman, 2008).

The number of components to keep in PCA regression on the side of X can be determined by Kaiser’s rule, which says to keep all those components with eigenvalues greater than 1 for the correlation matrix, or by using a cross-validation technique (Wold, 1978). The substantive meaning of derived components can also play a significant role in their selection contingent on whether or not the scientific nature of components matters to the scientist.

5.13 Partial Least-Squares Regression

Whereas principal components regression only uses x1 through xp in its construction of components, partial least-squares seeks out dimensionality or directions in the data that incorporates both the predictors and the response variable. That is, the components found in x1 through xp are not just relevant to the predictor side, but are also relevant to the response y. Partial least-squares, or “PLS” for short, is often considered a supervised alternative to principal components regression (James et al., 2013) since PLS will incorporate the response when determining the best “directions.”

As well described by Izenman,

PLS searches for a set of components (called latent vectors) that performs a simultaneous decomposition of X and Y with the constraint that these components explain as much as possible of the covariance between X and Y. In this manner, the derived variables in PLS are constructed in such a way as to retain most of the information in the X1 through Xp variables and is typically obtained via algorithm rather than optimization procedure (Izenman, 2008, p. 133).

To unpack what PLS actually accomplishes, recall once more what a linear combination looks like in the typical PCA:


z1 = e1x1 + e2x2 +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + epxp

In PLS, the coefficients in z1, those of e1, etc., are set to the coefficients resulting from a simple linear regression of y on x for each predictor. This coefficient (e.g., for e1) is proportional to the correlation between y and xj, the given predictor we are considering. That is, in computing the first component, variables x that are most strongly related to y (in a univariate sense) receive the most weight.

To obtain the second component, z2, each of the variables for z1 are first adjusted by regressing each variable on z1 and taking residuals of what is “left over.” If the first component accounts for all the information in the predictors, the residual will equal zero. More than likely, the first 253component will not account for all information, and hence the residual will be greater than zero. The second component z2 is computed using these residuals, which are orthogonal to the first component. The iterative approach continues for ensuing directions (i.e., components) of z.

It is clear then why the method is referred to as partial least-squares. It is so because it capitalizes on residuals that are orthogonal to previous component values. Hence, if PLS could talk, it would say, “After the predictive part is removed (or ‘partialled’), let’s now regress the new component on what is left over.” Partial least-squares, as is true of principal components regression, is not scale-invariant, and hence standardizing predictors is often advised. However, as noted elsewhere in the book, the decision to standardize should not be made without careful consideration of the nature (and specifically, scales) of the variables under study.

The sonar data above is made up of 208 data points collected on 60 predictors (only a few predictors are shown above). We would like to predict the response variable of two classes (M = metal cylinder, R = rock). We first divide the data into testing and training:

> set.seed(107)
> inTrain <- createDataPartition(
+ y = Sonar$Class,
+ p = .75,
+ list = FALSE)

The createDataPartition function is used here to divide the data into training and testing by “Class” in the sonar data set, which as we can see contains two categories:

We now define the training set as the .75 previously specified in inTrain, and the balance of this, which is .25, as the testing set, indicated by -inTrain to denote whatever was not included in inTrain:

> training <- Sonar[inTrain,]
> testing <- Sonar[-inTrain,]

We confirm there are now 157 cases in training and 51 in testing, for a total of 208 cases, whereby 157/208 is the previously designated proportion of .75 requested:

plsFit <- train(

5.13.2 Partial Least-Squares in Python

Partial least-squares regression can be fit in Python using PLSRegression. The following is a simple example with easy data:

from sklearn.cross_decomposition import PLSRegression
X = [[0., 0., 1.], [1., 0., 0.], [2., 2., 2.], [2., 5., 4.]]
Y = [[0.1, -0.2], [0.9, 1.1], [6.2, 5.9], [11.9, 12.3]]

We will request a 2-component solution:

pls2 = PLSRegression(n_components=2)
pls2.fit(X, Y)

We now obtain predicted values based on the two-component solution:

Out[5]: PLSRegression()
Y_pred = pls2.predict(X)
Y_pred
Out[7]:
array([[ 0.26087869, 0.15302213],
       [ 0.60667302, 0.45634164],
       [ 6.46856199, 6.48931562],
       [11.7638863, 12.00132061]])

The predicted values on each component extracted above are to be read vertically in a column. That is, the first component has predicted values of 0.26, 0.60, 6.46, and 11.76.

5.14 Multivariate Reduced-Rank Regression

Multivariate reduced-rank regression (Izenman, 1975) is a very general framework for the multivariate regression model and we mention it here only for pedagogical inclusion into the general regression framework. The classic multivariate linear regression model can be stated in its most general way as


Y = μ + CX + ε
(5.32)

where C is a matrix of regression coefficients or parameters on which there exists a set of linear constraints. These linear constraints in the case of reduced rank for C imply that C = AB, where both A and B are nonunique full-rank matrices (Izenman, 2008, p. 177), such that we can rewrite the classical multivariate model as


$$\begin{array}{l} {Y = \mu + {CX} + \varepsilon} \\ {\,\,\,\,\, = \mu + \left( {AB} \right)X + \varepsilon} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.33)

where in (5.33), we have simply substitued AB for C. That is, the reduced-rank multivariate model generalizes the classical multivariate model by, as summarized by Izenman (2008), relaxing the implicit constraint on the rank of C, which by consequence, allows for dimension reduction. The theme is already familiar by now; a matrix of less than full rank may very well have underlying 260dimensionality “disguised” within it. By estimating A and B, we effectively “treat” the reduced-rank condition of C. For a proof of why A and B are nonunique, see Izenman (2008, p. 177).

Several statistical models, including principal components analysis, exploratory factor analysis, canonical correlation, discriminant analysis, and even neural networks, can be conceptualized as special cases of the reduced-rank multivariate model. What is more, the Gauss-Markov theorem for regression discussed earlier in the book generalizes to the multivariate reduced-rank counterpart. Profile analysis and time series can also be conceptualized within the reduced-rank multivariate model.

5.15 Canonical Correlation

The canonical correlation is the bivariate correlation between sets of variables. It is, like Pearson r, a linear correlation. It is the linear correlation between linear combinations of variables. That is, for linear combinations l1 and l2, the correlation between them is given by:


$$r_{l_{1},l_{2}} = \frac{{cov}_{l_{1},l_{2}}}{\sqrt{s_{l_{1}}^{2}s_{l2}^{2}}}$$
(5.34)

where sl12 and sl22 are variances of the respective linear combinations (Denis, 2021a) and covl1, l2 is the covariance between linear combinations l1 and l2. The nonzero squared population canonical correlations are the nonzero eigenvalues λi of the following (Bilodeau and Brenner, 1999, p. 177; Rencher and Christensen, 2012, p. 387):


Σyy − 1ΣyxΣxx − 1Σxy

As a result of the eigenvalues providing the squared canonical correlations, the unsquared canonical correlations are thus equal to the square root of the eigenvalues, that is, $\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}$.

How are the squared canonical correlations found? There are a few ways of obtaining them, but perhaps the easiest way is through an eigen analysis of Σyy − 1ΣyxΣxx − 1Σxy, where such represents the matrix being analyzed in A in the classic form of the eigen equality:


Ax = λx

Recall that to find λ we set |A−λI|=0, where now instead of simply a matrix A,


A = Σyy − 1ΣyxΣxx − 1Σxy

and so we have


|A−λI|=0       →       |Σyy − 1ΣyxΣxx − 1Σxy−λI|=0
(5.35)

and hence since |A−λI|x=0, where x is an eigenvector associated with λ, the respective eigenvectors a and b of Σyy − 1ΣyxΣxx − 1Σxy are found by261


(Σyy − 1ΣyxΣxx − 1Σxy−λI)a = 0
(5.36)

and


(Σyy − 1ΣyxΣxx − 1Σxy−λI)b = 0
(5.37)

That is, the first linear combination is now l1 = a′x and the second l2 = b′y. Corresponding canonical variates for each dimension are uncorrelated, and each subsequent canonical dimension extracted is uncorrelated to previous dimensions. Izenman (2008, p. 216) summarizes canonical correlation:

The CVA technique ensures that every bit of correlation is wrung out of the original X and Y variables and deposited in an orderly fashion into pairs of new variables … which have a special correlation structure. If the notion of correlation is regarded as the primary determinant of information in the system of variables, then CVA is a major tool for reducing the dimensionality of the original two sets of variables.

Not surprisingly, canonical correlation can be interpreted as a special case of the aforementioned reduced-rank regression (Izenman, 2008). Variations of canonical correlation include deep variational canonical correlation (Wang et al., 2017) that extends and generalizes linear canonical correlation to nonlinear models within a deep neural network parameterization. Probabilistic canonical correlation is discussed by Bach and Jordan (2006). Tensor canonical correlation has also been proposed, where each observation in data consists of multidimensional arrays (tensors) (Min et al., 2020). Relationships between multivariate reduced rank, PCA, and CVA can be found in Izenman (1975).

5.15.1 Canonical Correlation in R

The package CCA in R (González & Déjean, 2023) can be used for canonical correlation as well as a version of regularized canonical correlation. The package also allows for numerous graphical visualizations of canonical correlation. Below is an example adapted from the package’s documentation on the nutrimouse data, where gene data is correlated to lipids on a group of mice:

6 Regularization Methods in RegressionRidge, Lasso, and Elastic Net

DOI: 10.4324/9781003376941-9

In the previous chapter we provided an overview of simple and multiple linear regression methods. We saw that the estimator of choice was an unbiased one, that is, a “BLUE” estimator. The quality of being unbiased seemed like a desirable feature to possess. Indeed, from elementary statistics courses onward, students are regularly taught that an unbiased estimator is one of the most favorable qualities of an estimator, in addition to other characteristics such as consistency, sufficiency, etc.

In some cases, however, especially where the matrix of predictors is ill-conditioned (e.g., collinearity), it may be worthwhile to drop the requirement of an unbiased estimator and instead adopt an estimator that is biased. At first glance, this may seem statistically unintuitive and borderline reckless. To actually prefer a biased estimator seems to go against all essential statistical teaching for favoring unbiased estimators. However, as we will see, choosing a biased estimator in regression has the effect of driving coefficients of predictors toward or to 0, thus potentially de-emphasizing predictors that are not essential to the regression solution. By driving coefficients to or toward 0, using a biased estimator can facilitate variable selection in multiple regression. In fact, we will demonstrate in this chapter that the residual sums of squares of ordinary least-squares is nothing more than a special case of regularized regression for a specific choice of hyperparameter.

Three popular estimators that are known to regularize a model are the ridge, lasso, and elastic net. Before discussing each of these, a general and broad introduction and overview of the principle of regularization is in order. Regularization as a general concept is not exclusively associated with any particular estimator per se, and shows up in many different statistical and machine learning methods. That is, regularization is an idea, not any specific particular methodology. This point is perhaps the most important to understand as it concerns regularization.

6.1 The Concept of Regularization

The main idea of regularization is getting a “handle” on a model to simplify its complexity so that it potentially generalizes better to new test data and hence minimizes overfitting. Equivalently, we can say that the goal of regularization is to improve performance on the test set by adding a penalty to the training loss (Kroese et al., 2020) so that the learner we do select is one that does not overfit on the training data and that generalizes relatively well on the test data. Regularization is all about preventing overfitting and increasing generalizability. It is often associated with so-called shrinkage and techniques such as ridge regression and the lasso, but it is important to understand that it is much more general and broader than this. One can regularize a model without implementing any specific algorithm. Regularization, the concept at least, is very simple and quite general.

To demonstrate the essence of regularization, consider an exceedingly simple example of regularization in the basic linear model:266


yi = β0 + β1xi + εi
(6.1)

The above models a linear relationship between response yi and predictor xi. But suppose the observed sample data exhibit nothing at all like a linear relationship. Suppose instead the plot of yi on xi is as depicted in Figure 6.1, with a correlation close to 0.

Now, consider if we fit the above linear model to this data. Would it fit well? No, and if it does not fit well, it likely will not generalize well to test data. To use statistical jargon, even a simple linear model on this data can be considered overfitting, and overfitting rarely leads to good generalizability. Hence, one solution is to simplify the model so that it no longer overfits and generalizes better. One way to simplify the model would be to simply constrain the slope parameter to equal 0, or equivalently, not estimate it:


$$\begin{array}{l} {y_{i} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{i} + \varepsilon_{i}} \\ {\,\,\,\,\, = \beta_{0} + \left( 0 \right)x_{i} + \varepsilon_{i}} \\ {\,\,\,\,\, = \beta_{0} + \varepsilon_{i}} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.2)

This “simpler” model is now just an estimate of the intercept (or “bias” term, to use neural network terminology) along with some error, εi. Simple as this example may be, we have just engaged in an act of regularization of a statistical model. The effect of simplifying the model has another implication; it expresses our belief that the true function is much less complicated than the linear function in this case. Hastie et al. (2009, p. 34) describe this idea beautifully:

Regularization methods, express our prior belief that the type of functions we seek exhibit a certain type of smooth behavior, and indeed can usually be cast in a Bayesian framework.267

Their point is that on a technical level, penalties (or regularization) reflect to some extent prior belief, which is a Bayesian idea. In our example of the line turned to intercept only, the penalty is implicit, and reflects our belief that the true function underlying the data is not as “complicated” as including the slope would suggest. It’s much simpler in that the intercept suffices to account for the true function. This is the idea or spirit of regularization.

Regularization can be very informal in practice and can be as simple as deciding to not model the slope in a simple linear regression problem. From a Bayesian point of view, we are imposing our belief that the true functional form underlying the data is simpler than hypothesizing a non-horizontal slope in the regression.

6.1.1 Regularization in Regression and Beyond

Consider for a moment the extent to which the above basic and simple concept might generalize to other modeling activities and methods. For example, when we constrain a parameter estimate in structural equation modeling so as to not overfit and hence improve generalizability, we are, in effect, engaged in model regularization. Likewise, when we decide on a simpler principal component solution instead of a more complex one for the purpose of generalization (such as in principal components regression, for instance), we are also regularizing the model. As we will see later, there are a variety of ways of regularizing a neural network, perhaps the most obvious or natural way by reducing the number of hidden layers or the number of nodes. Even early stopping of the iterative algorithm in neural networks constitutes a simple way to regularize a neural network.

In general then, anytime a model or method is simplified in some sense, it denotes an act of regularizing that model if such is done in an effort for it to generalize better to test data. In terms of regression, there are three more advanced and common ways of imposing a regularization parameter that go beyond our simple example of constraining the slope above. These include ridge, lasso, and elastic net regression. With the “spirit” of regularization now in place, we now survey these methods.

6.2 Ridge Regression

We begin with ridge regression because it is among the oldest and most significant and influential of the regularization techniques. These techniques often fall under the umbrella of “shrinkage,” where partial regression coefficients are driven toward or to values of 0. At first glance, it may seem questionable why you might ever want to “shrink” coefficients toward 0, but in the end, shrunken coefficients can greatly simplify, and hence regularize, a model. The ridge penalty (or similar, such as the lasso) is also generally known as weight decay and the L2 parameter norm penalty and ridge regression is commonly known as Tikhonov regularization in many circles (Goodfellow et al., 2016). The lasso penalty is commonly known as L1 regularization. Where the ridge penalty is in squared units, that is, a quadratic penalty, the lasso penalty is in absolute value units and is hence nonquadratic. The difference in penalties can have important consequences, especially for data in which the number of cases is greater than the number of variables. For an example of this latter point, see Hastie et al. (2009, p. 660). An advantage of L1 penalization is that such allows for feature selection through driving weights to, rather than simply toward, 0.

Ridge (and lasso, elastic net) can be applied to situations where one might have literally thousands of predictors, and hence shrinking becomes a good strategy for simplifying the model and making it more interpretable. However, just as regularization is a wide-ranging concept, so is 268shrinkage. Shrinkage is merely one way in which a model can be regularized. Be sure this is clear, as there is often some degree of misunderstanding that regularization is equivalent to shrinkage, but this is not the case. Subset selection, stepwise regression, forward regression, and even less formal techniques are all methods designed to regularize a model as well. A regularization method need not be associated with shrinkage.

As mentioned, another benefit to shrinking parameter estimates relates to the ratio of sample size n to the number of predictors p. If n is not that much larger than p, there can result inflated variability in the least-squares fit, which can result in overfitting and possibly poor predictions of future observations not used in the training. What is more, if p > n, there is no longer at all a reliable least-squares estimate, since the variance will be infinite. Under this situation, there exists simply too many ways to project the response variable onto the set of predictors (Hastie et al., 2009). Shrinkage is a tremendously valuable technique in such situations, since by shrinking the estimated coefficients in these cases, both when n = p and p > n, we can essentially reduce the variance at the cost of a negligible increase in bias.

6.2.1 Mathematics of Ridge Regression

To understand how ridge regression works, first recall ordinary least-squares regression. In least-squares regression, β0, β1, ..., βp are estimated via β̂ = (XTX) − 1XTy such as to minimize the residual sums of squares (RSS) function,


$$RSS = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( {y_{i} - \beta_{0} - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}{\beta_{j}x_{ij}}}} \right)^{2}}$$
(6.3)

Not surprisingly, in ridge regression we also seek to minimize a quantity, but instead through the ordinary least-squares (OLS) estimator


β̂ = (XTX) − 1XTy
(6.4)

the ridge estimator adds a small quantity λ to the trace of XTX such that


β̂ridge = (XTX+λI) − 1XTy
(6.5)

The quantity minimized in ridge regression is similar to that in least-squares regression, but with an extra term added:


$$RSS = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( {y_{i} - \beta_{0} - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}{\beta_{j}x_{ij}}}} \right)^{2}} + \lambda{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}\beta_{j}^{2}}$$
(6.6)

Note that the only difference between the two quantities that are minimized is in (6.6), we have added the trailing term $\lambda{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}\beta_{j}^{2}}$, where βj2 is simply the square of βj which we are already familiar. However, this quantity is “weighted” by λ, which is a tuning parameter that is imposed on the sum of the squared regression weights (i.e., $\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}\beta_{j}^{2}$). Taken together, the trailing term $\lambda{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}\beta_{j}^{2}}$ is known as a shrinkage penalty. But why add this penalty term to the original residual sums of squares? What is the theoretical consequence of doing so? We explore that motivation now.269

6.2.2 Consequence of Ridge Estimator

We first note that the residual sums of squares for ridge regression reduces to ordinary least-squares regression when the value for the tuning parameter is equal to 0, since


$$\begin{array}{l} {RSS = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( {y_{i} - \beta_{0} - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}{\beta_{j}x_{ij}}}} \right)^{2}} + \lambda{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}\beta_{j}^{2}}} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( {y_{i} - \beta_{0} - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}{\beta_{j}x_{ij}}}} \right)^{2}} + 0{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}\beta_{j}^{2}}} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( {y_{i} - \beta_{0} - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}{\beta_{j}x_{ij}}}} \right)^{2}}} \\ \end{array}$$

For values of λ greater than 0, we see that it has the effect of increasing the value of the residual sums of squares, since we are then adding on at least some of $\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}\beta_{j}^{2}$ to the least-squares residual.

Hence, ridge regression has the apparent effect of increasing the residual sums of squares over what it would have been had we simply used least-squares regression. This effect can seem contradictory to the purpose of conducting regression in the first place, as up to now, the goal in regression analysis has always been to minimize the objective function, which for classical least-squares has typically been the sum of squared errors. But now, with ridge regression, we are purposely adding on a “penalty” term that would seem to have the effect of increasing the sums of squared errors.

Why would we want to do this? We should have a good reason for doing so. It turns out that we do, and that is because we are no longer using the best unbiased estimator. Instead, ridge regression uses a biased estimator. Ridge regression has an explicit analytic solution, and so numerical methods are not required. Numerical methods will be required when we encounter a related technique called the lasso, as a closed-form solution for the lasso does not exist.

To understand why using a biased estimator may be advantageous over employing an unbiased one, we need to revisit the bias-variance tradeoff discussed earlier in the book.

6.2.3 Revisiting the Bias-Variance Tradeoff: Why Ridge Is Useful

To appreciate why ridge regression is effective and why using a biased estimator has an advantage over an unbiased one, we need to recall the bias-variance tradeoff concept:


E(y0−f̂(x0))2= Var(f̂(x0)) + [Bias[f̂(x0)]]2 + Var(ε)
(6.7)

where E(y0−f̂(x0))2 is the expected test mean squared error (i.e., MSE) at a given value of x, that of x0. The goal is to get E(y0−f̂(x0))2 down or reduced. All else equal in the equality, we see that an increase in [Bias[f̂(x0)]]2 will have the effect of increasing E(y0−f̂(x0))2, not decreasing it, again, all else equal. But here’s the key to understanding ridge regression: not all else is equal! For an increase in bias, the hope is that the variance of the function, that of Var(f̂(x0)), will decrease, which overall, for a constant Var(ε) implies that E(y0−f̂(x0))2 will decrease overall, not increase. Cutting right to the chase, ridge regression works by purposely introducing bias into the estimator to offset a reduction in variance, which we can summarize succinctly below:270


$$\begin{array}{l} \left. E\left( {y_{0} - \hat{f}\left( x_{0} \right)} \right)^{2} = \,\downarrow Var\left( {\hat{f}\left( x_{0} \right)} \right) + \uparrow\left\lbrack {Bias\left\lbrack {\hat{f}\left( x_{0} \right)} \right\rbrack} \right\rbrack^{2} + Var\left( \varepsilon \right) \right. \\ \left. \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = \downarrow E\left( {y_{0} - \hat{f}\left( x_{0} \right)} \right)^{2} \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(6.8)

That is, the net effect of using a ridge estimator is desirable because it typically results in a smaller MSE on test data. This last point is important. The smaller MSE is expected (and desired) on test data, not necessarily training data.

When performing ridge regression, it is common to recommend standardization of input variables prior to carrying out the procedure, despite the recommendation not being accepted by everyone (Izenman, 2008; Thisted, 1976).

6.2.4 A Visual Look at Ridge Regression

Ridge regression can be understood visually and is often referred to as penalized least-squares regression. The original motivation for the ridge estimator, as discussed, was the observation made by Hoerl and Kennard (1970) that potential instability in the OLS estimator could be tracked by adding a small constant k to the diagonal entries of XTX before taking its inverse. This is what results in the ridge estimator, or sometimes called the ridge rule. This has the effect of regularizing ordinary least-squares by shrinking toward a multiple of the identity matrix (Friedman, 1989).

But what is the significance of adding this small constant k? To understand this, consider the depiction in Figure 6.2 (left) featuring that of concentric ovals or ellipses for OLS, along with the search space for ridge estimators. We can see that the ridge estimate lies on the outer oval of the OLS ellipse, for both β1 and β2 (note that β1 and β2 are on the x and y axes, respectively).271

The concentric ellipses in Figure 6.2 represent possible and constant values of residual sums of squares for coefficients β1 and β2 for each ellipse. That is, no matter where RSS is on a given particular ellipse, it is the same value. Ellipses further away from the estimated coefficients have greater RSS. The OLS estimate (and corresponding RSS) in the plot is that RSS produced in regression for a combination of β1 and β2 values. Notice where the corresponding ridge estimate is; it is at a location where both β1 and β2 values have “shrunk” and are thus smaller than the OLS estimates (situated in the center ellipse), though typically not driven all the way to 0 since geometrically ridge features a circular constraint. That is, the circular constraint region is effectively the search space for ridge coefficients. That search is most likely to terminate on an edge of the circular region as shown in Figure 6.2 (left). The lasso, on the other hand, features a diamond search space with sharp edges instead (as a consequence of the L1 penalty), which illustrates that coefficients will not only be driven smaller, but may be “shrunk” to 0. That is, the search space is this time within the diamond, which means RSS will intersect a hard edge of the diamond rather than a smooth part of the circular region as in ridge. Hence, the lasso coefficient “lands” on a 0, such as for β1, as the first point that touches the lasso constraint region, that is, the lasso search space. For a more thorough discussion related to interpreting ridge (and lasso) regression this way, see James et al. (2013) for a deeper explanation of the geometry of ridge vs. lasso regression.

6.2.5 Ridge Regression in Python

Ridge regression can be performed very easily in Python. We create a simple example from sklearn’s ridge library:

from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
import numpy as np
n_samples, n_features = 10, 5

Note from the above that we have designated the number of samples equal to 10 and the number of features equal to 5, which we confirm below:

n_samples

n_features
Out[98]: 5

We now produce some random data on those samples and features, where rng.randn() generates data from a standard normal distribution:

rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
y = rng.randn(n_samples)
X = rng.randn(n_samples, n_features)
y
