clf = Ridge(alpha = 1.0)
clf.fit(X, y)
Out[146]: Ridge()

The default alpha in the above is 1.0. We could adjust it to other values. The smaller the value for alpha (regularization or tuning parameter), the more the solution will resemble ordinary least-squares regression. Recall that for an alpha of 0, the two solutions will converge. As sample size increases and alpha →0, both ridge and linear regression will also converge to generate the same output. With enough training data, the impact of regularization usually also becomes less prominent.

Now, let’s define some new data on each of the five features and predict a value based on that new data. The new data we will define by the name row:

row = [0, 2, 3, 4, 5]
yhat = clf.predict([row])
print(‘Predicted: %.3f’ % yhat)
Predicted: 4.059

We see that for the above new data on row, the predicted value for y is equal to 4.059.

We now cross-validate the solution. The RepeatedKFold cross-validator in Python performs k-fold n times with different randomization in each repetition. We will request ten splits (i.e., “folds”) with three repeats:

import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import RepeatedKFold
cv = RepeatedKFold(n_splits=10, n_repeats=3, random_state=1)
grid = dict()
grid[‘alpha’] = np.arange(0, 1, 0.01)

The above values from 0 to 1 in increments of 0.01 are values of the regularization parameter alpha. We will now run a grid search that scans the parameter values, finding the one that gives the smallest mean absolute error:273

search = GridSearchCV(clf, grid, scoring=‘neg_mean_absolute_error’, cv=cv, n_jobs=-1)
results = search.fit(X, y)
print(‘MAE: %.3f’ % results.best_score_)
MAE: -0.620
print(‘Config: %s’ % results.best_params_)
Config: {‘alpha’: 0.13}

Above, we see that the negative mean absolute error (i.e., MAE) is equal to −0.620 based on the most optimal parameter, equal to an alpha of 0.13.

Python also offers Bayesian ridge regression, where regularization parameters are updated systematically. To implement Bayesian ridge regression, see the BayesianRidge() function in Python. Also, for the example featured here, because we drew random data from a standard normal distribution (i.e., the data drawn were on the same scale), we did not standardize the resulting data to have a mean equal to 0 and standard deviation equal to one. However, such does not imply that standardization would not be worthwhile here. This is especially true in situations where variables occur naturally on different scales where one does not want the “importance” of one variable to exceed that of another simply due to the scale on which it is being measured. On the other hand, it is possible that this kind of “Bayesian prior” in terms of the original scale on which measurements are taken is precisely what is desired depending on the research setting and context, in which case the decision to standardize or not is a more difficult decision (Izenman, 2008). Either way, it is a good idea to compare results both with and without standardization when conducting most regularization methods. If one must choose one option over the other, it is probably a good idea to standardize (Hastie et al., 2009, p. 63) in most cases, but such should not be done without great care and consideration.

Indeed, beyond regularization methods, the decision of whether or not to standardize must be made in many other methods as well (e.g., principal components analysis). Offering a “cookbook” recommendation to “always standardize” is not good statistical teaching, especially without carefully considering whether or not it is desirable that the original variances of the measurement units play a role in the ensuing statistical analyses. Once more with the Bayesian prior concept, sometimes we want those variances to impact the solution, whereas other times we do not. The key point is that neither solution is definitively right or wrong, and the decision to keep measurements in their original units or transform them to standardized units needs to be made on a case-by-case basis.

6.2.6 Ridge Regression in R

Ridge regression in R can be performed using the lmridge package (Imdad & Aslam, 2018). For an excellent summary of this package, see Ullah et al. (2018). The package is outstanding in its coverage of all things “ridge.” In the following, we fit a ridge regression to the Hald data. The data relate to an engineering application that was concerned with the effect of the composition of cement on heat evolved during hardening. What is most relevant about this data for our purposes is that the features are relatively highly correlated and hence well-suited for ridge regression. Consult the package for further details on this specific example.

6.3 Lasso Regression

The ridge regression just featured is only one way that we may shrink parameter estimates. A second popular and modern way is through lasso regression. In lasso regression, the idea of minimizing E(y0−f̂(x0))2 over and above what OLS regression would accomplish remains through imposing a penalty term, but this time, instead of the penalty $\lambda{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}\beta_{j}^{2}}$ as in ridge, the penalty term is $\left. \lambda\left. \sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p} \right|\,\beta_{j} \right|$so that we are now minimizing the following:


$$\left. RSS = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( {y_{i} - \beta_{0} - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}{\beta_{j}x_{ij}}}} \right)^{2}} + \lambda{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}\left| \beta_{j} \right.} \right|$$
(6.9)

That is, instead of the tuning parameter being applied to the sum of squared regression weights, $\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}\beta_{j}^{2}$, it is now applied to the sum of the absolute value regression weights, $\left. {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}\left| \beta_{j} \right.} \right|$. Be sure to note however that whether adding a squared term in ridge regression or absolute value term in lasso regression, the general principle is the same, and that is to include a penalty term to the least-squares residual sum of squares to seemingly increase the error function. But again, it is worth asking why we would want to do such a thing. As before with ridge, it becomes “worth it” if such an addition of the penalty reduces MSE on test (not necessarily train) data. The only difference between ridge and lasso is the nature of the penalty. In both cases, as lambda λ increases, all coefficients in the regression will eventually go to 0, and hence a “stopping point” will be required; otherwise performing ridge or lasso regression would be trivial and meaningless. That is, while we would like to shrink some coefficients to or toward 0, driving all coefficients to 0 would be 277counterproductive. As we will soon see, in practice, the stopping point is typically selected via cross-validation.

According to Müller and Guido (2017), ridge is usually the first choice between that of ridge vs. lasso. Lasso might be most useful if you have a large number of predictors and expect only a few of them to be important, so that the rest can drop out. Remember, lasso can be used for variable selection because it drives some coefficients all the way to 0. This is the key distinguishing feature, in an applied sense, between using ridge vs. the lasso.

6.3.1 Lasso Regression in Python

We can perform lasso regression in Python using sklearn.linear_model by importing the lasso function. As with ridge, the tuning parameter is adjusted via alpha():

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso
lasso_reg = Lasso(alpha = 0.1)

Let’s first build some random data. We will request three columns for X and a single column for y:

X = 2*np.random.rand(10, 3)

The designation (10, 3) requests 10 rows by 3 columns, and hence 3 variables, each having 10 values:

X

6.3.2 Lasso Regression in R

Lasso regression in R can be fit using glmnet() in the glmnet package (Friedman et al., 2023). As was true for lmridge, glmnet is an outstanding package. The options are endless for performing lasso regression and a host of other regression models. Hastie et al. (2023) also published An Introduction to glmnet, which is equally outstanding and strongly recommended for getting started with glmnet.

We feature an example from the package:

> library(glmnet)
> data(QuickStartExample)
> x <- QuickStartExample$x
> y <- QuickStartExample$y

There are four predictors in x and a single response in y. We now fit the model (printing only a few cases):

> fit <- glmnet(x, y)
> fit

The number of nonzero coefficients is indicated by DF, with %Dev indicating the percent of deviance explained for various values of lambda, where the higher the deviance, the more that is explained by that particular case. The percent deviance explained is relative to the null deviance, which is a baseline model containing only the intercept term.

The plot() function (Figure 6.5) reveals the coefficient growth as a function of λ and consequently the L1 norm ∑|βj| of the coefficient vector, where the top axis (0–9) shows the number of nonzero coefficient for the given value of L1:

> plot(fit)
> plot(fit, label = TRUE)

Note that as values of L1 decrease toward 0, the “extreme” lasso solution is obtained with all coefficients equal to 0 implying that the number of nonzero coefficients (upper axis) is equal to 0. The right-most axis corresponds to the variable numbers. As evident in the plot, variable 1 has the largest coefficient. The second-largest (in magnitude) is variable 14 (the plot has been shrunk somewhat and so it cannot be seen; variable 14 is at the extreme lower right of the plot).

We can also perform cross-validation directly using the glmnet() function (Figure 6.7), which performs k-fold cross-validation (ten-fold by default).

> set.seed(123)
> cvfit <- cv.glmnet(x, y)
> plot(cvfit)

We can extract the horizontal line value (left vertical line) along with the corresponding coefficient for this value:

> cvfit$lambda.min
[1] 0.07569327

The value of lambda that generates the minimum is thus equal to 0.076. The natural log of this number is equal to −2.58, which is the left line shown in the above plot (Boehmke and Greenwell, 2020, p. 131). The vertical line to the right is that of lambda.1se, which is lambda equal to one standard error of the aforementioned minimum (cvfit$lambda.1se). We now obtain coefficients based on this minimum value (we print only the first few):282

Hence, via cross-validation, we have settled on a set of coefficients that we could deem “final” for our lasso regression, or could have also explored coefficients in the neighborhood of lambda.min. Automating the tuning parameter can further be performed using the caret package (Kuhn, 2008). Boehmke and Greenwell (2020, p. 133) provide an excellent summary of how to use the caret package for this purpose, where a grid search over values of lambda for various values of alpha is performed, where the alpha setting indicates whether we have performed ridge, lasso, or elastic net (to be surveyed next). That is, such a search will reveal the model with both the best (i.e., lowest RMSE) alpha parameter and lambda combined. A similar approach for searching for both alpha and lambda can be performed using cv.glmnet (see the package for details).

6.4 Elastic Net

A third option for shrinking parameters is that of elastic net, with penalty equal to


$$\left. {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}\left( \alpha \middle| \beta_{j} \middle| + \left( 1 - \alpha \right) \right.}\beta_{j}^{2} \right)$$
(6.10)

Elastic net is considered a compromise of sorts between the ridge and lasso, a kind of “hybrid” of the aforementioned estimators (Hastie et al., 2009). It can be shown that elastic net actually employs a linear combination of the ridge and lasso penalty functions (see Izenman, 2008, p. 153 for details).

Note that elastic net features two coefficients, βj2 and |βj|. To understand the role of α, the tuning parameter in this context, note that it is being applied to both βj2 and |βj|, both the losses that are used in the ridge and lasso, respectively (i.e., quadratic and absolute function losses). Hence, we can see that the role of α is to differentially weight βj2 and |βj|. This is why elastic net is interpreted as a “compromise” between ridge and lasso, and such compromise depends on the chosen value for α in differentially weighting the ridge and lasso L2 and L1 losses, respectively.

6.4.1 Elastic Net in Python

The library scikit-learn can perform elastic net. In what follows we fit an elastic net model on two features:

from sklearn.linear_model import ElasticNet
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
X, y = make_regression(n_features=2, random_state=0)
regr = ElasticNet(random_state=0)
283

We print only a few cases of X and y below:

print(regr.predict([[0, 0]]))

Not surprisingly, we see that the predicted value is equal to the intercept of 1.45 (try other values to see what predicted values you get).

As we did for the lasso, we can use the package glmnet to fit elastic net in R. We can also use a recently-proposed package fasterElasticNet (Ma et al., 2022) that purports to fit elastic net (and related models) very efficiently.284

6.5 Which Regularization Penalty Is Better?

To conclude our discussion of these regularization approaches, it should be noted that neither ridge nor lasso nor elastic net will universally dominate each other. There is no free lunch! Lasso might perform better when a few coefficients are close to 0 and the rest quite substantial, where ridge often performs best when all coefficients are approximately equal, or at minimum, of equal importance to the investigator. However, there are no guarantees. The use of cross-validation in some capacity is recommended to determine which approach is better for a given data set, with tuning parameters selected via grid search on different values and cross-validation employed to observe which gives the lowest test error. To reiterate, we want to minimize the test error, not necessarily train error. This is why cross-validation is so important to choosing an optimal tuning parameter. See Frank and Friedman (1993) for a comparison of ordinary least-squares to not only ridge regression, but also principal components regression and partial least-squares.

6.6 Least-Angle Regression

As we have seen when surveying variable selection techniques, forward regression selects variables in the candidate pool one at a time that improves model fit. Least-angle regression can be seen as a related technique to forward regression as it still selects based on a forward strategy, but does not necessarily select the entire variable. Instead, what enters into the selection is as much of the variable that is merited to the prediction, not all of it as in traditional stepwise routines. Hastie et al. (2009, pp. 73–74) describe the algorithm most succinctly:

At the first step it [least-angle regression] identifies the variable most correlated with the response. Rather than fit this variable completely, LAR (least-angle regression) moves the coefficient of this variable continuously toward its least-squares value (causing its correlation with the evolving residual to decrease in absolute value). As soon as another variable “catches up” in terms of correlation with the residual, the process is paused. The second variable then joins the active set, and their coefficients are moved together in a way that keeps their correlations tied and decreasing. This process is continued until all the variables are in the model, and ends at the full least-squares fit.

The algorithm begins with standardizing predictors to have a mean equal to 0 and variance equal to 1 (i.e., z-scores). At this initial step, the residual ri is computed having no predictors in the model, that is, $r_{i} = y_{i} - \overline{y}$, with all coefficients in the regression set to 0. That is, β1 = β2, ..., βp = 0. Next, the predictor having the largest correlation with this residual is entered into the model; however, not all of it. The predictor’s weight moves toward its least-squares coefficient until another predictor “catches up” and has as much correlation with the current residual as the first predictor. At this point, both β1 and β2 move in the direction of their joint least-squares coefficient until another predictor “catches up” to the current residual. The algorithm proceeds in this way until all predictors are entered and hence the least-squares solution is achieved for the model. In the case where the number of predictors is greater than sample size (more specifically, N-1), the algorithm will reach a zero residual condition after N-1 steps (Hastie et al., 2009, p. 74).

Hence, least-angle regression builds up a regression model by piecewise linear “partial” steps, adding single elements at each step by correlating the new variable with the current residual. As another variable “catches up,” the algorithm moves in a direction equiangular (i.e., having the 285same angle) to predictors. For this reason, least-angle regression has been called the “democratic” version of stepwise (Hastie et al., 2009). Both the lasso and forward stagewise regression models can be computed through the least-angle regression algorithm (Izenman, 2008). The key point to emphasize is that in least-angle regression, predictors essentially “catch up” to others in the selection process, then those variables move together. In Python, the Lars estimator can be used to fit a least-squares regression. The LARS lasso can also be used which implements the LARS estimator while driving some coefficients to 0, as is characteristic of the lasso.

6.7 Additional Variable Selection Algorithms

Other selection algorithms similar in spirit to the ridge and lasso include the Dantzig selector as well as the Garotte (Breiman, 1995). But why use different penalties in the first place? That is, why not use the same selection algorithm in all situations regardless of the data? The answer to this question once more lies in the No-Free-Lunch Theorem, discussed earlier in the book, which, recall, holds that no universal algorithm universally dominates all data sets. That is, one data set may have specific “peculiarities” for which one algorithm capitalizes, while another data set may not (James et al., 2021). Hence, different regularization techniques may generate slightly different results depending on the peculiarities of the given data set and it is virtually impossible to be certain that one algorithm or method will dominate others on any particular data set. Just as no single treatment is guaranteed to “work” on any given individual, no single statistical or machine learning method is guaranteed to dominate all others on any single data set.289

Still, the above admonition does not mean we cannot narrow things down to at least a “preferred” approach in “most” circumstances. According to Izenman (2008, p. 154), when comparing penalized regression approaches:

Extensive simulations comparing prediction accuracy under a wide variety of conditions and models … show that the Lasso, which tends to choose too many variables, almost always contains the correct model; the nonnegative garotte tends to select smaller models than the Lasso, and all-possible subsets, while more likely to choose the correct model than the Lasso, selects models that contain the correct model far less often than the Lasso.

7 Nonlinear and Nonparametric Regression

DOI: 10.4324/9781003376941-10

The regression methods surveyed thus far in this book have all featured one common assumption: that of the relationship between response variables and explanatory variables being modeled is linearly related. Why is linearity the focus of so many statistical methods? Huge books, some well over a thousand pages, are written primarily on linear methods alone. Why the obsession with linearity? We see two primary reasons for this focus on linearity:

  1. Many phenomena in the sciences can be well approximated by linear methods. The true function underlying the data may not be (and in fact, is usually not) linear, but linear models allow us to approximate those unknown functions rather well. In short, linearity “works” in many sciences because, though specifying the exact functional form underlying data is difficult to impossible, linearity is a useful assumption to make and makes for a nice approximation of scientific reality. The key words here are assumption and approximation. Very few data, if any, actually fall on a straight line.
  2. A second reason why linearity is popular is because it is simple and convenient. In the absence of knowing the true functional form, linearity provides reasonable prediction and generality analogous in some sense to why we use means and averages to describe many phenomena, even though such can be grossly misleading at times. Even in its sister discipline, linear algebra, linearity is, not surprisingly given its name, assumed in most applications. The convenience of fitting simple, functional forms comes at a price, however. Rarely, if ever, do those functional forms represent empirical reality. Reality is usually much more complex, or at least in many cases, we assume it is more complex. However, assuming a linear relationship generally guards against overfitting and hence can be more generalizable than if we try too much to model the exact form of the relationship that may underlie the data.

Though linear models dominate statistics and science, many, if not most phenomena in science are nonlinear. Seeking alternatives to linearity is often preferred to better capture the reality of scientific processes. Advancements in statistics and machine learning are often geared toward models and algorithms that help better unpack nonlinear features in data. Efforts to detect complex nonlinear patterns are at the heart of cutting-edge statistics and machine learning.

The truth of the matter is that most if not all relationships are nonlinear and may be even more complex than we could even ever model. Having surveyed the linear ground thus far in this book, our goal in this chapter is to survey a few methods that model nonlinear relationships. There are 291three general approaches that we will consider here that seek to capture nonlinearity in data: 1) polynomial regression, 2) regression splines, and 3) kernel regression, which we will first motivate by simple local-averaging.

7.1 Polynomial Regression

Recall the classic linear model,


yi = β0 + β1xi + εi
(7.1)

The above model is actually a special case of the more general polynomial regression model,


yi = β0 + β1xi + β2xi2 + β3xi3 + β4xi4+   ⋅  ⋅ ⋅   + βpxip + εi
(7.2)

A polynomial of order p can have p − 1 “bends.” For instance, a straight line of order “1” has p − 1 = 1 − 1 = 0 bends, which is what makes it a straight line (i.e., there are no “bends” in a straight line, at least macroscopically). A parabola has a single bend (i.e., 2 − 1 = 1), and so on. A constant-only model (e.g., the mean) implies p = 0.

Typically, polynomials of only degrees 1 through 4 are generally used in scientific practice, since the higher the order of the polynomial, the greater the possibility of overfitting. That is, while fitting a polynomial of say, degree 10 might provide an exceptional fit to your training data (you may in fact be connecting the dots if your sample size is rather small!), many of those higher degrees are likely simply capitalizing on chance factors or random noise in the training data and hence the fit will not generalize well when validated on test data. That is, a polynomial of excessive order is likely to overfit the data. Recall that when it comes to model validation, it is how the model fits on test data that matters most, not how it fits on training data.

A polynomial of order (or “degree”) p can have p − 1 “bends.” The complexity of a polynomial increases with the number of bends in it. Typically, polynomials of only up to degree 4 are used in scientific practice, as higher-order polynomials are likely to overfit the training data. However, higher-order polynomials may be useful depending on the nature of the scientific material and domain.

When we are fitting the classic linear model, we are in actuality performing polynomial regression, only that the polynomial is a rather simple one, that of a line. That is, the linear equation is simply a special case of the wider polynomial equation where only powers of one are included:


$$\begin{array}{l} {y_{i} = \left\{ {\beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{i}} \right\} + \beta_{2}x_{i}^{2} + \beta_{3}x_{i}^{3} + \beta_{4}x_{i}^{4} + \,\, \cdot \cdot \cdot \,\, + \beta_{p}x_{i}^{p} + \varepsilon_{i}} \\ \left. \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\downarrow \right. \\ {y_{i} = \left\{ {\beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{i}} \right\} + \varepsilon_{i}} \\ \end{array}$$

Another way of thinking of the above is that the linear model is a polynomial model in which all higher powers beyond unity are constrained or set to zero.292

7.1.1 Polynomial Regression in Python

We can fit a basic polynomial regression in Python quite easily using numpy.polyfit():

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

We would like to fit a polynomial to the following data:

x = [1,2,3,5,6,7,8,9,10,12,13,14,15,16,18,19,21,22]
y = [100,90,80,60,60,55,60,65,70,70,75,76,78,79,90,99,99,100]

We specify a third-degree polynomial (Figure 7.1):

mymodel = np.poly1d(np.polyfit(x, y, 3))
myline = np.linspace(1, 22, 100)
plt.scatter(x, y)
Out[209]: <matplotlib.collections.PathCollection at 0x1af74f20dd0>
plt.plot(myline, mymodel(myline))
Out[210]: [<matplotlib.lines.Line2D at 0x1af77d64cd0>]
plt.show()
import numpy
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score
print(r2_score(y, mymodel(x)))
0.9432150416451026

We can see from the R-squared that the proportion of variance explained by the polynomial is approximately 94%. The cubic model (i.e., degree 3) fits better than had we tried a quadratic one:293

mymodel = np.poly1d(np.polyfit(x, y, 2))
print(r2_score(y, mymodel(x)))
0.759777160189589

Had we fit a model of degree 4 (i.e., quartic), we would have obtained only a slightly larger R-squared than the cubic, which would have probably resulted in overfitting the data:

mymodel = np.poly1d(np.polyfit(x, y, 4))
print(r2_score(y, mymodel(x)))
0.9542030834699506

Polynomial regression can also be performed in Python using statsmodels.

7.1.2 Polynomial Regression in R

We illustrate polynomial regression on the Boston data set. This is data derived from information collected by the U.S. Census Service on housing characteristics and measures in the area of Boston, MA. We will use the tidyverse (Wickham et al., 2019) and caret (Kuhn, 2008) packages. A version of polynomial regression using this data can also be found in James et al. (2013, p. 115):

> library(tidyverse)
> library(caret)
> data(“Boston”, package = “MASS”)

There are a total of 506 observations in the Boston data. We will now split the data 0.8 into train and 0.2 into test:

> set.seed(123)
> training.samples <- Boston$medv %>%
+ createDataPartition(p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
> train.data <- Boston[training.samples, ]
> test.data <- Boston[-training.samples, ]

We confirm that the data has been split correctly:

> nrow(train.data)
[1] 407
> nrow(test.data)
[1] 99

The number of rows in the train data is 407 while the number of rows in the test data is 99. Recall we had requested that the train data be 80% of the entire data. The total number of cases is equal to 407 + 99 = 506, of which 407 is 80%.

We will now build the model, a polynomial model of degree 5 on the train data:

> model <- lm(medv ~ poly(lstat, 5, raw = TRUE),
+ data = train.data)

We can see that all degrees of the polynomial are statistically significant, most importantly the highest degree in this case, which is the fifth degree (p = 0.003421). The model explains approximately 68% of the variance in the response (i.e., Multiple R-squared). Adjusted R-squared is only slightly less at 0.6777.
We now obtain some predictions based on the test data:
> predictions <- model %>% predict(test.data)
> head(predictions)
      3          6          9          11     14         15
36.25964 31.52683 10.98130 14.57053 24.46163 22.15775

We can get an R-squared on the predictions as follows, which we can see is just a bit higher than the explained variance on the train data:

> R_squared = R2(predictions, test.data$medv)
> R_squared
[1] 0.6829474

We can also test smaller-degree models, such as simply a quadratic model. We can obtain coefficients for this model as follows:

> print(lm(medv ~ lstat + I(lstat^2), data = train.data))
Call:
lm(formula = medv ~ lstat + I(lstat^2), data = train.data)
Coefficients:
(Intercept) lstat I(lstat^2)
  42.5736 -2.2673  0.0412
295

The package polyreg (Matloff et al., 2022) can also be used to fit polynomial regression models.

7.1.3 Polynomial Regression as a Global Strategy

What is the problem with polynomial regression? There is no problem, really, if one wishes to model the entire range of xi by assuming a common functional form. That is, both the classic linear model and polynomial regression fit the data in a very global manner, similar in some sense to how the arithmetic mean summarizes a set of data from one end of the distribution to the other. For example, consider the small data set

2, 5, 8, 10, 15, 16, 170, 171, 172

The mean of this data is 63.2. But how well does the mean represent the data? Not that well, since, for example, the data points 170, 171, and 172 are very much greater than the rest of the data and the mean will thus be pulled upward because of these more extreme scores:

2, 5, 8, 10, 15, 16, 170, 171, 172

Computing the mean on the above set of data provides a very “global” summary of the data. We may not wish to model the data in this way, whether it is in computing the mean or conducting a regression, and may prefer a more local approach.

7.1.4 A More Local Alternative

For the above data, we may be better off calculating two averages, one for the data 2, 5, 8, 10, 15, 16, and one for the data 170, 171, 172. In doing so, we are essentially modeling the data at a more local level. Though this example is very simple, it demonstrates a strong but obvious point, and that is, fitting global measures to data provides a global summary of that data. If the data does not conform to a global representation, then fitting subsets of the data more locally may be preferable. Indeed, at its extreme, the most local we could go is to model each data point individually, but such would be foolish and detract from the purpose of modeling in the first place, except for extremely small data sets. Exact “curve-fitting” is essentially “connecting the dots,” which, for most purposes, defeats the goal of statistical modeling. In this case, we are not averaging anything; we are simply connecting observations on a descriptive level. The general goal of modeling is to estimate a general function over the data, even if local. The goal is not simply “connecting the dots” on the training data and achieving perfect fit. Anything less than “connecting the dots,” in most cases, can be considered a very general universal form of the aforementioned and discussed regularization concept as it concerns generalizability and minimizing test error.

7.1.5 Least-Squares Regression Line as a “Floating Mean”: Toward a Localized Approach

To further motivate localized regression approaches, recall that the classic least-squares regression line can be interpreted as a “floating mean” across the range of values of the predictor, xi. That is, the slope β1 in yi = β0 + β1xi + εi, analogous to the mean, is a kind of “summary statistic” because 296the model assumes it is constant across the range of xi. Even if the data suggested a different slope or functional form within a given range of xi, the classic least-squares line would not account for this. Likewise for polynomial regression, in which the polynomial is fit across the range of xi, essentially ignoring more “local behavior” within intervals of xi. Both linear and polynomial regression generalize over xi to provide a summary of the data in terms of model fit.

What if we wished, however, to consider local variation more carefully? Perhaps the easiest example is that of a scatterplot that you may have come across in introductory statistics, one featuring the presence of two “groups” within the plot, as in Figure 7.2.

Of course, for the data in Figure 7.2, a more localized approach to the regression could be as simple as modeling each group separately, with one slope for males and one slope for females. The locality of the data, in this case, is the group. But consider this example carefully and you will see that what we are actually proposing here, at least implicitly, is to recognize the potential for an interaction in the plot and not simply a main effect. That is, spotting the potential of an interaction in this sense is an effort to provide a more localized representation of the data.

A localized representation of data can be as simple as computing different averages by identifying different sets in data, or by modeling interaction terms in a regression (or ANOVA) context.

7.1.5.1 Zooming in on Locality

What if we take locality to the limit, to the extreme? As mentioned, to do so would be to narrow in on each individual data point in our plot, or, for the example of averages, to simply consider each data point by itself. It doesn’t get much more “local” than considering the case study without producing an average at all!

In the regression context, we could produce interaction terms with increasingly greater degrees of “split” or factor levels in ANOVA in one or more variables. Hence, instead of dividing the 297data into two groups, we could divide them into four or five, for instance. The general principle then in a localized approach to regression (or ANOVA) is that instead of assuming a general functional form across the range of xi, we wish instead to “zoom in” and inspect local variations within given intervals of xi. This is where localized methods of regression come into play. However, as we survey a few approaches to accomplish this, the reader should take away what we have discussed here: that zooming in locally on data can be as simple as splitting data in different ways or modeling interaction terms in regression or ANOVA. That is, local examination and modeling of data need not necessarily take the form of a sophisticated or advanced modeling strategy.

To understand and motivate local regression, it is imperative to first understand the nature of a basis function as it relates to regression and modeling in general. Basis functions are so general that they also open the door to understanding more advanced techniques such as neural networks as well, as there are intimate connections between basis functions and most other statistical and machine learning methods.

7.2 Basis Functions and Expansions

A basis function, or linear basis expansion (Hastie et al., 2009) is essentially the taking of a function of variable (or matrix, in this case) X, which we can express quite generally,


yi = β0 + β1b1(xi) + β2b2(xi) + β3b3(xi) + β4b4(xi)+   ⋅  ⋅ ⋅   + βpbp(xi) + εi
(7.3)

Note that the above is not polynomial regression; none of the (xi) are raised to exponents other than unity. The actual basis functions, which are functions of xi, are b1 through bp. For example, β1b1(xi) is the same as we would classically have in least-squares in that we are weighting xi by the regression parameter β1, but to be more precise, what is being weighted is not xi; we are instead weighting a function of xi, and that function is b1(xi). That is, we first weight xi by b1, then weight that product by β1. The basis function here is b1(xi).

To understand the above more clearly, consider the classic linear model as a special case of where basis functions occur. What basis function is inherent or “natural” in the classic linear model? To see this, we observe


$$\begin{array}{l} {y_{i} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}b_{1}\left( x_{i} \right) + \beta_{2}b_{2}\left( x_{i} \right) + \beta_{3}b_{3}\left( x_{i} \right) + \beta_{4}b_{4}\left( x_{i} \right) + \,\, \cdot \cdot \cdot \,\, + \beta_{p}b_{p}\left( x_{i} \right) + \varepsilon_{i}} \\ {y_{i} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}b_{1}\left( x_{i} \right)} \\ {y_{i} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}\left( 1 \right)\left( x_{i} \right)} \\ {y_{i} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}\left( x_{i} \right)} \\ \end{array}$$

and thus we end up with the classic one-predictor linear model. The basis function, b1(xi) is simply xi with b1 implied or set to 1.

Let’s now consider a primitive though arbitrary basis function simply to extend on this simple definition. Instead of b1(xi) = (1)(xi), suppose the basis b1 were equal to 2, making b1(xi) = (2)(xi). Note that none of this is related to the slope β1; the basis function here is simply an “action” directly on xi before the partial regression slope is applied to it. The question for us then, is what should the basis function comprise of? There are many possibilities, and the choice of a basis function will be motivated by the type of model we are considering. It doesn’t take long to realize that one could quite easily write an entire book titled Basis Functions for Prediction, which would encompass numerous possibilities and statistical models, which would include simple and multiple 298linear regression, polynomial regression, step functions, regression splines, analysis of variance, and a whole gamut of others. The common thread in all of these models is that they are identified by their bases, that is, their transformations of xi before weighting by least-squares or other technique; that is, before weighting by the parameter estimates in the given model.

7.2.1 Basis Functions and Locality

Among the chief benefits of basis functions is that they allow us to model the data at a more local level, much more local than polynomial regression ever could. The use of basis functions also allows us to model the relationship between y and x nonlinearly by adopting nonlinear basis functions. Because the basis function occurs inside of the expression “β1b1(xi)”, we could, in theory, allow b1 to be a whole host of nonlinear functions (Bishop, 2006), which include Gaussian basis functions such as the following,


$$\phi_{j}\left( x \right) = \exp\left\{ \frac{\left( x - \mu_{j} \right)^{2}}{2s^{2}} \right\}$$
(7.4)

or a sigmoidal basis function,


$$\phi_{j}\left( x \right) = \sigma\left( \frac{x - \mu_{j}}{s} \right)$$
(7.5)

among others, where s is the standard deviation in the aforementioned functions. The basis functions we have surveyed thus far have been all fixed beforehand; that is, they are not amenable or adaptable to the data. The curse of dimensionality will also limit the utility of fixed basis functions (Bishop, 2006). It will thus be advantageous to consider basis functions that are not fixed. We will encounter such basis functions, that is, those that are adaptive or recursive, when we survey neural networks later in the book and emphasize the connection between the regression methods of this chapter and neural network approaches.

A basis function, or linear basis expansion, weights the predictors in a regression model. Depending on the basis function chosen, this may allow for a more “local” examination of the fit at that particular point or region in the range of predictor values, or, may be limited to a more global representation of the data. In regression, this weighting occurs before weighting by the relevant partial regression slope. The basis functions employed in this chapter are fixed and hence can be quite limiting. Neural network basis functions are generally more adaptive to the data.

7.2.2 Neural Networks as a Basis Expansion: Generalizing the Concept

We mentioned above that we could title an entire book about basis functions or more precisely, basis expansions. We emphasized some of the more popular “special cases” of what we would include in such a book, namely simple and multiple regression, and so on. This was meant to 299emphasize how general basis expansions actually are and how many statistical methods can be understood or conceived in terms of basis expansions. Indeed, neural networks can be considered as a basis expansion as well and yet another special case of this wider framework.

In a classic neural network, as we will see later in the book, we take functions of functions, otherwise known as composite functions from elementary mathematics. Taking composite functions allows us to implement a similar idea of a basis expansion as we did just earlier. The general concept we need is that of a feature extractor (Murray, 2022):


f(x;θ) = Wϕ(x) + a
(7.6)

The parameters in the above are θ = (W,a) and if we were to write the classic functional equation, we would omit ϕ altogether. The key to the above, however, is the inclusion of ϕ which in our earlier regression example was β1b1(xi) where ϕ = b1. That is,


$$\begin{array}{l} {f\left( x;\theta \right) = W\phi\left( x \right) + a} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = Wb_{i}\left( x \right) + a} \\ \end{array}$$

where we now denote b1 as bi to eliminate any confusion in notation. What is the benefit to writing f(x;θ) this way? The answer is its generality. The more general form for f(x;θ) allows ϕ to be a more arbitrary and general function. More to the point, we are now permitting the feature extractor to have its own designated parameter, θ2:


f(x;θ) = Wϕ(x;θ2) + a
(7.7)

As we will see when we study neural networks, this allowance of the feature extractor to have its own parameter vector will generalize our current idea of basis expansion to much wider possibilities. The general idea is to specify functions of functions, which is what neural networks are all about.

We can see then that basis functions are an entirely general concept, and the choice of a basis function is essentially theoretically limitless. In the earliest of courses in introductory statistics, basis functions are indeed present in t-tests, ANOVA, regression, and so on; however they are simply not revealed and are usually implicit within the given method or procedure. Interactions in ANOVA, for instance, are yet another example of a basis expansion. Basis expansions essentially enrich the feature space. Support vector machines are yet another example of a basis expansion, which we survey later in the book.

In what follows and in returning to our discussion of nonlinearity, we focus on a particularly common basis function or expansion that will prove useful for modeling nonlinear regression, that of regression splines.

7.2.3 Regression Splines and the Concept of a “Knot”

We have discussed so far the benefit of leaving global functions behind and fitting more local functions to data. The general idea is to fit a model locally, or “zoomed in” to different parts of the data. Regression splines are a common way to get at the local structure of the data in a regression context.

But how can we define local subsets of the data range? An easy and common way to do so is via knots. A knot is something that divides areas of the data on xi into intervals, where the coefficients in the model change as to reflect a change in the data trend. In general, the greater the number 300knots, the greater the flexibility of the curve. As the number of knots increases without bound to infinity, we eventually obtain perfect fit. If we use too many knots, however, we are at risk of overfitting. The selection of the right number is thus crucial and is typically made by cross-validation or possibly simply by visualization. Smoothing splines, on the other hand, often use a maximal or near-maximal number of knots instead of that number being arbitrarily selected by the user (Hastie et al., 2009).

Figure 7.3 depicts the concept of a knot in spline regression, where it is clear that the coefficient of the curve changes in a rather dramatic and somewhat exaggerated way to illustrate the concept.

Recall that in the previous chapter we had chosen the tuning parameter in ridge, lasso, and elastic net by cross-validation to implement regularization. The choice of the number of knots can also be considered a form of regularization, and thus the number of knots can be thought of as a tuning parameter. That is, by reducing the number of knots, thus reducing the chance of overfitting, we are essentially regularizing the model. Indeed, this whole discussion of splines can actually be formally recast into the wider category of regularization (see Hastie et al., 2009, pp. 167–168 for a discussion). It is generally recommended that using 4 to 5 knots equally distributed, say at percentiles 20, 40, 60, etc., is a useful first strategy for their implementation in a typical regression problem (Fox, 2016).

Knots in regression splines define local subsets of a data range where coefficients typically change. The choice of the number of knots in spline regression can yet again be considered an instance of regularizing a model, just as selecting a suitable tuning parameter in ridge and lasso regression was a form of regularization. Hence, the number of knots can be thought of as a tuning parameter.301

7.2.4 Conceptualizing Regression Splines

How should we conceptualize the idea of a regression spline? Regression splines are best represented as a special case of the more general idea of basis functions or basis expansions that we just surveyed. Recall the basis representation developed earlier:


yi = β0 + β1b1(x1) + β2b2(x2) + β3b3(x3) + β4b4(x4)+   ⋅  ⋅ ⋅   + βpbp(xp) + εi

where b1 through bp are the basis functions. That is, they are transformations of xi before the relevant weighting by β1 through βp. The placement of the knots can, in theory at least, be arbitrarily chosen based on shifts in the function. However, as mentioned, a uniform, equally spaced distribution of knots is usually the more common and initial strategy (James et al., 2013).

Cross-validation can be used to determine the best number of knots, that which produces the smallest residual sums of squares in the test error. Cubic splines are often preferred because these naturally ensure the function is continuous and has continuous first and second derivatives at each knot (Murphy, 2022). The number of knots divides the data into one or more bins. For example, 4 knots divide the data into 4 + 1 bins. If we increased the number of knots to their limit, we would have the number of knots equal to the number of values for xi or data points. Using n knots to represent xi unique values results in what is generally known as a smoothing spline. Since there is typically not a fixed number of knots determined a priori, smoothing splines are usually regarded as nonparametric, as the number of splines is a function of the number of data points or values of xi in the data (Murphy, 2022, p. 395).

As noted by Fox (2016), spline regression models can also be considered a “bridge” between the linear and generalized linear model. In fact, the generalized additive model is one that extends the regression spline to the case of multidimensional inputs, assuming an additive form (i.e., no interactions). The generalized additive model can then be extended beyond regression and into classification, in which case one has the full-blown generalized linear model (Murphy, 2022).

7.2.5 Problem with Splines and Imposing Constraints

The great thing about splines is that we can be as flexible as we wish. However, too much flexibility entails a cost. For example, consider Figure 7.4. In this case, we are too flexible. That is, we have not imposed enough constraints on the knots. To remedy this, we begin imposing constraints, such as continuity from left to right to ensure there cannot be a jump (James et al., 2013). Recall what “imposing a constraint” means; it means we would like the curve to fit, but without, in this case of continuity, a jump. That is, we have taken the “jump” out of the possibility in the fitting or estimation of the curve; this is the constraint we are imposing.

This idea of imposing constraints on functions is not at all new. Indeed, virtually every statistical model has constraints either implicitly imposed that we cannot see or that the user imposes manually, such as in structural equation modeling where constraints are regularly imposed. As perhaps the simplest of examples, in linear regression the constraint of linearity is imposed, meaning that we will fit a functional form to data with the constraint that it assumes only a linear form. While this is an obvious example, it is nonetheless powerful and pedagogical; many researchers perform linear regression analysis without the awareness that they have implicitly constrained their predictive potential to that of lines at the expense of other curves such as a higher-order polynomial.302

Constraining a spline regression to have no jumps, or other constraints, gives the model less flexibility as when such parameters need to be estimated, in addition to limiting the type of spline fit so that it is scientifically meaningful to the researcher. Hence, if it is unreasonable to assume a jump can occur in one’s data, then constraining there to be no jumps (or other characteristic of the fitted curve) is perfectly reasonable. On the other hand, if such a jump is a reasonable possibility in the data, then imposing such a constraint would be ill-advised and the data should be modeled in some capacity that incorporates the discontinuity. In this regard, the science matters a great deal. If a discontinuity is a reasonable expectation for the given scientific data, it may make little sense to constrain it.

7.2.6 Polynomial Regression vs. Regression Splines

In our discussion above, we have presented regression splines as a special case of the more general idea of basis functions, and noted they are more local than methods such as polynomial regression. Which provides the better fit? As argued by James et al. (2013), regression splines often give superior results. Why? The reason that splines often give better results is that each polynomial regression and splines introduce flexibility in a different manner. Splines typically do it better. For polynomial regression, flexibility is introduced by increasing the degree of the function (e.g., from linear to quadratic to cubic and so on). Splines, on the other hand, introduce flexibility by keeping the degree fixed and instead increasing the number of knots, which can range from minimal to maximal. Hence, splines are simply more flexible than fitting a global polynomial, even of increasing degree of complexity, which usually means splines will perform better in cross-validation. What is more, as mentioned, regression splines can serve as a bridge to more generalized modeling such as the generalized linear model (Fox, 2016).

One-dimensional splines can also be generalized to multidimensional splines though these are beyond the scope of this book. Multidimensional splines are a straight generalization of the one-dimensional spline, however (Hastie et al., 2009). For an excellent overview of spline options across a variety of R packages, see Perperoglou et al. (2019). We can also use the spline2 package (Wang, 2024) to fit, in addition to natural cubic splines, other splines as well, such as more general B-splines, M-splines, among others, which we will not detail here (see the package for details). Another popular package for fitting splines in R is that of gss (Gu, 2014). One can also use the bspline package (Sokol, 2024) for estimating spline regression. The absorber package (Savino, 2024) is a variable-selection method using b-splines in multivariate nonparametric regression models that can be useful in choosing the “best” variables in a spline regression problem.303

7.3 Nonparametric Regression: Local and Kernel Regression

In our quest to model nonlinearity, we have thus far surveyed two possibilities: polynomial regression and regression splines. Polynomial regression provided a global fit to the data, while splines allowed us to model the data at a more local level. However, both approaches were parametric in nature, though splines, depending on the type and how we are using the terms parametric vs. nonparametric, are also often considered nonparametric (Fox, 2016, p. 511).

We now briefly survey two nonparametric approaches: 1) simple local-averaging, and 2) kernel regression. We will see that kernel regression is a generalization of simple local-averaging and the latter can be used to motivate the former. Kernel regression is our primary focus as a nonparametric technique.

To be more precise, kernel regression is a way to model a non-hypothesized form of the relationship, which will typically end up being some undesignated nonlinear form. It can be considered a nonparametric approach to regression (Fox, 2016). The nonparametric feature of kernel regression, as is true of kernel methods in general, allows the data to “speak” and tell us of its shape; we do not in advance assume a hypothetical linear or nonlinear form. That is, if the parametric linear model is


y = f(x,θ) + ε
(7.8)

then the nonparametric linear model is


$$\begin{array}{l} {y = f\left( x \right) + \varepsilon} \\ {\,\,\,\, = f\left( x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{p} \right) + \varepsilon} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.9)

where now there is no parameter vector, θ and instead the form of the relation is learned entirely by the data, x1, x2, ..., xp. Simple local-averaging on the other hand, is what is generally regarded as a “naïve” approach to regression where averages within predetermined subsets or bins along the x-axis are established in order to obtain a more local flavor in tracing the response variable. Kernel regression can be interpreted as a more general method of simple local-averaging.

7.3.1 Motivating Kernel Regression via Local-Averaging

In classical least-squares regression, recall that we typically assume that the conditional distribution of y/x is Gaussian (i.e., normal). More formally, we model p(y,x|D) where y is the response, x is the predictor, and D is the data. That is, in typical classical regression, we are tracing the mean function:


μ = E(y|x1,...,xp) = α + β1x1 +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + βpxp
(7.10)

Given the assumption that the conditional distribution is normal, consider if we backtracked for a moment and motivated ordinary regression via a naïve approach and dissected the explanatory variable into bins, that is, subsets of area or intervals along the x-axis. Not surprisingly, bias is minimized by making the bins as numerous and as narrow as possible (Fox, 2016). Sampling variance is minimized by using a small number of relatively wide bins, each with many observations. Hence, as usual, there is a trade-off between bias and variance here, encapsulating the classic bias-variance trade-off, as illustrated in Figure 7.5.304

We note in Figure 7.5 that as the bins get progressively narrower, we eventually “zero in” on the actual data points that make up the theoretical regression line as well as the actual points that happen to fall on the sample regression line. Hence, in this extreme version of nonparametric regression where each data point is a mean, we are simply connecting the means located within the bins. Clearly, such an approach would usually not be useful, and we are better off increasing the size of each bin. However, if we increase the bin size too much, we miss out on the locality of the data we initially were after; this is the nature of the trade-off.

What makes this approach nonparametric is that no assumptions about the population or form of the relationship are made. Sample size plays a crucial role here as well. As the sample size increases, the intervals become successively narrower, each containing more data, where in the limit as sample size gets larger, the naïve nonparametric regression coincides with the population regression (Fox, 2016). What happens with this approach when there are many explanatory variables? Not surprisingly, the previously discussed curse of dimensionality rears its ugly head. For simplicity, we focus on the case where we only have a single predictor.

A glaring weakness of this approach is that for a bin of a given size, assuming the bin is larger than each single data point, the estimate within each bin will be inexact for surrounding data points. That is, if the bin size contains 20 data points, the mean computed on these 20 data points will be a rather coarse representation of locality. Is there a way we can do better than the mean? Is there a way we can represent the data within each interval more “fairly” or precisely? The answer to this will be yes, via kernel regression.

7.3.2 Kernel Regression – “Locally Weighted Averaging”

Kernel regression seeks to improve on simple local-averaging by attempting to explicitly give more weight to observations that are close to the focal x0 and less weight to more remote values in the training data (Fox, 2016). What is a “focal x0”? This is the hypothetical value from which you wish to make a prediction of the response, y. This is an attractive idea, as doing so will provide a better representation of the data within each interval or “bin” of data. The distance xi from x0 can be represented by (Fox, 2016, p. 529):


zi = (xi−x0)/h
(7.11)

The scale factor here is h and is the bandwidth of the kernel estimator, controlling its degree of smoothness. As an example, suppose the distance (xi−x0) is equal to 5, with a bandwidth h equal to 1, yielding a zi equal to 5. If we increase the bandwidth to 2, then zi is equal to 2.5. The function of h then is to scale the distance (xi−x0). For a constant distance, as h grows larger and larger, the interval on the x-axis becomes smaller relative to h and we obtain a finer fit. The 305smoothness of the fitted function is thus largely influenced by the size of the bandwidth, h. In general, as h increases, the function becomes smoother. Too fine, or too smooth a fit could be detrimental in modeling scientific data, especially if the finer or smoother fit provides too “general” of a modeling approach across the span of the data where perhaps one strategy is more appropriate than another for particular ranges of the data space.

Scaling deviations xi − x0 by the bandwidth h is fine, but we can do even better and apply a kernel function to the scaled deviation to obtain final weights, wi:


wi = K[(xi−x0)/h]
(7.12)

Using the above weights wi, the fitted value at x0 is computed by weighted local-averaging of the yi values:


$$\left. \hat{f}\left( x_{0} \right) = \hat{y} \middle| x_{0} = \frac{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{w_{i}y_{i}}}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}w_{i}} \right.$$
(7.13)

We thus see that kernel regression is effectively a form of weighted regression, where the weights feature the use of a kernel.

7.3.3 A Variety of Kernels

Note that in our description of kernel regression and the computation of weights, wi, we have not yet described the nature of K, that is, the kernel function we are choosing to use for the given problem and by which we are applying to [(xi−x0)/h]. Not surprisingly, there are many choices for a kernel function. One choice, perhaps the default, is to use the Gaussian (or “normal”) kernel:


$$K\left( z \right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{- z^{2}/2}$$
(7.14)

where the bandwidth in (7.14) is the standard deviation. As noted by Fox (2016, p. 530), distances greater than 2h from the focal value of x0 receive virtually no weight due to the nature and shape of the normal density.

Following Fox (2016, p. 530), another possibility is to use the tricube kernel,


$$K_{T}\left( z \right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \left. \left( 1 - \middle| z \middle| {}_{3} \right)3, \middle| z \middle| < \,\, 1 \right. \\ \left. 0, \middle| z \middle| \geq 1 \right. \\ \end{array} \right.$$
(7.15)

or the rectangular kernel,


$$K_{R}\left( z \right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \left. 1, \middle| z \middle| < 1 \right. \\ \left. 0, \middle| z \middle| \geq 1 \right. \\ \end{array} \right.$$
(7.16)

There are other kernels we can choose from, however according to Fox (2016), the choice of kernel function is not that critical in carrying out the regression. There is nothing wrong with trying out a variety of kernels to study their impact on the given regression solution.306

7.3.4 Kernel Regression Is Not Nonlinear; It Is Nonparametric

We reiterate that kernel regression should not be considered specifically a nonlinear approach to regression in the same vein as polynomial regression (in terms of modeling nonlinear trends, not the model being nonlinear). Rather, it is a nonparametric approach, which implies that it learns from the data. If that learned form is linear, then so be it, but the point is that kernel regression does not a priori assume a linear or nonlinear form. It is first and foremost nonparametric because it essentially makes no parametric assumptions regarding the shape of the true function. Local-polynomial regression extends kernel regression where polynomials are instead fit at the focal value of x0; however this is beyond the scope of this book. For an excellent discussion of kernel regression (and much of anything else to do with regression), see Fox (2016).

7.3.5 Kernel Regression in R

Kernel regression in R can be fit using the package gplm (Mueller, 2016). We adapt an example from the package’s documentation below, where we first create data on 1000 observations for variable x:

> library(gplm)
> n <- 1000
> x <- rnorm(n)
> head(x)
[1] -0.71040656 0.25688371 -0.24669188 -0.34754260 -0.95161857 -0.04502772

We next create m as a function of x and then y as a function of m:

> m <- sin(x)
> head(m)
[1] -0.65214204 0.25406776 -0.24419733 -0.34058836 -0.81435593 -0.04501251
> y <- m + rnorm(n)
> head(y)
[1] 0.2638500 1.0546901 -1.1807664 -1.7413758 -0.6540784 -0.3189749
> plot(x,y,col=“gray”)
> lines(kreg(x,y),lwd=2)
307

The squiggly line (Figure 7.6) is the kernel regression estimate, using the Nadaraya-Watson estimator (see Nadaraya, 1964). See the package for many more functions that can be applied to the kernel regression, including extracting estimated fitted values.

The gplm package (Mueller, 2016) also features rather sophisticated 3-D visualizations of kernel regression. As an example (see the package for the code), Figure 7.7 is an advanced graphic generated, where the original function is on the left and the estimated function is on the right.

Kernel regression can also be fit using the np package (Hayfield & Racine, 2008).

  1. 1. Explain how simple or multiple linear regression are special cases of the more general polynomial regression model.
  2. 2. Generate data in Python and fit a quadratic polynomial. Generate the data so that the fit is quite good.
  3. 3. Perform the polynomial regression in #2 in R.
  4. 4. Explain the concept of a basis function and discuss how basis functions are apparent even in univariate procedures such as t-tests and linear contrasts.

  6. 6. Explain how kernel regression goes about providing a more “local” means of estimating the true function behind data.
  7. 7. Generate a plot of the rectangular kernel function either manually or using software.
  8. 8. Distinguish kernel regression as being nonlinear vs. nonparametric. Why might some refer to kernel regression as nonlinear?
  9. 9. Perform a kernel regression in R using the gplm package, where sample size is equal to 10,000. Be creative in how you generate vectors for y and x.
  10. 10. Suppose a kernel regression gives vastly different results than a linear regression; does such imply that one model is more “correct” than the other? Why or why not? Brainstorm and explain.

8 Generalized Linear and Additive ModelsLogistic and Related Models

DOI: 10.4324/9781003376941-11

Up to now in our discussion of modeling, we have assumed the response variable is more or less continuous, or at least “pseudo-continuous,” since no empirical variables are ever truly continuous in the idealistic mathematical sense. Continuity itself is an abstraction, a philosophical idea that is expressed mathematically using such things as epsilon-delta definitions in real analysis. More pragmatically, we have assumed the response exhibits a rather wide range of “dense” values and the goal has been to predict a value of the response along this continuum based on one or more predictors. While many of these models have been linear, we have also surveyed a number of nonlinear models. However, in all of these models, response variables have all been assumed to be continuous and treated as such in our analyses. There are many instances in modeling where the response variable is not continuous but is instead categorical. Such responses contain mutually exclusive categories instead of a continuum of numerical possibilities. Some responses having this property are naturally occurring (e.g., pass vs. fail), while others can be operationalized by the user into specific categories (e.g., numerical score on a test classified into the binary outcome of pass vs. fail).

How can statistical models deal with binary or categorical responses? Thanks to the theory of the generalized linear model (McCullagh & Nelder, 1989), binary and polytomous responses can be situated in the same general framework that we can find classic linear models. The generalized linear model contains the entire family of these models and is the topic of this chapter.

Before surveying the generalized linear model, we should ask an important question from the outset: Is “binning” a response a good idea? What are the advantages and disadvantages of doing so? We begin this chapter with a brief survey of the benefits and drawbacks of operationalizing the response as a binary or polytomous outcome.

8.1 How to Operationalize the Response

As mentioned, some response variables are naturally categorical. For instance, a salmon fish is either going “upstream” or “downstream,” and cannot be going both (though as we have all seen, they can just seemingly wade in the water without direction at times). When responses take on this quality, leaving the variable “as is” and treating it as binary is an easy decision since leaving it as is maintains it in its natural measured state. In other cases, however, the researcher may actually choose to bin the variable into mutually exclusive categories. In the machine learning literature, the pseudo-continuity of a variable before “binning” it is sometimes referred to as a pre-classifier (Kroese et al., 2020) because it is relatively continuous before forcing those values into categories.309

8.1.1 Pros and Cons of Binning

Whether or not to bin a variable is an important decision. Indeed, different operationalizations of a single variable can lead the resulting statistical model to “discover” different effects. As a simple example, the variable grade on a class test operationalized as pass vs. fail may be predictive of final grade, but operationalized as a numerical score may alter the predictive ability. The variable is the same, but how we have operationalized it is now different. What is more, the choice of how to operationalize a variable in analysis of variance (ANOVA) can influence the resulting mean squares and ultimately the rejection of the null hypothesis. There is a whole literature on the influence of operationalizing effects in ANOVA (for example, see Prentice & Miller, 1992).

8.1.2 Detecting New Classes or Categories

While we have discussed the pros and cons of binning, it is worth mentioning as well that in machine learning, there are also techniques that actually allow the algorithm to detect new classes or categories based on the algorithm’s examination of the data. Such is referred to as novelty detection in machine learning circles, so that instead of classifying cases in one of Ct classes, a new class label Ct + 1 is derived not by the researcher’s judgment or decision of how to bin, but from the actual algorithm discovering the new category. This process sometimes goes by the general concept of open set recognition (Murray, 2022). In this book, we do not survey methods that detect new categories. We assume the researcher is actively deciding how to operationalize their variables.

8.2 The Generalized Linear Model

The motivation behind the generalized linear model (GLM) is to encompass models that have continuous responses such as in classic ordinary least-squares (OLS) regression, but also incorporate models with binary or categorical responses. The GLM is the “parent” to all of these models and essentially features a transformation of binary or polytomous responses into linear and continuous ones. In developing the GLM, it is first best to recall the classic linear model featured earlier in our discussion of regression:


yi = β0 + β1x1 + β2x2 +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + βpxp + εi
(8.1)

Note that the above model is linear in the parameters, meaning that β0, β1, … βp are all raised to the exponent “1.” Even if x1, for example, was raised to the second power, x12, the model would still be regarded as a linear model so long as β0, β1, … βp remained raised to a coefficient of one; however, one could say it is no longer linear in the variables. Linear models require only that coefficients be raised to no terms greater than one. What basis transformations on the actual variables we perform is inconsequential as it pertains to the linearity or nonlinearity of the actual model in statistical parlance (Bishop, 2006). For example, the following model would rightly be considered nonlinear because it is nonlinear in the coefficients, notably the β22 term:


yi = β0 + β1x1 + β22x2 + εi
(8.2)

Note that the following model is also nonlinear because of β22 but not because of x22; it is considered both nonlinear in the parameter and variable:310


yi = β0 + β1x1 + β22x22 + εi
(8.3)

8.2.1 Intrinsically Linear Models

A useful distinction to make when it comes to linear vs. nonlinear models is that between intrinsic linearity vs. non-intrinsic linearity (Neter et al., 1996). A model that is nonlinear, but that can be linearized through a transformation is often referred to as an intrinsically linear model. Perhaps the most classic example of this is the exponential response, where if we were to take the log of the exponential in such a model, we would obtain a linear model. That is, we can transform the response into one that is linear. It is intrinsically linear because its nonlinearity is a product only of a transformation. A non-intrinsically linear model, on the other hand, is one that cannot be linearized via transformation.

8.2.2 General vs. Generalized Linear Models

Many of the models featured thus far in this book can be considered special cases of the wider general linear model. Regression and analysis of variance models are indeed special cases of this wider framework. But what defines a general linear model exactly? When we refer to a specific model arising from this “general” framework, we usually mean that the distribution of the error term, εi, has an expected normal distribution. The classic linear regression model, yi = β0 + β1x1 + εi is one such example where εi ∼ N(0,σε2), meaning that the error in the model is expected to be normal, having a mean of 0 and a finite and measurable variance, σε2. There are many situations, however, where we would not naturally expect the error term to behave this way. One classic and popular example is when the response variable is not continuous but instead binary. When a response variable is binary, the expectation of the error term is, not surprisingly, not normal. Nor could we reasonably expect errors to have constant variance (Fox, 2016).

The difficulty then on a theoretical level is how to deal with error distributions that have a non-normal expectation. They seem to be a different class of models altogether. However, thanks largely (but not exclusively) to the work of Nelder and Wedderburn (1972), a wider framework of statistical models was proposed that could encompass even these types of models with non-normal error distributions. Recall that understanding statistics is all about looking for hierarchies, of classifying “special cases” of models in the context of higher forms and generalities. This is precisely what these authors accomplished in proposing a framework for modeling that encompasses not only the classic linear model (regression, ANOVA) that features normally distributed error terms, but also models that contain non-normal error terms. This new class of models they called the generalized linear model, and hence a vast array of models can be situated in this general framework. That is, the generalized linear model encompasses models that contain normally and non-normally distributed error terms.

Essentially, the logic of the generalized linear model is to take an otherwise nonlinear model and make it mimic linearity through what is called a link function. Through the link function, the model becomes approximately linear and we can then treat the model more akin to how we would treat a classic linear model. This is the essential logic of the generalized linear model. An important distinction to make here is that it is the decision surface that is linearized, not truly the model entirely or necessarily (Bishop, 2006). Generalized linear models such as logistic regression engage in transformations that make them “linear-like” (Fox, 2016), such that otherwise nonlinear models can be “linearized” via the transformation (e.g., taking a link function such as the log of the odds in the case of logistic regression).311

One very special case of the generalized linear model that has historically been very popular across virtually all scientific fields, especially medical fields, is the aforementioned logistic regression model, which we survey next.

8.3 The Logistic Regression Model

The logistic regression model is known as the conditional Maxent model (Mohri et al., 2018) in machine learning circles, which is simply the multinomial regression model of which binary regression is a special case. The logistic function is given by the following,


$$p\left( x \right) = \frac{e^{\beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x}}{1 + e^{\beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x}}$$
(8.4)

where we can work with the formulation in (8.4) and get


$$\frac{p\left( x \right)}{1 - p\left( x \right)} = e^{\beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x}$$
(8.5)

The left-hand side of (8.5), p(x)/[1−p(x)] is what is referred to as the odds. In words, the odds is the probability of an event occurring, p(x), relative to the probability that the event does not occur, 1 − p(x). If the probability of an event occurring is the same as the probability of it not occurring, then the odds are equal to 1.0. For example, suppose p(x) = 0.5, then it stands that,


$$\frac{p\left( x \right)}{1 - p\left( x \right)}\frac{0.5}{1 - 0.5} = \frac{0.5}{0.5} = 1.0$$

Suppose we were to take the logarithm on both sides of


$$\frac{p\left( x \right)}{1 - p\left( x \right)} = e^{\beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x}$$

so that,


$$\log\left\lbrack \frac{p\left( x \right)}{1 - p\left( x \right)} \right\rbrack = \log\left\lbrack e^{\beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x} \right\rbrack$$
(8.6)

Recall that taking the log of an exponential function e has the effect of bringing the exponent down and so what we have from the above is


$$\begin{array}{l} {\log\left\lbrack \frac{p\left( x \right)}{1 - p\left( x \right)} \right\rbrack = \log\left\lbrack e^{\beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x} \right\rbrack} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.7)

That is, the log of the odds is assumed to be a linear function. The log of the odds goes by the name of the logit, and hence once we produce the logit, we are effectively now working with an approximate linear model similar in many respects to the classic linear model of regression. Of course, it is not exactly the same, since the units we are working in are no longer the natural units of the original variable, but instead are in units of the logged odds, or the logit, and hence the interpretation of parameter estimates will be in units of the logit.312

For example, suppose that in the model of (8.7), β1 were equal to 0.8; what would be the interpretation? In classic least-squares regression, the interpretation, as we recall, would be for a one-unit increase in X, we expect Y to increase by 0.8 units, given the model under test. In logistic regression, the interpretation is the same, only that the “units” now are not natural units of the original variable, but instead are units of the logit, and hence, our interpretation would be for a one-unit increase in X, we expect the logit of Y to increase by 0.8 logits, given the model under test.

8.3.1 Odds and Odds Ratios

Recall that we said the odds were defined as the probability of an event occurring relative to the probability of the event not occurring, that is,


$$\frac{p\left( x \right)}{1 - p\left( x \right)}$$

The odds ratio is, as the name suggests, a ratio of odds, comparing the odds for one variable, x1, or category of a response, to the odds of another variable, x2, or complement category to x1:


$$OR = \frac{\left( \frac{p\left( x_{1} \right)}{1 - p\left( x_{1} \right)} \right)}{\left( \frac{p\left( x_{2} \right)}{1 - p\left( x_{2} \right)} \right)}$$
(8.8)

For example, if the odds are the same for each variable or category, then the odds ratio is equal to one. An odds ratio greater than one implies that the odds for x1 are greater than the odds for x2. Conversely, an odds ratio of less than one implies that the odds for x1 are less than the odds for x2.
