> summary(ir.tr)
Classification tree:
tree(formula = Species ~ ., data = iris)
Variables actually used in tree construction:
[1] “Petal.Length” “Petal.Width” “Sepal.Length”
Number of terminal nodes: 6
Residual mean deviance: 0.1253 = 18.05 / 144
Misclassification error rate: 0.02667 = 4 / 150
376

We see above the residual mean deviance (0.1253) as well as the misclassification error rate of 0.02667. We now plot the tree (Figure 10.3), where pretty = 0 keeps the level names of factor splits unchanged (see the package for how this parameter can be adjusted):

> plot(ir.tr)
> text(ir.tr, pretty=0)

We can also obtain the misclassifications of the tree:

> ir.tr1 <- tree(Species ~., iris)
> misclass.tree(ir.tr1)
[1] 4
377

The number 4 agrees with the misclassification error rate reported above. We also see that the number of terminal nodes agrees with the tree we generated. That is, the endings of each branch terminate with either setosa, versicolor, versicolor, virginica, virginica, or virginica.

We now prune our original tree, which will allow us to observe misclassification error rate as a function of tree size:

> cv.iris = cv.tree(ir.tr, FUN=prune.misclass)
> cv.iris
$size
[1] 6 4 3 2 1
$dev
[1] 8 8 11 95 112

The output $dev refers to the cross-validation error rate (“misclass” in the plot below). We see that it is equal at a value of 8 for trees of size 6 and 4 terminal nodes, as we can more easily see in the plot in Figure 10.4 (plot (cv.iris, type = “b”) will produce a similar plot):

> plot(cv.iris)

We now obtain the pruned tree with 4 nodes (Figure 10.5):

> prune.ir.tr = prune.misclass(ir.tr,best = 4)
> plot(prune.ir.tr)
> text(prune.ir.tr)
378

We now obtain misclassifications on the tree,

> prune.ir.tr = prune.misclass(ir.tr, best = 4)
> misclass.tree(prune.ir.tr)
[1] 4

The number of misclassifications is equal to 4. Note that had we chosen a much more crude tree, say with 2 nodes, the misclassification error rate would have skyrocketed, such as in the following where we request only 2 nodes (best = 2):

> prune.ir.tr = prune.misclass(ir.tr, best = 2)
> misclass.tree(prune.ir.tr)
[1] 50

The package rpart (Therneau et al., 2023) can also be used to fit decision trees. We will fit a tree to the iris data:

> library(rpart)
> iris.rpart <- rpart(formula = Species ~., data = iris, method = “anova”)
> iris.rpart
n= 150
node), split, n, deviance, yval
    * denotes terminal node
1) root 150 100.0000000 2.000000
  2) Petal.Length< 2.45 50 0.0000000 1.000000 *
  3) Petal.Length>=2.45 100 25.0000000 2.500000
    6) Petal.Width< 1.75 54 4.5370370 2.092593
      12) Petal.Length< 4.85 46 0.9782609 2.021739 *
      13) Petal.Length>=4.85 8 2.0000000 2.500000 *
    7) Petal.Width>=1.75 46 0.9782609 2.978261 *
> library(rpart.plot)
> rpart.plot(iris.rpart)
> plotcp(iris.rpart)
379

Percentages of sample size in respective nodes are depicted in Figure 10.6. We note from the figure that a tree size of 3 or 4 gets the relative error down to fairly low levels, where “cp” on the x-axis is the cost complexity parameter (Therneau et al., 2023). In general, setting cp to a smaller value will generate a fuller tree (Boehmke and Greenwell, 2020). See the package for further details regarding the computation of cp.

There has been some research done on multivariate responses for decision trees (Canete-Sifuentes et al., 2021, Zhang & Ye, 2008). Survival trees (Izenman, 2008), also known as conditional inference trees, have also been advanced. Multivariate adaptive regression splines (MARS), due to Friedman (1991) is a generalization of recursive partitioning and is a nonparametric regression approach which uses basis functions. For details, see Izenman (2008, p. 311). Work has also been done on Bayesian additive regression trees (Chipman et al., 2010).

10.4 Committee Machines

As mentioned at the outset of this chapter, “committee machine” is a general term referring to combining weaker learners to generate a stronger learner. By far the most popular and useful of committee machines are those of bagging and boosting.

10.5 Overview of Bagging and Boosting

We have so far in this chapter discussed decision trees and have focused on their construction. We have emphasized that a single tree, especially if not pruned, likely significantly overfits the data. That is, it is easily subject to random perturbations in the data such that if we changed a few data points here or there, the outcome of the tree would be different. In statistical learning theory, as we 380know by now, this is referred to the method having high variance. Note carefully this is not the data having high variance. We are referring here to the method. The data are what they are. We are more interested in evaluating the method used to evaluate the data. Unstable methods are usually not preferred to more stable ones. Decision trees are not the only statistical method that is unstable, but in what follows, we will use them as an example in our discussion of bagging and boosting.

How can we reduce the variance of an otherwise unstable method? Though there are many ways of accomplishing this reduction in variance, two methods are often used: bagging and boosting; however, boosting prioritizes reducing bias over reducing variance. Bagging, which is short for bootstrap aggregating, is random and probabilistic. By essentially averaging bootstrapped samples, one could get different bagging results depending on the given sampling procedure. Boosting, on the other hand, is not random or probabilistic. It is instead systematic or deterministic. Boosting generates predictable non-random perturbations of the training data by successive reweighting of the training set, where the most current and updated weights depend on misclassification history. We survey boosting shortly. First, we more fully develop the idea of bagging.

10.5.1 Bagging

Bagging is essentially a procedure of taking many bootstrapped samples and then aggregating (averaging) them. By averaging results, the goal is to reduce variance. For example, as already discussed, in a typical decision tree, any particular tree likely suffers from high variance, which basically means that a given tree is subject to random fluctuations in the data. That is, if we perturbed the data somewhat, the resulting tree would be different. By averaging trees (or whatever method we are using), the hope is to reduce the overall variance. In fact, the success of bagging actually depends on how originally unstable the data are; the more unstable, the more perturbing the data set causes a change in prediction, the more advantageous it is to bag to improve accuracy (Breiman, 1996). Be sure to understand what we have just said. We emphasize that the more unstable a learning method, the more it stands to benefit from aggregating. If the learning method is stable, bagging will, in general, be less efficient. In fact, for relatively stable methods, bagging has been found to work less well and has been found to actually degrade the performance of stable procedures (Breiman, 1996).

10.5.2 A Familiar Example: Bagging Samples and the Variance of the Mean

The simplest conceptual example of bagging would be to designate a sample of say, 100 observations, bootstrap 10 samples, on each compute a sample mean, then average those means. The average of those averages $\mu_{\overline{y}}$ will have less variance than any of the individual averages, $\overline{y}$. Averaging (in this case, of means) reduces variance. If each of the subset samples has a variance equal to σ2, then the variance of those means, as is well known, is equal to σ2/n, with standard error $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$.

Hence, when we think of bagging, it is convenient to simply think of the word averaging. Averaging reduces variance. As an analogy, imagine taking betting predictions for a sporting event from one forecaster vs. ten forecasters. If you averaged the results from ten forecasters, the prediction would have less variance. On average, the forecast might be more “stable” than if you relied on the prediction of a single, stronger forecaster. This is the idea of bagging, except that we will apply it to bootstrapped samples instead of to actual empirical divisions of the data. In theory, if we had enough data, we could feasibly take segments of the data and average results, but usually, 381we do not have enough data to do this. This is why bootstrapping is utilized in bagging – because of an insufficient amount of real data.

10.5.3 A Deeper Look at Bagging

Let us look more closely into how bagging works. First, we begin with the most ideal and fanciful but unrealistic of situations. Suppose we apply a statistical learning method to some data and compute a function on many different empirical subsets of that data. Let’s suppose for a moment that we were able to partition the data perfectly and have all subsets of the data represented. Then, the average of all those subsets would be the following:


$${\hat{f}}_{avg}\left( x \right) = \frac{1}{B}{\sum\limits_{b = 1}^{B}{{\hat{f}}^{b}\left( x \right)}}$$

where B is the number of subsets that we are drawing and computing on each a function on x. The estimated function is f̂b(x). Thus, f̂b(x)/B is the average of all those computed estimated functions. But why is this situation unrealistic? It is so because we are likely to not have access to all partitions of the data, or, the number of partitions of the data would likely simply be too large to be practical. Data is usually expensive (at least in some fields), and so the idea of having large partitions of data available may not be pragmatic. However, it should be emphasized that if this were possible, it would be the ideal situation to shoot for. Real data is always better than simulated data.

The way around the above problem will be to bootstrap samples from the only sample we do have and compute the average of all such bootstrapped samples:


$${\hat{f}}_{bag}\left( x \right) = \frac{1}{B}{\sum\limits_{b = 1}^{B}{{\hat{f}}^{*b}\left( x \right)}}$$

Notice that the only thing that has changed is where before favg(x) was the average of all partitions of the training data, now f̂ * b(x) is the average of all the bootstrapped samples. Hence, we are averaging a subset of all samples via the bootstrap procedure. That is, we are aggregating the bootstrapped samples. This is precisely what bagging means. It simply means taking an average of functions via bootstrapping. For a good theoretical discussion of just why bagging works on a technical level superseding our intuitive conceptual explanation, see Breiman (1996, p. 129). Breiman justifies that the degree of instability in the method is paramount to determining whether bagging will or will not be effective.

Bagging is simply taking an average of bootstrapped samples. The reason for taking bootstrapped samples is that dividing up the data into many divisions is impractical. Dividing the actual empirical data into subset samples would, theoretically, be our first choice, however, if practical.

When working with decision trees, bagging can combine hundreds or even thousands of bootstrapped trees. Think of what this means for a moment – we have a single sample, we bootstrap many samples from this sample, and on each, we compute a separate decision tree. We then average the results of all the decision trees we compute. Each tree alone suffers from high variance, 382but when we bag (i.e., average) all of the bootstrapped trees, we reduce variance. As already discussed, bagging is especially useful when dealing with predictors that tend to overfit the data, such as in decision trees, where the unpruned tree structure is very sensitive to small changes or perturbations in the training set.

10.5.4 Out-of-Bag Error

Once we bag, we would like to know how well the bagging procedure performed. We need a way of evaluating the results of the bagging. To properly evaluate, it would make little sense to validate on the bagged decision trees (or whatever statistical learning method we used). This would be akin to evaluating how well a boxing fighter performs on practice opponents; it is not a true test of the boxer’s skill.

To evaluate the goodness of bagging, we require observations that were not part of the bagging procedure. That is, as with other cross-validation, we require a kind of test set on which to evaluate bagging. Observations that were not part of the bagging procedure are referred to as out-of-bag (OOB) observations. These are the observations that are part of the training set, but not used to generate the given bagged tree. In spirit, they serve the same purpose as in typical cross-validation; however, the out-of-bag observations are simply the set of observations (roughly 1/3; James et al., 2013) in the training data not used in generating the given bootstrapped tree.

10.5.5 Interpreting Results from Bagging

When we bag, there is no easy way to interpret the result since now we have a number of trees rather than a single tree. Hence, while bagging does tend to improve prediction accuracy, as is true of so many machine learning algorithms, it does so generally at the expense of interpretability. There is simply no easy way to combine trees and read off the “meaningfulness,” in some sense, of the individual predictors.

The situation is not entirely hopeless, however. There are some measures of importance that can be used. For bagging regression trees, as already discussed, a decrease in RSS can be used to evaluate the importance of a predictor due to its split inclusion. A large decrease in RSS suggests the given predictor is valuable to the decision tree. In a classification context, decreases in the Gini index can be used in a similar way to evaluate the importance of a given variable. Large decreases in the Gini index suggest the variable under consideration may be important.

It should be emphasized as well that bagging does not always improve performance and relies very much on the base models being unstable. There are some situations where bagging will not improve performance or prediction. For instance, Buja and Stuetzle (2000) found bagging to, at times, increase bias; however, the increase or decrease in mean squared error was contingent upon the given statistic and its distribution. There is no free lunch, and hence bagging on one data set may perform better or worse than bagging on another.

10.5.6 Bagging in R

Many packages can be used to bag in R such as baguette (Kuhn, 2024). Bagging for classification in R can be performed using ipred (Peters & Hothorn, 2023) and rpart (Therneau et al., 2023). Below we feature an example from the package ipred, which uses data on breast cancer from the package mlbench (Leisch & Dimitriadou, 2024) featuring various characteristics of cells:383

> library(ipred)
> library(MASS)
> library(survival)

10.6 Random Forests

We have seen how bagged trees (or whatever statistical learning method we are using) can help reduce variance in the method by averaging results. The question now is, can we improve on bagging? It turns out that we can. The technique of random forests is yet another committee machine. Random forests take bagging to the next level, seeking to improve upon it. To appreciate how random forests improve on bagging, we first need to consider what is lacking in bagging in the first place.

10.6.1 The Problem with Bagging Decision Trees

We know that in building decision trees, overfitting can occur because the nodes will contain the “best option” at each split. That is, a decision tree is, in a sense, optimized to produce the best outcome and hence is capitalizing on the training data a great deal. Thus, we can expect trees to be similar in many respects when bagged because each tree is built with the same optimization strategy in mind. Of course, if you build trees with the same optimization, this will quite naturally and quickly lead to overfitting.

Random forests are an ingenious way to combat the overfitting problem of combining decision trees. How they do this is by introducing a randomization feature into each node split in an effort to combat overfitting. That is, each node is split in a random manner where a random sample of predictors is chosen as split “candidates” from the full set of possible predictors. This improves over bagging alone because when we bag, if there is, say, one strong predictor, most of the trees developed will use this strong predictor in the top split, and hence, all bagged trees will look similar, which produces predictions that are highly correlated. Where bagging reduces variance and potentially bias for full-grown trees, a random forest reduces the correlation between 385tree-structured classifiers. That is, random forests essentially decorrelates the trees through this randomization process. Random forests forces each split to consider only a subset of the predictors, which is what “decorrelates” the trees.

The problem with bagging decision trees is that the trees are correlated. Averaging many highly correlated quantities reduces variance, but not as much as averaging many uncorrelated quantities. Random forests overcomes this problem by introducing a randomization process regarding how predictors are chosen at each split.

10.6.2 Equivalency of Random Forests and Bagging

The observant reader may have noticed that there is a certain condition in which random forests must be equivalent to bagging. Indeed, random forests have a natural relationship to bagging when the random forest is built using the number of trees equal to the number of predictors. Under this condition, random forests equate to bagging. Random forests then can be considered, in this context, simply a special case of bagging where a randomization feature is introduced, or vice versa, one can also consider bagging a special case of random forests where no randomization feature is implemented.

Random forests can be considered a special case of bagging in which a random sample of decision trees are selected from the bootstrapped “bagged” samples in an effort to decorrelate the trees. When all predictors are used in the random forest and hence there is no randomization element, this then reduces to bagging.

10.6.3 Random Forests in R

The package randomForest (Liaw & Wiener, 2002) can be used to build a random forest in R. We demonstrate on the iris data, where we combine an ensemble of trees (see package for more details on this example):

> library(randomForest)
> data(iris)
> rf1 <- randomForest(Species ~ ., iris, ntree=50)
> rf2 <- randomForest(Species ~ ., iris, ntree=50)
> rf3 <- randomForest(Species ~ ., iris, ntree=50)

10.7 Boosting

Boosting is another committee machine that again essentially operates on combining weak learners, analogous to how bagging averages many bootstrapped samples. However, boosting does this systematically and deterministically, not randomly. As explained by James et al. (2013, p. 321) in reference to boosting with regression trees:

Each tree [or single predictive tool, more generally] is grown using information from previously grown trees. Boosting does not involve bootstrap sampling; instead, each tree is fit on a modified version of the original data set.

Boosting, in general, is what is known as a slow learner, which in general, performs better than fast or greedy learners. An analogy to boosting would be you and your friend drawing a picture. Suppose you get the picture started and your strengths are on full display, but also your weaknesses. For instance, suppose you are good at drawing the general shapes of objects, but not so good at filling in some of their more specific characteristics. After you are finished doing what you can, your friend steps in and focuses specifically on drawing the elements that you were poor at drawing, including giving specific attention to errors that you made in your contribution. The combination of both of you generates a rather strong painting even though you were both weak at drawing particular individual elements of the painting.

Another prototype example for understanding how boosting works is the spam e-mail paradigm described by Izenman (Izenman, 2008, p. 511). Suppose we wish to know whether an e-mail is spam or not before opening it. If the e-mail contains the word “money,” this by itself is a weak identifier because identifying it as spam might appear as random and misclassify the result. In other words, this is a weak classifier. Indeed, another classifier that is weak is one that classifies as spam if the e-mail contains the word “credit,” for instance. Taken on their own, weak classifiers are not very good and are bound to misclassify many cases. However, as was the case for bagging, if we combine these weak classifiers, we may be able to substantially improve classification. This is what is behind the idea of boosting. In this example, classification based on the word “money” will be imperfect and rather weak, but the second classifier trained will try to make up for the error generated by the first classifier. When combined, they make a pretty decent classifier. Boosting relies on the assumption that each of the weak hypotheses has accuracy that is just a bit better than chance levels. This assumption is generally referred to as the weak learning condition (Schapire, 2001).

We draw on James et al. (2013, p. 323) quite heavily as well as Bishop (2006, p. 658) in giving a formal, if not brief, summary treatment of boosting. Suppose in a regression tree problem f̂(x) is the estimated function. At the initial step of the algorithm, we will set f̂(x) = 0 and residuals ri = yi, that is, residuals equal to the values of the response variable in the training data. We then fit a regression tree with d splits to the training data. We call this tree f̂b. We then update the original function f̂(x) = f̂(x) + λf̂(x) with a shrunken (weighted) version of the new tree:


f̂(x) = f̂(x) + λf̂b(x)
(10.5)

where in (10.5) λ is a shrinkage parameter regulating the rate of learning, which notice is being applied to the new tree, f̂bthat has d splits. Next, we update residuals by389


ri′ = ri − λf̂b(xi)
(10.6)

This process is repeated for all b models and the final boosted model is produced, which is the sum of all weighted estimated functions, f̂b,


$$\hat{f}\left( x \right) = {\sum\limits_{b = 1}^{B}{\lambda{\hat{f}}^{b}\left( x \right)}}$$
(10.7)

Hastie et al. (2009, p. 341) show that boosting is a simple example of an additive model and yet another instance of a basis expansion. There are many boosting algorithms in existence. However, one particular algorithm has historically dominated boosting, that of AdaBoost, short for adaptive boosting and generally used to classify into one of two binary categories (Schapire, 2001). The algorithm works by modifying probabilities of drawing instances as a function of error similar to the generic boosting algorithm described earlier (Alpaydin, 2020). AdaBoost has been found to be equivalent to forward stagewise additive modeling where an exponential loss function is minimized (Hastie et al., 2009). Gradient boosting, and extensions, are more general than AdaBoost where additional loss functions can be minimized. See Izenman (2008) for details.

10.7.1 Boosting Using R

In R, we can use the package ada (Culp et al., 2016) for AdaBoost for binary responses. A very popular package for gradient boosting in R is gbm (Ridgeway et al., 2024).

We adapt the example for boosting on the iris data in the ada package:

> library(ada)
> data(iris)

We note the confusion matrix results in perfect classification. We can also see from the above output that the out-of-bag error is equal to 0.017 for iteration = 6. As iterations increase, overfitting becomes a concern. These results can be visualized to observe fluctuations on the training error across iterations (Figure 10.8). Note that by iteration 9, the training error has bottomed to 0, which agrees with the output above. We note as well that kappa (Figure 10.8), which measures the agreement between observed and predicted classification, is also maximized by iteration 9 (these figures are reported in the above output, train.err1 = 9, train.kap1 = 9), where TRUE, TRUE controls the reporting of training and kappa curves:

> plot(gdis, TRUE, TRUE)

391

Now, we add the testing data and evaluate both training and testing error:

> gdis=addtest(gdis, iris[teind, -5], iris[teind, 5])
> plot(gdis, TRUE, TRUE)

We can see from the left plot in Figure 10.9 that the training error decreases while the testing error remains relatively constant until it elevates toward the end of the iterations, likely due to overfitting. The kappa accuracy reflects the extent to which there is agreement between the observed classification and the predicted classification. We see from the plot that kappa increases on the train data as the number of iterations increases, which is what we would expect, as the higher the kappa score, the greater the degree of agreement. Kappa decreases, however, on the test data as we near the final iteration, which is likely again a sign of overfitting.

Finally, we can obtain a variable importance plot as in Figure 10.10.392

> varplot(gdis)

We can see from Figure 10.10 that in the boosted sample, sepal length is most important, followed by sepal width. See Hastie et al. (2009, Chapter 10) for the computation of variable importance in this context. Re-running the model at various iterations may be useful both to regulate overfitting and also to observe changes in variable importance.

Whereas bagging and boosting combines weak “base” learners to produce a stronger learner, so-called stacked models seek to combine weak to strong learners into an even stronger one via optimizing the weighting of each model, a so-called super learner. This is generally referred to as stacking or stacked generalization (Hastie et al., 2009). Stacked learners will often outperform individual base learners. Breiman (1996, p. 51) summarizes the benefits of stacking:

The results show that stacking can produce predictors with substantially reduced prediction errors. Stacking never does worse than selecting the single best predictor. We note that the biggest gains came when dissimilar sets of predictors were stacked, i.e., subset selection and ridge regressions. The more similar the predictors, the less advantage there is in stacking.

In R, we can use the package h2o (Fryda et al., 2023) for model stacking. For details on stacked generalization, see Hastie et al. (2009).393

11 Principal Components Analysis, Blind Source Separation, and Manifold Learning

DOI: 10.4324/9781003376941-14

In this chapter, we survey the method of principal components analysis, or “PCA” for short, as well as other related techniques. As we will see, principal components analysis can be interpreted as a special case of more general methods that generally fall under the name of blind source separation and manifold learning. PCA can be regarded, in fact, as a special case of manifold learning where in the case of PCA the manifold is linear. The more general manifold can take on nonlinear shapes and most often the phrase “manifold learning” will refer to nonlinear dimensionality reduction. Virtually all dimension-reduction techniques can be crudely classified into linear vs. nonlinear.

The motivation for PCA is to take a set of observed variables and generate linear combinations of those variables. Substantively, PCA is often advertised as being able to “discover” underlying dimensions of data. However, as we will learn in this chapter, the word “discovery” is potentially misleading and problematic. All that PCA can guarantee, for certain, is to derive linear composites of variables that maximize variance in the original variables. Whether those composites are meaningful in any substantive sense is not a question that can be answered by PCA and is only answerable by the user with reference to scientific theory and the domain of application. What is more, is that maximizing variance in observed variables may not result in dimensions that are in any way interesting. This is an important point, as there are many other competing techniques that claim to discover more interesting patterns in data and have their own criteria for doing so other than maximizing variance. In short, maximizing variance in components does not necessarily imply those components will be of value or interesting in themselves. They may, from a substantive point of view be entirely meaningless given current theory or application. Indeed, from a scientific point of view, the results of any dimension-reduction or manifold learning technique should be interpreted with caution as it is entirely possible that the given algorithm “causes” interesting geometric patterns or trends that in the end are not supported by the data (Meila & Zhang, 2023).

Principal components is only one of many techniques that seek to reduce the dimensionality of data. That is, PCA is a (i.e., only one) dimension-reduction technique; it is not equivalent to dimension reduction. In its most general sense, dimension reduction may be said to be taking observed data in a high-dimensional context and reducing that data to a lower-dimensional context but ensuring that it still conveys similar information (Nanga et al., 2021). That is, a good dimension-reduction technique should retain essential properties of the original data. If the information contained in the lower dimensions is misleading or at odds with the information at a higher dimension, then the reduction may lead to faulty interpretation. Hence, this is one important reason for understanding the nature of the dimension-reduction technique one is using as the conclusion provided by one technique may differ from the conclusion reached from another. Dimension reduction is as much a function of the method as it is of the data. A question worth asking is if the visualization of one technique is different from another, which then is most correct? The only answer to this question is that none are “correct”; they simply accomplish different things.395

Most dimension-reduction techniques are nonparametric in nature (Murray, 2022), which essentially implies that they focus heavily on the training data often without attempting directly to generalize to out-of-sample data. These include techniques such as the aforementioned PCA, but also classical multidimensional scaling, kernel PCA, Isomap, Laplacian Eigenmaps (Belkin & Niyogi, 2003), and t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE), non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), among others. Alternative names for PCA include Karhunen-Loeve transform (Karhunen, 1947), empirical orthogonal functions, common principal components analysis (Flury, 1998), and others. The different names are largely due to the same method being developed in various disciplines or as special cases or extensions of classic PCA. For instance, the Karhunen-Loeve transform features the option of using class information on data before applying PCA to each class, then takes an average of class PCA (Alpaydin, 2020). This is similar to common PCA where similar components are hypothesized to arise in different data sets. Hence, not all names are identical to classic PCA, but at their core are still “PCA.” Once more with jargon in statistics and machine learning, one can know a given method well but fail to “recognize” it in a given field because it is named something different!

Many dimension-reduction techniques are justified based on a fundamental theorem, the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma. It holds that for a number of points in high-dimensional space, such points can be mapped to a much lower dimension with an upper limit to how much pairwise distances can be distorted. That is, the lemma essentially holds that dimension reduction can be performed while still preserving fundamental properties of the data. For further details on the lemma, consult Mohri et al. (2018, p. 354).

11.1 Dimension Reduction and Jargon

As we have mentioned, what can make dimension reduction challenging is that many of the same techniques have evolved in various scientific fields under somewhat different names and for different purposes. For instance, in psychometrics, one may wish to produce orthogonal linear combinations to represent attitudes of respondents, whereas in more physical applications such as images in information theory, this same idea translates to the compression of an image. The same technique can almost have unrecognizable and diametrically opposed applications. While this can be said of virtually any technique and not just dimension-reduction ones, the jargon is especially “rich” in dimension analysis.

However, just as is true for simple arithmetical operations such as addition, it is not what is being added that matters when it comes to understanding addition; it matters more in understanding what addition does. The technique must be studied, at least to some extent, from an abstract point of view exclusive of application. Only in that sense can one understand what the technique actually accomplishes without being “swayed” by what we “wish” it to accomplish to satisfy our Freudian id on this or that data set.

If dimension reduction is so vast a subject, why begin with PCA? We begin with PCA simply because it is generally considered the most common and oldest method of the family of dimension-reduction methods, having its origins with Karl Pearson in 1901. It is also the easiest (though deceptively simple) to understand and hence forms a good grounding for understanding other more advanced techniques as extensions or derivatives of essential PCA. Since the time of Pearson, several other dimension-reduction methods have been developed, PCA now considered only a special case of a wider family of blind source separation techniques (Izenman, 2008). Many of the more modern techniques feature latent variables which are analogous to hidden variables in neural networks (Izenman, 2008) and are also featured extensively in exploratory and confirmatory factor-analytic models as well as structural equation models. In its most general interpretation, 396blind source separation involves separating out signals from noise, such that the signals extracted possess certain mathematically desirable properties, such as orthogonality in the case of classical PCA and many versions of exploratory factor analysis, or independence in the case of independent components analysis or independent factor analysis.

Principal components analysis can also be considered purely from an essential linear algebra point of view, equivalent to best subspace approximation using the singular value decomposition, or “SVD” for short (more precisely, reduced SVD). Singular value decomposition itself dates back to Beltrami (1873) and is a method for obtaining eigenvalues and eigenvectors from a matrix, mathematical objects that are at the very crux of PCA. SVD is able to decompose via factorization of a rectangular matrix X such that


X = VDWT
(11.1)

where X in a statistical application is a data matrix of observations on a number of variables, V and W contain orthonormal columns (i.e., orthogonal and of length equal to one), and D is a diagonal matrix (Jolliffe, 2002, p. 44). From the SVD, singular values and singular vectors can be obtained of even rectangular matrices, and hence SVD can be considered a pathway to generating principal components.

We can also conceptualize PCA as a rotation, such that PCA transforms or rotates empirical data by deriving new axes from which the data are projected onto these new axes. These new axes are the eigenvectors of the rotation. The best basis theorem states the best orthonormal basis is given by the leading eigenvectors of the transformation.

Whether one uses eigen analysis or SVD to compute principal components will result in the same components, though SVD is often preferred due to computational benefits (Murray, 2022). For extremely large dimensional problems, a randomized SVD algorithm (Murray, 2022) can be used to handle increasingly large dimensional data. In Python, for instance, sklearn features a randomized solver. PCA is also associated with the Eckart-Young and Schmidt-Mirsky theorems in mathematics as these both account for the mathematics that underlie the dimension-reduction technique.

In modern statistics and machine learning, there are a whole host of dimension-reduction techniques. What unites them all is the attempt to “uncover” a lower-dimensional manifold from higher-dimensional data. That data could be attributes on a scale or an image that needs to be “decoded” by color, or even sound signals from a musical symphony.

11.2 Deriving Classic Principal Components Analysis

As mentioned, classical PCA has its roots with Pearson in 1901. The term “principal component” was coined by Hotelling in 1933. Classical PCA is motivated as follows. Suppose we have a set of observed variables x1 through xp. From these observed variables, we wish to produce linear combinations of these variables that have desirable statistical properties. Recall more generally the nature of a linear combination from our earlier review of linear algebra:397


li = a1y1 + a2y2 +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + apyp

where a linear combination li is a weighted sum of products and where a1 through ap are the weights applied to observed variables y1 through yp. For our data on x1, ..., xp, the linear combination becomes


zi = a1x1 + a2x2 +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + apxp

where now zi is the name of the linear combination and x1 through xp are the observed variables. A principal component is a unique kind of linear combination such that the weights a1 through ap correspond to values of allied eigenvectors extracted from an eigen analysis performed on the covariance or correlation matrix of variables x1, ..., xp. Hence, if we denote the weights a1 through ap by e1 through ep to denote eigenvector weights, the first principal component is defined as


z1 = e1x1 + e2x2 +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + epxp
(11.2)

The first principal component possesses an important property; it is the linear combination that accounts for the most variance in the observed variables. What this means is that the variance of the resulting zi will have maximum variance compared to any other linear combination that we could have derived from the data. If you think about this for a moment, you might agree that it is a favorable quality to have for a linear combination. It suggests that instead of needing x1, ..., xp variables, perhaps we could account for a great deal of the variance in those observed variables by considering only the first principal component. That is, the first component makes up a large proportion of those observed variables.

However, the first principal component will likely not account for all of the variance in the variables. To account for more, we will have to consider the second and successive principal components.

More formally, if the total variance E|x−μ|2 is defined by


$$\left. E \middle| x - \mu \middle| {}_{2} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{p}{{var}x_{i} =}}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{p}\sigma_{ii}^{2}} = {tr}\Sigma \right.$$
(11.3)

where trΣ is the sum of variances σii2 along the main diagonal, PCA essentially constructs orthogonal variables (i.e., linear combinations) the variance of which, in totality, equal trΣ.

The first principal component is that which accounts for maximal amount of the variance in the original variables as possible. Ensuing components will account for increasingly less variance.398

11.2.1 The Second Principal Component

The second principal component is that linear combination that accounts for maximal variance in the variables, as was true for the first component, but with an additional important property, that it accounts for variance not captured by the first principal component. How can we express this idea mathematically? Recall that in linear algebra, linear combinations that account for different sources of information (in a sense) more generally in the original variables are called orthogonal. Hence, the second principal component is that linear combination accounting for maximal variance in the observed variables but orthogonal to the first component:


z2 = e1x1 + e2x2 +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + epxp

where now e1, ep represent elements of the second eigenvector. More precisely, the eigenvectors are orthogonal, the components are uncorrelated, though it is fine to use the terms “uncorrelated” and “orthogonal” interchangeably in this context so long as one is aware of the difference. We need not stop there! We can continue to derive principal components from our data each accounting for a successive amount of variance unaccounted for by prior components. Note that in our development of classical PCA, we have applied the technique to the entire training data at once. That is, we have assumed the entire training data is readily available. An alternative to this approach is known as incremental PCA (Lippi & Ceccarelli, 2019), where the updated covariance matrix Σn + 1 is based on the “old” covariance matrix, Σn. That is, incremental PCA adds new observations (the  + 1 in n + 1) to the covariance matrix and thus has computational advantages over traditional PCA. The benefit is that not all data has to be saved in memory and the algorithm can be applied when the data set is expected to grow quickly or if the stationary data set is itself very large, too large to fit into memory at once (Lippi & Ceccarelli, 2019). Incremental PCA is available in Python in sklearn via IncrementalPCA.

11.2.2 PCA as a Least-Squares Technique and Minimizing Reconstruction Error

As is the case with most statistical methods, there is more than a single interpretation of principal components analysis. Our interpretation thus far has been via eigen analysis or SVD, but we can also interpret it as a least-squares technique similar to that of least-squares regression, with which we are already familiar. Instead of projecting from higher-dimensional space to lower-dimensional space such that we minimize the sum of squared errors in a response as in the typical ordinary least-squares regression, in PCA we also seek a projection, but this time from higher-dimensional space to lower-dimensional space such that the sum of squared perpendicular distances are minimized, where “perpendicular” is equivalent to orthogonal.

For example, in Figure 11.1 is a projection from two-dimensional space to a single hyperplane such that the orthogonal squared data distances from the principal component are minimized.399

In fact, in the typical PCA analysis, we seek to minimize what is known as the reconstruction error (Murphy, 2022). Not coincidentally, it can be shown that the reconstruction error is minimized when the resulting components are eigenvectors of an eigen analysis of the covariance matrix. Details of the derivation can be found in Bishop (2006) and Murphy (2022). The average reconstruction error is given by:


$$l\left( W,Z \right) = \frac{1}{N}{\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{N}\left| \middle| x_{n} - Wz_{n} \middle| \right|^{2}}$$
(11.4)

where xn are the original data points, zn are the derived data points based on the projection, and W is an orthogonal matrix. The optimal solution (i.e., l(W,Z), which is a loss, is minimized) is obtained when Ŵ = UL, where UL are the eigenvectors of a covariance matrix, and hence by definition for a symmetric matrix with distinct eigenvalues, orthogonal. Note that Wzn is essentially trying to produce the least amount of deviation from xn and under the most ideal of circumstances where the reconstruction of data based on the obtained eigenvectors (i.e., loosely, components) is perfect, then l(W,Z) = 0. Minimizing this reconstruction error is equivalent to maximizing the variance in the variables (Murray, 2022) which was the original interpretation of PCA we started out with. Again, as is the case with most statistical methods, there are a variety of different ways to derive the PCA technique, where in this case it can be shown that minimizing the reconstruction error is mathematically equivalent to maximizing the variance of the data projected by the components solution. Different ways of perceiving a statistical or machine learning technique from various angles and perspectives can pay dividends in truly understanding it in depth.

In addition to PCA being computed by eigen analysis or (truncated) SVD, components can also be gotten by the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm and has advantages over eigen analysis such that it is often faster (Murphy, 2022).400

11.2.3 Choosing the Number of Derived Components

Under most conditions of a well-behaved matrix, the number of components that we can obtain is equal to the number of observed variables subjected to the components analysis. That is, if x1, ..., xp consists of say, 100 variables, then under usual (and most common) conditions, the number of components computed on these variables will equal 100. In brief, a PCA on observed variables does not, by itself, reduce the information in the data. In the case of the 100 variables, choosing less than 100 computed components is where the actual data reduction occurs, else all the PCA has done is disproportionately load most variance hopefully onto the first few components. What this means is that PCA is simply “packaging” (or re-packaging) the variance of observed variables into successive linear combinations. But it is not truly dimension “reduction” in an applied sense until we select less than the total number of components generated. This is the logic of PCA as a dimension-reduction technique. PCA is first and foremost only a transformation.

11.2.4 Why Reconstruction Error Is Insufficient for Choosing Number of Components

As a result of PCA attempting to account for as much variance in the variables as possible, when choosing the number of dimensions (components) to retain, one cannot simply use the reconstruction error or variance explained as a guide, since the more components one keeps, the more variance one will explain and the smaller will be the consequent reconstruction error. This is somewhat analogous to the effect of adding more predictors in a multiple regression – variance explained will virtually always increase (except in very unusual situations of zero correlation), and hence choosing the “best” regression model based on variance explained alone is not a good strategy. This limitation of using reconstruction error as a guide will also resurface when we consider cluster analysis later in the book and seek a measure to justify the number of clusters to retain. Since reconstruction error typically and necessarily reduces as the number of clusters increases, reconstruction error is not a sufficient measure for making decisions on how many clusters to retain.

To determine the number of components to keep, one should primarily use substantive judgment in addition to statistical indicators, and in the end, a bit of common sense. For example, if the first two components explain 70% of the variance, but the third component only explains an additional 1%, then obviously the two-component solution will dominate under most circumstances (depending on the substantive nature of the investigation). Graphical measures such as the scree plot can be used to visualize both the reconstruction error as well as the variance explained, and one typically looks for a “bend” in such plots to indicate where the reconstruction error (or variance explained) suddenly “drops.”

PCA, under most circumstances, will generate as many components as there are variables. The actual “data reduction” occurs by selecting the first few components to account for as much of the variance in the variables as possible, or equivalently, minimizes the reconstruction error. Choosing the number of components to keep or maintain is largely dependent on the research or scientific context and often based on user judgment.

11.2.5 Constraints on Components

Recall that we mentioned that the eigenvector weights e1 through ep were applied to observed variables in order to generate components. In deriving these components, we shall impose the 401constraint on these eigenvector weights so that the sum of their squares is equal to unity. That is, the sum of squared eigenvector weights we will set equal to one,


$${\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}e_{i}^{2}} = 1$$
(11.5)

When we impose such a condition on each component, the component is said to have been normalized. There is no absolute requirement that the sum needs to be 1; it could in theory be any other constant positive value. Setting it equal to 1 implies that the length of the component is equal to unity. But why impose such a constraint at all? The purpose of this constraint is such that if we did not impose at least some constraint on the loadings, then in theory we could allow the component’s variance to increase without bound. By imposing this constraint, or other positive constant for the variance, we are assured that the variance of the component will not simply be a reflection of increasingly large eigenvector weights.

As we have seen throughout this book, constraints such as the above are not atypical in statistical or machine learning methods. It is a regular occurrence in mathematical modeling more generally that some quantities are fixed or constrained to particular values so that other variable quantities can be more freely estimated under these constraints. Constraints such as these, in the end, simplify problems.

11.2.6 Centering Observed Variables

Observed variables are also often (though need not necessarly be) centered before being subjected to the components analysis, so that each variable has a mean equal to 0. By centering here we simply mean subtracting the mean of each observed raw variable. For example, if the observed variable is xi with mean $\overline{x}$, then centering the variable means generating $x_{i} - \overline{x}$ for each observation. The reader will recognize centering here as a precursor to computing z-scores where the centered deviation is then further divided by the standard deviation, s. As a simple example of centering, consider the following vector of data in R having original raw mean equal to 6.2:

> v <- c(0, 4, 8, 9, 10)
> mean(v)
[1] 6.2

To center this data, we simply subtract the mean from each observation:

> v.center <- v - mean(v)
> v.center
[1] -6.2 -2.2 1.8 2.8 3.8

We can then easily confirm that, within rounding error, the mean of the centered data is equal to 0:

> mean(v.center)
[1] -1.775489e-16
402

11.2.7 Orthogonality of Components

As mentioned already, one of the attractive features of components analysis is that derived components are guaranteed to be orthogonal (i.e., eigenvectors) and uncorrelated to one another. Recall what orthogonality means, it means derived components are at right angles, or perpendicular to one another (that of 90 degrees). From a substantive point of view, orthogonality ensures that each component accounts for, or explains a differing proportion of variance in the variables and that there is no overlap. It is important to emphasize that orthogonality is not the same as statistical independence. Statistical independence is, in a sense, a stronger property than orthogonality in this case and principal components will only be both orthogonal and independent if the data are multivariate normal. For components to be both orthogonal and independent beyond the assumption of multivariate normality one must go beyond traditional PCA and instead perform an independent components analysis, to be discussed later. Assuming all components are nonzero, however, orthogonality of components will imply linear independence (as opposed to statistical independence).

Classic principal components analysis ensures orthogonality of components but does not guarantee their statistical independence. Statistical independence is the stronger property in this case, reserved for the technique of independent components analysis.

11.2.8 Proportion of Variance Explained by Each Component: Covariance vs. Correlation Matrices

Having computed components in decreasing order of variance explained, a natural question worth asking now is: how much variance is actually accounted for by each component? Recall that components analysis does not change the amount of variance in the original variables. It merely reconstructs that variance along new dimensions (called the components, which are in effect, eigenvectors of the transformation). Hence, it stands that the total variance in the totality of components should be equal to the total variance in the original variables. That is, when we sum up the variance accounted for by all of the components, that sum should equal the total variance in the original variables. In a covariance matrix, that sum of variance will equal the sum of variances across all observed variables. In a correlation matrix, that sum will equal to the total number of variables because in a correlation matrix, the variance contributed by each variable is equal to one. Whether one analyzes a covariance or correlation matrix can result in quite vastly different outcomes. Principal components analysis is not invariant to type of matrix analyzed. This fact may at first seem to go against intuition, such that one might have assumed or expected that both the covariance and correlation matrices would yield similar results, or at minimum, one result would be a trivial transformation of the other. However, this is not the case. A PCA performed on a correlation matrix will usually yield different eigenvalues and eigenvectors than a PCA performed on a covariance matrix.

Given this distinction, the question becomes: which matrix to analyze? While some hold the covariance matrix is more in spirit with PCA (e.g., see Rencher & Christensen, 2012), others recommend that PCA should virtually always be performed on the standardized covariance matrix, otherwise known of course as the correlation matrix (Bilodeau & Brenner, 1999; Murray, 2022). Of course, there is no harm in trying both solutions and comparing them. The important point, however, is to recognize that performing PCA on one versus the other will, in general, not produce the same result. Principal components analysis also requires at least some covariance (or 403correlation) among pairs of variables. In the absence of such covariance, that is, if all covariances or correlations are equal to 0 and only variances remain along the main diagonal, PCA will be of little use. At most, PCA will simply generate components that are a reflection of the original variables but in descending order of variance (Chatfield & Collins, 1980). For now, we will assume we are working with the covariance matrix. Given that the eigenvalues are variances of each component, then the following relation should then hold:


∑s2 = ∑λi
(11.6)

That is, the sum of variances of the original variables should equal the sum of eigenvalues from the components analysis. We can easily demonstrate this on empirical data. Consider some data on x, y:

> x <- c(2.5, 0.5, 2.2, 1.9, 3.1, 2.3, 2.0, 1.0, 1.5, 1.1)
> y <- c(2.4, 0.7, 2.9, 2.2, 3.0, 2.7, 1.6, 1.1, 1.6, 0.9)

The variances of each variable are the following:

> var(x)
[1] 0.6165556
> var(y)
[1] 0.7165556

The sum of these variances is

> sum(var(x), var(y))
[1] 1.333111

When we compute the components analysis on the covariance matrix from this data, we obtain via eigen analysis eigenvalues of 1.284 and 0.0491, which when summed total 1.3331, which we note is the same total as that generated by summing the original variances of the variables. Hence, we have demonstrated through empirical data that PCA has not changed the variance in the variables, it has merely reconstructed the variance onto new dimensions instead of on the original variables. The variance accounted for by the new components is the same variance in the original variables. This is why again we dislike the idea of PCA “discovering” dimensions. We prefer say that PCA is simply reorganizing the variables onto dimensions that are mathematically assured by the decomposition. For the majority of data sets and well-behaved matrices, PCA will generate components. It is whether such components can be interpreted and whether they are meaningful that is the real question of interest.

11.2.9 Principal Components as a Rotation of Axes

We have seen that principal components analysis can be explained by eigen analysis or by reference to a least-squares argument in which squared perpendiculars are minimized instead of vertical distances. The real “mystery” of principal components analysis lies in eigen analysis. Once we accept that eigen analysis can be performed, it is a relatively simple matter to accept that we can generate components. It is the substantive understanding of these components that then matters. 404What we mean by this is that if one truly wants to understand PCA, one needs to truly understand eigen analysis.

Our understanding of PCA can also benefit from understanding some of its geometry. Geometrically, PCA is nothing more than a rotation of the original Cartesian axes. To demonstrate such a rotation, consider once more our data on PCA (Smith, 2002):

> x <- c(2.5, 0.5, 2.2, 1.9, 3.1, 2.3, 2.0, 1.0, 1.5, 1.1)
> y <- c(2.4, 0.7, 2.9, 2.2, 3.0, 2.7, 1.6, 1.1, 1.6, 0.9)

We now generate a dataframe from these vectors as well as the corresponding covariance matrix:

> data <- data.frame(x, y)
> data
X y

> cov(data)
X y

X

0.6165556

0.6154444

Next, we perform an eigen analysis on this data to extract eigenvalues and eigenvectors from the covariance matrix:405

> eigen(cov(data))
eigen() decomposition
$values
[1] 1.2840277 0.0490834
$vectors
[,1] [,2]

[1,]

0.6778734

-0.7351787

[2,]

0.7351787

We note the first eigenvalue is equal to 1.284 with eigenvector 0.6779, 0.7352 (the eigenvectors corresponding to each eigenvalue are in columns above, not rows). The second eigenvalue is equal to 0.0491 with eigenvector −0.7352, 0.6779. But what do these eigenvectors represent? We can consider them to be factors of rotation of the original axes (Young, 2023). The eigenvectors are first and foremost vectors, and as such, can be easily plotted in space (Figure 11.2).

Note carefully that each eigenvector appears to account for the scatter of points. The first eigenvector, from bottom left to upper right, seems to account for most of the variance in the data. This is not a surprise, since the first eigenvalue is equal to 1.284 and is much larger than the second of 0.0491. The proportion of variance accounted for by the first eigenvector is 1.284/(1.284 + 0.0491) = 0.96, or 96%. Clearly, the first eigenvector (component) is accounting for the majority of the variance in the original variables.

We can also see that the angle between the eigenvectors is one of 90 degrees. That is, the rotation of the original axes did not change the angle between them but instead kept it as orthogonal as were the original basis Cartesian axes. In linear algebra, this type of transformation is regarded as a rigid rotation of the axes and we have simply found an optimal new basis from which to project the data. Mathematically, this is all that PCA accomplishes.

11.2.10 Principal Components, Discriminant Functions, Canonical Variates: Linking Foundations

As mentioned at the outset of this book, if there is a common theme running throughout most of it, one of many, it is that of dimension reduction. Even the analysis of variance, long before we knew it in undergraduate statistics, on a deeper theoretical level could be said to be generating new dimensions on which data can be projected. It may thus appear to the reader at some point that many of the methodologies surveyed in this book and beyond are performing a similar task. Indeed, dimension reduction is common to most in one way or another, though there are of course important differences regarding how various methods go about such a task.

Recall that we had said earlier in the book that discriminant functions were underlying dimensions such that they maximized separation between groups. Successive dimensions were 406uncorrelated to one another. Both discriminant analysis and principal components analysis execute a “flavor” of dimension reduction, but they go about it in different ways. For one, in PCA, dimensions are obtained that maximize variance, not maximize separation between groups. Second, while discriminant functions are uncorrelated to one another, they are typically not orthogonal, while principal components are uncorrelated and orthogonal. Components have the stronger property of orthogonality (Rencher & Christensen, 2012). This is also true of canonical variates in canonical correlation; they are uncorrelated but not orthogonal. As mentioned earlier, components can be made independent (or nearly so), but that requires independent components analysis and not classical PCA. PCA only ensures that components are uncorrelated, which is a weaker property than statistical independence (Jolliffe, 2002, p. 396).

A second feature that distinguishes PCA from linear discriminant analysis (LDA) (and canonical analysis) is that obtaining components does not involve the computation of an inverse matrix. In discriminant analysis, we were required to obtain eigenvalues and eigenvectors from E − 1H and hence E − 1 had to exist. In PCA, no such inverse is computed. Of what consequence is this fact? Recall that inverses exist only for matrices that are nonsingular. A singular matrix has determinant equal to 0, which also implies or equates to linear dependence among select rows or columns. However, if the computation of an inverse is not required, then this implies that PCA can be performed on a covariance matrix that is singular. Under this condition some eigenvalues will equal 0 (Rencher & Christensen, 2012). In such a case, these components are to be ignored, as they explain zero variance. A second case in which singularity can arise is when the number of observations is less than the number of variables. PCA can still be performed on such data, whereas LDA or canonical analysis on such data would, analytically, be problematic.

11.2.11 Principal Components in Python

We consider a very easy example of PCA in Python on fictional data:

import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
X = np.array([[-1, -1], [-2, -1], [-3, -2], [1, 1], [2, 1], [3, 2]])
pca = PCA(n_components=2)
X
Out[95]:
array([[-1, -1],
      [-2, -1],
      [-3, -2],
      [ 1, 1],
      [ 2, 1],
      [ 3, 2]])
pca.fit(X)
Out[72]: PCA(n_components=2)
print(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)
[0.99244289 0.00755711]

We see from the above that the proportion of variance explained by the first component is 0.99, while the proportion of variance explained by the second component is 0.0075. Clearly, the first 407component is most important to the analysis. Note that the cumulative sum of the proportions equals 1 (i.e., 0.99244289 + 0.00755711 = 1.0).

As mentioned earlier, incremental PCA can be beneficial when the data are so large that it cannot fit in memory at once, and can be fit using IncrementalPCA. Heatmaps can also be used to visualize components (see Müller & Guido, 2017, pp. 148–149 for examples).

11.2.12 Principal Components in R

Conducting a basic PCA in R is very easy. For example, we can use the Rdimtools package (You & Shung, 2022) on the iris data:

> library(Rdimtools)
> data(iris)
> set.seed(100)

Below we will sample 50 observations from numbers 1 through 150:

> subid = sample(1:150, 50)

We then create the matrix X made up of variables 1 through 4 (in columns) in the iris data, which are the plant features (i.e., sepal length, sepal width, etc.), followed by the designation of species (i.e., label):

> X = as.matrix(iris[subid,1:4])
> label = as.factor(iris[subid,5])

We now conduct the PCA, requesting two dimensions (ndim = 2):

> PCA <- do.pca(X, ndim=2)
> PCA
$Y
[,1] [,2]

[1,]

1.50866388

-0.491302038

[2,]

1.90078112

-0.156616064

[3,]

-0.245114259

[4,]

1.18816125

0.114116172

[5,]

0.13988863

-0.543760253

The above are the component scores resulting from the PCA (only the first five scores are shown). Next, we are given the variances associated with each component:

$vars
[1] 3.8646558 0.2000033
$projection
[,1] [,2]

[1,]

0.37088025

0.63842394

0.72546180

408

We can see that the variance of the first component is 3.86 while the variance of the second component is 0.200. The component weights (eigenvectors) are given next which are to be read vertically for each component. We can obtain a visualization of the projected component scores (Figure 11.3, left):

> plot(PCA$Y, pch = 19, col = label, main = “PCA”)

Incidentally, we encourage the reader to try a competing alternative to the above PCA simply to get a glimpse and appreciation of how drastically the dimension reduction (or “embedding,” a term we will use shortly) can change as a function of method employed for the data reduction. For example, had we conducted a Laplacian Score, we would have obtained the plot to the right of the above PCA (Figure 11.3, right). Instead of do.pca(), we code do.lscore():

> lap = do.lscore(X, ndim=2)
> plot(lap$Y, pch = 19, main = “Laplacian score”)

Clearly, as is evident from the two different methods of dimension reduction, the expression “what you find in data is largely a function of what you use to do the finding” rings true!

Curvilinear component analysis is yet another option and can be fit by R with the package ProjectionBasedClustering (Thrun & Ultsch, 2021).409

11.2.13 Cautionary Concerns and Caveats Regarding Principal Components

Principal components analysis can seem like a relatively simple procedure, but it has a lot of hidden complexities associated with it that often bypass the novice. In statistics, PCA is probably the simplest procedure that has the most complexity associated with it and things that can “trip you up” if you’re not careful. Its simplicity is deceiving. Understanding PCA is actually quite challenging, which might explain why there are entire books devoted to the subject. The graduate student learning PCA for the first time, concluding it is an “easy” procedure simply lacks the experience to appreciate its “latent” (pun intended!) complexity. We list a few of the more common caveats below. These are things you should be well aware of before using or interpreting the technique. Some we have already mentioned elsewhere in the chapter, and we emphasize here again only to reiterate their importance:

  1. 1. Principal components are not scale-dependent. That is, whether the PCA is performed on the covariance or correlation matrix usually results in different findings. Variables with greater variance will have greater influence on the PCA solution than variables with lesser variance. The typical way to get around this issue is to scale variables so that they all have the same variance, which amounts to analyzing the correlation matrix instead of the covariance matrix. While this may seem like a good solution to be adopted in all circumstances, if variables are not originally conceived to be of equal importance (almost in the sense of a Bayesian prior), then the covariance matrix should be analyzed over the correlation matrix (Chatfield & Collins, 1980, p. 71) as the analysis of covariance matrices is more in the spirit of PCA (Rencher & Christensen, 2012).
  2. 2. The first principal component, as mentioned, is the one with the largest variance. However, this does not necessarily imply that it is the component of most interest. There is no guarantee that the first principal component will be more theoretically interesting than the second, or the third, etc. It is the “best” component only in the sense of maximizing variance. Other components may be preferred based on their correlation with other variables or how they perform in ensuing regression analysis for instance, or even how they cluster in a cluster analysis (Marden, 2015). Variance explained is only one criterion that should be used in addressing the “importance” or “relevance” of a component.
  3. 3. Principal components will under most circumstances generate as many components as there are original variables. PCA, under most circumstances, will necessarily generate components. However, there is absolutely no requirement that the components obtained are meaningful or useful. The fact that you ran a PCA on variables and obtained components is not a “finding.” It is a mathematical certainty that existed long before you performed the components analysis. Whether you believe the transformation is in some sense “interesting” will likely depend on your substantive science and even philosophy of mathematics. That is, if the components look “meaningless” now substantively, does the mathematical transformation still imply they are nonetheless “real?” This isn’t a statistical question, it is one of the philosophy of mathematics. If you believe mathematics corresponds to “reality,” then regardless of whether you can “make sense” of the components or not you may still believe them to nonetheless “exist.” This is an exceptionally interesting topic, but far beyond the scope of this book.
  4. 4. Related to #3, components are only as good or interesting as the input variables subjected to the components analysis. Hence, the first and primary concern of interest is subjecting PCA to a set of variables that is inclusive of all the variables you wish to analyze. If the data set is not interesting or you leave out important variables from the ensemble of variables, conducting a PCA on such data will likely be limiting, or your components analysis will be misspecified.410
  5. 5. It is possible, even if unlikely, that a PCA generates eigenvalues that are equal or near equal in size. Further, population eigenvalues are usually not exactly equal to eigenvalues generated by the sample. Inferential tests for eigenvalues exist (e.g., Camargo, 2022), but are rarely used. Tests have been developed and usually require the normality assumption (Collins & Chatfield, 1980; Peres-Neto et al., 2005).
  6. 6. Components derived in PCA depend more on the ratios of correlations in a correlation matrix than the correlations themselves. As noted by Collins and Chatfield (1980, p. 67), dividing all off-diagonal correlations by a constant greater than 1 reveals that the eigenvalues change but that the eigenvectors, which implies the components as well, do not.
  7. 7. PCA does not assess the dimensionality of the variables; it assesses the linear dimensionality of the variables. If the data are nonlinear, which amounts to the underlying manifold being nonlinear, then classical PCA will fail to capture this nonlinearity. As discussed later, techniques such as kernel PCA will be more effective at uncovering a nonlinear underlying manifold.
  8. 8. Related to the previous point (#7), PCA is, in its most general sense, a type of manifold learning where the manifold is assumed to be linear. Nonlinear techniques may be more effective at uncovering the true manifold. A failure to uncover meaningful components using PCA should never be taken as conclusive evidence that deeper dimensionality is nonexistent underlying the variables. Such interesting dimensionality may indeed exist, but it may be nonlinear in form, a structure that PCA will be limited in uncovering.

11.3 Independent Components Analysis

In the classical PCA just discussed, we required components to be linear functions and orthogonal to one another. We sought to reduce the rank of the matrix of observed variables into one of smaller rank, but that accounted for most of the variance in the original variables, preferably in the first few components. The fact that the components were orthogonal to one another was a key feature of principal components analysis.

In independent component analysis (ICA), we require components (i.e., the latent variables) to be mutually independent and typically non-Gaussian (Izenman, 2008). That is, the goal in ICA is to find a linear representation of non-Gaussian data so that the components are statistically independent, and if not perfectly so, then as independent as possible. This is a different requirement than simply requiring orthogonality. As noted by Jolliffe (2002), the links between classical PCA and independent components analysis are, perhaps surprisingly, not that strong, and ICA is closer in relation to factor analysis than it is to components analysis.

The ICA model (Izenman, 2008) can be stated as follows:


X = f(S) + e
(11.7)

where X is a vector of random observed “manifest” variables, S is an unobservable random vector variate of sources whose components are independent latent variables, each having zero mean, and e is a random vector representing noise, for instance, in the measurements taken on X. The key point is that the independence of the sources implies that each individual source signal is hypothesized to be generated by a process unrelated to any other source signal (Izenman, 2008). Without e, the model is referred to as noiseless ICA. When e is included, we refer to the technique as noisy ICA.411

In ICA, projected points P are obtained as a product of the original data D and an unmixing matrix Mu, where the mixing matrix is equal to M. Hence, P = DMu. ICA essentially looks for rotations of data that have (approximately) independent coordinates. This will necessarily be true for all rotations from samples from multivariate normal distributions (Venables & Ripley, 2002, p. 313), and hence ICA will not be of most interest for such a “trivial” situation. Instead, ICA is most valuable and useful for data arising from distributions that are not normal, that is, non-Gaussian.

11.3.1 Principal Components vs. Independent Components Analysis

How does independent component analysis relate to PCA? It stands that there should be some relation between them, and indeed there is. PCA can be considered a special case of ICA, where PCA yields orthogonal components while ICA generates independent components.

Jolliffe (2002, p. 396) best summarizes the difference between PCA and ICA:

PCA has as its main objective the successive maximization of variance, and the orthogonality and uncorrelatedness constraints are extras, which are included to ensure that the different components are measuring separate things. By contrast, independent components analysis (ICA) takes the “separation” of components as its main aim. ICA starts from the view that uncorrelatedness is rather limited as it only considers a lack of linear relationship, and that ideally components should be statistically independent. This is a stronger requirement than uncorrelatedness, with the two only equivalent for normal (Gaussian) random variables [emphasis added]. … This is much closer to the set-up for factor analysis, and it is this “model” that ICA generalizes.

Jolliffe goes on to emphasize that simply because ICA is most appropriate in non-Gaussian contexts, this does not imply that classical PCA assumes normality, since it does not. One need not make any distributional assumptions to conduct a PCA as it is simply a mathematical decomposition of variance. If one chooses to make inferences of components to populations, then that is a different matter that would require corresponding parametric assumptions.

Hence, whereas PCA seeks to find or uncover a reduced-rank representation of variables, ICA attempts to represent data as independent sub-elements. ICA tries to separate the signals in one’s data, while PCA attempts to “load” the data onto the first few important or “principal” components. These are two quite different objectives. The reader will better appreciate how ICA is more similar to factor analysis when we survey factor analysis later in the book. Factor analysis is a proper statistical model and thus includes an error term, making it comparable to ICA. In PCA, no such error term is typically included nor is any statistical “model-like” structure advanced.

PCA and ICA are not the same technique. PCA seeks a lower-dimensional linear representation of the variables, whereas ICA seeks to separate the observed data into independent signals. Independence is a stronger property than uncorrelatedness under the assumption of non-Gaussian distributions.

As a simple example of independent components analysis, consider Figure 11.4.412

We begin with a mixed signal. The goal of ICA is to essentially “unmix” the signals. In sound analysis, for instance, a variety of components make up any sound, and ICA has been found useful for unmixing those composite sounds (e.g., “black box” recordings following an airplane crash). Independent components analysis can also prove useful in “unmixing” mixtures of image components in a picture.

For further details on ICA, see Izenman (2008). For an excellent discussion that summarizes the primary features of ICA and elaborates greatly on the required assumptions (and why they are necessary), see Hyvärinen and Oja (2000). For a concise discussion of the differences between PCA and ICA, see Jolliffe (2002, p. 396). Kernel ICA is a relatively recent development (Bach & Jordon, 2002) at least in comparison to classical PCA and is discussed in Izenman (2008, pp. 575–576). Independent components analysis can be fit using Python’s Fast ICA algorithm. In R, the package ica (Helwig, 2022) can perform ICA as well as the package e1071 (Meyer et al., 2023).

We feature an example in R from the package ProjectionBasedClustering (Thrun et al., 2024), where the Hepta data (three-dimensional) contain pre-defined clusters but with different variances:

> library(ProjectionBasedClustering)
> data(Hepta)
> Data = Hepta$Data
> Proj=ICA(Data)
