11.4 Probabilistic PCA

In classical PCA, there is an absence of an associated probabilistic model for the data. That is, classical PCA is not probabilistic in any way; it is merely a mathematical transformation of the variables onto new axes such that it establishes a new basis (i.e., one that is orthogonal) from which the data are projected. As many writers on PCA have emphasized, PCA is not a “model” per se, it is simply a rotation of axes on which data are projected in correspondence to this rotation. Components are not obtained with reference to any kind of density-estimation framework. Be sure to note that in this distinction we are referring to the construction of the components, not the estimation of the components in the population. As mentioned, inferential procedures for components analysis do exist but are rarely used, with users preferring visualization techniques (e.g., scree plots) and eigenvalue magnitudes as aids to determining how many components to retain. When inference is employed, the inferential aspect of PCA makes components analysis probabilistic, but only in that particular sense of inference, not in the sense of actually deriving the components via eigen analysis.

It is possible, however, to derive the PCA approach based on a probabilistic formulation even without regard to estimation. Probabilistic PCA was first proposed by Tipping and Bishop (1999) to provide an alternative approach to PCA, one that is probabilistic and thus exists in a density-estimation framework (Tipping & Bishop, 1999).

We give the case of probabilistic PCA, which can also be regarded as a special case of factor analysis, where W is a loading matrix and where the covariance matrix S can be written as


S ∼ WWT + σ2I
(11.8)

Notice the noise term σ2in the probabilistic model. Classic principal components analysis is a special case of probabilistic PCA as σ2→0, or at minimum is infinitesimally small and essentially converges to zero. Noise dimensions are also uncorrelated, which above is indicated by σ2I, since in the identity matrix only values of 1 lie along the main diagonal and zeroes everywhere else. The inclusion of σ2I as the “error term” here instead of only σ2 simply denotes the fact that we are working in the context of several variables and hence require a matrix representation.

The principal axes of probabilistic PCA can be derived as maximum-likelihood parameter estimates computed by the usual eigen-decomposition approach. There is no closed-form solution and hence parameter estimates for W and σ2I must be obtained iteratively (Tipping & Bishop, 1999). We can also approach the construction of components via an iterative, computationally efficient expectation-maximization approach. For details, see Murphy (2022). For an excellent introduction to the probabilistic PCA model from the ground up starting with classic non-probabilistic PCA, see Tipping and Bishop (1999) who provide a very good overview.

11.4.1 Motivation for Probabilistic PCA

Why seek out a probabilistic approach to PCA in the first place? Why add a noise term similar to how factor analysis includes an error term? There are at least a couple benefits to doing so over the simpler and more conventional PCA approach:

  1. 1. Using a probability model allows us to extend the scope of conventional PCA and may also be useful in cases of missing data. It also allows for a comparison with other probabilistic approaches which dominate statistics, facilitating statistical testing and allowing for the application of Bayesian approaches (Tipping & Bishop, 1999).415
  2. 2. Probabilistic PCA can be utilized as a constrained Gaussian density model (Tipping & Bishop, 1999). This allows for the efficient computation of maximum-likelihood estimates directly from the data principal components.

11.4.2 Probabilistic PCA in R

Probabilistic PCA can be performed in R using the Rdimtools (You & Shung, 2022) package. The following is an example, adapted from the package (p. 184), that compares probabilistic PCA (PPCA) to PCA on the iris data:

> set.seed(100)
> subid = sample(1:100, 50)
> X = as.matrix(iris[subid,1:4])
> label = as.factor(iris[subid,5])

11.5 PCA for Discrete, Binary, and Categorical Data

Up to now, we have assumed that the data subjected to PCA is numerical and relatively continuous in nature. This is fine, so long as the data in one’s study adheres to this nature. However, oftentimes data come in a variety of forms that are hardly continuous. For example, binary (e.g., yes vs. no) data are common in polling, and categorical data (e.g., A, B, C) are quite popular as well.

Can PCA be used for data of different types? According to Jolliffe (2002, p. 339), the answer is “yes”:

When PCA is used as a descriptive technique, there is no reason for the variables in the analysis to be of any particular type … the variables could be a mixture of continuous, ordinal or even binary (0/1) variables. It is true that variances, covariances and correlations have especial relevance for multivariate normal data x, and that linear functions of binary variables are less readily interpretable than linear functions of continuous variables. However, the basic objective of PCA – to summarize most of the “variation” that is present in the original set of p variables using a smaller number of derived variables – can be achieved regardless of the nature of the original variables.

While PCA can be conducted on a mixture of variables, multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) is usually the preferred technique for dimension reduction using categorical data, as PCA is most often used for dimension reduction featuring numerical measurements. Kalantan and Alqahtani (2019) also feature a method of PCA for mixed data. Murphy (2022, p. 670) gives the case of PCA for categorical data.418

11.6 Nonlinear Dimension Reduction

11.6.1 Kernel PCA

As we have seen, classical or “standard” principal components analysis allows for linear dimensionality reduction. However, we must ask the question of how often the true dimensionality of the variables or data lies in a subspace that is precisely linear. Probably not that often just as most data subjected to regression models are hardly linear, which is why techniques such as polynomial regression, splines, and other nonlinear and nonparametric approaches were surveyed earlier in the book. Though linearity is a useful approximation for dimension reduction, the true underlying dimensionality of most sets of variables is probably nonlinear. That is, the true manifold is likely, in the end, a nonlinear structure, not a linear one. We emphasize again that the linear vs. nonlinear underlying dimensionality always refers only to the set of variables you are working with and have included in your set of chosen variables. Dimension analysis, as is the case with any mathematical technique, can only operate on the set of variables you have subjected to analysis. All analyses are on what might be called restricted universes of variables and their respective interrelationships. This seems like an obvious point to make, but is one worth emphasizing: a PCA, or any statistical method can only provide results on the variables on which it is analyzed! If you leave out important variables, your entire analysis will be misspecified. What you “find” is entirely related to what you supply the “machine” doing the searching. All is context-dependent all of the time.

Kernel principal components analysis (KPCA) allows one to generalize standard PCA to nonlinear dimensionality reduction. As we will see, it is one of many nonlinear options to choose from when it comes to uncovering nonlinear dimensions.

11.6.2 How KPCA Works

Recall that the big idea of using kernel methods in general, not just for PCA (but for example, support vector machines), is that data that may not be separable in its current feature space may benefit from being projected into higher dimensions. For example, instead of having variables x1 and x2 only, an enlargement of the feature space might be x1, x2, x12, x22. This enlargement of the feature space makes the data more linearly separable. This is the very essence of what kernel methods, and kernel PCA in particular, seek to accomplish. Through the calculation of a kernel, we can then apply PCA in higher-dimensional space without ever having to really go there. When you think about it, this is truly a marvel! Indeed, kernel methods can be applied to many algorithms that can be formulated in terms of inner products in the feature space.

By projecting data that is nonlinear into higher-dimensional space, we make otherwise nonlinear data in the data space more linearly separable in the feature space. This is the essence of how kernel PCA (and other kernel methods) work.

To further unpack how kernel PCA may be useful, consider Figure 11.7 consisting of data in two dimensions. Clearly, the data are not linearly separable. That is, we cannot draw a line through the data to separate the circles from the crosses. A more complex decision surface would provide much better separability. Mapping the problem from two dimensions to higher, we make the problem linearly separable, and it now looks as in Figure 11.8.419

The mapping from two dimensions to higher dimensions has made the data linearly separable, and thus a linear method can now be applied to the transformed “kernelized” data. This is the essence of kernelizing data in the context of PCA, that of transforming the data via kernels so that otherwise nonlinear data becomes linearly separable in the feature space and an “ordinary” PCA can then be applied to the transformed “kernelized” data.420

11.6.3 Kernelizing and Computational Complexity

There is another benefit to kernelizing. When we move from two dimensions to three, or, more generally, from lower dimensions to higher, such can seriously increase computation time. For smaller problems, this is usually not a problem, but for larger dimensionality tasks it becomes prohibitive. Hence, an immediate problem with high dimensionality is that of computational complexity. We would like to get around this problem and still capitalize on the benefits of working in higher-dimensional feature space. If we can compute in lower-dimensional space but actually work in higher-dimensional space, such would be ideal. This is precisely what the kernel trick allows us to do in terms of facilitating computation. That is, we can take advantage of higher-dimensional representations without having to actually work in those higher configurations. Instead, we can remain in lower dimensions and nonetheless conduct our analyses there. This is accomplished by computing kernels, which even though computed in lower dimensions, contain information about higher-dimensional representation.

The above result is due to Mercer’s theorem, which the reader may recall was discussed earlier in the book in relation to support vector machines. In brief, the computational complexity of kernel PCA does not one-to-one increase with the dimensionality of the feature space (Schölkopf et al., 1998, p. 4), and so even if we are working in very high-dimensional space theoretically, the computational complexity can be “tamed” somewhat by computing in a lower-dimensional space. This is thanks to the fact that we can compute kernels to represent this higher-dimensional inner product (Hilbert) space, and the fact that kernels are relatively simple to compute. Again, kernelizing is a marvel!

What is more, with kernel PCA no nonlinear optimization is involved. We can simply solve an eigenvalue-eigenvector problem as we would in traditional PCA but now on the kernelized data. The benefit of this is that getting “stuck” in local optima, in this case, minimums, is not a problem as it might be using other nonlinear methods. That is, global optima can be attained in kernel PCA (Belkin & Niyogi, 2003, p. 1374). Clearly, kernel PCA has computational benefits to employing direct nonlinear methodologies.

The kernel trick allows us to work and compute in lower dimensions but benefit from higher-dimensional representation. The advantage of this is to both account for potential nonlinearity in the data but also to simplify computation time since we do not have to actually access the higher-dimensional space or surfaces in order to account for it. This is more generally known as the “kernel trick” and is due to Mercer’s theorem.

11.6.4 Reconstruction Error in Kernel PCA

As was the case for classic PCA, the goal in kernel PCA will be to minimize the reconstruction error. It should make sense as to why this goal has not changed when moving from classical PCA to kernelized PCA; both methods are essentially doing the same thing, but simply on different transformations of the variables and data. At first glance, it may appear that enlarging the feature space would increase the dimensionality in which we need to compute. However, contrary to what we may expect, this is not what occurs, thanks again to the kernel trick. As we have emphasized, due to the kernel trick, we will not actually have to do any calculations in the higher-dimensional feature space. Computation of kernels occurs in the original lower-dimensional space of the data. As summarized by Hastie et al. (2009, p. 547):421

Kernel PCA expands the scope of PCA, mimicking what we would obtain if we were to expand the features by non-linear transformations, and then apply PCA in this transformed feature space.

To add to all this, the higher-dimensional space could very well turn out to be infinite dimensional. This is why it’s called a “trick,” because we can simply compute kernels in lower dimensions and learn something of the higher dimensions without actually doing complex computations in higher dimensions. By analogy, it would be somewhat like being able to add two numbers, a very simple operation, to learn more about how the numbers relate in very complex ways (e.g., whether the distance between the numbers is a prime number). The kernel trick allows for a simple computation to represent a much more complex reality or “space” behind those numbers. Inexact analogy to be sure, but approximates the idea somewhat in spirit. The takeaway message is that the kernel trick is a big deal in statistics and machine learning.

11.6.5 The Matrices of Kernel PCA

Mathematically, kernel PCA relies on the fact that principal components can be obtained from a data matrix X by computing inner products of that data matrix,


K = XXT
(11.9)

Eigen analysis is then performed on the double-centered version of K, where K̃ is now equal to


Kc = (I−M)K(I−M)
(11.10)

and where M = 11T/N which serves to center K (Hastie et al., 2009, p. 547). That is, we are computing a kernel matrix K̃ that contains all pairwise dot products between data points. The double-centering here ensures the mean of every row and column is equal to 0. Whereas classical PCA uses the covariance matrix and scales regarding the number of input dimensions, kernel PCA scales with respect to the number of data points rather than dimensions in that the eigen analysis occurs on the K̃ matrix and not the covariance matrix as in PCA.

As is true when using kernels, a variety of kernels are available, such as the radial kernel and others. However, the choice of kernel is critical, and the expression “what you find is a function of what you put in” is very relevant here; one kernel over another can drastically generate different findings (for an example of this, see Hastie et al., 2009, p. 549). What does the eigen problem look like? Recall classic eigen decomposition:


Ax = λx

For kernel PCA, A is now the kernel matrix K̃, and by simple substitution (Bishop, 2006, p. 588) the eigenvalue problem becomes,


Ax=λx→K̃x=λNx
(11.11)

or as simply422


K̃x = λ̃x

if λ̃ = λN (Izenman, 2008, p. 611). Note that we are performing eigen analysis on the K̃ matrix and not the covariance or correlation matrix as in traditional PCA (Bishop, 2006). Once we have the eigenvalues and eigenvectors, we can now project the data onto each new dimension.

Kernel PCA can be conceptualized as an “ordinary” PCA, but instead of weighted by input variables by values of the eigenvector, it is the kernel of the data points that is weighted by values of the eigenvector. Hence, KPCA simply replaces the variables (dimensions) with the kernel of observations, so that the kernel trick can “do its magic.”

11.6.6 Classical PCA as a Special Case of Kernel PCA

We have seen that kernel PCA allows for nonlinearity. Hence, it stands that with some constraints imposed, classical linear PCA should be able to be obtained and operationalized as a special case of kernel PCA. Indeed, it should be evident from our earlier discussion that classical PCA must simply be a special case of KPCA (Bishop, 2006, p. 589) in which the kernel is the linear kernel. This is powerful insight. In general, many linear methods can be regarded as special cases of a more general nonlinear framework. The set of nonlinear statistical “possibilities” is much wider than the smaller set of linear models, and hence linear methods are a subset of that wider set, not only in the case of kernel PCA in relation to PCA but for most statistical methods in general.

11.6.7 Kernel Trick Is Not Simply about Cost

The kernel trick is useful since it saves on computational cost in accessing the higher-dimensional feature space. However, it should be emphasized that that is not the only reason for its utility. The primary benefit to using kernel methods is not only as a way around computational complexity. To reiterate, the kernel trick allows us to work in higher dimensions without knowing the specific details of that dimensionality. That is its key benefit. Hence, though often kernel methods in general are advertised or evaluated for their computational properties in “accessing” higher dimensionality, applying kernel methods in general is far from simply a way to ease computation. Even if the computations are laborious, which they can be in computing dot products of large matrices, kernel methods are useful since they allow access to those higher dimensions in the first place. In general, kernel methods allow access to higher dimensionality while working in lower dimensions, often all for a more reasonable computational cost than if we were to access those higher dimensions directly.

11.6.8 Kernel PCA in Python

We will perform kernel PCA in Python using the KernelPCA function:

import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import KernelPCA
X = np.array([[-1, -1], [-2, -1], [-3, -2], [1, 1], [2, 1], [3, 2]])
X
Out[24]:
array([[-1, -1],
     [-2, -1],
     [-3, -2],
     [ 1, 1],
     [ 2, 1],
     [ 3, 2]])
423

We will request a kernel PCA for two components using a radial basis function (i.e., kernel = “rbf”):

kernel_pca = KernelPCA(n_components = 2, kernel =“rbf”, gamma = 0.03)

We have requested two components (n_components = 2) as well as the radial basis kernel (kernel = “rbf”). We have also set gamma equal to 0.03, which is the kernel coefficient for the radial basis function (rbf).

final = kernel_pca.fit_transform(X)
print(final)
[[-0.3149893 -0.17944928]
[-0.46965347-0.0475298 ]
[-0.62541667 0.22697909]
[ 0.3149893 -0.17944928]
[ 0.46965347-0.0475298 ]
[ 0.62541667 0.22697909]]

The above are the two components resulting from the kernel PCA. Of course, the result looks very similar to what we might have obtained had we performed a classic PCA (i.e., two columns of eigenvectors), but remember that because it is a kernelized PCA, eigenvectors were computed on transformed “kernelized” data, not the original (and typically centered) data we would ordinarily use for a traditional PCA.

129

The above has produced 70 values from data with a range of 1 through 150. We now specify the kernel PCA, requesting that two features be extracted. We set the kernel equal to the radial basis “Gaussian” kernel (rbfdot) and eta, which is the Hebbian learning rate, equal to 0.01 (the default is 0.005). Sigma (sigma = 0.2) is the inverse kernel width for the radial basis kernel function, which we can set as a flexible parameter. We set the maximum number of iterations equal to 65:

> kpc <- kha(~., data=iris[-test, -5], kernel=“rbfdot”,
+ kpar=list(sigma=0.2), features=2, eta=0.01, maxiter=65)

To print the components, we code:

> pcv(kpc)

The above provides the component vectors (we print only a few rows):

> plot(predict(kpc, iris[,-5]), col=as.integer(iris[, 5]),
xlab = “1st Principal Component”, ylab = “2nd Principal Component”)

We can see from the plot (Figure 11.9) that a classic linear PCA would have likely never captured the complex configuration of the data. However, kernel PCA was able to quite nicely uncover the nonlinear and rather complex dimensionality.

11.7 Principal Curves

Recall that in classic PCA, we fit a hyperplane such that the sum of the squared perpendicular distances is minimized. Principal curves are more general than PCA. As we will see, PCA in fact can be considered a special case of the wider principal curve framework just as we considered it a specialized case of kernel PCA. Instead of providing a line of “best fit” as in PCA, principal curves seeks to find a curved approximation, a curved manifold of dimensionality two or greater. However, as an estimation algorithm principal curves does not result in dimension reduction (Meila & Zhang, 2023, p. 9). More simply, principal curves fits a curve to a swarm of data points, as illustrated in Figure 11.10.

The fit provided by principal curves is nonlinear and nonparametric, meaning that their exact form is suggested or “learned” by the data (Hastie & Stuetzle, 1989). A precise definition of a principal curve was given by Hastie and Stuetzle (1989) who first proposed the method: “an infinitely differentiable finite length curve that passes through the middle of the data.”

A feature of the curve is that it is self-consistent, meaning that every point on the curve is the expected value of the data points projecting onto this point (Ozertem & Erdogmus, 2011). What this means is that if we arbitrarily selected a point on the curve and amassed all the data that project onto this point, the average of all those points would coincide with the point on the curve (Hastie & Stuetzle, 1989, p. 502); hence, “self-consistent.” We can immediately see that if the curve is a straight line and is self-consistent, then the principal curve will be that of a principal component. Algorithms used for principal curves essentially iterate until this convergence of self-consistency is achieved (Hastie & Stuetzle, 1989). Details of the algorithm are given in Hastie and Stuetzle (1989, p. 506).

Note that the definition of a principal curve is different from that of a principal component or even ordinary least-squares line in regression. Both of these latter methods fit a constant straight-line hyperplane to the data regardless of what the data are. There are no “bends” in the curve to follow the data. That is, in PCA and ordinary least-squares (OLS), we are imposing a linear form 426on the data; the data are not telling us what form of polynomial we should fit. In contrast, principal curves provide a rather “smooth” fit to the data; the fitted curve is essentially “guided” by the data.

In classic PCA or OLS regression, we impose a linear form on the data, regardless of whether the data actually follow a linear form or not. In contrast, in principal curves, the form of the curve is suggested or “learned” from the data, and is hence, nonparametric in nature.

Essentially, principal curves find the “middle” of the data in some sense (the “self-consistency” sense) when fitting the curve. Not surprisingly, there are various notions of how “middle” is defined. Global or top-down algorithms begin with an initial line, which is usually the first classic principal component, then through iterations, “bend” this line until some convergence criteria are met. The curve that is fit is a result of successive iterations and is a smooth local average of points, where the definition of “local” is based on the distance in arc length of the projections of the points onto the curve found in the previous iteration (Hastie & Stuetzle, 1989). As summarized by Hastie and Stuetzle (pp. 502–503):

We formally define principal curves to be those smooth curves that are self-consistent for a distribution or data set. This means that if we pick any point on the curve, collect all the data that project onto this point, and average them, then this average coincides with the point on the curve … the algorithm for finding principal curves is equally intuitive. Starting with any smooth curve (usually the largest principal component), it checks if this curve is self-consistent by projecting and averaging. If it is not, the procedure is repeated, using the new curve obtained by averaging as a starting guess. This is iterated until (hopefully) convergence.

Other more local, or bottom-up approaches estimate the curve essentially “step by step” moving through the data cloud (Delicado, 2001). These more local approaches are generally more flexible but have higher variance since small perturbations in the training data can drastically affect the location of the curve. Local principal curves is one technique that models segments of the curve within a certain bandwidth. The concept of principal curves can be extended to that of principal surfaces when working in higher dimensions.

11.7.1 Principal Components as a Special Case of Principal Curves and Surfaces

We can now see how principal components can be conceptualized as a special case of principal curves in which the “curve” in PCA is linear (Sandilya & Kulkarni, 2002). Principal curves are the more general procedure. That is, while principal curves uses the data to fit a curve, principal components in a sense still uses the data to determine the placement of the components, but the curve is always a hyperplane. Indeed, if we extend curves to surfaces, then PCA becomes a special case of principal curves which in turn is a special case of principal surfaces. This is also clear from the fact that the principal curve algorithm begins with fitting a principal component, until it iterates to successfully fit the corresponding curve based on the arrangement of the data (Hastie et al., 2009).

11.7.2 Principal Curves in R

The package princurve (Hastie et al., 1989) can be used to fit a principal curve in R. We adopt an example from the package and produce a plot of the resulting curve:427

> library(princurve)
> x <- runif(100, -1, 1)
> head(x)
[1] -0.81697944 -0.08094903 0.19879631 0.83944382 0.96564815 -0.92439484

The above generates 100 cases of random data from a uniform distribution with limits −1 to 1. We will now transform the data to make it quadratic by including an x^2 term:

> x <- cbind(x, x^2 + rnorm(100, sd = 0.1)
+ )

We now fit the principal curve on x and plot the result along with lines and whiskers characterizing the fit:

> fit <- principal_curve(x)
> plot(fit)
> lines(fit)
> points(fit)
> whiskers(x, fit$s)

The output generates a plot (Figure 11.11) with whiskers (left), where the whiskers correspond to deviations of data points from which the curve was fit. We can also fit a lowess smoother to the data (right), which reveals the actual data points:

> fit_smooth <- principal_curve(x, plot = TRUE, smoother = “lowess”)

11.8 Principal Components Analysis as an Encoder

An encoder is a general term that has many variations and connotations depending on the exact context, but in its most general sense, is some function that translates or transforms data or information into another form, usually, and most generally, into a form with desirable properties. There are two parts to an encoder, the encoding element and the decoding element.428

An autoencoder is a special type of encoder that encodes through some latent path such as a hidden layer in a neural network. If the autoencoder has more than a single hidden layer, it is generally referred to as a deep autoencoder. The key feature of a classic autoencoder is that there are as many inputs as there are outputs (Alpaydin, 2020). An autoencoder in which the new function is required to have a lesser dimension than the inputting function is sometimes referred to as an undercomplete autoencoder (Goodfellow et al., 2016). Autoencoders generally belong to the family of unsupervised techniques.

A classic example of an autoencoder at a conceptual level is that of encoding cell phone data into the cloud, then decoding that data back to the cell phone. The important feature here is that, for the classic autoencoder at least, the data has not really changed dimensionality; it has simply changed forms. Had we constrained the data in the cloud to assume a lesser dimensionality than the original cell phone data, this would have been an example of the aforementioned undercomplete autoencoder.

More formally, the encoder in an autoencoder can be given by


z = Encode(x|W)

where W are the parameters of the encoder and x is the vector being encoded. The decoder is thus given by


x = Decode(z|V)

where V are now the parameters of the decoder and z is the vector being decoded.

Autoencoders can be linear or nonlinear. For example, consider the two images in Figure 11.12, one a linear encoder and one a nonlinear encoder, the only difference being the form of function in the hidden nodes (i.e., linear vs. nonlinear).

11.9 Neural Networks and PCA as Autoencoders

The classic case of an encoder, as featured just above, is that of a neural network where the mappings are no longer linear but instead nonlinear. As we will see when we survey neural networks, there is nothing necessarily and intrinsically nonlinear about a neural network; technically the 429activation function can be linear if chosen as such. However, neural networks typically feature nonlinear activation functions in an effort to capture more complex configurations in the data.

This is where now PCA comes in. An autoencoder with a single fully connected hidden layer combined with a linear activation function and a squared error cost function is closely allied to classical PCA. Essentially, a neural network that is trained to learn the identity function is what an autoencoder actually is since we are not interested in “changing” the data at all, we are simply interested in reconstructing it (Plaut, 2018), such as the example with the phone data being transmitted to the cloud. This sounds very much like PCA! Indeed, it can be shown that the subspace formed by the first few components of a PCA is near equal to the vectors formed from encoding an autoencoder neural network and the reconstruction error from each is approximately the same (Oken, 2017). Autoencoders reconstruct the data as efficiently as possible, and hence PCA can be regarded as a special case of the more general autoencoder idea. Recall however that PCA does not by itself perform dimension reduction. We do, by choosing among the components the first few that explain most of the variance. Essentially, an autoencoder multilayer perceptron with one hidden layer of units (a linear encoder) implements PCA.

Sparse PCA has also been proposed (Zou et al., 2004) which seeks to regularize coefficients in the components model by penalization, such as l1 regularization. As we will briefly discuss in the following chapter, a similar regularization penalty can be adopted in factor analysis as well giving birth to the sparse factor analysis model.

11.10 Multidimensional Scaling

Multidimensional scaling (Kruskal, 1964; Torgerson, 1952, 1958) is a nonparametric technique used for dimensionality reduction with the goal of preserving pairwise distances between observations. It is perhaps the simplest type of manifold learning (Murray, 2022). Recall that the problem of visualizing data in high dimensions is essentially to reduce the dimensionality and visualize resulting projections in those lower dimensions. In this sense, dimension reduction, as it pertains to visualization, is a way of answering the question:

What would this high-dimensional data look like if the points existed in a much lower dimension?

This is the goal of many dimension-reduction techniques, to learn how high-dimensional data “live” or “exist” in lower dimensions. As an example, suppose we consider the distances between cities in miles. We then put these distances into a matrix and perform multidimensional scaling on that matrix. What we will obtain is the coordinate map in two dimensions with the city distances preserved as much as possible.

As summarized by Chatfield and Collins (1980, p. 189):

Multidimensional scaling is the term used to describe any procedure which starts with the “distances” between a set of points (or individuals or objects) or information about these “distances,” and finds a configuration of the points, preferably in a small number of dimensions, usually 2 or 3.

Or, as remarked by Venables and Ripley (2002, p. 306),

The most obvious of the distance methods is multidimensional scaling (MSD) which seeks a configuration in Rd such that distances between the points best match (in a sense to be defined) those of the distance matrix.

Most generally, MDS takes a distance matrix of observed variables and seeks to find a lower-dimensional representation of those distances. It takes a distance matrix of say, ten dimensions, 430and asks the question “Can we represent this ten-dimensional matrix in terms of only a few underlying dimensions, and if so, what are the coordinates that best give rise to the observed distances/dissimilarities?” In this sense, MDS seeks to accomplish a similar (though not exact) goal as PCA and other dimension-reduction techniques. In fact, classical multidimensional scaling with a Euclidean distance metric is equivalent to plotting the first k principal components, without rescaling to correlations (Chatfield & Collins, 1980; Murray, 2022; Venables & Ripley, 2002). A related interpretation of MDS is to uncover underlying dimensions such that the observed distances between points are maintained or “preserved” as closely as possible (Meila & Zhang, 2023; Rencher & Christensen, 2012). Most embedding algorithms do not preserve Euclidean distances, instead resulting in a distorted geometry to at least some extent (Meila & Zhang, 2023, p. 19).

Depending on whether we have a distance matrix already computed, classical MDS can begin with a matrix of raw data, X, or the distance matrix D. Beginning with X, we compute a matrix B, which is the matrix of sums and squares and cross-products,


B = XX′
(11.12)

It stands that the matrix B can be converted into a matrix of distances, D, where we can obtain the squared Euclidean distances between rows of X as a function of the elements of B:


dij2 = bii + bjj − 2bij
(11.13)

These are squared Euclidean distances (Chatfield & Collins, 1980, p. 198), yet in the above formulation, it can be difficult to appreciate what is being computed and it is helpful to recall what a Euclidean distance actually is,


$$\begin{array}{l} {d\left( x,y \right) = \sqrt{\left( x_{1} - y_{1} \right)^{2} + \left( x_{2} - y_{2} \right)^{2} + \cdot \cdot \cdot \left( x_{p} - y_{p} \right)^{2}}} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = \sqrt{\left( x - y \right)'\left( x - y \right)}} \\ \end{array}$$

where d(x,y) is the distance between vectors x and y. It should be emphasized that the distance matrix D does not need to contain Euclidean distances. Many other options are available, which we briefly survey when we discuss cluster analysis later in the book. What is important for D is that the distances featured satisfy basic essential properties of distances dij where i and j correspond to points i and j. These properties include dij ≥ 0, dii = 0, and dij = dji (Chatfield & Collins, 1980). Beyond such essential properties, MDS does not really “care” where D comes from. Though, of course, the scientist should. Distance measures (sometimes called similarity coefficients) can also be obtained for binary data (see Chatfield & Collins, 1980, p. 194 for details).

Given the correspondence between B and D, an eigenanalysis can then be computed on B, which, assuming B is of full rank, will yield as many eigenvalue-eigenvector pairs as there are rows or columns of B. The resulting eigenvectors are new dimensions from which the data can be projected. As in PCA, we can then evaluate the size of respective eigenvalues relative to the sum of eigenvalues to determine the “importance” of the given dimension, where proportions greater than 0.8 are suggestive of an at least reasonable fit (Everitt, 2007, p. 95), however such “cut-off criteria” should not be taken rigidly and like PCA will depend on the nature and context of the problem. To emphasize, the matrix of raw data in X was not actually required had we already had D. That is, MDS only requires a distance matrix, it does not operate directly on the raw data 431(Hastie et al., 2009). Of course, in most cases, raw data is all the investigator has, and hence such will usually be the starting point to computing an MDS, that of computing the matrix D from X. But theoretically, one can perform an MDS having only knowledge of the distance matrix, similar to how one can perform a PCA having only knowledge of the covariance or correlation matrix. How these matrices “arise,” MDS cares little about.

As mentioned, MDS comprises several related techniques and versions. The method surveyed above is generally known as classical scaling. A competing version of MDS, called Kruskal-Shepard scaling, seeks values or points p1, p2, ..., pn that minimize the following so-called stress function:


$$S = {\sum\limits_{i,j}\left( d_{ij} - \middle| \middle| p_{i} - p_{j} \middle| \middle| \right)^{2}}$$
(11.14)

where dij is the distance between two data points i, j in the original data and ||pi−pj|| is the corresponding “distance” i to j between reconstructed or “embedded” data points p based on the dimension reduction. It should be noted these latter distances may not represent actual distances and may not agree with classical properties of distances; in the case of nonmetric MDS (to be discussed shortly), they are only used to help determine the monotonicity of the original distances, dij (Rencher & Christensen, 2012). On the other hand, in a version of metric MDS in which dij represent more than an ordinal ranking, interpreting ||pi−pj|| as the distance between observed and reconstructed points is more acceptable.

An alternative scaled way of defining the stress function is,


$$S = \frac{\sum\limits_{i,j}\left( d_{ij} - D_{ij} \right)^{2}}{\sum\limits_{i,j}d_{ij}^{2}}$$
(11.15)

where dij is once more the distance between two data points i, j in the original data and Dij=||pi−pj|| is once more the distance between the newly constructed, estimated, or “mapped” points (Chatfield & Collins, 1980). The lower the stress, the better the fit. The most ideal situation is for dij = Dij under which case ${\sum\limits_{i,j}\left( d_{ij} - D_{ij} \right)^{2}} = 0$ and thus $S = 0/{\sum\limits_{i,j}d_{ij}^{2}} = 0$. Stress increases as $\sum\limits_{i,j}\left( d_{ij} - D_{ij} \right)^{2}$ increasingly deviates from zero but has limits [0, 1] due to the denominator, $\sum\limits_{i,j}d_{ij}^{2}$ which serves to scale (not standardize) the squared distances. Stress decreases as the number of dimensions increases (Chatfield & Collins, 1980, p. 208).

When the distance is Euclidean, PCA and classical MDS will coincide. This is because S, the sample covariance matrix of PCA is proportional to B = XX′. This can be seen by inputting B into the eigenvalue-eigenvector characteristic equation and observing these two equalities,


      Bai = λiai

where ai are eigenvectors and λi corresponding eigenvalues. We see that the eigenvalues will be the same and eigenvectors will also be subject to a linear transformation (Chatfield & Collins, 1980, p. 200). As noted by Jolliffe (2002), PCA operates on a matrix of similarities between variables, whereas principal coordinate analysis (i.e., classical MDS) operates on a matrix of similarities between observations (i.e., individuals). However, both can lead to the same results.

Consult Chatfield and Collins (1980, p. 201) for a fruitful discussion of how PCA and MDS relate to one another and why these authors recommend that PCA, not MDS, be performed if 432distances are Euclidean. Jolliffe (2002, p. 90) seconds this recommendation, except notes that when the number of cases is less than the number of variables (i.e., n < p), even though both MDS and PCA will yield results, MDS will have computational advantages over PCA.

Multidimensional scaling is equivalent to classical principal components analysis when Euclidean distance is used as a metric on the non-standardized correlation matrix, that is, the covariance matrix. When non-Euclidean distances are used, the equivalency no longer necessarily holds.

The classical form of MDS is called principal coordinate analysis, which is usually a metric version of scaling (see below for a discussion of metric vs. nonmetric approaches).

11.10.1 Merits of MDS

When compared with other dimension-reduction techniques (e.g., classical PCA), metric multidimensional scaling carries with it many advantages. For one, it is not restricted to linear projections of the data and hence can handle nonlinear problems. Second, it can be applied to any metric space, not only Euclidean (Demaine et al., 2021). Distances can also be arrived at subjectively, for instance, subjects stating their preferences for a given product as an estimate (Rencher & Christensen, 2012). This choice will depend on the preferred metric, which we discuss shortly. The issue of what the proximity matrix contains is a substantive one; to reiterate, MDS itself, or any other statistical procedure does not care where the numbers came from, which is why measurement, not analysis, should be the primary concern of any investigation. Poorly measured attributes are not usually worth analyzing, either statistically or any other way.

A last point worth mentioning regarding the merits of MDS is that it emphasizes, and thus attempts to minimize, squared differences. While this may be ideal in some contexts, it may be less so in others. In some contexts, smaller distances may actually matter more than larger ones. Sammon mapping is one technique that puts greater emphasis on preserving smaller distances and hence attempts to capture more of the local structure of the manifold than does classical MDS. The stress function for salmon mapping can be given as follows,


$$S = \frac{1}{\sum\limits_{i < j}d_{ij}}{\sum\limits_{i < j}\frac{\left( d_{ij} - D_{ij} \right)^{2}}{d_{ij}}}$$
(11.16)

A comparison of the above stress function to that of MDS reveals that distances (dij−Dij)2 are divided by dij to provide a sense of “relativity” to the squared distances. That is, if (dij−Dij)2 is found to be large, the stress function for Sammon mapping recognizes that this may in part be due to the squaring of the distance, and so relates it to dij, which is not squared. It is in this sense that Sammon mapping puts more emphasis on smaller distances than MDS. This also has the potential for Sammon mapping to be able to generate a nonlinear map (Alpaydin, 2020). The constant $\frac{1}{\sum\limits_{i < j}d_{ij}}$ is simply to ease the computation of the gradient (van der Maaten & Hinton, 2008, p. 2597).

The fact that Sammon mapping focuses more on smaller distances still does not prevent one or two distances from dominating the cost function. As we will soon see, t-SNE attempts to 433remedy this by not focusing so much on these raw magnitudes of separation in the data (van der Maaten & Hinton, 2008, p. 2597) and instead more closely modeling them as having equal local to global importance.

The package ProjectionBasedClustering (Thrun et al., 2024) can perform Sammon mapping:

> library(ProjectionBasedClustering)
> data(‘Hepta’)
> Data=Hepta$Data
> Proj = SammonsMapping(Data)
Initial stress : 0.07779
stress after 10 iters: 0.05981, magic = 0.092
stress after 20 iters: 0.04725, magic = 0.213
stress after 30 iters: 0.04026, magic = 0.491
stress after 40 iters: 0.03924, magic = 0.500
stress after 50 iters: 0.03923, magic = 0.500

We can see the stress numbers decrease as a function of iterations. After 50 iterations, the stress is equal to 0.03923. The magic number (i.e., magic = 0.500) is the initial value of the step size constant in diagonal Newton’s method and need not concern us. We can obtain a projection of the points as follows (Figure 11.13):

> PlotProjectedPoints(Proj$ProjectedPoints, Hepta$Cls)
434

The package Rdimtools (You & Shung, 2022) performs Sammon mapping via the function do.sammon().

11.10.2 Metric vs. Nonmetric (Ordinal) Scaling

If we have actual distances available, that is, distances that are numerical or computational, this is generally referred to as metric multidimensional scaling, also generally known as classical scaling or principal coordinate analysis (Rencher & Christensen, 2012). If, on the other hand, the distances are arrived at via human judgment or other procedure such that all we can really know is how distances are ranked (i.e., we do not actually have the real numerical distances), this is generally referred to as nonmetric or ordinal multidimensional scaling (Chatfield & Collins, 1980, p. 190). In metric MDS, we attempt to dimension reduce based on actual numerical distances. In nonmetric MDS, we dimension reduce based on rankings or other more inexact distance derivation. Most commonly, for nonmetric, distances are often converted to ranks somehow, or in some applications, only the ranks exist in the first place without any access to more precise numerical measurements (Murray, 2022).

11.10.3 Weakness of MDS: “Closeness” Can Be Arbitrary

There is a limitation to multidimensional scaling, in that just because it considers two points to be “close” in some sense, this comes with the assumption that they are close on a relatively simple manifold. If the true manifold happens to be more complex, for instance a curved manifold, then the actual distance along the manifold might be much larger. Hence, one can perform MDS on data and obtain results, but those results are only as good as the assumption of the nature of the underlying manifold. MDS also may be limiting as a result of its objective function being nonconvex (Demaine et al., 2021). Recall what this implies. Optimization of a nonconvex function can result in there being multiple solutions in the form of minima instead of settling on a global minimum.

One technique that seeks to improve on MDS is that of Isomap. Isomap uses geodesic distances instead of Euclidean and thus is able to usually uncover manifolds that are more complex geometrically than what MDS is able to capture. In fact, this is true of most of the more advanced manifold learning algorithms. They all share a common goal in that they seek to uncover a more sophisticated manifold than is possible with simpler techniques such as classical PCA or MDS. This is precisely why these more advanced procedures, as we will soon see, are so attractive.

MDS also suffers from not having an explicit projection function (Yin, 2008). That is, if one adds even a single data point to the dataset, one must recompute the entire MDS algorithm.

Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) typically assumes distances on the manifold are Euclidean, whereas more complex methods of dimension-reduction such as Isomap feature the use of non-Euclidean distances such as geodesic distances, which are not necessarily Euclidean. Allowing for greater complexity in how distances are defined is what makes more advanced methods of dimension reduction so attractive and popular.

11.10.4 Standardization of Distances

Distances in MDS are often standardized so that each variable has a mean of zero and standard deviation of one. However, even with standardization, such does not by itself take into account 435the correlation between objects (Chatfield & Collins, 1980). To take correlations into account, one could instead compute


D2 = (xi−xj)′S − 1(xi−xj)
(11.17)

which is a standardized version of Euclidean distance, typically called squared Mahalanobis distances (1936). Other measures of dissimilarity also exist (see Chatfield & Collins, 1980, p. 193). What is more, there is no “best” measure of similarity or dissimilarity. Instead, a researcher should choose one which seems most appropriate for his (or her) particular problem. There is also nothing at all wrong in trying out different distance measures in an exploratory sense to see how they compare in the final solution. Especially with the speed and ease of computing power, this should be easy to do. As usual when it comes to statistics, what you find in your data is often a function of what tools you use to do the searching. MDS is no different in this regard.

We demonstrate MDS in Python on the make_blobs data set, where we extract two dimensions:

X, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=100, n_features=3, centers=2, random_state=42)

We note now that all distances are positive numbers and can proceed to fit MDS:

> fit <- mds(valsD)
> fit
Call:
mds(delta = valsD)
Model: Symmetric SMACOF
Number of objects: 10
Stress-1 value: 0.195
Number of iterations: 17
> plot(fit)

The above plotting function is enough to produce the configuration of psychological variables along both dimensions in Figure 11.15 (Can you possibly name the dimensions on which the configuration was constructed?):439

> circle <- fitCircle(fit$conf[, 1], fit$conf[, 2])
> draw.circle(circle$cx, circle$cy, radius = circle$radius, border = “gray”)

A further option is to use the fitCircle() function, which fits a circle into a two-dimensional point configuration (Figure 11.16). Using this option will not change the plot at all, it will only draw a circle on the existing plot (left):

To the right of the dimension plot in Figure 11.16 is a Shepard diagram, obtained by

> plot(fit, plot.type = “Shepard”)

The Shepard diagram relates the distances obtained by the MDS dimension reduction (on the y-axis, the configured distances) to the distances observed in the empirical data. The extent to which the slope is positive with minimal scatter is the extent to which configured or “reconstructed” distances relate well to the original empirical distances, which is the ideal. Many additional plots are available in the package. The ProjectionBasedClustering package can also be used to fit MDS.

The MASS package (Venables & Ripley, 2002) can also perform multidimensional scaling on categorical data. The daisy() function in the cluster package can produce dissimilarity matrices for both continuous and categorical data (Maechler et al., 2023).

11.11 Self-Organizing Maps

Multidimensional scaling can be slow because it must incorporate all distances between variables into its final computation (Venables & Ripley, 2002). An alternative to MDS, for large-scale problems especially, is the self-organizing map (Kohonen, 1990, 1995), which instead of using the entire matrix of distances, focuses on a rectangular or hexagonal two-dimensional lattice of 440representative points. SOM can also be considered from the vantage point of cluster analysis, it being a special “constrained” case of k-means clustering where data are “encouraged” to lie in a one or two-manifold feature space (Hastie et al., 2009). While most of the work on SOMs occurred in the 1990s and beyond, the initial principle for SOM first appeared in the early 1980s (Kohonen, 1990).

There are several versions of algorithms for SOM. A simple version of the SOM algorithm operates similar to k-means clustering, in that given an observation from the data, xi, the closest data point mj is selected. Then, a neighbor of mj, called the neighbor mk, is moved toward xi via the following update rule (Hastie et al., 2009, p. 528; Kohonen, 1990, p. 1467),


mk←mk+α(xi−mk)
(11.18)

where α is the learning rate and where 0 < α < 1. The updating is run for each input vector and the process should be run at least 500 times the number of nodes (Izenman, 2008). The updating function can be more complex than a simple weight (Kohonen, 1990). For example, instead of simply a weight α, one can specify a function of the weight,


mk←mk+αhk(xi−mk)
(11.19)

where hk now can be a function such as a kernel (e.g., a Gaussian kernel).

The algorithm is detailed in Yin (2008, p. 725). Self-organizing maps can also be generally considered in the family of neural network algorithms (Oliveira & Levkowitz, 2003) and can be integrated with other visualization techniques. The very idea of naming the method self-organizing arose from biology and sets of neurons essentially competing with one another, which is why often self-organizing maps are discussed under the machine learning topic of competitive learning. We quote Kohonen (1990, p. 1464):

It [self-organizing map] is a sheet-like artificial neural network, the cells of which become specifically tuned to various input signal patterns or classes of patterns through an unsupervised learning process.

Hence, in mimicking biological neuronal processes (or at minimum, hypotheses about such processes), self-organizing maps start with cells that “organize themselves” via updating themselves during training, a version of Hebbian learning (Yin, 2008). Such training concludes with the approximation of a smooth manifold (Bishop, 2006). Since there is no objective function to optimize, initial parameter estimates are crucial, perhaps “too important” since they could, in the end, essentially determine whether structure exists in the ensuing map (Bishop, 2006). The SOM algorithm can also be applied in a variety of contexts and customized to such applications. For example, various similarity measures can be adopted that suit the task at hand. That is, it need not be a distance function of the kind xi − mk discussed earlier, but instead can be an inner product (Yin, 2008, p. 726). SOMs have also been extended to incorporate mixture distributions. Work has also been done on kernelized versions of SOMs.

Self-organizing maps can be fit in Python using sklearn’s SOM and in R using the package aweSOM (Boelaert et al., 2022).441

11.12 Manifold Learning

Principal components analysis assumes the data lay in a linear subspace. Sometimes however, perhaps actually most often, the data are best represented by a nonlinear subspace, such as in Figure 11.17, which is the classic “S-curve” shaped manifold.

In Figure 11.17, what is generally referred to as a manifold, sometimes called a topological manifold, since it satisfies certain topological conditions, such as being able to define continuous functions on that manifold. A manifold, first and foremost, is a topological space. A topological space is, roughly, a geometrical space where, for our purposes, measuring distances between points may prove challenging. A manifold is a topological space that is further locally Euclidean (Murray, 2022), which essentially generalizes the concept of a generalized surface in space. “Euclidean” here implies a differentiable mapping (Hubbard & Hubbard, 2002). By “locally Euclidean” we mean simply that at each point the space appears or resembles to be Euclidean, or, more crudely, flat. The space or neighborhood around each point should also consist of an open set, where by open set we may consider to be a higher-space generalization of an open interval on the one-dimensional real line in mathematics (Meila & Zhang, 2023).

A classic and practical example of such a manifold is the earth, a curved two-dimensional surface, but everywhere on the earth it appears locally flat (Murray, 2022). The local two-dimensional space is sometimes referred to as the tangent space. Hence, when you walk down the street on what appears to be a relatively flat surface on the earth, you are exploring the tangent space of a locally sectioned part of the earth. The earth is round, but the tangent you are on appears flat. Indeed, a two-dimensional map of a country is not a perfect representation since the actual surface is not actually flat but instead spherical. ℜn is a manifold since everywhere you look you can be in ℜn space. Any finite-dimensional vector space can be regarded as a manifold as well.

A one-dimensional manifold is a smooth curve, for example that of a wire or garden hose (Hubbard & Hubbard, 2002). An ordinary line is a special case of a curve and thus a one-dimensional manifold as well. A smooth manifold is generally one that is many times differentiable or even infinitely differentiable in some cases. The absolute value function f(x)=|x| is an example 442of a simple manifold (curve) that is not smooth, as it is not differentiable at zero. The existence of a manifold is also independent of coordinates and can be easily translated.

Manifold learning and topology are largely about how to calculate on local areas of these more complex generalized surfaces. Differentiable manifolds are preferred as they allow one to perform calculus operations on the manifold. Topology essentially generalizes concepts of metric spaces (which are used to specify a distance function on that space) to the concept of neighboring points without having to specify a distance function explicitly.

The image in Figure 11.18 gives a clear picture of what manifold learning is about, that of taking a high-dimensional space and reducing it down to say, a two-dimensional scatterplot.

The hope of manifold learning is that the right-most plot contains pretty much the same information, in some sense, as the left plot, or that only a minimal amount of information is “lost” in the transformation (i.e., the dimension reduction). Another way of saying this is that in the dimension reduction, the essential elements of the geometry are preserved. Of course, we can immediately deduce that classical principal components analysis, for example, is a special case of manifold learning, since a high-dimensional space is reduced to a lower-dimensional topological space via linear transformation. The previously discussed multidimensional scaling, Sammon mapping, and self-organizing maps also can be included under the more general theme of manifold learning.

11.12.1 Manifold Hypothesis

The manifold hypothesis holds that even though data may appear in higher dimensions, it is possible to place it in a lower-dimensional manifold (Murray, 2022). That is, the learning of a manifold is an attempt to take high-dimensional multivariate data and reduce it down to a lower dimensionality. One can think of a manifold as being an embedding from a higher- to lower-dimensional Rn space. Most embedding algorithms have the priority of identifying the set of eigenvectors associated with the most important (largest) eigenvalues. These methods are often referred to as spectral embedding methods (Izenman, 2008), however some reserve the classification of an embedding as distinct from other methods that necessarily preserve geometric and topological data properties.

Manifold learning is generally equated with nonlinear dimensionality reduction since in most cases the actual true manifold underlying the data will be nonlinear and the linear hypothesis is merely a special case of the more general nonlinear framework. It is not an exaggeration to say that most linear manifold methods seek out global structure whereas most nonlinear manifold methods seek out more local nonlinear structure. This parallels the idea of a line capturing global behavior of a scatterplot whereas a curve (or spline, for example) would capture potential nonlinear and more local behavior.

Lee and Verleysen (2005, p. 30) describe the goal of nonlinear dimension reduction:443

The standard task in nonlinear dimensionality reduction consists of taking a set of data points sampled from a smooth, low-dimensional submanifold of a high-dimensional Euclidean space and to re-embed those points in a low-dimensional Euclidean space while preserving the local structure of the submanifold. The purpose is to find useful new coordinates for the data.

Of course, very little of the data the scientist will encounter will lie exactly on a linear or nonlinear manifold and hence approximation of the manifold will be a key concept in all of this.

11.12.2 Example of a Simple Manifold

It should be emphasized that while manifold learning generally refers to higher-dimensional spaces, manifolds themselves can be extremely simple in lower dimensions. For example, the following simple function, simple as it is, is nonetheless a manifold:


f(x) = (x/10)3

The above will generate a one-dimensional plot (curve in this case) that is nonlinear (try plotting it). What dimension-reduction techniques will do is find a lower-dimensional representation. For example, we saw that PCA found the major axes underlying the variables in a very global fashion (i.e., based on the entire data). As we will see, Isomap will accomplish something similar, but will also preserve linearity locally, not only globally as is the case with PCA. That is, Isomap finds a nonlinear manifold but not directly through a global function as in PCA, but instead through connecting smaller local linear functions. Locally linear embedding does something similar to Isomap but goes about the task by finding weights that perform local interpolations between data points that closely approximate the data. We survey these approaches shortly.

11.12.3 Nonparametric Manifolds

When we perform dimension reduction of any kind, we can be said to be trying to find the intrinsic “true” dimensionality that underlays the data. Nonparametric manifolds are generally those that learn a low-dimensional embedding often at each point in the training data, but in general do not learn a mapping function that can be applied universally to out-of-sample data. That is, they typically do not impose an overall functional form, but instead focus heavily on what the current data have to say. Recall this has been one of our definitions of nonparametric, such that they utilize the current data maximally and do not, in general, impose implicit parametric forms on the data that come laden with prior assumptions.

A nonparametric manifold learns a low-dimensional embedding often at each point in the training data but in general does not learn a concise and universal mapping function that can be applied to out-of-sample data. That is, nonparametric manifolds are, generally, “built” around the training data.

11.12.4 Geodesic Distances

The shortest distance between any two points on a manifold is called the geodesic distance. Key to a geodesic distance is that it is the shortest distance or “path” connecting two points on a surface. 444If that surface happens to be on a plane, then the geodesics of the plane are straight lines (Tanton, 2005). If the surface happens to be more complex, then the geodesic will likewise be more complex and may not even be unique (e.g., for a sphere the distance between poles is not unique). The use of geodesics assumes there are no gaps in the manifold on which they are measured, and also assumes the data do not lay outside of the data manifold (Ozertem & Erdogmus, 2011). Geodesics often have no closed-form formula such as Euclidean distances and hence are usually difficult to calculate, requiring numerical methods. In R, geodist (Padgham & Sumner, 2024) can compute such distances.

11.13 Locally Linear Embedding

Local linear embedding (LLE) recovers global structure by using linear “patches” in the wider structure. Each “patch” of the manifold is approximately linear. That is, LLE does what many other local methods do, whether in dimension-reduction or even nonparametric regression, and that is to “zoom in” on narrow slices or patches where things can be regarded as linear because the slice or patch is so small (think of a magnifying glass “zooming in”). As the slices become larger, the local linearity concept begins to vanish and so the slices cannot be too large. LLE uses this local linearity idea to essentially find a weight-based representation of each point of the manifold using its neighbors so that there are locally linear “neighborhoods” in the manifold. As the name suggests, the “embedding” is locally linear, even if the global manifold is not (i.e., the global manifold is typically highly nonlinear). The hope, however, is to capture the nonlinearity through smaller linear areas (i.e., patches) of the manifold.

Recall at the outset that one overarching theme we gave for statistical learning methods; they either impose a global structure onto data, or, they focus in more locally to observe segments of the data. Hastie et al. (2009) brilliantly introduce the whole edifice of statistical learning emphasizing this one key distinction. Nearest-neighbor methods essentially use local information in accounting for the data. These are generally nonparametric techniques because they heavily use the data that surrounds the given observation and rely exclusively on training data. This is in contrast to more global parametric methods that impose parametric structure on the data, such as linear or polynomial regression models. These methods are less concerned about the training data and are more interested in generalizing to future observations. The local parameterization of LLE is such that one can “embed” a new set of points in a lower-dimensional manifold. Such preserves, to the extent that is possible, the same relative positioning information (Ihler, 2003) via a nearest-neighbor approach.

More specifically, locally linear embedding hypothesizes that the best linear approximation around a given data point xi can be found by predicting the data point xi as a linear combination of its k-nearest neighbors using reconstruction weights. The weight vector is found by minimizing the following cost function,


$$\hat{W} = \min_{W}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}\left| \middle| x_{i} - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{N}\left. w_{ij}x_{j} \middle| \right|^{2}} \right.}$$
(11.20)

where the sum of weights wij equals 1, and where wij denotes the “contribution” of xj to the eventual reconstruction (to be discussed shortly). We must choose a suitable neighborhood of points from xi when computing $\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{N}{w_{ij}x_{j}}$. That is, $\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{N}{w_{ij}x_{j}}$essentially constitutes the neighborhood of the focal point, xi. We wish to weight the neighbors via wij such that Ŵ is minimized. 445If the neighborhood is too large we lose the local linearity of local embedding. The neighborhood can be chosen by criteria such as k-nearest neighbors or by imposing a sphere around xi with a minimal radius ε (Ihler, 2003). The possibility also exists to use different values for ε for different segments of the input space to help assure that ε is never too large to significantly weaken the embedding (Alpaydin, 2020; Saul & Roweis, 2003). Standard algorithms for k-nearest neighbors can be used as a more efficient method for determining neighbors. A randomized approximate nearest-neighbor algorithm can also be used (Jones et al., 2011).

A weight is also set to 0 if the neighboring point is the actual point we are building a neighborhood around, hence, this necessitates the idea of considering only points that are truly “neighbors” instead of the actual focal point (Roweis & Saul, 2000). The corresponding weights in Ŵ are then used in reconstructing values of Y, which correspond to the lower-dimensional representation.

How many dimensions should Y consist of? The lower dimension projected points are obtained by minimizing a similar function as we did for the original higher-dimensional scores xi, only that now, the minimization is relative to yi instead of xi,


$$z = {\sum\limits_{i}\left| \middle| y_{i} - {\sum\limits_{j}\left. W_{ij}y_{j} \middle| \right|^{2}} \right.}$$
(11.21)

such that ${\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{y_{i}y_{i}^{T}}} = I$ and also that $\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{y_{i} = 0}$. The first condition guarantees that points will be uncorrelated, whereas the second condition centers the output on the origin. Together, both conditions impose a unit covariance matrix for z which now contains the new coordinates as a function of the weights in W. That is, E(z) = 0 and Cov(z) = I (Alpaydin, 2020). The function for z is then minimized via an eigen analysis on


E = (I−W)T(I−W)
(11.22)

thus obtaining d eigenvalue-eigenvector pairs that correspond to the new embedded dimensionality of the original data (Belkin & Niyogi, 2003), keeping the eigenvectors that correspond to the lowest (nonzero) eigenvalues. Such will yield a set of orthogonal coordinates (Roweis & Saul, 2000) corresponding to the d-dimensions chosen for the eigen analysis, where d is a free parameter set by the user. In essence then, LLE first establishes points as a function of some arbitrarily chosen definition of nearest neighbors, then reconstructs new points in lower dimensions, given the constraint that such “new” points are reconstructed subject to the aforementioned concept and definition of neighborhoods. In this sense, the reconstruction implements the concept of “linear patches” in reconstructing points in lower dimensions.

An advantage of LLE is that it is unlikely to get “stuck” in local minima as the optimization is convex. A disadvantage is that it does not learn a new mapping such that we can predict new values for z for new inputs (Alpaydin, 2020). Note that LLE also makes no attempt to measure geodesic distances. This will prove to be a significant difference when we compare it to procedures that do, such as Isomap.

11.13.1 LLE in Python

We consider an example of LLE in Python. We will see how the original data can be transformed into an embedding computed via local linear embedding. First, we load the relevant libraries:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import make_swiss_roll
from sklearn.manifold import LocallyLinearEmbedding
446

Next, we generate some data, specifying the number of neighbors for this problem equal to 10:

n_samples = 1000
n_neighbors=10

We now construct the data which will represent the classic “swiss roll”:

X, _= make_swiss_roll(n_samples=n_samples)
X, _

array([[ 7.80833394, 0.48066359, 11.03910558],
      [ 1.59837552, 2.65730412, 7.47431048],
[-8.91500526, 3.57885813, 2.20113125],
      ...,
      [11.34728421, 11.47912824, -4.45900994],
      [ 4.7570084 , 13.86156279, 5.30120852],
      [ 2.33270015, 5.81407082, 7.16947349]])

Our goal is to reduce the dimensionality of the swill roll manifold into a two-dimensional structure. Now we perform the LLE and plot the result for two components (n_components=2):

lle = LocallyLinearEmbedding(n_neighbors=n_neighbors, n_components=2)
X_reduced = lle.fit_transform(X, _)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.scatter(X_reduced[:, 0], X_reduced[:, 1], cmap=‘viridis’)
Out[54]: <matplotlib.collections.PathCollection at 0x18fd4114b10>
447

We can see from Figure 11.19 that the reduced data, that is, the locally linear transformed data, captures an embedding in the original data that is much more interesting had we simply performed something like classic “linear” PCA. Classical PCA would have never “uncovered” such an interesting nonlinear embedding.

Locally linear embedding in R can be performed using the package Rdimtools (You & Shung, 2022).

11.14 Isomap

Recall that classical multidimensional scaling (MDS) attempts to output coordinates (i.e., the principal coordinates) that seek to preserve pairwise distances. If the true manifold is complex, then classical MDS using Euclidean distances may not recover it. What Isomap (isometric feature mapping) does is use the geodesic distance (not Euclidean distance as is usually used in classical MDS), which, recall, is essentially “the shortest curve length which respects the geometry of the data” (Ihler, 2003). Isomap seeks to preserve this geodesic distance when reducing the dimensionality. That is, if two points are distant in higher dimensions, we would like to preserve that distance in lower dimensions, and vice versa. The distance xi − xj is sought to be preserved when transformed to a geodesic distance. According to its innovators, “ours [Isomap] efficiently computes a globally optimal solution, and, for an important class of data manifolds, is guaranteed to converge asymptotically to the true structure” (Tenenbaum et al., 2000, p. 2319). The convergence is justified by a theorem that holds that as n→∞ distances on a manifold (so-called graph distances), increasingly provide better and better approximation to true geodesic distances (Tenenbaum et al., 2000). This result is assured because the approximation can be achieved by much shorter Euclidean distance “hops.”

Since by definition a manifold is a structure that is locally Euclidean, meaning once more that at any area on the structure it is flat (again, think of the earth as an example), it stands that the k-nearest neighbors in the original high-dimensional space should, ideally, also be the k-nearest neighbors on the manifold. Hence, the first step in Isomap is determining which points are neighbors based on the familiar notion of distance, di = xi − xj. What constitutes a “neighbor” can be determined by a flexible radius ε parameter. Not surprisingly, for points that are very close, Euclidean distances approximate geodesic distances quite well, however this is not the case for points that are increasingly further apart. Selection of a suitable neighborhood size is a crucial input to conducting Isomap.

Next, geodesic distances are estimated between all pairs of points i, j. The more dense the sampling of points, the better estimates one will obtain. Dijkstra’s algorithm (Dijkstra, 1959) or competing algorithm can be used to estimate the shortest paths, which are approximated by the sum of local distances. Lastly, classical MDS is then computed on the geodesic distances. Essentially then, Isomap performs a multidimensional scaling (eigen analysis) on the high-dimensional data, but instead of using Euclidean distances as classical MDS, it performs the MDS on geodesic distances. Using geodesic distances carries the benefit of capturing nonlinear and complex dimensions that could otherwise not be “tapped” using Euclidean distances.

The cost function that is minimized in Isomap is given by


E=||τ(DG)−τ(DY)||L2
(11.23)

where DG is a matrix of geodesic distances, DY is a matrix of Euclidean distances resulting from the embedding and preserving the manifold’s essential geometry, and τ is an operator that 448converts distances into inner products. See Tenenbaum et al. (2000, p. 2322) for the precise details regarding the computation of τ.

We can see then how Isomap is related to MDS. But what about LLE? Where does LLE fit into all this? While LLE and Isomap are similar, LLE makes no effort to estimate the true geodesic distances, whereas Isomap does. LLE instead attempts only to measure local linear “patches.” Furthermore, Isomap makes additional assumptions over LLE, such as the data being located in a convex region of ℝq and that the data was originally embedded in ℝp by some isometric transformation, both assumptions which may not hold for any particular data set. The assumption of convexity, however, has been challenged recently (see Trosset & Buyukbas, 2020 for details).

For all of its strengths, the problem with Isomap is that it first relies on finding “neighboring” distances on the manifold, which could be faulty. In seeking out the nearest neighbors, if k is too small, then the graph may not even be connected. If k is too large, then the graph may be too dense giving us wrong distances on the manifold. That is, finding the “right” k, if it exists at all, is quite hard. Stochastic Neighborhood Embedding (SNE), as we will soon see, attempts to address and solve some of these problems. Another issue with Isomap, as was true of MDS as well, is that neither approach learns a general mapping function that can be applied to new points. Hence, if a new data point is added to the original data point, the entire algorithm needs to generally be repeated to incorporate that point (Alpaydin, 2020).

A key difference between local linear embedding and Isomap is that LLE makes no effort to estimate the true geodesic distances, whereas Isomap does.

11.14.1 Isomap in Python

The following is an example of Isomap in Python. We first import the relevant libraries:

from sklearn.datasets import make_s_curve
from sklearn.manifold import Isomap
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Next, we generate the S-curve data:

X, color = make_s_curve(n_samples=1000, random_state=42)
X
