13.10 Chapter Review Exercises

  1. 1. Distinguish between exploratory vs. confirmatory factor analysis. How are they similar? Different?
  2. 2. Explore the idea of causality through online searches. Why is causality so difficult to define precisely and poses so many philosophical challenges to philosophers of science?
  3. 3. Distinguish between observable vs. unobservable variables. If you were to classify all variables of one type, which would it be?
  4. 4. Is it possible for a system of variables to have no endogenous variables? Why or why not?
  5. 5. How is the confirmatory factor analysis model a special case of the wider structural equation model?
  6. 6. What is the null hypothesis for a structural equation model? What constitutes a rejection of the null? How is this similar or different from traditional null hypothesis significance testing?
  7. 7. What is the influence of q in the root mean square residual? As q increases or decreases, does this have any effect on the value of RMR?
  8. 8. Compare the Tucker-Lewis index to that of Bollen’s ρ1. Which would you consider to be a better measure of model fit? Why?
  9. 9. Compare the nonlinear structural equation model to that of the semiparametric structural equation model. How are they similar? Different?
  10. 10. Building on the example in the chapter, run the same SEM model but where Z is indicated by only z1 and z2. How do your results compare to the results in the chapter? Discuss.

498

14 Cluster Analysis and Data Segmentation

DOI: 10.4324/9781003376941-17

Cluster analysis, also known as data segmentation, is a general name for a variety of methods and analyses designed to discover, in some sense, groups of cases that, again, in some sense, “go together.” Perhaps the most significant challenge to cluster analysis is in defining what exactly is a cluster. Indeed, unpacking the phrase “in some sense” is very much the goal of this chapter. As noted by Izenman (2008), determining the exact nature of a cluster “is a difficult question to answer mainly because there is no universally accepted definition of exactly what constitutes a cluster. As a result, the various clustering methods usually do not produce identical or even similar solutions” (p. 408). Hence, as we will see, there is no universal single cluster solution when it comes to cluster analysis. Rather, there are a variety of algorithms that will potentially generate disparate results depending on the algorithm used in performing the clustering and the data on which that algorithm is interacting.

A good clustering algorithm, in general, should intuitively be one for which pairwise distances between cases are smaller for cases within the same cluster than for cases between clusters. More formally, cluster analysis attempts to discover multiple convex regions (i.e., convex meaning circular or sphere-like) of the variable space that essentially contain modes of the probability distribution of that variable space (Hastie et al., 2009). One can also seek to “cluster the clusters” such that the clusters that are most alike are classified into a larger “super cluster.” At first glance, the establishment of clusters may seem to resemble very much techniques such as PCA. However, in PCA the number of generated dimensions could never be more than the number of original dimensions (i.e., variables) subjected to the PCA. And while in cluster analysis one cannot typically generate more clusters than there are cases, the dimensionality of the new “clustered” space can actually be more numerous than in the original variables (Alpaydin, 2020, p. 178).

14.1 Cluster Paradigms and Classifications

There are a variety of cluster classification paradigms that attempt to literally “cluster” the types of clustering algorithms. One rudimentary distinction often made is that between top-down vs. bottom-up approaches. In the top-down approach, one might designate the number of clusters one wishes to “extract” from the data or allow an algorithm to find smaller clusters from a much larger initial one. In the bottom-up approach, the algorithm begins with individual cases and builds up clusters by fusing case memberships, usually in a hierarchical manner. As we will see, the classic k-means clustering algorithm is one such example of a top-down approach (Hastie et al., 2009, p. 503) while agglomerative clustering is an example of a bottom-up method to clustering.

Following Hastie et al. (2009), we can also more generally classify clustering algorithms into one of the following three types:499

Combinatorial algorithms. These are applied directly to the data without reference to an underlying probability model. These are sometimes known as hard clustering algorithms, because cases are deterministically allocated to cluster membership. That is, there is no probability associated with a case being allocated to a given cluster, or, if we prefer to be all-probability-inclusive about it, cases are allocated with probability equal to 1.0; that is, the case either belongs in the cluster or it does not. This is what we generally mean by hard clustering. Combinatorial algorithms can also be interpreted as encoders in which the encoder is the kth cluster in an analysis, to which any given observation in the data is assigned (Hastie et al., 2009).

Mixture modeling assumes an underlying probability model and is thus part of the family of probability-based clustering. Mixture models have a similar goal as combinatorial algorithms but use association rules to construct simple descriptions (also known as conjunctive rules) that describe regions of high density. Mixture modeling is an example of soft clustering, where a case is not deterministically guaranteed to belong to a given cluster. Rather, it belongs to a given cluster with an associated probability. Mixture models are especially useful when working with binary data. More specifically, in mixture models we assume observed data arose or was originated from a mixture of distributions, that is, the data were “generated” based on those distributions. For this reason, not surprisingly, mixture models are often regarded as generative. The choice of distribution is often Gaussian, but is essentially variable, and allows the user to incorporate prior knowledge of the cluster distributions. In this sense, a prior probability idea is utilized in clustering. In such probabilistic mixture models, as opposed to non-probabilistic models, the log-likelihood can be used as a metric to determine the success of clustering (Murray, 2022), though this approach will not necessarily be effective in entirely evaluating the clustering that is discovered by the model.

Mode seekers or “bump hunters” are nonparametric approaches to clustering and seek to estimate distinct modes of a probability density function. Classification of cases to respective clusters is made by assignment of cases to the cluster for which the observation is the closest. Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) is a popular method of density-based clustering, one which we will survey in this chapter.

The above are not the sole categorizations possible for clustering algorithms. For instance, Xu and Tian (2015) provide nine different categories by which clustering algorithms can be differentiated and distinguished. For instance, traditional k-means and k-medoids are generally referred to as algorithms based on partition due to their way of segregating data. This is in contrast to algorithms such as DBSCAN which is in its own clustering category of those based on densities (i.e., the category of density-based clustering algorithms). For our purposes in this chapter, we stop short of classifying algorithms too finely and are generally content with the above aforementioned classification.

This chapter features a survey and discussion of the more popular methods of clustering, which include k-means, hierarchical clustering, density-based clustering (DBSCAN), and cluster mixture models.

14.2 Are Clusters Meaningful?

Cluster analysis, whatever the algorithm, will typically always “find” clusters since they are designed to do just that. However, whether those clusters are meaningful in any sense other than mathematically is often left to the user to ultimately determine. Unlike supervised methods that typically feature a loss function to quantify the extent to which predictions are in error, unsupervised methods, of which cluster analysis is one, do not generally feature such “hard” measures to assess how “far off” one is from an ideal solution. This is especially so if natural groupings are 500unknown before carrying out the cluster analysis, which is in most cases why we are employing cluster analysis in the first place. In evaluating cluster solutions, as Hastie et al. (2009, p. 487) remark,

One must resort to heuristic arguments not only for motivating the algorithms, as is often the case in supervised learning as well, but also for judgments as to the quality of the results. This uncomfortable situation has led to heavy proliferation of proposed results since effectiveness [emphasis added] is a matter of opinion and cannot be verified directly.

Indeed, Venables and Ripley (2002, p. 316) issue a rather dire warning on relying on cluster analysis exclusively in discovering groupings:

Do not assume that “clustering” methods are the best way to discover interesting groupings in the data; in our experience the visualization methods are often far more effective. There are many different clustering methods, often giving different answers, and so the danger of over-interpretation is high.

Perhaps the take-away message from the above warnings in that, as is the case with so many statistical models, to be aware that what you find is often a function of what tool you use to do the finding. There is no such thing as the definitive “existence” of clusters. Rather, as was the case with previously studied dimension reduction techniques in this book, the “existence” of a dimension or cluster solution will be intimately tied to the algorithm that “discovered” the solution. Naturally, this reality has huge philosophical implications and raises many questions. For instance, that one cannot make immediate sense of a cluster solution should not necessarily imply the solution is not sensible. All we can really conclude is that it currently is not sensible to the user at this point in history, given the context and current state of the science in which he or she practices. Indeed, this dilemma makes for an interesting philosophical debate regarding whether the existence of cluster solutions is primarily mathematical or whether it is primarily substantive. It is not a debate we will have here but is an important one in the philosophy of statistics and mathematics and is something the user should keep in mind as we survey a variety of cluster algorithms.

14.3 Dissimilarity Metrics: The Basis of Clustering Algorithms

Most clustering centers around the idea of a dissimilarity metric. For some types of clustering, dissimilarity or similarity is defined explicitly, while for other clustering approaches such as mixture modeling, a distance metric is usually implied from the way the clustering is performed. If the data are qualitative rather than quantitative, then mathematical distance cannot be computed and some measure of similarity will be required in its place (Xu & Tian, 2015).

In mathematics, a dissimilarity coefficient d may be symmetric, meaning d(A, B) = d(B, A), as well as being non-negative, that is, d(A, A) = 0. We can also easily deduce from a dissimilarity metric that for points A, B, C, where B lies between A and C,


d(A,C) ≤ d(A,B) + d(B,C)
(14.1)

We can also express d(A,B) as an ultrametric,501


d(A,B) ≤ max (d(A,C),d(B,C))
(14.2)

where A, B, C can also be conceived as clusters with points existing within each cluster. The ultrametric holds that the distance between clusters A and B is less than or equal to the maximum distance between points in clusters A and C or between points in clusters B and C. Venables and Ripley (2002) note that hierarchical approaches to cluster analysis can be largely interpreted as ultimately approximating an ultrametric dissimilarity. Indeed, Simovici and Hua (2019) have found that a dissimilarity space (which empirically, is a set of data) is more clusterable the closer such space is to an ultrametric.

14.4 Association Rules: Market Basket Analysis

Association rules are a relatively primitive way of clustering. The idea behind association rule analysis, also commonly referred to as market basket analysis (since it is commonly used in marketing analysis of products) is to, not surprisingly, find associations between variables, typically binary variables (Hastie et al., 2009). Much of association rule analysis reduces down to the familiar idea of conditional probabilities, that is, the probability p(y|x) where y is what is being purchased but conditional on product x. For example, we may want to know the probability of a customer purchasing a computer monitor given that that same customer has just purchased a desktop computer or the probability of purchasing a television stand given one has just purchased a new television. Many of the algorithms for association analysis reduce to finding modes or what are called “bumps” in the data, whereby collections of prototype x values are associated with probability densities (i.e., the “bumps”).

More formally, association analysis seeks to find intersections of subsets of variables on x, that is, overlapping spaces of the kind


$$p\left\lbrack {\underset{j = 1}{\overset{p}{\cap}}\left( x_{j} \in s_{j} \right)} \right\rbrack$$

where the intersection of such subsets is known as a conjunctive rule (Hastie et al., 2009). These subsets naturally occur for qualitative variables, where for quantitative variables the subsets sj consist of intervals along some continuum.

Clustered association rules have also been proposed that seek to essentially group association rules themselves into categories instead of operating by several individual rules (Lent et al., 1997). Association rules have their modern origin with Agrawal et al. (1993), who provide a highly readable and highly recommended introduction to the topic. The package arules (Hahsler et al., 2024) in R can be used for mining association rules. For further details on market analysis, see Aggarwal (2015).

14.5 Why Not Consider All Groups?

The first question that arises in the study of cluster analysis algorithms is that of why not look at all groups of cases, and then decide which is optimal by some metric? For example, when considering the possible clusters of two objects from three available objects, it would be foolish to not simply consider all possibilities of the simple combinatorial problem 3 choose 2, equal to 3. Indeed, it would at first glance seem that using a combinatorial algorithm from the combinatorial paradigm of clustering is the obvious choice, that is, simply enumerate all possibilities and choose the solution that maximizes or minimizes some objective function. That is, choose the “best” cluster in this sense, and be done with the task.502

While the above solution is highly recommended for very small data sets, it unfortunately will be ineffective or impractical for any data set of even moderate size. The reason for this is that the number of ways of partitioning n cases into g clusters is literally gargantuan in number, and can be shown to be equal to


$$N\left( n,g \right) = \frac{1}{g!}{\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{g}\left( \begin{array}{l} g \\ k \\ \end{array} \right)}\left( - 1 \right)^{g - k}k^{n}$$
(14.3)

More succinctly, the number can also be approximated rather well by gn/g!. This approach is sometimes referred to as the sledgehammer approach. Not only is the approach impractical from a substantive point of view, it is absolutely prohibitive from a computational vantage point as well since to evaluate this vast number of combinations would require a huge amount of computational time and capacity. While smaller data sets will never experience these upper limits of capability, increasingly large data sets will, and given the vast amounts of data that can be clustered today in the era of big data, computational capacity becomes a determining and influential factor when deciding on how to cluster. A good algorithm isn’t only one that clusters well; it must also be computationally efficient.

Hence, what is needed are ways to group cases together in some sense that is efficient without searching through every single possible combinatorial pattern. That is, we need to consider or hypothesize a much smaller set of enumeration possibilities. This is precisely why cluster analysis algorithms exist. Algorithms are designed to partition cases such that mathematically meaningful groups emerge which may or may not simultaneously be substantively meaningful (i.e., the user and research community can make “sense” of what the clusters might represent). Yet good algorithms do not consider all possible groupings; they only consider the best ones, in the sense of the most efficient, creative, and greedy ways to generate such groupings, where “greedy” implies that many algorithms consider what is best “here and now” and not two or three steps down the road. By way of analogy, the carrot cake with enough sugar to make you dizzy sounds great right now without any thought of how you will feel in a couple of hours.

14.5.1 What Makes a “Good” Clustering Algorithm?

Some have suggested criteria for a good clustering algorithm. For instance, some have proposed that clustering algorithms should require minimal requirements of domain knowledge to determine input parameters, as appropriate values are typically not known in advance when working with large databases. A good cluster algorithm should also not automatically assume clusters will be spherical in shape, as empirical evidence has shown that many empirical clusters are drawn out, linear, or elongated, etc., which are shapes that a technique such as traditional clustering algorithms like k-means may fail to detect. This last point is very important in cluster analysis, as an entire literature in statistics and machine learning exists with the goal of discovering non-spherical cluster shapes. A good clustering algorithm, as already emphasized, should also provide reasonable efficiency on large databases. This of course is coupled with computational concerns and the limitations of software and hardware to carry out such clustering.

Whatever the clustering algorithm adopted, many clustering procedures, as is the case with most statistical and machine learning methods, essentially come down to maximizing or minimizing some quantity, that is, some objective function of the data. That is, good clustering, from a mathematical point of view, becomes simply a problem of optimization. What makes for a good optimization strategy for clustering? It seems reasonable to require that within-cluster variation be minimized. That is, an ideal goal to strive for might be to minimize the sum of within-cluster variation across each cluster,503


$$MIN{\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{K}{Within\left( C_{k} \right)}}$$

where Ck is a given cluster k. The above reads the sum from k = 1 to K of within-cluster variation is minimized, that is, as small as it can be through successive iterations. This amounts to the clusters being as homogeneous as possible.

More specifically, the within-cluster distance is usually specified by an average squared distance function:


$$Within\left( C \right) = {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{K}N_{k}}{\sum\limits_{C(i) = k}\left| \middle| x_{i} - {\overline{x}}_{k} \middle| \right|^{2}}$$
(14.4)

where ${\overline{x}}_{k}$ is the mean for the kth cluster, and $\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{K}N_{k}$ simply represents the sum across all clusters k to K. That is, we are summing across all clusters k the squared distances from respective cluster means, ${\overline{x}}_{k}$. The objective is to minimize this average within-cluster distance. Once this objective is minimized, the clustering algorithm is said to have converged on a solution. As we will discuss later in this chapter, the k-means clustering algorithm seeks to accomplish just this and provides a local optimum (James et al., 2021).

Cluster analysis algorithms do not typically consider all partitions of the data since such are too numerous and would be far too labor intensive. Combinatorially, there are simply too many ways of generating groups. Instead, they seek to partition cases in a way that is mathematically meaningful which usually translates to them optimizing some “greedy” function of the data.

14.6 Distance and Proximity Metrics

As already mentioned, virtually all of cluster analysis techniques available, despite their individual differences, are based on the notions of similarity or distance between objects. Indeed, as discussed at the outset of this book, one can even say that most, if not all statistical and learning machine methods eventually boil down in some capacity or another to notions of distance when inspected at the most foundational level (Johnson & Wichern, 2007). Distances will generally be organized into a distance matrix that contains non-negative entries. That is, it is assumed that distances are a non-negative integer. To measure proximity of cases, we require a measure of distance, where the distance dj between xij and xi′j is, most generally,


dj(xij,xi′j) = (xij−xi′j)

and squared distances are thus given by504


dj2(xij,xi′j) = (xij−xi′j)2

There are several such distance measures available. The most common is that of Euclidean distance. The Euclidean distance between two p-dimensional objects, x = [x1,x2,...,xp] and y = [y1,y2,...,yp] is given by,


$$\begin{array}{l} {d\left( x,y \right) = \sqrt{\left( x_{1} - y_{1} \right)^{2} + \left( x_{2} - y_{2} \right)^{2} + \cdot \cdot \cdot \left( x_{p} - y_{p} \right)^{2}}} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = \sqrt{\left( x - y \right)'\left( x - y \right)}} \\ \end{array}$$
(14.5)

A statistical distance can also be used, where distances x − y are scaled by the covariance matrix, S,


$$d\left( x,y \right) = \sqrt{\left( x - y \right)'S^{- 1}\left( x - y \right)}$$
(14.6)

Other metrics are also available. For instance, the Minkowski metric is given by


$$d\left( x,y \right) = \left\lbrack {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{p}\left| x_{i} - y_{i} \right|^{m}} \right\rbrack^{1/m}$$
(14.7)

for which when m = 2, the Minkowski metric reduces to the Euclidean distance,


$$\begin{array}{l} {d\left( x,y \right) = \left\lbrack {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{p}\left| x_{i} - y_{i} \right|^{m}} \right\rbrack^{1/m}} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = \left\lbrack {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{p}\left| x_{i} - y_{i} \right|^{2}} \right\rbrack^{1/2}} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = \sqrt{\left( x_{1} - y_{1} \right)^{2} + \left( x_{2} - y_{2} \right)^{2} + \cdot \cdot \cdot \left( x_{p} - y_{p} \right)^{2}}} \\ \end{array}$$

Yet another distance metric is that of city-block, also known as Manhattan distance,


$$d\left( x,y \right) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{p}\left| x_{i} - y_{i} \right|}$$
(14.8)

One place where the Manhattan distance is used is in the k-medians approach to cluster analysis (Aggarwal, 2015) which we will feature shortly when we survey algorithms from the k-representatives family.

The importance of choosing an appropriate distance metric cannot be overstated. As emphasized by Hastie et al. (2009, p. 506):

Specifying an appropriate dissimilarity measure is far more important in obtaining success with clustering than choice of clustering algorithm. This aspect of the problem is emphasized less in the clustering literature than the algorithms themselves, since it depends on domain knowledge specifics and is less amenable to general research.505

A good summary of the more popular distance measures used in clustering algorithms is provided in Xu and Tian (2015).

14.7 Is the Data Clusterable?

Before engaging in clustering, we might ask the question of how “clusterable” is a data set to begin with? A first answer to this might be that it does not matter and to just give clustering a “try” and see what comes out. However, this strategy can be somewhat problematic. Cluster analysis in most cases will find a solution, the algorithms are designed specifically to do just that! Hence, a test for clusterability before engaging in cluster analysis, if that test is a good one, should give us an idea of whether the data should be clustered in the first place and whether any clusters we do observe will be more a function of the algorithm than the actual empirical existence of clusters. As remarked by Adolfsson et al. (2019, p. 1), “perhaps an even more fundamental issue than algorithm selection is when clustering should, or should not, be applied.”

The Hopkins statistic is one popular measure that can be used to assess the clusterability of data. It can be interpreted as a measure of clustering tendency of a data set (Aggarwal, 2015; Wright, 2022). In this approach, pr values are randomly generated as well as pd points randomly sampled from the data. For both sets of points, distances to their nearest neighbors in the data are computed. That is, if we let xi be a nearest neighbor, then what we wish to compare are the distances pr to xi, which we will call Drandom vs. pd to xi′, which we will call Ddata. That is, we are interested in knowing how the distances to nearest neighbors compare based on a random data set vs. actual data points in the data set.

The Hopkins statistic is thus defined as


$$H = \frac{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{r}D_{i(random)}}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{r}\left( D_{i(data)} + D_{i(random)} \right)}$$
(14.9)

For uniform randomly generated data, the expectation for Hopkins is in the neighborhood of 0.5. This is as a result of Di(data) and Di(random) being similar. If the data are clusterable, Di(data) is typically less than Di(random) and hence H will increase. Values of H greater than 0.75 have been found to equate to clustering “confidence” at 90% (Lawson & Jurs, 1990; Wright, 2022). Adolfsson et al. (2019) provide an extensive review of so-called clusterability methods (many other techniques exist over and above Hopkins), and have found that the Hopkins statistic may be a somewhat limited measure when clusters touch or overlap.

The package hopkins (Wright, 2023) is available in R for computing the Hopkins statistic. As an example from the package, we compute a Hopkins statistic on the iris data (sepal length through petal width, excluding species), where we compute Hopkins on m = 15 observations (or sampled rows of the data, the default is 1/10th of the rows if not set specifically):

> library(hopkins)
> hopkins(iris[, 1:4], m=15)
[1] 0.9986529

We can also obtain a p-value for the computed Hopkins statistic where x is the value of the computed Hopkins and n is the number of observations sampled:506

> hopkins.pval(x = 0.9986529, n = 15)
[1] 0

As a result of the value for Hopkins being so large, the p-value is extremely small (it is rounded to 0, p-values never equal 0 exactly). Suppose instead we obtained a Hopkins equal to 0.5, the p-value would thus be

> hopkins.pval(x = 0.5, n = 15)
[1] 1

The value is equal to 1 since recall the expectation of Hopkins for a uniform distribution is equal to 0.5. The further away from 0.5, the lower the p-value, as demonstrated once more,

> hopkins.pval(0.1, 15)
[1] 3.925226e-08
> hopkins.pval(0.9, 15)
[1] 3.925226e-08

We see that for both values of 0.1 and 0.9, identical p-values are obtained. As usual with a significance test, as n increases, all else equal, p-values drop. Using our previous example but increasing n to 100 not surprisingly yields

> hopkins.pval(0.9, 100)
[1] 0

14.8 Algorithms for Cluster Analysis

In this section we survey some of the more popular clustering algorithms, which include k-means and associated k-representatives, hierarchical or agglomerative clustering, density-based clustering (specifically DBSCAN), and clustering via mixture models.

14.8.1 K-Means Clustering and K-Representatives

The k-means clustering algorithm is probably the simplest and well-known, most used form of cluster analysis. K-means is a special case of the wider group of representative-based algorithms for clustering that rely on the concept of distance between observations as the basis for clustering. These approaches are also sometimes called partitional (Madhulatha, 2012) or unnested methods since they seek to partition the data into groups or clusters by assigning cases nearest cluster centroids whereas hierarchical clustering is considered a form of nested clustering that builds clusters by essentially fusing smaller subordinate clusters. The centroids in this case are the so-called “representatives” of the given clusters. Other representative-based algorithms include k-medians, k-medoids, and kernel-based k-means. Briefly, the k-medians approach uses the median instead of the mean and is thus more robust to extreme and outlying cases than is the k-means approach. In the k-medoids approach, initial starting points to initiate the algorithm are drawn from the original database, and in kernel-based k-means, a kernel function via the familiar kernel trick is applied in generating clusters.

As mentioned, representative-based algorithms are usually contrasted to hierarchical approaches which take an either bottom-up or top-down approach to building clusters and generally require the storage of a distance matrix. Nonhierarchical clustering methods are generally 507more efficient than hierarchical methods since they do not require the storing of a distance matrix. The jargon can differ slightly depending on the source one reads, so it behooves the reader investigating clustering algorithms to be sure of how terms are being used by the author.

14.8.2 How K-Means Works

K-means clustering attempts to partition cases into distinct clusters where the number of clusters is requested by the user beforehand. In k-means, the sum of squared distances to their closest representatives is optimized and an observation belonging to one cluster cannot simultaneously belong to another. That is, cluster membership is mutually exclusive. This will typically not be the case in some other clustering methods such as density-based or mixture modeling clustering. So-called fuzzy clustering algorithms also allow for a case to be clustered into more than a single cluster.

The k-means algorithm also clusters every object, implying that there will not be any observations left out of the clustering. In this sense, k-means is regarded as a complete clustering algorithm such that it seeks to cluster every case. This is in contrast to partial clustering algorithms that allow some cases to go unclustered. For example, DBSCAN, a density-based clustering algorithm which we will survey shortly, typically does not produce complete clustering since it defines some cases as simply noise points rather than classifying them to clusters. These “noise” points are those that do not seem to “fit” in any of the clusters being generated. And while k-means is often regarded as an “algorithm” today, there is nothing special about the word “algorithm” as it applies to the procedure. Indeed, in the past, k-means was often called a data-analytic procedure or method. Like many statistical and machine learning approaches today, it is often referred to as an “algorithm” largely, though not exclusively, due to the zeitgeist that we currently find ourselves in. Otherwise excellent works on cluster analysis may not once even mention the word “algorithm” and may simply describe the process by which clusters are derived.

K-means is a special case of the wider group of representative-based clustering algorithms. Hierarchical algorithms on the other hand can be divided into bottom-up and top-down approaches.

14.8.3 Defining Proximity for K-Means

Recall that there are a host of distance metrics and proximities available for cluster analysis, including that for k-means. The most typical choice of distance metric in k-means is that of the squared Euclidean metric,


$$\begin{array}{l} {d\left( x_{i},x_{i}^{'} \right) = {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}\left( x_{ij} - x_{i'j} \right)^{2}}} \\ \left. \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = \, \middle| \middle| x_{i} - x_{i'} \middle| \right|^{2} \\ \end{array}$$
(14.10)

such that the quantity being minimized is that of the average within-case or within-point scatter variation discussed earlier:508


$$Within\left( C \right)\, = {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{K}N_{k}}{\sum\limits_{C(i) = k}\left| \middle| x_{i} - {\overline{x}}_{k} \middle| \right|^{2}}$$

We follow James et al. (2021) quite closely in detailing precisely how the k-means algorithm goes about clustering:

  1. 1. Each observation in the data receives a random number 1 to K. These are the initial cluster assignments.
  2. 2. For each of the K clusters, the cluster centroid is computed, where “centroid” is another word for arithmetic mean in this case. More generally, a centroid in mathematics is simply a center point, and thus it is, at least in theory, open and flexible regarding how we wish to define it. For example, the median can also be regarded as a centroid in cluster analysis. In classical k-means, the arithmetic mean is featured as the centroid.
  3. 3. Assign each observation to the cluster whose centroid is closest. The measure of “closeness” is defined by the squared Euclidean metric or some other distance function we have chosen a priori. There is nothing preventing the user from trying out different distance metrics on the same clustering problem and study the patterns that result.
  4. 4. Iterate on steps 2 and 3 until the minimization criterion is achieved, which as mentioned earlier is typically Within(C), the within-cluster sums of squares.

The algorithm is guaranteed to decrease the value of the objective function at each step and optimizes a non-convex function (Murphy, 2022), which recall implies that achieving a global minimum is more difficult in k-means since numerous local minima exist in its place, and hence the algorithm will typically converge to local minima. As a result of the non-convexity, how the algorithm is initialized can make a big difference in the final cluster solution. For this reason, choosing several random starts is often advised to learn if the various cluster solutions more or less converge on a single solution (Murphy, 2022) or whether any of the single cluster solutions obtained are favorable to the user. Another approach is successively selecting points that are more distant from cluster centroids thus ensuring that initial seeds are well separated. This should be done with caution, however, as to not exclusively sample outliers.

14.8.4 Setting k in K-Means

A key decision in k-means clustering is that of deciding how to set k. One could set it by trial and error to learn what kinds of clusters emerge and decide whether they are substantively meaningful, but it would be advantageous to have some statistical “objective” criteria to help us determine an optimal value for k. We could at first attempt to set it such that it minimizes the reconstruction error. The problem with this approach is that reconstruction error will naturally decrease with increasing k, and hence setting this as a criterion to minimize will be meaningless as we could always minimize the error further by increasing the number of clusters desired, somewhat akin to forever increasing R2 due to increasingly adding more predictors to the model. Since we know that R2 must virtually always increase with increasing numbers of predictors, an inflating R2 is a poor measure of anything, which recall is why Radj2 or some other penalized statistic (e.g., AIC) is typically recommended over, or at least in conjunction with, R2. This situation occurs also in probabilistic mixture models that we will survey later in which we can compute the log marginal likelihood of the solution as an aid to determining an “ideal” number of clusters such that whichever cluster solution yields the largest likelihood may be considered “best.” In this context, however, it will be 509entirely possible for a solution with fewer clusters to generate a more favorable substantive finding than a solution with a greater number of clusters.

14.8.5 Weakness of K-Means

K-means comes with it a host of weaknesses. As noted by Müller and Guido (2017):

Even if you know the “right” number of clusters for a given dataset, k-means might not always be able to recover them. Each cluster is defined solely by its center, which means that each cluster is a convex shape. As a result of this, k-means can only capture relatively simple shapes. K-means also assumes that all clusters have the same “diameter” in some sense; it always draws the boundary between clusters to be exactly in the middle between the cluster centers.

(p. 175)

This implies that k-means clustering essentially comes with it a prior idea of what the clusters should look like to some extent, and if the empirical realities do not conform to that idea, then recovering them can be quite difficult or even impossible. K-means implicitly also assumes a spherical shape for each cluster, and as we will see when it comes to mixture modeling, the EM algorithm is capable of discovering a broader class of elliptical clusters. Once again, this is a general problem when it comes to clustering algorithms. To reiterate, what you find often depends on what tool you use to do the searching. As warned by Meila and Zhang (2023, p. 26) with regard to manifold learning more generally, “Are the features observed really in the data or artifacts of the algorithm?” Add to this difficulty that in most applications of cluster analysis there is typically no ground truth, as it is sometimes called, to the data. That is, we do not usually know the labels before we do the clustering. Only in toy problems do we typically have this benefit (e.g., species membership on the iris data).

14.8.6 K-Means vs. ANOVA vs. Discriminant Analysis

We said above that the goal of k-means was to minimize within-cluster difference. Does this criterion sound familiar? This minimization of such an objective function may have caught the eye of the reader and reminded them of what occurs in the analysis of variance or discriminant analysis. Consider the following conceptual comparison of approaches:

ANOVA – goal is to maximize between-group differences and minimize within-group differences.

Discriminant analysis – goal is essentially the same as in ANOVA, except in reverse roles of the independent and dependent variables such as to maximize group separation.

K-means cluster analysis – goal is to minimize within-group differences and maximize separation between clusters.

To be clear, ANOVA, discriminant analysis, and k-means clustering are not the same procedures and have their own individual respective roles in data science. However, they often seek to minimize a similar objective function and can be, to some extent, likened to one another. Indeed, one way to think about k-means clustering, where there is no a priori ground truth, is such that we seek to discover groups. In classic ANOVA or discriminant analysis, the investigator comes to the analysis already with a theory in mind in the form of either a factor with various levels in ANOVA or a response variable in discriminant analysis featuring a binary or categorical grouping. That is, in ANOVA and discriminant analysis the user advances the hypothesized grouping structure. Is it the best grouping structure in some sense? Not necessarily, but it is the one hypothesized by the 510researcher. In cluster analysis, we typically do not yet have a hypothesized grouping structure in mind and seek to “find one” via the algorithm. This is a powerful conceptual way to relate these approaches, even if their technical details will differ substantially.

14.8.7 Making K-Means Probabilistic via K-Means ++

We have seen that k-means assigns cases that are closest to cluster centers but have noted that initial cluster seeds can have a significant impact and influence on the determination of clusters. Given this impact, we have said that it is usually recommended to try a variety of initial seeds and not simply rely on a single “run” of seeding. But how exactly should this be done? We could simply rerun the k-means algorithm manually a few times and settle with that approach to determining initial seeds. While this is not a terrible way of doing things, such an approach is not very efficient and could take a long time to execute.

A much more efficient approach to the above problem is to extend the traditional k-means algorithm and adopt a method in which the initial seeds are selected at random as in classical k-means, but then subsequent points are selected subject to being probabilistically proportional to the square distance to the point’s nearest cluster center (Murray, 2022, p. 719). The approach here is to try to, essentially, “cover” the data as much as possible. This approach is called farthest point clustering, or k-means ++.

14.8.8 Using the Data: K-Medoids Clustering

We have seen that k-means clustering assigns cases to the cluster for which it is closest to the cluster centroid. In k-means, that “representative” centroid is that of the arithmetic mean while in k-medians clustering it is the median. Note that both of these approaches use a representative that is a function of the data and not the data itself. That is, the mean is a summary statistic of the data; it is not an actual data point in the data. In this sense, the mean does not “exist” in the data, it is simply an abstract measure we apply to the data set. Even if the mean happens to equal a particular data point, it is still not being drawn from the data itself, and likewise with the median; the median may or may not exist in the data. The bottom line is that whether we are using the mean or median, we are nonetheless using a function of the data and not the data itself.

A variant of such approaches is that of k-medoids. In k-medoids clustering each cluster center is estimated not through computing a function of the data, but instead by choosing an actual empirical data value from the actual data set that is “optimal” in some sense. How should we choose this value? One strategy is to select it such that its average dissimilarity to all other points in the data set is a minimum. The empirical value, or representative object, that is, the medoid, may also be chosen randomly. The key advantage of k-medoids, in addition to being less sensitive to outliers than k-means, is that it can be applied to spaces that are non-Euclidean which do not necessarily permit the computation of an average (Leskovec et al., 2014). In such cases, a representative can be calculated called a clustroid, of which there are many ways of choosing the relevant clustroid for a given problem (see Leskovec et al., 2014 for details).

The algorithm typically used in k-medoids is called the partitioning around medoids (or PAM) algorithm. Essentially, the algorithm exchanges medoids for non-medoids in an iterative fashion recomputing the cost each time to learn whether the exchange was advantageous in minimizing the cost. If the exchange was worthwhile, it is kept. An allied method to PAM is the Voronoi iteration. See Murphy (2022) for details.511

Cluster purity is a measure of how well the algorithm classifies relative to the ground truth, if available (Sikhakolli & Sikhakolli, 2023). If the algorithm performed perfectly, then out of 150 cases total, 150 should have been clustered correctly. If we let pj be the proportion representing the maximum number of points clustered correctly into the given class, and $\frac{N_{i}}{N}$ be the total fraction of cases eligible to be clustered for the given class from the total number of cases N, then cluster purity is given by


$$cluster\, purity = {\sum\limits_{i}\frac{N_{i}}{N}}p_{j}$$
(14.11)

For the iris data, if all cases were clustered correctly, the cluster purity would equal (50 + 50 + 50)/150 = 1.0 as a result of there being 50 cases per species of iris. For our actual data, the cluster purity is computed to be (50 + 48 + 36)/150 = 0.893. This is a shorthand calculation since Ni/N = 50/150 for each class of species. To be more precise, the full computation is the following:

> purity <- (50/150)*(50/50) + (50/150)*(48/50) + (50/150)*(36/50)
> purity
[1] 0.8933333

The package funtimes (Lyubchich et al., 2023) computes cluster purity as well as reproducing results initially observed in the aforementioned confusion matrix:516

If the ground truth is known before the clustering, then cluster purity in this example is simple to conceptualize, it is essentially assessing the total proportion of cases that were clustered correctly into their ground truth classifications. For instance, if setosa had 50 cases, and all of those cases were clustered into “setosa,” then such would constitute perfect cluster purity for setosa. The cluster purity for versicolor is not quite as good because out of the 50 cases that should have gone into versicolor, only 48 ended up classified into that class. Virginica had the worst cluster purity at only 36 out of 50. The overall cluster purity is effectively summing up these class-specific purity ratios.

We can also plot the within sums of squares for the optimal number of clusters (code from Boehmke & Greenwell, 2020, p. 409) as shown in Figure 14.2. The function fviz_nbclust() helps visualize and determine the optimal number of clusters, where get_dist computes a distance function, in this case based on the correlation method of spearman (other options include pearson and kendall, minkowski, etc.); see the package factoextra (Kassambara & Mundt, 2017, for details):

> library(factoextra)
> fviz_nbclust(iris.data,
+ kmeans,
+ k.max = 3,
+ method = “wss”,
+ diss = get_dist(iris.data, method = “spearman”))

We can see from the plot that the ideal number of clusters is 2 or 3, with 3 generating the lowest within sums of squares (method = “wss”):

14.9 Sparse and Longitudinal K-Means

There are numerous variations of k-means clustering. For instance, in sparse cluster analysis, permutations of the data can be obtained such that the features in the permutated data set are uncorrelated 517with each other. In R, sparse cluster analysis can be performed with KMeansSparseCluster(). Longitudinal k-means is also a possibility where clusters can be tracked over successive time points. The kml package in R (Genolini et al., 2024) can perform k-means on longitudinal data. The package longitudinalData (Genolini et al., 2024) is also useful, as kml relies on it.

14.10 Hierarchical Clustering

As we have seen, in the k-family or k-representatives of clustering the number of clusters is specified a priori. Methods such as k-means and their variants rely on distance matrices to perform their clustering. An alternative approach to clustering is hierarchical clustering, in which the number of clusters is not requested a priori, but instead the algorithm will build a tree, a dendrogram, that displays the historical linkages made as the algorithm progresses from single cases to fused conglomerates of cases subject to some minimization criterion. A variety of linkages can be used that define case similarity, which we will survey shortly. Hierarchical clustering can either be agglomerative or divisive. Agglomerative clustering begins with single cases and fuses cases together building up the dendrogram. Divisive clustering begins with one big cluster and separates into smaller clusters at each step. We only survey the agglomerative case here as it is the most common.

Figure 14.3 is an example of a simple dendrogram where we can easily visualize the history of where cases were joined from the bottom up in the dendrogram. We see that cases 2 and 3 were first fused, followed by the fusing of those cases to case 4. Lastly, this cluster made up of cases 2, 3, and 4 was fused to case 1 to form the largest cluster.

As mentioned, there are competing linkages one can use in fusing cases and clusters, including complete, single, average, and centroid methods, each having its strengths and weaknesses. In single linkage (also known in the literature as MIN), the minimum distance between cases is used as a criterion for fusing, while in complete linkage (also known in the literature as MAX) that of the maximal furthest distance between cases is employed. Average linkage, not surprisingly, takes an average of distances between groups. Dendrograms in single and complete linkage are invariant under monotone transformations of pairwise dissimilarities, however this is not true for average linkage (Izenman, 2008). These are not the only linkages possible but are the most common ones.

For a good discussion of linkages used in hierarchical clustering, see Johnson and Wichern (2007). The key point for now is to recognize that employing different linkages could lead to different solutions.

Hierarchical clustering can be expensive computationally because it operates on what are potentially quite large dissimilarity indexes. The slower speed of hierarchical clustering can be considered a drawback of this approach and of agglomerative approaches more generally as they 518can be quite expensive since they require entire distance matrices as inputs. Another drawback to hierarchical approaches is that contrary to k-representative clustering, there is usually no clear single optimization criteria or objective that is optimized in the final solution (Murphy, 2022). Further, once cases are fused, they cannot be unfused. Rather, the user typically has to mostly rely on substantive theory in determining whether a cluster solution is successful.

14.10.1 Agglomerative Clustering in Python

We demonstrate a simple agglomerative clustering routine in Python on the iris data:

import seaborn as sns
iris = sns.load_dataset(“iris”)
df = iris[[‘sepal_length’, ‘sepal_width’, ‘petal_length’, ‘petal_width’]]
iris.drop([‘species’], axis=1, inplace=True)
iris

We produce a series of scatterplots between variables (Figure 14.4).

import seaborn as sns
sns.pairplot(iris)

We now perform a single-linkage cluster analysis, using Euclidean distances:519

from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering
groups = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=3,
affinity=’euclidean’, linkage=’single’)
groups.fit_predict(iris)

What follows are the cluster assignments, which we also plot for variables petal length by petal width (Figure 14.5). We note from the plot that clusters 0 and 2 are somewhat intermixed:

14.10.2 Agglomerative Clustering in R

The following is a basic hierarchical clustering routine in R using Euclidean distance via the function hclust. Dendrograms based on single and average linkage are easily generated (Figure 14.6).520

d <- dist(iris.data, method = “euclidean”)
clust.single <- hclust(d, method = “single”)
clust.average <- hclust(d, method = “average”)
plot(clust.single)
plot(clust.average)

We can also produce a variety of plots in addition to the dendrograms in Figure 14.6. For example, triangle, unrooted, and fan plots are possibilities (Figure 14.7) using the ape package (Paradis & Schliep, 2019).

> library(ape)
> dendro <- as.dendrogram(clust.single)
> plot(dendro, type = “triangle”, ylab = “Height”)
> plot(as.phylo(clust.single), type = “unrooted”, cex = 0.6, no.margin = TRUE)
> plot(as.phylo(clust.single), type = “fan”)
521

Of course, the plots in Figure 14.7 are challenging to visualize due to the size of the data, but they are enough to get a sense of the general idea that there are two larger clusters that come out of the data. To produce a colored dendrogram, consult the package sparcl (Witten & Tibshirani, 2018).

In helping determine the number of clusters to keep, we can produce what is called a silhouette plot as well as compute the gap statistic (Figure 14.8), where larger values of these statistics are indicative of a preferred solution:

> library(factoextra)
> p1 <- fviz_nbclust(iris.data, FUN = hcut, method = “silhouette”, k.max = 10)+
+ ggtitle(“(B) Silhouette method”)
> p1

We can see that the ideal number of clusters is equal to 2 for the silhouette method, which more or less agrees with the dendrogram on this data. Silhouette values are computed for each data point and then averaged per cluster. A greater than not value for average silhouette values indicates that data points are essentially “matched” well for the given cluster, and hence cluster solutions with a higher than not silhouette average value are preferred.

> p1 <- fviz_nbclust(iris.data, FUN = hcut, method = “gap”, k.max = 10)+
+ ggtitle(“(B) Gap method”)

The number of clusters suggested by the gap statistic is equal to 6 (however, gap values are relatively strong for anything greater than three or so clusters). Gap values correspond to the difference between within-cluster dispersion relative to a reference or null distribution. For details on how the gap statistic is calculated, see Tibshirani et al. (2001). For further details on the silhouette method, see Rousseeuw (1987).522

14.11 Density-Based Clustering: DBSCAN

We have thus far in this chapter surveyed k-means and k-representative clustering approaches as well as hierarchical and agglomerative paradigms. These are perhaps the most traditional and common ways of clustering across the sciences.

A third general approach to clustering which is especially useful for detecting clusters of arbitrary shape goes by the name of density-based clustering. One such approach is the popular DBSCAN algorithm, which is an acronym for density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise. DBSCAN is especially efficient for large databases. The method is similar to what are referred to as grid-based methods (Aggarwal, 2015), but uses circular regions as building blocks for the clusters. To understand DBSCAN, we must first understand the notions of dense points and crowded regions.

14.11.1 Dense Points and Crowded Regions

DBSCAN operates differently than k-representative clustering or hierarchical clustering. Instead of building up clusters by establishing random seeds and then computing distance functions, DBSCAN identifies points that are in so-called crowded regions of the feature space, that is, where many points are in some sense already “close together.” These regions are sometimes referred to as dense regions. Hence, we already see a key difference between this approach and that of k-means. In k-means, the algorithm did not seek out dense spaces of any kind but instead simply selected random points to begin the clustering process. In DBSCAN clustering, we actually seek out what appear to be clusters first as defined by the density of those regions. But how exactly to define density? For this we need to implement a distance function.

The density of a data point in DBSCAN is defined by how many points lie within a given radius ε of the point (Aggarwal, 2015). All points that lie within a radius of ε are considered to be in the same cluster as the core point so long as they are equal to or less than MinPts, another parameter set by the user specifying the minimum number of points (or “neighbors”) required to form the so-called “dense region” within radius ε. Points that are within a dense region are called core samples or core points. Other points are either border or noise points. Border points are those that are contained within the radius ε but have insufficient points around them by the criterion MinPts to consider themselves a core point. That is, border points fall within the neighborhood of core points but are not significant enough to be core points themselves because they do not have MinPts points around them. Noise points are those that are neither core points nor border points.

The algorithm essentially connects core points that are within ε (or “eps”) of one another, which is a flexible parameter that can be freely adjusted by the user. A choice for ε too large and what will result is a cluster with density equal to the number of cases. On the other hand, for ε set too small will have virtually all points essentially being their own cluster. Border points are then assigned to the cluster for which they have the highest connectivity, meaning that it is not sufficient on its own to be a core point (due to not meeting the MinPts criterion), so is classified to the cluster for which it is closest to a core point. The groups that result are the clusters and the remainder of the points are noise points. The precise steps of the algorithm are detailed in Schubert et al. (2017, p. 3).

The DBSCAN algorithm can actually be viewed as a more robust generalization of the single-linkage method where instead of only detecting spherical clusters as in k-means, it can find arbitrarily shaped clusters (Aggarwal, 2015). DBSCAN can also be considered a modification of single-linkage agglomerative clustering by treating border and noise points with special consideration relative to other methods where they are not given any special treatment. That is, in classic 523single-linkage clustering, for instance, border and noise points have no meaning in such an algorithm, and hence are just more points around which to compute linkages. As noted by Aggarwal (2015), the benefit of DBSCAN over single linkage is that with the consideration of border and noise points, the sensitivity of outliers is diminished in addition to the algorithm being able to detect clusters of arbitrary shape rather than only spherical ones such as in k-means approaches. Recall that we said from the outset that one of the chief difficulties with clustering algorithms is that they often make prior assumptions about the shape of clusters (e.g., spherical in the case of k-means). DBSCAN is useful because it is not limited to detecting spherical or other pre-defined shapes. DBSCAN has also been found to have better cluster classification when used on smaller data sets.

525

The nearest-neighbor distance plot sorts all data points by their corresponding k-nearest neighbor distances, where here k is equal to 4 (Figure 14.10, left). A sudden increase in the distance, a so-called knee in the plot suggests that most points to the right are likely outliers, and hence choosing a value for eps at the location of such a knee is recommended (Hahsler et al., 2024, p. 6). According to Hahsler et al., points to the right of approximately 0.7 seem to suggest the location of the knee and thus points to the right may be primarily regarded as noise. Hence, a suitable value for eps would be 0.7. A horizontal line can be drawn at 0.7 by coding (Figure 14.10, right):

> abline(h=.7, col = “red”, lty = 2)

14.12 Clustering via Mixture Models

The clustering algorithms we have surveyed thus far, those of k-means (and k-representatives), hierarchical clustering as well as density-based approaches such as DBSCAN, have made no assumptions about where the data have been sampled. That is, they have not made any parametric assumptions about the data or prior assumptions about the nature of the clusters (aside from assuming they must be spherical in shape in k-means or in dense regions as in DBSCAN), nor have they invoked anything to do with probability. They have simply relied on the empirical data to essentially tell the story of whether or not clusters might exist and have proceeded as such through hard-rule algorithmic processes of assigning cases to clusters.

An alternative approach to these clustering approaches is to assume the data arise from a mixture of (typically) Gaussian distributions or other parametric distributions (e.g., Poisson for discrete data, etc.). These distributions, both kind and number, are often chosen by the user based on prior substantive experience in the area and prior knowledge or hypotheses about the mixture components, though in most cases where specific knowledge is not known, Gaussian distributions are usually the default. The number of components, however, can be regarded as a hyperparameter 526that the user must specify (Alpaydin, 2020). If the number of clusters is known a priori and hence the “ground truth” of the number of clusters exists, specifying the number of components is easy. However, and as usual, cluster analysis is performed when knowledge of the number of clusters is not known a priori, in which case prior knowledge of what the user might expect to see may be useful in designating the number of components.

A mixture model, as the name suggests and as we have seen already in other contexts, is a mix of probability density distributions which for cluster analysis has the general form,


$$f\left( x;\theta \right) = {\sum\limits_{g = 1}^{G}{\pi_{g}f_{g}\left( x;\theta_{g} \right)}}$$
(14.12)

where there are g = 1 to G clusters, πg is the probability of an observation arising from the gth cluster (πg represents the mixing proportions), fg(x;θg) is the probability density function in the gth cluster, and θg is a vector of parameters that requires estimation. The usual form to assume for fg(x;θg) is that of multivariate normality, implying that θg will therefore consist of a mean vector and covariance matrix (Jolliffe, 2002).

Once the mixture model is fit, posterior probabilities p(y/θ) are obtained. The most popular mixture model, as mentioned, is that of a Gaussian mixture model (Murray, 2022) with density N(y|μg,Σg) where now N(y|μg,Σg) denotes a multivariate normal distribution with mean vector μg and covariance matrix Σg. A more robust version here would utilize the t-distribution instead of the normal (McLachlan & Chang, 2004).

The statistical objective in a mixture model is to estimate the parameters of the model by maximizing the likelihood function of the data to generate posterior probabilities of cluster membership with respect to the data, given knowledge of the model parameters. A problem can occur when maximizing the likelihood in a mixture of Gaussians, however, which is the problem of potential singularities. A singularity can occur if one of the components of the mixture model has a mean equal to that of a single data point. As noted by Bishop (2006), under this condition, a single data point contributes a single term to the likelihood function,


$$N\left( x_{i} \middle| x_{i},\sigma_{j}^{2}I \right) = \frac{1}{\left( 2\pi \right)^{1/2}}\frac{1}{\sigma_{j}}$$
(14.13)

where σj2 is the variance of the jth component and xi is a given data point, which, as a consequence of the singularity, is equal to the mean of the given component, that of μj. The problem occurs as σj gets closer and closer to 0, and in the limit,


$$\lim\limits_{\sigma_{j}\rightarrow 0}\left( {\frac{1}{\left( 2\pi \right)^{1/2}}\frac{1}{\sigma_{j}}} \right) = \infty$$

and hence the log-likelihood will go to infinity due to 1/σj = 1/0. In cases where this does occur, a random value for the mean can be “reset” to help avoid the “collapsing” of a point on the likelihood in this way. For a more thorough description of this problem, see Bishop (2006).

As mentioned, the user can select from different choices of model distributions and parameters which have the effect of inducing flexibility with regard to the probability distribution for each component. The advantage of a mixture modeling approach is that resulting clusters will tend to 527have high peaks resulting from relatively tightly and distinct cluster centers and hence the mixture model can account for cluster data relatively well in many cases.

Mixture models are part of the wider family of probability-based clustering algorithms which feature the idea of soft clustering, where a case is assigned to a cluster not deterministically but instead, probabilistically. These models are often referred to as generative models such that they assume observations were generated from one or more probability distributions. The reader may recognize “Bayesian” tones in this idea. More technically, the underlying idea behind a generative model is that one can generate synthetic data by drawing values from a marginal distribution (Bishop, 2006).

A popular method for the estimation of these probability-based models is that of maximum likelihood (ML) using the well-known EM algorithm. Recall that the EM algorithm is a general optimization routine typically employed for the treatment of incomplete data, but has been found to be especially valuable for fitting mixture models in cluster analysis, consisting of the E-step and M-step in its iteration. The E-step (expectation) and M-step (maximization) are iteratively executed to convergence to determine optimal parameters, where in the end posterior probabilities are estimated and a probabilistic model is obtained with soft assignments in place of hard assignments of cases to clusters. It turns out that special cases of the EM algorithm are equivalent to a soft version of the k-means algorithm, where the representative distances are used to define soft EM assignment probabilities (Aggarwal, 2015).

14.12.1 Model Selection for Clustering Solutions

At first glance, model selection in a cluster analysis mixture model environment might be performed by simply maximizing the marginal likelihood, or more specifically, its logarithm, and choosing the cluster solution for which the log-likelihood is the greatest for g1,g2, ...G solutions. However, formal tests for this are difficult to come by (McLachlan & Chang, 2004). A formal test of H0 : g = g0 vs. H1 : g > g0 (where g0 is the number of clusters under a null and alternative, respectively) is possible via the bootstrap, where bootstrap samples are drawn from a given fitted mixture model for a specific H0 of g = g0 components and the value of  − 2log λ is computed both for H0 and for H1 : g > g0. A p-value can then be obtained to learn whether adding another component is, in a statistical sense, worthwhile.

The likelihood we seek can also be approximated by the following BIC statistic,


$$BIC\left( g \right) = \log p\left( x \middle| g,{\hat{\theta}}_{g} \right) - \frac{v_{g}}{2}\log\left( n \right)$$
(14.14)

where θ̂g is the maximum-likelihood estimate of θg, vg is the number of estimated parameters associated with the model with g components (Baudry et al., 2010), and n is the sample size. Note that in this case, greater values for BIC are preferred over smaller values as the goal is to maximize the first part of the equation, log p(x|g,θ̂g). The penalty or correction factor is in the second term, $\frac{v_{g}}{2}\log\left( n \right)$, which includes the number of parameters vg required to obtain the given maximum for given g components. To the extent that more parameters vg are required over less, $\frac{v_{g}}{2}\log\left( n \right)$ will be increasingly large and hence we are subtracting an increasingly larger number from log p(x|g,θ̂g). Hence, as usual with BIC, more parsimonious models are typically preferred. Cut-off criteria here are generally discouraged and what denotes a “good” clustering solution will depend on the research area and user judgment. Note as well that there are different versions of BIC and related model selection statistics for mixed models in cluster analysis. What we have presented here is 528only one possibility. It is good practice to always verify how the given author or software is defining the particular model selection statistic featured before interpreting it.

The package mclust (Scrucca et al., 2023) can perform mixture modeling in R.

14.13 Cluster Validation

Having surveyed the most essential algorithms and approaches to cluster analysis which have included k-means, hierarchical, density-based, and mixture models, we close out this chapter with a brief discussion and recap of the cluster validation problem and revisit criteria for choosing the number of clusters.

In general, there are two types of validation one may perform on a cluster solution: 1) internal validation criteria, and 2) external validation criteria. The most preferred of these is, of course, external validation, since externally validating a cluster solution puts us back in touch with the empirical world akin to cross-validation of a model on test data helps us know how the model or algorithm will perform on data it has not yet seen. Internal validation approaches can be useful however when external validation criteria are not available or otherwise difficult to come by.

Internal methods of validation include sums of square distances to centroids, which is, as the name suggests, a measure of variability of cases from their corresponding centroids. A better than not cluster solution generally has a smaller sums of squares distance than a poorer solution. This measure can be used with k-means but not with density-based clustering such as DBSCAN. A ratio of the intracluster distance (distance within) to the intercluster distance (distance between) can also be computed (Aggarwal, 2015, p. 196) where smaller values than not are suggestive of a better solution. Other measures of internal validity include the silhouette coefficient as well as probabilistic measures. See Aggarwal (2015, pp. 196–197) for details. Tibshirani, Walther and Hastie (2001) have also proposed the aforementioned “gap” statistic which in some cases can be useful as well. The gap essentially compares total within-cluster variation for a given cluster solution (e.g., k-cluster solution in k-means) to what would be expected under a null distribution. An increasingly large gap is thus indicative of a more refined cluster solution.

For mixture models, as we have seen, log-likelihood statistics can be computed as well as BIC for helping determine the number of components to the mixture model. It should be noted that mixture models are of the few clustering methodologies that generally allow for significance tests to be performed since they are probabilistic. A device called the clustergram has also been proposed (see Fleischmann, 2023 for details).

External methods of cluster validation are most useful when knowledge of the actual clusters, sometimes called the ground truth, is known a priori or beforehand to performing the cluster analysis (such as in the case of clustering the iris data). The benefit of using external methods of validation over internal ones is that they are not biased by the particular algorithm doing the clustering (Aggarwal, 2015). To externally validate a cluster solution, something as simple as a confusion matrix, as the reader will recall from discriminant analysis, can be generated to learn how well the clustering solution “mimics” reality, or ground truth. While simple visualization of smaller confusion matrices may be sufficient, for especially larger confusion matrices measures of cluster purity can be computed as we did earlier when we clustered the iris data. As might be suspected, while these and other measures are useful, final decisions on the number of clusters usually come down to substantive interpretation and should be highly influenced by how pragmatic the cluster solution proves to be given the research or scientific context.529

14.14 Cluster Analysis and Beyond

In this chapter we surveyed the most common and foundational techniques of cluster analysis and data segmentation. These have included techniques such as k-means and other k-representatives, hierarchical and agglomerative approaches, density-based methods such as DBSCAN and mixture models. The reader should be aware that the current chapter has literally only scratched the surface when it comes to the literature on cluster analysis. New clustering techniques are continuously being developed in the statistical and machine learning literatures. However, as is the case with other methods surveyed in this book, if the reader is strong on the foundations of the techniques surveyed here, they will be in a reasonable position to generalize that knowledge to future techniques as they come across them.

Where to go from here? The extensions of the methods surveyed are almost limitless. The k-means clustering approach in this chapter can be extended to the kernel k-means algorithm. The DENCLUE algorithm is based on kernel-density estimation (Aggarwal, 2015). Ensemble methods can also be used in choosing a cluster solution, since different methods may provide conflicting solutions but combining them may paint a clearer picture. K-means is used in vector quantization related to data compression, often used in the analysis of images (see Bishop, 2006, p. 428 for details).

Cluster analysis can also be applied to categorical data, but with more difficulty; k-modes clustering is one option for categorical analysis. A hierarchical algorithm that has been found useful for categorical data is that of ROCK, which stands for Robust Clustering Algorithm for Categorical Attributes. See Aggarwal (2015) for details. Semi-supervised methods of cluster analysis are also available.

Other options for cluster analysis include spectral clustering which features an eigen analysis of a similarity matrix (Aggarwal, 2015) as well as biclustering which involves clustering rows or columns of a data matrix. See Murray (2022, p. 731) for details.

15 Artificial Neural Networks and Deep Learning

DOI: 10.4324/9781003376941-18

Throughout much of this book, we have surveyed and previewed neural networks while in the midst of discussing other techniques. This was done intentionally to illustrate and emphasize the extent to which other models could be understood as related or even as special cases of the more general neural network design. Indeed, this was one of the major objectives of this book, to “demystify” neural networks and other models by relating them to similar methods. As with any new statistical or machine learning model the reader may come across, it is helpful, in fact virtually essential in understanding them to relate them to other techniques. This is one reason why introductory books and courses on statistics and machine learning should emphasize foundations at the expense of surveying every method or algorithm under the sun. If students properly learn foundations, they are then in a good position to generalize and extend on that knowledge as needed later in their careers. Without a grounding in foundations, however, one risks not only misunderstanding additional methods, one also risks misusing and misinterpreting those same methods. Foundations are always the key to a good education.

In this chapter, we finally arrive at the full neural network and unpack it in its full generality. In our treatment, our hope is that the reader will appreciate more fully how neural networks are related to other statistical procedures but also why they have essentially revolutionized data analysis in the last 20–30 years. We begin the chapter with a brief survey of the motivation behind the rise of neural networks. We then introduce what a neural network actually is, emphasizing that even a simple linear regression can be regarded as a simple single-layer feedforward neural network. Based on this foundation, we then inspect more closely the nature of activation functions, a concept that is central to neural networks, surveying different types of activation functions and differentiating between saturating vs. non-saturating functions. We then generalize the feedforward network to the multilayer perceptron, which is the most common neural network in use today. Incidentally, in our discussion of neural networks we do not strongly distinguish between what is a neural network vs. what is a perceptron, and at times use the terms interchangeably. However, due to their history, the term perceptron is usually reserved for neural networks having discontinuous step-function nonlinearities as hidden units (Bishop, 2006) while classic neural networks are typically understood to have continuous nonlinearities in the hidden units. So long as this distinction is appreciated, there is no harm in using the terms interchangeably as authors sometimes do.

15.1 The Rise of Neural Networks: Original Motivation

Artificial neural networks are often what first comes to mind when we think of modern machine learning. The origins of machine learning as it pertains to artificial neural networks dates back to at least psychologist Rosenblatt and his work on the human nervous system, developing a machine for recognizing the letters of the alphabet. This “machine,” he called a perceptron. The 532McCulloch-Pitts neuron was featured in the seminal publication “A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity” in 1943, which is often considered to be one of the initial “seeds” of the artificial intelligence movement that is in full bloom today. Abraham (2002) details the historical origins of this important publication as well as the contributors to it. Beginning in the 1930s, the mathematical description of the brain was becoming an important topic and these pioneers were of the earliest to apply mathematics in developing such networks.

Drawing on Turing’s work at the time, which was itself groundbreaking, McCulloch and Pitts reasoned that the task of computation could be described logically in a finite number of steps, and that Turing’s “machine” could be perceived as a “logic machine” (Abraham, 2002). Of course, from today’s perspective, these developments are obvious as key contributions to the modern algorithm and discipline of machine learning more widely, but at the time these realizations were quite novel. As well summarized by Abraham (2002):

What distinguished the McCulloch-Pitts neural network from previous concepts of networks was its basis in axioms and definitions, and their use of such axioms to construct a logical calculus of the relations between neurons … McCulloch’s and Pitts’s goal was to represent the functional relationships between neurons in terms of Boolean logic: to embody the mental function of reasoning in the actual physiology of the brain.

(pp. 19–20)

The classic McCulloch-Pitts neuron is drawn in Figure 15.1 where x1…xp are inputs and where each input has a value of 0 indicating “off” or 1 indicating “on”; $S = {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{p}x_{j}}$ represents the sum of the inputs, a total excitation of the neuronal connections.

The total for S is then compared to a threshold value, T. If S ≥ T, the output is 1 and the neuron fires, which means it transmits the signal to Y. Otherwise, Y is 0 and the neuron does not fire. This is known as a threshold logic, or in neurology, the all-or-none principle which was thought to govern how neurons behave. Mathematically, this can be represented using the heavyside function, which is nothing more than a step function having values “1” if the neuron fires and “0” otherwise, that is,


$$f\left( x \right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {1,\,\,\,\,\, x \geq 0} \\ {0,\,\,\,\,\, x < \, 0} \\ \end{array} \right.$$
(15.1)

which when plotted, looks like that in Figure 15.2.533

Contrary to what most believe about McCulloch and Pitts’ early intentions, they themselves did not hold too strongly to this all-or-none binary principle and acknowledged that the process could be continuous as well rather than only binary (Abraham, 2002). It is also worth noting that McCulloch and Pitts recognized from the outset that their neuronal model was likely not an exact representation of neuronal function. As noted by Abraham:
