Their goal in the paper was not to present a factual description of neurons, but rather to design “fictitious nets” composed of neurons whose connections and thresholds are unaltered … They noted emphatically that they were not arguing that any “formal” equivalence between their nets can be part of a “factual explanation” … in no way did McCulloch and Pitts claim their model was a true description of known networks.

(pp. 20–21)

In this early depiction, or shall we say “idealization” of the nature of neuronal transmission, there are no adjustable parameters or weights (Izenman, 2008, p. 321). That is, each of x1, x2, ..., xp are not weighted by scalars but instead are simply summed, and if that sum exceeds a given threshold, then the signal is activated. To forecast further developments of the neuron and to be even more general, we could say that x1, x2, ..., xp are implicitly weighted, but by scalars of one for each input. However, these weights are not adjustable, and hence as noted by Izenman (2008), they were not a sufficient model for biological systems to “learn.” Forecasting to later developments up to the modern day neural network, it is the adjustable nature of these scalars that will constitute learning in modern neural networks. Of course, this idea of “adjustable scalars” is nothing new since virtually all statistical models beginning with regression in the 1890s featured adjustable weights and scalars. Adjusting the weights based on learning from the data is what statistical modeling, or statistical learning, has always been about since its inception. Optimizing weights is what learning actually is, from a statistical point of view.534

Hence, though the McCulloch and Pitts neuron was not thought to “mimic” brain activity exactly, it was a pretty good start and first stab at mathematically representing the communication between neurons. Computational advances would have to take place before one could seriously think of modeling neuronal activity. In the brain, there are approximately 86 billion neurons, many of which are interconnected and can stimulate other neurons (Cheng & Titterington, 1994). To mimic the parallel processing of neurons, parallel processing in computing power would have to arrive in full, which would have to wait until the 1980s. It is the computer that provides the capacity for neural networks and many other statistical and machine learning methods to actually become pragmatic for use. However, the mathematics underlying these and other models is distinct from computation. Mathematical studies of the perceptron continued with Rosenblatt (1959) but it was Novikoff (1963) who became more widely known for providing the conditions for convergence of the perceptron.

In the early McCulloch-Pitts neuron, though input values were summed and then subjected to a threshold “activation” function, none of the inputs were weights nor were they adjustable. Hence, there was no way, from a modern point of view, for the neuron to actually “learn.” At the time, regression models had long been on the scene since the 1890s and featured adjustable weight parameters.

15.2 Rosenblatt’s Perceptron

Rosenblatt aimed to improve the MC neuron which meant applying weights to the inputs. His ideas were influenced by Donald Hebb’s book in 1949 called The Organization of Behavior (Hebb, 2002). The book conceptualized memory traces via sets of connected neurons which help determine future behavior. Such connections were referred to as Hebb synapses. As Izenman (2008) notes, Hebb’s book was a significant development in behavioral neuroscience even if its findings have been largely overturned since its writing. Hebb’s ideas motivated a large body of work.

Rosenblatt was not convinced that most neural connections were random and that cell assemblies could self-generate within a purely homogeneous mass of neurons. He believed instead that he could improve upon Hebb’s work and constructed a “minimally constrained” system he called the perceptron (Rosenblatt, 1958, 1962). A perceptron is nothing more than a McCulloch-Pitts neuron but now with adjustable connection weights. The magnitude of the weights communicates the strength of the connection. The perceptron is hence more flexible than the aforementioned MP neuron.

In Rosenblatt’s perceptron, depicted in Figure 15.3 (right), we see the extension of the MC neuron (left):535

Recall that for the MP neuron, the neuron either fired or did not fire subject to the threshold or heavyside function (e.g., +1, −1). Rosenblatt’s perceptron is similar to the MP neuron, but with one crucial difference; the inputs xi are now associated with “connection weights,” β1 ⋅  ⋅  ⋅ βp, where positive weights βp> 0 are excitatory synapses, and negative weights βp< 0 are inhibitory synapses. These weights could then be summed to obtain the overall action of the neuron or the strength of the connection (Izenman, 2008, p. 322).

Does all this sound familiar? Of course it does. It sounds very much like regression analysis where β1 ⋅  ⋅  ⋅ βp are simply partial regression weights. As with the MP neuron, the sum of values in Rosenblatt’s perceptron is computed and then subjected to the threshold binary logic. The difference, of course, is that the sum this time consists of weighted values of xi, that is, $S = {\sum\limits_{j}\beta_{j}}x_{j}$. Thus, it is easy to see that the MP neuron is a special case of the perceptron where, as previously mentioned, β1 ⋅  ⋅  ⋅ βp are all understood to be unity such that


$$S = {\sum\limits_{j}\beta_{j}}x_{j} = {\sum\limits_{j}\left( 1 \right)}x_{j} = {\sum\limits_{j}x_{j}}$$

or other fixed constant. A final component to the perceptron is the inclusion of what is known in neural networks as a bias element, β0, which is nothing more than the familiar intercept in regression.

15.3 Big Picture Overview of Machine Learning and Neural Networks

Having surveyed the McCulloch-Pitts neuron and Rosenblatt’s perceptron, we now consider neural networks in greater generality. First and foremost, in its most general and wide interpretation, machine learning can be said to be about function approximation. Of course, the problem of approximating functions was not at all “new” at the time machine learning arose since scientists and mathematicians had been working on function approximation in one way or another since at least the Greeks. Even the derivative in calculus is a way of approximating a nonlinear function with one that is linear, which is the tangent to the curve. The integral can also be said to be an approximation to the area under a curve. The Greeks’ method of exhaustion in approximating the integral was just that, an exercise in approximation theory. Indeed, approximation in mathematics is an ancient concept and one that in one form or another has been applied countless times over history.

What was new, however, with regard to neural networks, were the algorithms and methods advanced to accomplish such function approximation. The infamous backpropagation algorithm, which is central to modern neural networks, actually had its origins in the 1960s, but was only fully recognized in the 1980s and constituted a major step in the advancement of function approximation and hence neural networks as well. Deep neural networks are thought to have originated in the mid-1980s (Dechter, 1986). What made these networks “deep” was the idea of layering of networks, that of including more than a single layer in the given neural network. Essentially, this meant that one could approximate the approximation of a function and do this iteratively through the chain of layers. By the mid-1990s, Cortes and Vapnik (1995) introduced the support-vector network, which showed great promise when compared to more traditional methods. This work initiated further work in machine learning.

More modernly, neural networks are increasingly popular and are used in addressing very meaningful and complex applied problems such as self-driving cars, detecting financial fraud, medical diagnoses, among many others. Why is this the case? What makes neural networks so attractive to practitioners, perhaps more so than any other statistical or machine learning technique? Alpaydin (2020) nicely summarizes their appeal:536

Deep learning methods are attractive mainly because they need less manual interference. We do not need to craft the right features or suitable basis functions or kernels, or worry about optimizing the exact network architecture. Once we have the data – and these days we have “big” data – and sufficient computation available, we just wait and let the learning algorithm discover by itself all that is necessary.

(p. 315)

Kroese et al. (2020) also do a nice job of contextualizing machine learning algorithms relative to the previously discussed early (and perhaps in some cases, overly ambitious) origins that sought to mimic neuronal activity:

The attempts at building efficient machine learning algorithms by mimicking the functioning of the human brain have been as unsuccessful as the attempts at building flying aircraft by mimicking the flapping of birds’ wings. Instead, many effective machine algorithms have been inspired by age-old mathematical ideas for function approximation.

(Kroese et al., 2020, p. 324)

15.3.1 What Is a Neural Network? Minimizing the Hype

Neural networks can become very complex, but in understanding just what is a neural network, it is helpful, as is true with all statistical methods surveyed in this book, to strip them down to their most basic elementary level, akin to explaining the nature of an algorithm with an example as something as simple as long division. The power in understanding, in general, is that of coming across a term or concept that you believe must be very complex, then realizing you already know what it is through deeper examination and reminders of simpler examples and prototypes with which one is already familiar. Indeed, this has been the pedagogical approach adopted throughout this book. As we will discuss with reference to neural networks, in a strong sense, we already know what they are because we have already surveyed models that we will find to be extremely similar to them. Indeed, as remarked by Sarle (1994) regarding the relatively early days of neural networks,

NN [neural network] researchers routinely reinvent methods that have been known in the statistical or mathematical literature for decades or centuries, but they often fail to understand how these methods work.

(p. 1)

Perhaps a bit extreme and exaggerated, Sarle’s argument does have some merit. Neural networks are their own methodology, but they do hold equivalencies (or near equivalences) to other methods under specific special case conditions. Our goal here is to strip them down to their essential constituents to learn and appreciate what is actually there instead of getting lost in the verbiage and hype of their jargon. The jargon and fanciful statements made about neural networks are useful for marketing them, but as one who wishes to truly understand them, the reader must truly seek to comprehend what is going on, as it were, under the hood.

15.3.2 Neural Networks Are Composite Functions

First and foremost, a neural network could be as simple as a linear regression model, or as complex as several nonlinear models. A neural network can also be nonparametric. One reason why neural networks are often referred to as “deep” learning is simply because they take model functions of 537functions. The “depth” is in the layering of what are referred to as hidden layers. Multiple levels of composition are what neural networks are all about (Goodfellow et al., 2016).

As a very simple example of so-called “depth,” consider the function f(x) = x2 which is that of a parabola. The function $g\left( f\left( x \right) \right) = \sqrt{x^{2}}$ is more complex and deeper since it arises as a result of taking a function of the first function. That is, the outside function g(x) is applied to the inside function f(x), which constitutes a composite function, in our case, the square root of x-squared. Shallow neural networks typically contain only a single hidden layer with only a few nodes. A deep network consists of several layers with many nodes, each of which might range in complexity. In a deep network, at each hidden layer we are taking (typically) relatively complex functions of prior layers. As we increasingly take functions of functions, the network is learning characteristics of the features at an increasingly more complex level of abstraction, capitalizing on even the smallest of discriminators that will help better predict the output. These often include nonlinear and interacting relationships on the journey from input to output.

Because of their complexity, neural networks have often been called “black boxes” as a result of the numerous nonlinear and interacting elements that are not explicit (Yosinski et al., 2015). That is, neural networks may indeed perform well under many circumstances, but their “black box” nature prevents us from knowing exactly why. This is one of the drawbacks to these networks, in contrast to other techniques such as regression where one can obtain a listing of partial regression coefficients in an attempt to evaluate the relative performance of predictors in a model. A neural network typically does not provide such precise individual variable performance information, and in some cases, this is understandable and for good reason; the number of parameters modeled in a neural network can be upward of over 50 million and hence attempting to understand how those parameters relate to one another is a gargantuan, and most likely, impossible task. Efforts to better understand the performance of neural networks via sophisticated visualization techniques is an ongoing area of research that may assist in “decoding” the black box of these networks and untangling their interacting, nonlinear components (Yosinski et al., 2015).

We can thus far then sum up the fundamental property of neural networks, which holds that neural networks, at their ultimate core, are combinations of combinations, that is, they are composite functions. For now, we characterize them as composite functions without any further constraints such as nonlinearity or linearity for the reason that neural networks need not be nonlinear in nature. As we will see, they are often nonlinear, such that they can transform nonlinear inputs into more linearly separable abstract features (Dubey et al., 2022), but the key point is that they need not be nonlinear.

Neural networks can be attractive approaches to data analysis due to their inherent complexity and nonlinearity possibilities which do not need to be modeled overtly and instead can be relegated to a “black box” approach. By taking composite functions as many times as desired, the network becomes “deep” as it learns more about the variables in the model and their interactions at successively deeper levels of abstraction. While neural networks usually feature the modeling of nonlinearity, at a technical level, a neural network can still be linear.

To understand the nature of a neural network, it is best to begin with the simplest case of such networks – the feedforward neural network with a single layer, which as we will see, the simple linear regression model can be considered a special case.538

15.4 Single-Layer Feedforward Neural Network

We begin with the simplest example of a neural network, which is a single-layer feedforward network, or sometimes called the single-unit perceptron, illustrated in Figure 15.4.

The network is called a feedforward neural network for the reason that information “flows” (in necessarily a mathematical sense only) from input to output and there are no reverse feedback loops. When a network contains feedback paths, it is usually referred to as a recurrent neural network (Goodfellow, 2016).

In Figure 15.4, we see that all inputs, x1 through xp, are weighted by β1 through βp, where a bias term, β0 is also added, which is the familiar intercept term in classic regression. The inputs x1 through xp are nothing more than observed variables as we would have in a model such as multiple regression (as opposed to “latent” ones as we encountered in structural equation modeling, for instance). In actuality, what we have in Figure 15.4 is in effect the familiar multiple regression model where yi is nothing more than a function of an intercept βo and a set of weighted predictors, βixi:


$$y_{i} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{p}{\beta_{o} + \beta_{i}}}x_{i}$$

Why call it a neural network if it is simply a multiple regression model? In this most simple of situations, we do not have to. However, the benefit of doing so is the gateway to understanding neural networks in their full generality. The model in Figure 15.4 is a multiple regression only because the implied activation function is an identity function. A multiple linear regression does not allow us to change the nature of the activation function. This is where neural networks become more general than the classic multiple regression model. In neural networks, we will be free to choose activation functions more complex than the identity function that is naturally implied or implicit in the multiple regression framework.

Activation functions are central to neural networks, and as we will see later, can be chosen from a variety of possibilities. However, as we have said, if we choose the identity function in this case, the neural network reduces to that of a multiple regression. Recall an identity function is the following:539


f(x) = x

which reads what you put into the equation you get out; there is no transformation at all on the input variable. Had we chosen a different activation function, perhaps a more complex nonlinear one, then we would have no longer had a simple or multiple regression and would have had a more complex neural network. For instance, instead of taking the identity function, we could have instead taken the log of the function as one example,


$$\begin{array}{l} {y_{i} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{p}{\beta_{o} + \beta_{i}}}x_{i}} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\, = \log\left( {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{p}{\beta_{o} + \beta_{i}}}x_{i} \right)} \\ \end{array}$$

making the activation function no longer an identity function but instead a logarithmic one. Activation functions are what give neural networks their life. For example, a perceptron with a threshold activation function, that is, a “yes” vs. “no” binary outcome,


$$f\left( x \right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {1\,\,\,\,\, if\,\,\,\,\, x > \, 0} \\ {0\,\,\,\, otherwise} \\ \end{array} \right.$$

becomes a binary linear discriminant analysis and hence the perceptron in this case is imposing a familiar hyperplane. If the output is multi-valued and categorical, it becomes a multiple logistic function featuring a softmax activation function:


$$soft\text{max}\, f\text{(}x\text{)} = \frac{e^{x_{i}}}{\sum\limits_{j}^{}e^{x_{j}}}$$
(15.2)

Neural networks essentially act as a type of parametric/nonparametric regression model (more on this distinction later), which allows the user to model complex and often unknown nonlinear functional forms based on what the data have to say, rather than assuming a prior parametric form such as in the classic linear model. Be sure to note that this does not forbid us from assuming a functional form, but the point is that it does not require us to do so. This is why neural networks are often considered first and foremost, nonparametric. The parametric case in which prior assumptions are invoked is simply a special case of the larger nonparametric framework in which such assumptions are not advanced. If the relationship between inputs and outputs is known a priori to be linear, then typically a linear regression will usually outperform a neural network in terms of prediction (King, 1999).

How often do we know the exact functional form of a relationship? How many scientific phenomena actually follow perfect linear trends? As we have noted throughout this book, many phenomena are rather complex with unknown parametric forms, which is why so many machine learning techniques are nonparametric in nature allowing us to skip over the assumptions and get right to what the data have to say. That is, the algorithm learns from the data, not from our prior beliefs (theory) about the data or imposed (induction biased) parametric structures. Recall that we had said at the outset of this book that this was one of the distinguishing features made between classical statistics and the machine learning revolution, or perhaps even “rebellion.” Where classical statisticians have historically arrived at a problem with a priori functional forms and assumptions 540largely already imposed on their data, machine learning types became more interested in simply wanting to know what the data have to say. Classical statistics and machine learning approaches overlap a great deal, of course, but the emphasis and approach to problem-solving can differ somewhat, especially in the age of massively large data sets and tremendous computing power where making distributional assumptions may not seem as relevant as with the smaller samples of yesterday. Of course, there is not simply one or two things that distinguish these fields; they overlap a tremendous amount and each field benefits from the other. Much of machine learning, despite its advancements, has relied on the field of statistics to make such headwinds.

We have said that neural networks are all about activation functions. We now survey such functions in more detail.

15.5 What Is an Activation Function?

Activation functions are at the very core of neural networks. An activation function is basically, at its most foundational and rudimentary level, simply a function, often better understood in the context of the previously discussed composite function. A composite function, as we have seen and as the reader may recall from basic calculus, is a function of a function. In theory, we can layer as many of these composites as we like and iteratively take functions of functions of functions, and so on. That is,


f(x;θ) = fL(fL − 1(⋅⋅⋅(f1(x))⋅⋅⋅))
(15.3)

where in (15.3) θ is the parameter vector. The most “inside” function is that of f1(x). From there, we are iteratively taking functions of functions, where fL is the most “outside” function, followed next by fL − 1. This idea of taking composite functions is precisely the concept of what makes a neural network deep. To put this into context again, recall that linear regression can be conceived, from the most global perspective, as a neural network. It is simply an elementary one that is linear, and for which the composite function is that of the identity function. That is, though we do not operationalize regression this way, we could in the way of composite functions by identifying f1(x) as the regression function and fL − 1 as the identity function where fL − 1 = I(x). Hence, the trivial neural network would be


$$\begin{array}{l} {f\left( x;\theta \right) = f_{L - 1}\left( f_{1}\left( x \right) \right)} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = I\left( f_{1}\left( x \right) \right)} \\ \end{array}$$

where in the above, fL − 1 = I. When fL − 1 is, for instance, a nonlinear function, then we have a more traditional representation and application of a neural network. This is the typical rationale given to activation functions in the literature, that they allow nonlinearity to be incorporated into the network. However, an activation function need not necessarily be nonlinear to still make it a proper neural network. Many writers require a neural network to be nonlinear in order to define it as a proper neural network and the reader should be aware of this.

The use of a composite function in neural networks, as we will see, also accounts for why backpropagation works so well, since it is based on the chain rule of differentiation in calculus, which as the reader may recall is all about differentiating composite functions. Hence, complex and as powerful as neural networks can become, they are all based on these very fundamental and elementary foundations.541

15.5.1 Activation Functions Do Not “Activate” Anything

As we have said throughout this book, many statistical terms unwillingly denote “movement” or “action” of some kind. To one who is knowledgeable of how these terms are being used, no harm is done. However, to the newcomer, the use of such power and action words can be tremendously misleading. Indeed, recall that we earlier in the book discussed how mediation and moderation in no way necessarily implied movement or action. They are simply names for partitioning variance in different ways. If the substantive context of the problem implies movement or action, then that’s an entirely different matter. The point, however, is that statistical modeling, whatever the kind, could never on its own imply such movement no matter how “sexy” of terms used to describe the modeling.

The same can be said of activation functions. The outside function in g(f(x)) is not “activating” f(x) in any way other than being applied, mathematically, to f(x). Yet, the word “activating” seems to suggest a more important role, a physical movement of sorts, a more “exciting” story! Indeed, activation functions are sometimes referred to as transfer functions, but this again is hyped-up jargon, as activation functions, by themselves, do not “transmit” anything. A mathematical function, on its own, cannot physically transmit a thing! Now, neurologists might claim that neurons in the brain might transfer information, but that is a scientific matter, not solely a statistical one. Neural networks may have originally been influenced by neuronal activity as a paradigm, but in the end they are simply mathematical abstract functions. As was the case with so-called “causal modeling” in our survey of structural equation modeling, if a neural network is applied to model the electrical activity of the brain or some other presumed physical activity, then the word “transfer” may indeed make more sense. But such is not a property of the statistical model; it is a property of the neural activity.

Bounded activation functions (e.g., 0 to 1 or −1 to 1) are also often referred to as squashing functions (Sarle, 1994). For instance, as we will see, the sigmoid function has this property of “squashing” values into a bounded interval (Lederer, 2021). Again, this is not meant to imply any physical action, but only to communicate that the activation function has the effect of outputting values within a bounded interval. Activation functions need also not be consistent across each output and different activation functions can be used for each.

15.5.2 Types of Activation Functions

As we have seen, we are unlikely to simply use identity functions and will prefer to use more complex functions, most of which will be nonlinear in order to capture complex nonlinear aspects of the data or processes we are seeking to model. The most popular activation functions in use in neural networks are, generally, the logistic, tanh, and ReLu (Lederer, 2021), however novel functions have recently been proposed, including softplus, elu, selu, and swish. We survey some of these activation functions shortly. Lederer (2021) provides an exceptional review of these functions and many more. According to Lederer (2021), softsign and ReLu should be the preferred activation functions in practice. The softsign function has been found to have computational advantages over tanh due to its simplicity (Lederer, 2021).

There are some important things to consider in choosing an activation function, however. Indeed, the choice of an activation function can have rather dramatic effects on the performance of a neural network, and hence how to choose a “good” activation function has been ongoing research in the neural network community for years with entire literatures devoted to the subject. As noted by Lederer (2021), “the literature contains an entire zoo of different activation functions, and arguments for and against specific activation functions are often based on heuristics and anecdotal 542evidence” (p. 2). Also, predicting which activation function will work best for a given situation can be very difficult to impossible (Goodfellow, 2016).

15.5.3 Saturating vs. Non-Saturating Activation Functions

Ideally, activation functions should be differentiable at most points and generally also increasing. Beyond that, we have the choice to select from a wide range of activation functions, some more preferable than others depending on the context. One very important distinguishing feature of activation functions is whether they are saturating or non-saturating. Non-saturating activation functions are generally preferred over saturating ones. The requirements for activation functions are not absolute, however, which is to say these requirements are flexible to some extent and not always preferable in all contexts.

A saturating activation function implies that for large inputs, the function asymptotes at a constant value, such as 0 or 1. This is a characteristic of the logistic sigmoid activation function (Dubey et al., 2022; Murphy, 2022),


$$Logistic\,\, Sigmoid\left( x \right) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{- x}}$$
(15.4)

which saturates (or “asymptotes”) at values of 0 and 1 (Dubey et al., 2022). That is,


$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\left( \frac{1}{1 + e^{- x}} \right) = 0$$

and


$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow + \infty}\left( \frac{1}{1 + e^{- x}} \right) = 1$$

These functions essentially “squeeze” or “squash” the input to be within upper and lower bounds. Unfortunately, as we will soon discuss, saturating activation functions will generate a vanishing gradient problem, where the gradient of the objective function becomes very close to 0, and hence updating weights becomes virtually impossible. The tanh function,


$$\tanh\left( x \right) = \frac{e^{x} - e^{- x}}{e^{x} + e^{- x}}$$
(15.5)

also quite popular, also squashes the inputs, but this time between −1 and 1 (Dubey et al., 2022).

Hence, one of the keys to training very deep neural networks is to select activation functions that are non-saturating (Murphy, 2022). A non-saturating activation function is one that does not asymptote at a constant value and hence typically goes to infinity. That is,


$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f\left( x \right) = \infty$$

The rectified linear unit (or “ReLU” for short) is one such non-saturating activation function,543


$${Re}LU\left( x \right) = \max\left( 0,x \right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {x,\,\,\,\,\, if\,\,\,\,\, x \geq 0} \\ {0,\,\,\,\,\, otherwise} \\ \end{array} \right.$$
(15.6)

It is non-saturating because the range of the function is from 0 to positive infinity, that is, [0,∞) as we can see from Figure 15.5 featuring a few competing activation functions.

We see from Figure 15.5 that the sigmoid function is saturating, squeezing input values to be within [0, 1]. The tanh function is saturating for similar reasons, this time squeezing inputs to be within [−1, 1]. The arctan, another activation function, is also saturating. It is easy to see that the ReLU function is non-saturating, being constant at 0 for values equal to or less than 0 and increasing linearly for values greater than 0 and hence still allowing for updates to occur even for large values of x (Alpaydin, 2020). However, for negative inputs, the vanishing gradient problem still rears its ugly head (Dubey et al., 2022).

A saturating activation function essentially “squeezes” the input values to be within specified bounds (e.g., 0, 1). A non-saturating activation function does not “bind” the input in this way and instead allows the function to typically go to infinity. When it comes to choosing an activation function for a neural network, non-saturating ones are often preferred over saturating ones.

Incidentally, all of these functions can be easily plotted in software. For instance, a sigmoid activation function in Python (plot not shown) can be generated quite simply as:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import math
x = np.linspace(-20, 20, 100)
y = 1/(1 + np.exp(-x))
plt.plot(x, y)
plt.xlabel(“x”)
plt.ylabel(“Sigmoid(X) Activation Function”)
plt.show()
544

15.5.3.1 The Problem with ReLU

The ReLU function, also commonly known as the positive-part function or ramp function due to its shape, is one of the most common activation functions used in neural networks. The positive part of the function is merely the identity function, linear with slope equal to 1. It is this near linearity of ReLU that in part, makes ReLU attractive in the sense that it can allow for easy optimization using gradient-based methods as is the case with most linear models (Goodfellow et al., 2016). The negative part of the function is constant at a value of 0. A look at the ReLU function more closely reveals these characteristics (Figure 15.6).

We can see that the ReLU “cuts out” values less than 0 but activates values greater than 0 in a steady “ramp” fashion. One benefit of the ReLU function is that the function and its derivatives are very easily implemented at a relatively low computational cost (Lederer, 2021).

For all of its advantages, there is nonetheless a weakness with ReLU. The problem is if initialized weights are large and negative such may translate into many ReLU nodes being inactive during a big part of the training process, which can make it difficult or impossible for the algorithm to learn increasingly complex models. That is, there is no information going into the network for values less than 0 since they are set to equal 0 by default of the way the function defines negative values. This is known in the literature as the dead ReLU problem. It is a version of the vanishing gradient problem (Dubey et al., 2022; Lederer, 2021). Possible solutions to the problem include choosing a lower learning rate or replacing ReLU by leakyReLU, which we now discuss.545

15.5.3.2 LeakyReLU

The leakyReLU is given by (where weight a = 0.01 is featured)


$$L{Re}LU\left( x \right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {x,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, x \geq 0} \\ {0.01\left( x \right),\,\,\,\,\, x < 0} \\ \end{array} \right.$$
(15.7)

A comparison of ReLU vs. leakyReLU appears in Figure 15.7.

We see that instead of the function being equal to 0 for all values less than 0, as was the case for ReLU, leaky ReLU will simply equal some very small negative number instead of the constant zero. This translates to a small negative slope for values less than 0. Consequently, the range of leakyReLU is (−∞,∞) instead of [0,∞) as it is for ReLU. This allows for updates for values less than 0 and avoids the vanishing gradient problem (Alpaydin, 2020). As Dubey et al. (2022) note, a problem with leakyReLU is in determining the correct slope for negative inputs, as different slopes may be appropriate or most relevant for different types of problems. The parametric ReLU (PReLU) attempts to rectify this by considering negative inputs as a training parameter, however this can lead to overfitting. See Dubey et al. (2022) for details.

Another activation function that attempts to improve on the ReLU is the elu, or exponential linear unit, which is a smooth function and thus has an advantage over ReLU:


$$elu\left( x \right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {x,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, x \geq 0} \\ {\alpha\left( e^{x} - 1 \right),\,\,\,\,\, x < 0} \\ \end{array} \right.$$
(15.8)

In elu, α is a trainable hyperparameter in α(ex−1). While elu has shown positive results, its theoretical backing is lacking (Basirat & Roth, 2019). A variant of elu is selu, where the “s” stands for “scaled” and constrains the slope larger than one for positive inputs (Dubey et al., 2022; Lederer, 2021).

We could continue to detail a whole host of activation functions by looking at their algebraic functions, but it is perhaps most convenient to simply view the most common ones graphically as their graphs immediately tell more of their form than interpreting their algebraic counterparts will ever. In Figure 15.8 are a few of the more popular activation functions which include and extend on some we have surveyed thus far.546

15.5.4 Which Activation Function to Use?

As discussed at the outset of our review of activation functions, according to Lederer (2021), softsign and ReLU (or leakyReLU) should be the preferred activation functions in practice. According to Basirat and Roth (2019), most deep learning approaches use ReLU largely due to its simplicity and reliability. Izenman (2008) notes that algorithms that feature the tanh function generally tend to converge more rapidly than those featuring the logistic, however the tanh itself has been found to be computationally inefficient (Dubey et al., 2022). As discussed, the sigmoid and the tanh, originally motivated by the biological neuronal firing of the brain in the early days of neural nets (Dubey et al., 2022), suffer from the vanishing gradient problem (Basirat & Roth, 2019) due to the fact that they are squashing functions. Recall this is because the gradient becomes very close to 0, resulting in virtually no update in parameters during training. With ReLU, since the derivative of positive inputs is equal to one, the gradient cannot vanish.

There is an entire literature and specialization within machine learning and mathematics devoted to evaluating existing activation functions as well as proposing new ones. Recent work has also introduced the idea of learning/adaptive activation functions, which, as the name suggests, contain learnable parameters to exploit more of the data’s complexity. These include such activation functions as the Adaptive Piecewise Linear (APL), the swish, e-swish and more. Consult Dubey et al. (2022) for a thorough and excellent review of the strengths and weaknesses of a variety of non-adaptive and adaptive activation functions and who also give a series of recommendations regarding which activation functions to use under a variety of conditions. While ReLU is commonly a default choice, these authors also recommend the swish, mish, and PAU (Padé activation unit) to be tried for most problems. Of course, there is absolutely nothing wrong with trying out a variety of activation functions for any given problem. There is no theoretical “type I error rate” on activation functions that would restrict the user from trying out a handful, so long as the resulting network is ideally subjected to cross-validation.

15.6 The Multilayer Perceptron – A Deeper Look at Neural Networks

We have thus far considered a very simple and basic neural network such that when the activation function was an identity function, mimicked a multiple regression. We now consider a more complex neural network, one that is more representative of neural networks actually used in practice 547across scientific fields. The neural network we are about to discuss features a layer of hidden units over and above the single layer in the feedforward network surveyed earlier. The addition of one or more layers gives rise to the multilayer feedforward network, depicted in Figure 15.9.

As we will emphasize later when we compare neural networks to other statistical methods, the layering concept of a neural network, along with its depth, can be thought of as yet another basis expansion of the original inputs to the network (Hastie et al., 2009). However, these parameters are not imposed or a priori determined as in the basis expansion methods we surveyed earlier in the book (e.g., regression splines). Instead, they are arrived at by effectively learning from the data. This idea of depth in these networks was influenced historically by the ideas of connectionism, which essentially held that though one neuron may not be able to accomplish much on its own, several neurons acting together and interacting can possibly exhibit intelligent behavior (Goodfellow et al., 2016).

As we did with the single-layer network, we will unpack the multilayer network. In the network in Figure 15.9, a given hidden unit, hi, is equal to the sum of products of the inputs xi multiplied by the weights βi:


$$h_{i} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{p}{\beta_{i}x_{i}}}$$

The hidden layers in a multilayer feedforward network consist of variables arranged in successive layers, which are traditionally called nodes, neurons, or processing units (Izenman, 2008). Calling them “nodes” is probably the most general, as neurons and “processing units” implies something 548that mathematics, by itself, cannot do. We can see in Figure 15.9 that there are two layers at which computation takes place, the hidden layer and the output layer. There are four input nodes and two output nodes, and three nodes in the hidden layer. This network can be then specified for regression or classification. In a multiple regression, there is only one output variable yi, whereas in multivariate multiple regression there are many output variables yi....yn + 1. In a binary classification, there is only one output variable yi with values 0 or 1.

As was the case in the simpler neural network discussed earlier, an activation function is applied to the given hidden unit. That is, we take a function of the given hidden unit, which as we know by now that function is usually one that is nonlinear chosen from a set or family of prespecified activation functions. This is where, for instance, we could take the aforementioned logistic sigmoid,


$$Logistic\,\, Sigmoid\left( x \right) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{- x}}$$

or many other of the activation functions previously discussed. Simplified, as we move our way toward the output, that output is now a function of the hidden layer. That is, the output is a function of a function of the inputs:


$$f_{i} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}h_{i}}\left( \beta_{i}x_{i} \right)$$
(15.9)

where in (15.9), N is the number of hidden units, and βi is the weight from the hidden unit to output. The final step is the outputting of a function of fi,


$${\hat{y}}_{i} = g\left( f_{i} \right) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{- f_{i}}}$$
(15.10)

where we see now fi, that is, the inner function, takes the place of x in the sigmoid function. As we continue to move from layer to layer in the network, the concept of composite functions is very apparent. That is, neural networks continuously take functions of functions in arriving at their eventual final output.

15.7 Training Neural Networks

We have discussed the architecture of neural networks in some detail, but we have not yet surveyed how the weights in a neural network are optimized or trained. How are the weights in a neural network chosen? As with many statistical methods, they should be chosen in such a way as to maximize or minimize some function. The selection of the weights thus becomes a problem of optimization as has been the case in most other models surveyed in this book. That is, the “training” of the neural network consists of finding optimized weights similar to how we found optimal weights in linear regression using ordinary least-squares or discriminant analysis, for instance. “Training” a statistical or machine learning model means running the model through the data such that weights (or coefficients) are optimized by some criteria. In the past days of statistics, we fit models to data; today we train them in machine learning. Some of this terminology is simply due to a shift in zeitgeist. However, in a wide variety of statistical learning, the “learning part” is usually the updating of scalars in line with obtaining maxima or minima subject to some algorithm. That is, a big part of “learning” is simply optimization.549

15.7.1 Backpropagation and Minimizing Error Sums of Squares

To optimize a neural network, backpropagation (sometimes called error backpropagation) is typically employed. It should be emphasized that backpropagation is used to compute the gradient, while a gradient descent algorithm uses this computed gradient to perform the learning (Goodfellow, 2016). Hence, the backpropagation algorithm and gradient descent are used in conjunction with one another, not in place of each other. Backpropagation has also been called the delta rule (Hastie et al., 2009; Widrow & Hoff, 1960). The algorithm consists of two phases, the forward phase and the backward phase. Essentially, the forward phase provides an opportunity for the model to initially learn the weights based on the data; the backward phase gives the model a chance to “correct” or “improve” on the weight estimates based on feedback for how it performed in the forward phase. It is in this sense that neural networks learn, just as a human being learns from his or her errors (in studying statistics, for instance) and improves performance. This is why the popularization of the backpropagation algorithm in the 1980s was so important to neural networks. It would not be an exaggeration to say that the modern rise of neural networks is mostly related to the discovery of the backpropagation algorithm along with the computational power to handle increasingly large networks.

But what function shall the neural network optimize when doing the learning? While a number of functions can be minimized, one convenient and familiar function for continuous responses is that of minimizing error sums of squares with respect to the network’s connection weights,


$$E^{2} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}\left( y_{i} - {\hat{y}}_{i} \right)^{2}}$$
(15.11)

The extent to which E2 is minimized can also be used as a performance metric for the neural network. The backpropagation algorithm itself is an iterative gradient-based algorithm, using randomly chosen initial values for the weights and employing primarily the chain rule from calculus in conducting its optimization. Essentially, backpropagation features repeated application of the chain rule to compute and update weights in the network by differentiating relative to an error function (e.g., error sums of squares),


$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ij}} = \frac{\partial E}{\partial s_{i}}\frac{\partial s_{i}}{\partial net_{i}}\frac{\partial net_{i}}{\partial w_{ij}}$$
(15.12)

where E is the error function, wij are the weights from neurons j to i, that is, the elements we wish to optimize, si is the output, and neti is the weighted sum of the inputs for a given neuron i (Riedmiller & Braun, 1993, p. 586). The gradient $\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ij}}$ is then updated via


$$w_{ij}\left( t + 1 \right) = w_{ij}\left( t \right) - \varepsilon\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ij}}\left( t \right)$$
(15.13)

where t is the iteration and ε is the learning rate. That is, wij(t+1) denotes the weight wij at iteration t + 1, where wij(t) is the current weight at iteration t, from which we subtract550


$$\varepsilon\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ij}}\left( t \right)$$

which denotes the learning rate ε multiplied by the gradient $\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ij}}$ at time (iteration) t. We see there are two steps, one is computing the gradient, the other is updating the weights wijat (t+1). If the learning rate is set too small, it may take a longer time to train the neural network than if the learning rate is set at a larger value; if set too large, such may result in less than optimal solutions. Aggarwal (2015) suggests beginning with a relatively large weight then gradually reducing the weight as more optimal values are settled upon.

Another option is to use a momentum adaptation,


$$\Delta w_{ij}\left( t \right) = - \varepsilon\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ij}}\left( t \right) + \mu\Delta w_{ij}\left( t - 1 \right)$$
(15.14)

where μ is a momentum parameter (Riedmiller & Braun, 1993, p. 586) which serves as a direct scaling factor for the previous step (i.e., wij(t−1)). The effort to adapt weights took a big step with the work of Riedmiller and Braun (1993) who proposed resilient propagation, commonly known today as simply resilient backpropagation, which provides an improved adaptation process. Details of the algorithm are given in Riedmiller and Braun (1993) and Riedmiller (1994). Resilient backpropagation is what is used in the R package neuralnet that we will feature later in the chapter as a demonstration of neural networks using software. For much deeper details on how optimization works in the multilayer network, see Izenman (2008) or Warner and Misra (1996, pp. 288–289), who provide an excellent account and overview.

As noted, backpropagation helped neural networks “rise to fame” in the 1980s. The development of the backpropagation algorithm is primarily responsible for the relatively recent resurgence of interest in neural networks (Warner & Misra, 1996). The training of neural networks is a major challenge that requires both ingenuity and much experimentation. The algorithms for training neural networks with great depth are collectively referred to as deep learning methods.

Despite its success, there is no proof that the backpropagation algorithm always converges. Further, it can be a slow learner, its estimates may be unstable, and there may exist many local minima as the function being optimized is a nonconvex function of the model parameters (Bishop, 2006). Further, because backpropagation utilizes the chain rule, derivatives are multiplied which can cause problems of the gradient either vanishing or exploding (Alpaydin, 2020). Overfitting can also be a problem in backpropagation and attempts for it to converge can be addressed by early stopping as well as through other approaches we will soon discuss.

15.8 How Many Hidden Nodes and Layers to Include?

How many nodes and layers should a network have? This is an empirical question, and surprisingly continues to be an open question in the literature on neural networks. In general, the closer the approximation desired, the larger the number of hidden nodes required. In this sense, deep neural networks are usually preferred over shallow ones and empirical and theoretical evidence supports this. Yet at the same time, Ockham’s razor should be kept in mind, keeping the model as simple as possible while maintaining its ability to generalize well. Cross-validation can be used, as well as trial-and-error in determining the number of hidden nodes and layers. As we will see shortly when we discuss the universal approximation theorem, it can be shown that a multilayer perceptron with only a single hidden layer is a universal approximator. Such implies that a multilayer perceptron can model any suitably smooth function to any desired level of accuracy assuming a sufficient number of hidden units (Murphy, 2022).551

It should be emphasized as well that a feedforward neural network with linear activation functions and n layers is equivalent to a linear neural network without hidden layers. Hence, the idea of “adding layers” in this case does not increase the approximation “power” of a linear neural network at all, unlike for nonlinear neural networks. In this sense then, the nonlinearity of neural networks is essential when it comes to better approximating functions based on increasing hidden layers. This is one reason why neural networks are almost always described as nonlinear. However, formally, they need not necessarily be so. If the number of hidden units in a single-layer neural network is chosen to be smaller than the number of inputs and all activation functions are linear, then information is essentially lost in the dimension reduction, in which case the neural network would essentially mimic a principal components analysis (Bishop, 2006).

15.9 Overfitting in Neural Networks

Overfitting is a problem with neural networks perhaps more so than in any other technique. This is largely due to their complexity. It is very easy to design a quite complex network that will provide a reasonably good fit to one’s training data. However, as emphasized throughout this book, what is a good fit on the training data does not necessarily imply an equally good fit on test data. We have just discussed that the complexity of neural networks should be minimized, all else equal, as to avoid an unnecessarily complex network when a simpler one will garner the same or similar fit. Beyond that general principle, the question then is how to prevent overfitting? We survey some of the more common methods, though many more approaches can be found in the literature.

15.9.1 Early Stopping

One approach to preventing overfitting is to simply stop the model short of fully iterating. This is known as the early stopping solution to mitigating overfitting. The longer a network is trained, the more it capitalizes on noise or chance factors and thus fits the training data quite well, but at some point will increasingly generalize poorly to validation data. The complexity of the system is increased with training and hence generalizability suffers (Alpaydin, 2020). In other words, the network might fit really well on the training data, but error increases substantially on new data because, essentially, what the network was so “good” at on the training data past a certain point was in effect capitalizing on chance or random noise. The case study analogy once more works well here, such that the network becomes an “expert” on the current case, but the theory (i.e., in the form of optimized estimated weights) developed on that case does not do nearly as well predicting the outcome of new cases. If one purposely stops the network early from iterating fully, one can possibly mitigate overfitting.

15.9.2 Dropout Method

A second method to dealing with overfitting is that of the dropout approach, which prevents complex adaptation of the hidden units (Srivastava et al., 2014). The method purposely drops some of the units out on each iteration and hence each unit learns to perform well even if some other units are missing. This approach estimates what is known as a noisy version of the weights since dropping weights equates to adding noise to units. As a result of the method randomly dropping weights, it is generally referred to as a stochastic regularization technique. An excellent summary and implementation of the dropout method is provided in Srivastava et al. (2014).

A related solution to the dropout method is instead of randomly dropping weights, to instead equate (or in some forms of the method, encourage equality) some of the weights as a way of 552regularizing the model and discouraging overfitting. This solution is known as soft weight sharing (Bishop, 2006; Nowlan & Hinton, 1992). Details are in Bishop (2006, p. 269).

15.9.3 Regularized Network

A third approach to prevent, or at least reduce the possibility of overfitting is to introduce a regularization parameter, that is, a penalty function to shrink estimates similar to what is accomplished in ridge and lasso regression, for instance. One form of regularization used in neural networks is that of weight decay where a penalty term is added to the error function. As detailed in Hastie et al. (2009), if the error function for the parameter vector θ is R(θ), then the error function plus penalty is equal to


R(θ) + λJ(θ)
(15.15)

where J(θ) is some penalty (e.g., see Hastie et al., 2009) and λ a tuning parameter. It is easy to see that as λ increases for J(θ) ≠ 0, R(θ) will increase which implies the error of the model will be larger than not and weights will be shrunk toward 0. For regularized least-squares specifically, the error function becomes (Bishop, 2006),


$$\begin{array}{l} {E\left( w \right) = R\left( \theta \right) + \lambda J\left( \theta \right)} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = E\left( w \right) + \frac{\lambda}{2}w^{T}w} \\ \end{array}$$

where w is the weight vector and which is an example of L2 regularization.

So, what could be the benefit to increasing error? As was the case with ridge and lasso regression, imposing a penalty has the effect of shrinking weights toward 0 and hence reduces overfitting. Both L1 and L2 are possible for neural networks just as they were for ridge and lasso regression. For further details, consult Hastie et al. (2009), who also provide a powerful demonstration of regularizing a neural network through weight decay (pp. 402–403). The weights used to initialize a network can be a factor in weight decay as well. Initial weight values should be small, random, and typically in the neighborhood of [−0.01, 0.01] (Alpaydin, 2020) from a uniform distribution, though much larger intervals have also been proposed.

15.10 Types of Networks

As we saw when we considered the simpler neural network, the multilayer network is likewise not that far removed from traditional regression. In fact, multilayer networks are analogous to nonlinear regression models for continuous responses and to discriminant analysis models for binary outcomes (Sarle, 1994).

A fully connected network is one in which all input nodes are connected to the nodes in the first hidden layer, and all nodes in the first hidden layer are connected to all nodes in the second hidden layer, and so on. If some of the connections are missing, then we have a partially connected network. By setting or constraining some of the weights to zero, we can obtain a partially connected network from a wider and more general fully connected network. This idea of constraining parameters is familiar by now; most models constrain select parameters either implicitly or explicitly. In general, in any statistical model we entertain, parameters can be fixed or constrained to particular values, or even more generally chosen to not be estimated at all. Usually, substantive theory and prior knowledge of the research situation will help determine which weights to fix. Sometimes 553fixing parameters is a necessity to aid in identifying the model as in structural equation modeling. The important point for now is to appreciate the similarity of fixing weights in a neural network to that of fixing weights in other statistical models. It is an entirely general concept which simultaneously frees up degrees of freedom (such as we saw in regression splines when constraining the solution to have no jumps or discontinuities).

The neural networks we have surveyed thus far are all examples of what are known as feedforward neural networks such that the “flow” of the network is from one end to the other (typically from left to right). However, there are many other types of networks. In fact, feedforward networks can be viewed as special cases of recurrent networks, where recurrent networks are not necessarily always forward-feeding and instead allow output from some nodes to influence nearby or subsequent inputs to those very nodes. Recurrent neural networks are often used in the processing of sequential data (Goodfellow et al., 2016). Convolutional networks are yet another type of network which typically feature the use of kernels and are usually subjected to regularization to mitigate overfitting. Such networks are often used in image and video recognition to help narrow in on specific or local regions in the case of an image, for example, and combine local features (e.g., the smaller details of what in totality make up a vehicle called a “truck”) to generate compound features (e.g., identifying the object as a truck instead of a car). Both recurrent and convolutional networks are well beyond the scope of the current text, and can become quite complex. For a good introduction, see Goodfellow et al. (2016) or Bishop (2006).

15.11 The Universal Approximation Theorem: The Appeal of Neural Networks

We have discussed thus far the architecture of neural networks, but we have not yet discussed why, theoretically, they are so appealing. Why bother with building a neural network? The key motivation behind neural networks, just as is the wish for any statistical method, is that they are remarkably good at approximating functions. This concept is housed in the universal approximation theorem and is the key to understanding the more theoretical side of neural networks. The theorem, as stated by Hornik (1991, p. 359) word for word, is the following:

Standard multilayer feedforward networks with as few as one hidden layer using arbitrary squashing functions are capable of approximating any Borel measurable function from one finite dimensional space to another to any desired degree of accuracy, provided sufficiently many hidden units are available. In this sense, multilayer feedforward networks are a class of universal approximators.

This is a very profound and remarkable result! For instance, Cybenko (1989) has shown that a two-layer feedforward neural network with a sufficient number of hidden units can approximate any continuous function to any degree of accuracy. The approximation theorem also holds for a great deal of activation functions except for the polynomial (Bishop, 2006). See Hornik (1991) for approximation capacities for arbitrary bounded and nonconstant activation functions.

Typically, the closer the approximation desired, to reiterate, the larger the number of hidden nodes required (Izenman, 2008), but the key point to emphasize is that we are able in the first place to approximate functions as closely as we would like using neural networks. The theorem, due to Kolmogorov (1957) tells us that any continuous high-dimensional map can be represented as the function composition of much simpler one-dimensional maps. Again, this is a very powerful idea, as Izenman (2008) summarizes very well:554

The universal approximation theorem is an existence theorem: it shows, theoretically, that one can approximate an arbitrary continuous function by a single hidden-layer network. Unfortunately, it does not specify how to find that approximation; that is, how to determine the weights and the number, t, of nodes in the hidden layer (a problem known as network complexity). It also assumes that we know the continuous function being approximated and that the available set of hidden nodes is of unlimited size. Furthermore, the theorem is not an optimality result: it does not show that a single hidden layer is the best-possible multilayer network for carrying out the approximation.

(p. 334)

What does it take for the theorem to work? It turns out that the only thing that is required to realize the approximation are mild assumptions on the activation function. And while the theorem typifies modern neural networks, its mathematical origins can be traced back to Hilbert’s 13th problem or conjecture, which held that all high-dimensional continuous functions are a combination of two-variable continuous functions (Kratsios, 2020). In machine learning, more generally, universal approximation is about “a model class’s ability to generically approximate any member of a large topological space whose elements are functions, or more rigorously, equivalence classes of functions” (Kratsios, 2020, p. 2). For a highly theoretical read of the approximation theorem, see Kratsios (2022).

15.11.1 Visualizing the Universal Approximation Theorem

Approximating functions has a long history in mathematics. Indeed, as Steffens (2006) has remarked regarding the centrality of approximation in mathematics, “Whenever one computes, one approximates” (p. vii). But what exactly does function approximation mean? Perhaps the easiest way to understand it is to liken it to what occurs in differential calculus as the prototypical elementary example of function approximation. For example, consider the function in Figure 15.10, that of a parabola along with its graph (left):


f(x) =  − x2 + 3

Suppose we would like to approximate the function at a value of x =  − 1. Of course, we could compute the slope of the line at x =  − 1 which would give us the derivative, shown in Figure 15.10 555(right). The derivative, as the reader will recall, is the slope of the tangent to the curve (or, more precisely, the limit of the slope of secant lines approaching the given point). That is, the derivative is approximating the function at that particular point. Indeed, if we computed derivatives at all infinitesimally small and infinite numbers of points along the x-axis and summed them up, we would have approximated the actual function of the inverted parabola.

As may seem obvious to the reader, the more derivatives we use the better the polynomial approximations become. They get better as well if we use higher-order polynomials to better capture the curve. These ideas suggest a much more general result which is that of the Taylor polynomial of degree n (Pn(x)), which x for near x0 is given by,


$$P_{n}\left( x \right) = f\left( x_{0} \right) + f'\left( x_{0} \right)\left( x - x_{0} \right) + \frac{f''\left( x_{0} \right)}{2!}\left( x - x_{0} \right)^{2} + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \frac{f^{(n)}\left( x_{0} \right)}{n!}\left( x - x_{0} \right)^{n}$$
(15.16)

and for which (15.16) is called the nth Taylor polynomial for f at x0. The approximation for points near x0 is given by x − x0, and the approximation is rarely perfect, yielding a remainder term f − Pn (i.e., the actual function minus the approximation). If we allow the degree n of the polynomial to go to infinity, that is, n→∞, then the Taylor polynomial becomes simply a Taylor series. That is, a Taylor series is simply a Taylor polynomial of infinite degree. Put differently, a Taylor series is the limiting sum of a Taylor polynomial as n→∞.

Though a bit more complicated and involved than the simple Taylor series featured here, the essential idea is analogous in neural networks. Approximating functions is what neural networks, in the end, actually do. Often these functions are unknown and must be “learned” from the data. This is, in part, the nonparametric element of neural networks.

15.12 Neural Networks and Projection Pursuit

There is often a link drawn in the literature between neural networks and a nonparametric technique called projection pursuit (Friedman & Tukey, 1974; Friedman & Stuetzle, 1981; Kruskal, 1969). Understanding the latter can provide a window into better understanding neural networks. As the name suggests, in projection pursuit we are “pursuing” the best means by which to make a projection. The primary qualification for the pursuit is that the projection be in some sense, interesting. The original conception of projection pursuit was formulated by Kruskal (1969, 1972).

More to the point, projection pursuit is the search in a potentially nonlinear structure of high-dimensional data lower-dimensional linear projections (Posse, 1995). It is considered nonparametric since nonparametric estimators (smoothers) are used in the estimation process. Many excellent examples of projection pursuit can be found in Posse (1995). Projection pursuit is primarily a visualization technique with limited output as is traditional with methods such as principal components analysis (Laa & Cook, 2020).

Projection pursuit itself was first coined by Friedman and Tukey (1974) in what is an exceptionally well-written paper “A Projection Pursuit Algorithm for Exploratory Data Analysis,” but as mentioned had its origins somewhat earlier with Kruskal (1969). Friedman and Tukey introduced the method as an algorithm that seeks to find one- and two-dimensional linear projections of multivariate data that are relatively highly revealing:

Mapping of multivariate data onto low-dimensional manifolds for visual inspection is a commonly used technique in data analysis. The discovery of mappings that reveal the salient features of the multidimensional point swarm is often far from trivial. Even when every adequate description of the data requires more variables than can be conveniently perceived (at one 556time) by humans, it is quite often still useful to map the data into a lower, humanly perceivable, dimensionality where the human gift for pattern recognition can be applied.

(Friedman & Tukey, 1974, p. 1)

Interestingly, Friedman and Tukey chose not to treat nonlinear dimension reduction techniques stating that they are more difficult to interpret but also for their computational complexity, a problem that has since been overcome by the modern uprise in computing power. Projection pursuit uses a projection index as a quantity that needs to be optimized in the search for interesting projections. Hence, we see immediately that principal components analysis can be regarded as a special case of projection pursuit where the index is that of maximizing variance of orthogonal linear combinations.

Components analysis, as we have seen, is by far not the only way to project data. For instance, returning to a simpler example, one could project data via ordinary least-squares. Most of the indexes used in projection pursuit are built around detecting departures from known distributions, such as multivariate normality, or projections that are best able to distinguish between groups (Laa & Cook, 2020). As Jolliffe (2002) notes, most projection pursuit techniques begin by assuming that multivariate normality is the least interesting basis for a projection, and hence many indices in the projection essentially measure deviations from this “uneventful” status. Numerically, the actual index is a scalar computed in the d-dimensional space and is maximized over all possible d-dimensional projections of a data set. A number of indexes are discussed in Laa and Cook (2020). For a concise summary of projection pursuit, see Jolliffe (2002, pp. 219–221).

15.12.1 Projection Pursuit Regression and Relation to Neural Networks

The model for projection pursuit regression, which can be considered a special case of the wider more general projection pursuit framework, can be stated as follows:


$$y_{i} = \beta_{0} + {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{r}{f_{j}\left( \beta_{j}^{T}x_{i} \right) + \varepsilon_{i}}}$$
(15.17)

where the model looks pretty much the same as we would expect from a typical linear regression model,


$$y_{i} = \beta_{0} + {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{r}{\left( \beta_{j}^{T}x_{i} \right) + \varepsilon_{i}}}$$

However, note the key difference, the inclusion of fj in the projection pursuit of (15.17). For convenience, we will drop the error term εi for now and simply focus on the systematic portion of the model. In projection pursuit, we can have numerous functions m through M and hence we account for these via summation,


$$\left. y_{i} = {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M}{f_{j}\left( \beta_{j}^{T} \right.}}x_{i} \right)$$

and seek to minimize the following error function557


$${\sum\limits_{i}^{N}\left\lbrack \left. y_{i} - {\sum\limits_{m = 1}^{M}{f_{j}\left( \beta_{j}^{T} \right.}}x_{i} \right) \right\rbrack}^{2}$$
(15.18)

We can think of βjT in projection pursuit as containing directions instead of merely scalars as we might typically think of such in ordinary regression (Hastie et al., 2009) though it definitely does not hurt to think of these weights as directions in classical regression as well. In projection pursuit, fj(βjTxi) is called a ridge function, with its direction determined by values in βjT. We note that essentially the only difference between this and the classic linear model is the inclusion of fj, where these are a collection of unknown smoothing functions (i.e., “unknown” until they are “learned” from the data). That is, in fj(βjTxi) we are taking a function fj of another function βjTxi and hence once more, we are taking a composite function just as we do in a neural network. The number of these smoothing functions we will take is a flexible hyperparameter. When that number is one the model is sometimes referred to as a single index model (Hastie et al., 2009). Cross-validation can be used to determine an optimal number of smoothing functions. Its value can also be determined based on how much each successive term improves the model in terms of visualization.

We can see that the projection pursuit model is entirely general. Indeed, as noted by Hastie et al. (2009, p. 390), “the operation of forming nonlinear functions of linear combinations generates a surprisingly large class of models.” The link to neural networks is rather obvious then, such that in neural networks we are taking, as we saw, (typically) nonlinear functions of linear (or nonlinear) combinations. In projection pursuit, we could do the same if we chose a linear function instead of smoothing functions. That is, with a bit of generality, projection pursuit can be conceptualized as a layered neural network where fj essentially becomes the activation function. Once we make fj a classic activation function such as the sigmoid function instead of smoothing functions, projection pursuit essentially becomes analogous to a simple neural network.

One key difference between projection pursuit and neural networks, however, is that the activation function in the former can be different for each hidden unit and is typically estimated nonparametrically, where in neural networks such are usually prespecified parametric functions. However, this does not make neural networks entirely parametric, since they are especially useful when we have no theoretical preconceptions about the data. That is, neural networks “learn” from the data, which is a very “nonparametric” idea. And while it is technically possible to assign a unique activation function to each hidden unit in a neural network, it is not the norm.

Sarle (1994) perhaps distinguishes best between the parametric vs. nonparametric debate as it pertains to neural networks:

With a small number of hidden neurons, an MLP [multilayer perceptron] is a parametric model that provides a useful alternative to polynomial regression. With a moderate number of hidden neurons, an MLP can be considered a quasi-parametric model similar to projection pursuit regression … An MLP with one hidden layer is essentially the same as the projection pursuit regression model except that an MLP uses a predetermined functional form for the activation function in the hidden layer, whereas projection pursuit uses a flexible nonlinear smoother. If the number of hidden neurons is allowed to increase with the sample size, an MLP becomes a nonparametric sieve that provides a useful alternative to methods such as kernel regression and smoothing splines. MLPs are especially valuable because you can vary the complexity of the model from a simple parametric model to a highly flexible, nonparametric model.

(p. 5)558

Differences between the two methods also include the fact that parameters in a neural network are typically estimated simultaneously where in projection pursuit regression they are usually fit successively for each hidden unit (Klinke & Grassmann, 2000). Though not an exact analogy, the optimal number of hidden units in a neural network can be likened to the number of terms to add in a projection pursuit.

Thus, projection pursuit is often considered an historical and conceptual “precursor,” especially pedagogically, to understanding neural networks, and according to Hastie et al. (2009), projection pursuit was not widely used at the time of its inception largely due to computational requirements for obtaining a solution, computational “roadblocks” that have long been overcome with modern computing advances. Perhaps had more computing power existed back in the day of projection pursuit, these models would have a more significant legacy. Pedagogically, however, projection pursuit is very valuable in putting neural networks and other models (e.g., PCA and generalized linear models) into proper context. Indeed, a generalized version of PPR, aptly named Generalized Projection Pursuit Regression (Roosen & Hastie, 1993) has been proposed that is similar in structure to the generalized linear model paradigm of McCullagh and Nelder (1989) in its use of link functions and that allow for binary responses.

Lastly, it can be shown that as the number of smoothing functions increases without bound to infinity, for an appropriate set of functions in fj, as was the case for neural networks, projection pursuit regression can approximate virtually any continuous function and is considered a universal approximator. How many smoothing functions to include in the approximation? There are different recommendations regarding this. For example, Friedman et al. (1984) found that adding more terms than necessary then using a backward selection algorithm helps avoid getting stuck in local minima. Roosen and Hastie (1993) have found that adding terms to maximize generalized cross-validation then pruning back somewhat may be an effective strategy.

Having compared projection pursuit to neural networks, it is also useful to recap where we began this discussion, in that projection pursuit can be understood as a higher-order and more general framework to principal components analysis. Such emphasizes that the latter is but only one type of projection, not the unique projection or dimensionality reduction of data. As we have seen throughout our discussion of dimension reduction techniques, what one technique might reveal from the data another technique may do better. There is no such thing as finding the unique dimensions of one’s data; what you find is as much to do with what tool you use to do the finding, which, incidentally is why some dislike statistics in the first place as it is perceived to provide no “hard” truths, a misguided perception based on an incomplete understanding of the subject.

Principal components analysis is only one type of projection of the data. Projection pursuit (and by extension, neural networks) makes this clear – how you project your data will, to a large extent, determine what you find, and thus “see” from that data.

Projection pursuit in R can be performed using the R package tourr (Wickham et al., 2011). It can also be performed using ppr() in R.

15.13 Summary, Warnings, and Caveats of Neural Networks

Neural networks can be easily misunderstood by the uninitiated. Their very name can encourage newcomers to give them powers they may not have, or at minimum, exaggerate the powers they actually do have. Neural networks are tremendously useful, but in learning them for the first time, it is important to understand exactly what they are and what they are not. Throughout this chapter 559we have issued many caveats and warnings about neural networks. We summarize, and in some cases extend on those caveats and warnings in what follows.

15.13.1 Neural Networks Are Not Biological Nor Are They Machines

A first obvious point is that though neural networks were motivated by psychological and biological entities in the brain, they themselves have nothing to do with psychology or biology! They have everything to do with abstract mathematics. What is more, though they, like virtually all other statistical or machine learning methods are run on high-speed computers, there is nothing about neural networks themselves that have anything to do with computers or other “machines.” A neural network can, at least in theory and with enough time, be fit by pencil and paper just as any other mathematical technique. “Enough time” is more lifetimes than anyone might ever have, hence the benefit of using computers.

Why is this point so relevant? It is so because too often some users get into the habit of drawing conclusions from data based on the jargon of the statistical or machine learning method. As we discussed earlier in the book, in social statistics, for instance, all too often researchers will surprisingly conclude that such and such variable mediates or moderates another and impose an action quality on those words when no action is necessarily supported by the research design or the organicity of the variables used in the modeling.
